BOOMING AMONG SAILORS

Pages 33-33

G among sailors denotes the application of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOM">boom</a> to the sails. A ship is said to come <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOMING">booming</a> forwards, when she comes with all the sail she can make.

BOONEN

Pages 33-33

Arnold, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORT">Dort</a> in 1669, and at first was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Arnold Verhuis, a painter of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and portrait. Afterwards he placed himself with Godfrey Schalcken, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> with that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> for six years. The sweetness of his colouring, and the neatness of his touch, with a striking likeness in his portraits, procured him a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of admirers. He painted in the manner of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, particularly subjects by candlelight, which were very delicate, and very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>; and much more of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was requested by the lovers of the art than it was possible for him to undertake. He had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to paint the portraits of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CZAR">czar</a> of Muscovy; of Frederick I., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>; of the victorious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>, as well as many of the princes of Germany; and most of the noblemen who attended the czar. His style of colouring was extremely good, and he had an elegant manner of disposing the attitudes of his figures; his handling was neat, and the whole had so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> that he was justly ranked among the ablest artists of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The small pictures of Boonen are in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of his master Schalcken; but his excessive application, to answer the multitude of his engagements, impaired his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, and destroyed while it enriched him. He died in 1729.

BOOPS

Pages 33-33

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of balana. See Balana, Cetology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BOOSHATTER

Pages 33-33

formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTICA">Utica</a>, famous for the retreat and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Cato, lies about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles inland from Porto Farina in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>. Nothing remains of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> except <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> aqueduct, some cisterns, and other magnificent ruins, which cover a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of ground, and show it to have been a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, it is known, came up anciently to this city, though now seven miles distant.

BOOT

Pages 33-33

a leathern cover <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> for the leg, used on horseback, both to keep the body more firm, and defend the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> from the injuries of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. Boots seem to have taken their name from the resemblance they bear to a sort of jacks or leathern bottles formerly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, and called botte, in the old French boots. Borel derives the name from the old French word bot, a stump, by reason the boot gives the leg this appearance. The Chinese have a kind of boots made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> or fine stuff lined with cotton, a full inch thick, which they always wear at home. This people are always booted; and when a visit is made them, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they happen to be without their boots, their guest must wait till they put them on. They never stir out of doors without their boots on; and their scrupulousness in this respect is the more remarkable as they are always carried in their chairs. The boot was much used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, by the foot as well as by the horsemen. It was called by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> orea; in middle-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers, greva, gambria, bainberga, bembarga or bembarga. The boot is said to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the Carians. It was at first made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, afterwards of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and was <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> both against cuts and thrusts. It was from this that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> calls the Greeks brazen-booted. The boot only covered half the leg; some say the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> leg, which was more advanced than the left, it being advanced forwards in an attack with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; but in reality it appears to have been used on either leg, and sometimes on both. Those who fought with darts or other missile weapons, advanced the left leg foremost, so that this only was booted. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">Fishing</a>-Boots, are a thick strong sort used in dragging ponds and the like. Hunting-boots, a thinner kind used by sportsmen. Jack-boots, a kind of very strong boots used by the troopers. Boot, is likewise a kind of torture for criminals; to extort a confession, by means of a boot, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STOCKING">stocking</a>, or buckskin of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>; which being put on the leg moist, and brought near the fire, in shrinking squeezes the leg violently, and occasions intolerable pain. There is also another kind of boot; consisting of four thick strong boards bound round with cords: two of these are put between the criminal's legs, and the two others placed one on the outside of one leg and the other on the other; then squeezing the legs against the boards by the cords, the criminal's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> are severely pinched, or even broken, &c. The boot is now disused in England and Scotland; but it subsists still in some other countries. Boot-Tree, or Boot-last, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used by shoemakers to widen the leg of a boot. It is a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> slit into two parts, between which, when it is put into the boot, they drive by main force a wedge or quoin.

BOOTES

Pages 33-33

a constellation of the northern hemisphere, consisting of 23 stars according to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s catalogue, of 18 in Tycho's, of 34 in Bayer's, of 52 in Hevelius's, and of 54 in Mr Flamsteed's catalogue.

BOOTH

Pages 33-34

Barton, a famous English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>, born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a> in 1681, and educated in Westminster school under the celebrated Dr Bushby, where his success in the Latin plays customarily performed by the scholars gave him an inclination for the stage. He was intended for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; but running away from school to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, he there commenced actor. His first appearance was in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Oroonoko, in which he came off with every testimonial of approbation from the audience. From this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> daily improving; and, after two successful campaigns in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, conceived thoughts of returning to his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and making a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of his abilities on the English stage. To this end, he first, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, reconciled himself to his friends; and then, as a farther step towards injuring his success, obtained a recommendation from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Fitzhardinge (one of the lords of the bedchamber to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> George of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>) to Mr Betterton, who with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> candour and good <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> took him under his care, and gave him all the assistance in his his power. The first part Mr Booth appeared in at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> was that of Maximus in Lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALENTINIAN">Valentinian</a>, his reception in which exceeded even his most sanguine expectations; and very soon after his performance of Artaban, in Rowe's Ambitious Stepmother, which was a new tragedy, established his reputation as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> at least to his great instructor. Pyrrhus, in the Distressed Mother, was another part in which he shone without a rival. But he was indebted to a happy coincidence of merit and chance, for that height of fame which he at length attained in the character of Cato, as drawn by Mr Addison, in 1712. For this play being considered as a party one, the Whigs, in favour of whose principles it was apparently written, thought it their duty strongly to support it, while at the same time the Tories, who had too much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> to appear to consider it as a reflection on their administration, were still more vehement in their approbation of it, which they carried to such a height, as even to make a collection of 50 guineas in the boxes during the performance, and present them to Mr Booth, with this compliment, "That it was a slight acknowledgment for his honest opposition to a perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a>, and his dying so bravely in the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>." Besides this, he had a present of an equal sum from the managers, in consideration of the great success of the play, which they attributed in a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to his extraordinary merit in the performance; and certain it is, that no one since that time has ever equaled, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even nearly approached, his excellence in that character. But these were not the only advantages which were to accrue to Mr Booth from his success in this part; for Lord Bolingbroke, then one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> secretaries of state, in a little time after procured a special licence from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, recalling all the former ones, and nominating Mr Booth as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> manager with Wilkes, Cibber, and Doggett; none of whom were pleased at it; but the last especially took such disgust as to withdraw himself from any further share in the management. In 1704, Mr Booth had married a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir William Barkham Bart. who died in 1710, without issue. Being now established in the management, he once more turned his thoughts towards matrimony; and in the year 1719 united himself to the celebrated Miss Hester Santlow, a woman of a most amiable disposition, whose great merit as an actress, added to the utmost <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> and prudential economy, had enabled her to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> up a considerable fortune. During the 20 years in which Mr Booth continued a manager, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> was in the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>; and his illness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened on the 10th of May 1733, contributed not a little to its decline. Mr Booth wrote a dramatic entertainment called Dido and Æneas; but his masterpiece was a Latin inscription to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Mr William Smith, a celebrated actor, who died while he was young.—As an actor, his excellency lay wholly in tragedy, not being able to endure such parts as had not strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> to inspire him. And even in this walk, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> rather than complacency, rage rather than tenderness, seemed to be his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. For a particular idea of his abilities, we must refer to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> Mr Cibber has given of him in his Apology; and the admirable character drawn of him by that excellent judge of dramatic perfection, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a> Hill, Esq. in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> published by him called the Prompter, which may be seen at length in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a>, Cibber's Lives of the Poets, and Chetwood's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Stage.—His character as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was adorned with many amiable qualities, among which, a goodness of heart, the basis of every virtue, was remarkably conspicuous; and so particularly was he distinguished and careful, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> sought by the great, that, as Chetwood relates of him, not one nobleman in the kingdom had so many sets of horses at command as he had.

BOOTY

Pages 34-34

whatever is taken from an enemy in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>.—Among the Greeks, the booty was divided in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, the general only claiming a larger share. By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, spoils taken from the enemy belonged to the republic, particular persons having no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to them. The generals who piqued themselves on their probity carried it wholly to the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>. Sometimes indeed they divided it among the soldiery, to animate them, and serve in lieu of a reward. But this distribution depended on the generals, who were to conduct themselves herein with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a> and moderation; otherwise it became a crime of peculate to lay <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> on the pillage, as regularly belonging only to the state. The consuls <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> and Vatinius were condemned for having sold the booty taken from the Equi.—Among the Jews, the booty was divided equally between the army and the people, though under the kings a different kind of distribution obtained.—Among the Mahometans, two thirds of the spoils are allowed to the army; the other third to God, to Mahomet and his relations, and to the orphans, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and the pilgrims.—Among us, formerly the booty was divided among the soldiery. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the general be in the field, every body takes what he can lay hold on; if the general be absent, the booty is distributed among the soldiery, two parts being allowed to the cavalry, and one to the infantry. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> is allowed ten shares, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> five, and a cornet four.

BOPPART

Pages 34-34

a town of Germany, in the circle of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREVES">Treves</a>; it is seated at the foot of a mountain near the Rhine, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 35'. N. Lat. 5° 19'.

BOPSINGEN

Pages 34-34

a town of Swabia in Germany, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol8.html#article-EGER">Eger</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 55'. N. Lat. 48° 51'.

BOPTHALMUS

Pages 33-33

a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGATE">agate</a> with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> circles in it, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> some resemblance to an ox's eye, from whence it has got this name.

BOQUINIAN

Pages 34-34

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heretics, so called from Boquinus their founder, who taught that Christ did not die for all mankind, but only for the faithful, and consequently was only a particular Saviour.

BORAK

Pages 34-34

among Mahometans, a fabulous animal, supposed to be of the middle kind between an ass and a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULE">mule</a>, whereon their prophet was carried in his nocturnal flight from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> into the heavens. This animal the Arabians call Al-Borak, q. d. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>. The night when the journey was performed is called Lailat al-Meeraag, i.e. the night of ascension; and the flight itself Al-Meeraag; concerning which there is a multitude of traditions.

BORAX

Pages 34-35

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> in appearance somewhat similar to crystals of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, brought originally from Borbetoma from the East Indies in an impure state, and afterwards freed from its impurities by certain processes in the European countries. It was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of uncertainty whether this salt be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> factitious substance in those countries from whence it is brought; but it is now beyond a doubt, that it is naturally produced in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Thibet, from which other parts of the eastern continent are supplied. According to an account in the Philosophical Transactions, vol. lxxvii. by Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLANE">Blane</a>, it is produced in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Jumlate, about 30 days journey <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> from Betowle, a small principality about 200 miles northeast of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUCKNOW">Lucknow</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it is found is said to be a small valley surrounded with snowy mountains, in which is a lake about six miles in circumference; the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of which is constantly so hot that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> cannot bear it for any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Around this lake the ground is perfectly barren, not producing even a blade of grass; and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> is so full of a saline matter, that after falls of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> or snow it concretes in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> flakes on the surface like the natron of Hindoostan. On the banks of this lake, in the winter season, when the falls of snow begin, the earth is formed into small reservoirs six inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>: when these are filled with snow, the hot water from the lake is thrown upon it; which, together with the water from the melted snow, remains in the reservoir, to be partly absorbed by the earth and partly evaporated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; after which there remains at the bottom a cake of sometimes half an inch thick of crude borax, which is taken up and referred for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. It can only be made in the winter season, because the falls of snow are indispensably requisite, and also because the saline appearances upon the earth are strongest at that time. When once it has been made on any spot, it cannot be made again on the same until the snow has fallen and dissolved three or four times, when the saline efflorescence appears as before. See Chemistry and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BORBETOMAGUS

Pages 35-35

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Vangiones on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>; now <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">Worms</a>, in Germany. BORBONIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BORBORITES

Pages 35-35

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Gnostics, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, who, besides embracing the errors of these heretics, denied the last judgment. Their name comes from the Greek Borbores, "filth;" on account of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> they had of daubing their faces and bodies with dirt and filth.

BORCH

Pages 35-35

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGDEBURG">Magdeburg</a> in Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12° 14'. N. Lat. 52° 25'.

BORCHLOEN

Pages 35-35

a town of the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a> in Germany, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 28'. N. Lat. 50° 50'.

BORCOVIUM

Pages 35-35

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Ostadini in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, now Berwick on Tweed.

BORD-HALFPENNY

Pages 35-35

a small toll by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> paid to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the town for setting up boards, tables, booths, &c., in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>. Bord-Lands, the demesnes which lords keep in their lands for the maintenance of their board <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. Bord-Lode, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> required of tenants to carry <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> out of the woods of the lord to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. It is also used to signify the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of provision which the bordarii or bordmen paid for their bord-lands. Bord-Service, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> of bord-lands, by which some lands in certain places are held of the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and the tenants now pay sixpence per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>, in lieu of sending provision anciently for their lord's table.

BORDAT

Pages 35-35

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, a small narrow stuff, which is manufactured in some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, particularly at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, and Damietta.

BORDE

Pages 36-36

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, is made to enclose parterres, that they may not be injured by walking in them. Borders are made either circular, straight, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in curves; and are turned into knots, scrolls, volutes, and other compartments. They are rendered very ornamental by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, yews, &c., that are raised in them. They are always laid with a sharp rising in the middle; because, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are flat, they are nowadays agreeable to the eye; and as for their breadth, the largest are allowed five or six feet, and the smallest <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> four.

BORDEL

Pages 36-36
Peter, a learned physician, was the son of James Borel who published several poems, and was born at Castris in 1620. He applied himself to the study of physic, of which he was created doctor, and practised with great success in the city of Castris. Towards the end of the year 1653, he went to Paris, and was soon after made physician in ordinary to the king. In 1674, he was received into the academy of sciences, and distinguished himself by writing a great number of works. The most esteemed are: 1. Historiarum et observationum medico-physicarum centuria quarta. 2. Bibliotheca chymica, duodecimo. 3. De vero teleopii inventore, cum brevi omnium consipicillorum historia. He died in 1678.

BORDELLI

Pages 36-36

John Alphonsus, a famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and mathematician, born at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> the 28th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1608. He was professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> in some of the most celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, particularly at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a>, where he became highly in favour with the princes of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Medici; but having been engaged in the revolt of Messina, he was obliged to retire to Rome, where he spent the remainder of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> under the protection of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTINA">Christina</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, who honoured him with her friendship, and by her liberality towards him softened the rigour of his hard fortune. He <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> two years in the convent of the regular clergy of St. Pantaleon, called the phous scholae, where he instructed the youth in mathematical studies. He died there of a pleurisy, the 31st of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1679, in the 72nd year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He wrote in Latin, 1. Euclid restored. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the influence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> in medicine, deduced from physical causes. 3. Of percutive force. 4. Of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> motions depending upon gravity. 5. An historical and meteorological account of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of Mount Etna, in the year 1669. 6. Of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of animals; and several other works, some of which are in Italian.

BORDEU

Pages 36-36
or Bordone, Paris, an excellent Italian painter, was born at Venice about the year 1512; and, being of a noble family, had a polite education. He was the disciple of Titian; but has been admired more for the delicacy of his pencil than for the truth of his outlines. He was at the court of France in the reign of Francis I., who had a great esteem for him, and for whom he drew not only abundance of history-pieces, but the portraits of several court-ladies, in so fine a manner, that original nature was hardly more charming. He at length returned to Venice, laden with riches and honour; and having gained great reputation in all parts of Italy, died in 1587, aged 75.

BOREAS

Pages 36-36

a Greek name, now in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. Pezron observes, that anciently Boreas signified the north-east wind blowing at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> solstice. The Greeks erected an altar to Boreas. He is represented on the temple at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> with his robe before his mouth, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he felt the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> over which he presides, agreeably to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of Ovid, who calls him gelidus tyrannus, "the shivering <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>," Met. vi. ver. 711. But he is usually described by the Roman poets as violent and impetuous; ibid. ver. 686—ver. 707. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, he is generally represented like an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> with a horrible look, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> covered with snow <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hoar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROST">frost</a>, with the feet and tail of a dragon. M. Spierlingius has a treatise in praise of Boreas, wherein he shows the honours paid to him by antiquity. Boreas, according to this author, purifies the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, renders it calm and salubrious, preserves buildings from decay, drives away the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> and other noxious diseases, and expels locusts and other <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a> hurtful to the grounds.

BORGHIA

Pages 36-36

Cæsar, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> son of Pope Alexander VI. was a brave general, but a most abandoned villain. See (<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of) <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>.—It is incredible what numbers he caused to be taken off by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; and it is notorious that swarms of assassins were constantly kept in pay by him at Rome, for the sake of removing all who were either obnoxious or inconvenient to him. He experienced various turns of fortune; and was sometimes very prosperous, sometimes the reverse. He very narrowly escaped dying by poison in 1503; for having concerted with the pope a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of poisoning <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> newly created cardinals at once, for the sake of possessing their effects, the poisoned wine, destined for the purpose, was by mistake brought to and drunk by themselves. The pope died of it; but Cæsar, by the vigour of his youth, and the force of antidotes, after many struggles, recovered. He only recovered to outlive his fortune and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, to see himself depressed, and his enemies exalted; for he was soon after divested of all his acquisitions, and sent a prisoner to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in order to free Italy from an incendiary, and the Italian princes from those dangers which the turbulent and restless spirit of Cæsar made them fear, even though he was unarmed. He escaped from thence; and got safe to Navarre to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> John his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, who was then at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with his subjects. Cæsar served as a volunteer in that war, and was killed in 1507.

BORGO

Pages 36-37

BORGO, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Nyland. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 26° 25'. N. Lat. 60° 34'. Borgo de St Sepulcro, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, situated in E. Long. 13° 0'. N. Lat. 43° 32'. Borgo de Val de <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FARO">Faro</a>, a town of Italy, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Parma, in E. Long. 10° 36'. N. Lat. 44° 35'. Borgo Forte, a town of the Mantuan in Italy, situated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Po and Menzo. E. Long. 11° 0'. N. Lat. 44° 50'. Borgo San Domino, a town of Italy, in the duchy of Parma, with a bishop's see. E. Long. 10° 31'. N. Lat. 41° 53'.

BORIA

Pages 37-37

a small town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Arragon. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 2'. N. Lat. 41° 50'.

BORING

Pages 37-37

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the art of perforating, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> making a hole through any <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> body. Boring of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>. The method of boring water-pipes is as follows. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> of alder, which is a very useful wood in making pumps, water-pipes, &c., being laid on horses or trusses of a foot height, to rest the auger upon while they are boring, they set up a lathe to turn the least end of the poles, to fit them to the cavities of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> end of the others. They turn the small ends of the poles about five or six inches in length, to the size they intend to bore the bigger ends about the same depth, viz. five or six inches. This is designed to make a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> to shut each <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of poles together, the concave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> part, and the other the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> of the joint. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the male part, they turn the channel in it, or a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a> at a certain distance from the end; and in the female part they bore a small hole to fit over this channel. This being done, they bore the poles through; and to prevent them from boring out at the side, they stick great nails at each end to be a guide in boring. It is usual, however, to bore them at both ends; so that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a pole be crooked one way, they can bore it through and not spoil it. Boring, in Farriery, a cruel and absurd method of treating a wrenched shoulder. See Farriery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Boring, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a>, a method of piercing the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> with scooping irons, which being drawn back at proper times, bring up with them samples of the different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> through which they have passed; by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of which the skilful mineralogist <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be able to guess whereabouts a vein of ore or a stratum of coal may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a>, or whether it will be worth while to Boriuen open a mine for the purpose of working it.

BORIQUEN

Pages 37-37

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, near that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PORTO_RICO">Porto Rico</a>. The English formerly had a settlement there, but were driven away by the Spaniards. It is at present without inhabitants, though agreeable and fertile; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> being wholesome, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> good. There are a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRABS">crabs</a>, whence some have called it Crab-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 64° 35'. N. Lat. 18° 0'.

BORISTHENES

Pages 37-37

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the largest river of Sarmatia Europea, thus described by Mele, who copies verbatim from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>: "It runs through a cognominal people, is the most pleasant of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCYTHIA">Scythia</a>, and calmer than all of them in its course, and very agreeable to drink: it feeds very rich pastures, and produces <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fish of the best flavour, and without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>; it comes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> way, rising from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> unknown; its course is a distance of 40 days, and so far it is navigable." It is now called the Dnieper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Nieper.

BORKELO

Pages 37-37

a strong town in the United Provinces, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZUTPHEN">Zutphen</a>, seated on the river Berkel, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 30'. N. Lat. 52° 15'.

BORLASE

Pages 37-38

William, a very ingenious and learned writer, was of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in Cornwall, and born at Pendean, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">Just</a>, Feb. 2. 1693-4. He was put early to school at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENZANCE">Penzance</a>, and in 1709 removed to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1712-13, he was entered of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1719, took a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. In 1720, he was ordained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>; and, in 1722, instituted to the rectory of Ludgvan in Cornwall. In 1732, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> presented him to the vicarage of St Just, his native parish; and this, with the rectory aforesaid, were all the preferments he ever had. In the parish of Ludgvan were rich <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> works, which abound with mineral and metallic fossils; and these, being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and inquisitive turn, he collected from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time, and thence was led to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>. He was struck at the same time with the numerous monuments of remote antiquity that are to be met with in Cornwall; and, enlarging therefore his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, he determined to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> as accurate an acquaintance as possible with the Druid learning, and with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and customs of the ancient Britons, before their conversion to Christianity. In 1750 he was admitted a fellow of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>; and, in 1753, published in folio at Oxford his "Antiquities of Cornwall;" a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition of which was published, in the same form, at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 1769, with this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, "Antiquities, historical and monumental, of the county of Cornwall; consisting of several essays on the ancient inhabitants, Druid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, customs and remains of the most remote antiquity in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and the British isles, exemplified and proved by monuments now extant in Cornwall and the Scilly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; with a vocabulary of the Cornu-British <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Revised, with several additions, by the author; to which is added a map of Cornwall, and two new plates." His next publication was, "Observations on the ancient and present state of the islands of Scilly, and their importance to the trade of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Britain; Oxf. 1756," 4to. This was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> which had been read before the Royal Society in 1753. In 1758 came out his "Natural history of Cornwall; Oxf." fol. After these publications, he sent a variety of fossils and remains of antiquity which he had described in his works, to be repolished in the Ashmolean <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>: for which, and other benefactions of the same kind, he received the thanks of the university, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from the vice-chancellor, Nov. 18. 1758; and, March 1766, the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of laws. He died in 1772, aged 77 years, leaving two sons out of six, whom he had by a lady he married in 1724. Besides his literary connexions with many ingenious and learned men, he had a particular correspondence with Mr Pope; and there is still existing a large collection of letters written by that poet to Dr Borlase. He furnished Pope with many of the materials which formed his grotto at Twickenham, consisting of curious fossils; and there may at present be seen Dr Borlase's name in capitals, composed of crystals, in the grotto. On which occasion Pope says to Borlase in a letter, "I am much obliged to you for your valuable collection of Cornish diamonds: I have placed them where they may best represent yourself, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>, but shining;" alluding to the obscurity of the doctor's situation, and the brilliancy of his talents. Besides the above works, he sent many curious papers to the Philosophical Transactions, and had in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> several other works.

BORNE

Pages 38-38

a market town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a> in England. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 20. N. Lat. 52. 40.

BORNEO

Pages 38-39

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the East Indies, and one of the three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUNDA">Sunda</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. It is thought to be the largest island in the world, next to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-NEW_HOLLAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; being 1,500 miles in circumference. It is seated under the equator, that line <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> it almost through the middle. It is almost of a circular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; abounds with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; and the finest diamonds in the Indies are found in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, being probably washed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the hills by torrents. Here are also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> and tin, and leadstones. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">Bird</a>'s nests are to be had in this island, which are eatable, and reckoned a great delicacy. The beasts are, oxen, buffaloes, deer, goats, elephants, tigers, and monkeys. This island has fine rivers, especially towards the west and south. In their monsoon from April to September, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> is westerly; and they have continual heavy rains, attended with violent storms of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>. The rainy season continues for eight months of the year; and as during that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> all the flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> is overflowed, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is rendered very unhealthy, and the inhabitants are forced to build their houses on floats, which they make fast to trees. The houses have but one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, with partitions made with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a>; and the roofs are covered with palmetto leaves, the eaves of which reach within four <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> five feet of the bottom. The west and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> coasts of the island are almost deserted, and the east is but little known. The inland parts are very mountainous; and the southeast, for many leagues together, is a flanking morass, which, being overflowed in the wet season, is very unhealthy. The Portuguese, who first discovered Borneo, had arrived in the Indies about 30 years before they knew anything of it more than the name, and its situation, by reason of their frequently pausing by its coast. At last one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Edward Corril had orders to examine it more narrowly; and being once acquainted with the worth of the country, they made frequent voyages thither. They found the coasts inhabited by Malayan Moors, who had certainly established themselves there by conquest; but the original inhabitants still remain in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and are styled Beajus, which in the Malay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> signifies a wild <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. The most authentic account of these people is the following, which was extracted from the papers of Father Antonio Ventimiglia, an Italian missionary. He was sent to Borneo from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACAO">Macao</a>, on board a Portuguese ship, converted great numbers to Christianity, and died on the island about the year 1691. The Beajus have no kings, but many little chiefs. Some are subject to the Moorish kings, and pay them tribute; but such as live far up the country are altogether independent, and live according to their own customs. They are generally very superstitious, and much addicted to augury. They do not adore idols; but their sacrifices of sweet wood and perfumes are offered to one God, who, they believe, rewards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> in heaven, and punishes the wicked in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>. They marry but one wife; and look upon any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of conjugal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, either in the man or woman, as a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> offence. The Beajus are naturally honest and industrious, and have a brotherly affection for one another. They have a notion of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, which yet does not render them covetous. They sow and cultivate their lands; but in the time of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>, each reaps as much as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> serve his family, and the rest belongs to the tribe in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>; by which means they prevent <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> or disputes. With the Moors on the coasts the Portuguese for some time carried on a considerable trade, and at their request settled a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a> there; which, however, was afterwards surprised and plundered by the Moors, who put most of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORNHOLM">Bornholm</a>, the people to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. The most considerable river in Borneo is called Banjar, at the mouth of which our East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> have a factory.

BORNHOLM

Pages 39-39

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, to the south-east of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Schonen in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. It is twenty-one miles in length, and above thirteen in breadth. It has three considerable <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, Rattum, Sandwick, and Nexia; with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of villages; and is fertile and populous. It was conquered by the Swedes in 1658; but the inhabitants, under the conduct of Jens Roefods, voluntarily surrendered it to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, on account of the bad usage they received from the former. In 1678, a body of 5000 Swedish troops, in their passage from Pomerania to Sweden, being shipwrecked on this island, such of them as remained were made prisoners of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The inhabitants defend the island by their own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, without any expense to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. The commandant <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> governor resides at Rattum. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 56. N. Lat. 55. 15.

BORNOU

Pages 39-39

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Zaara in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, extending from 12 to 22 degrees of east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and from 17 to 21 degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. The northern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and like the rest of the provinces of Zaara: but all the rest is well watered by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> that tumble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with a dreadful noise from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; rendering the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> prolific in corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and giving it a pleasing aspect. The eastern and western frontiers are divided into mountains and valleys, the latter being all covered with flocks of cattle, fields of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> and millet, and many of the mountains with wood, fruit-trees, and cotton. On the north-west stands the mountain of Tariton, having plenty of good <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>; and on the south flows the river <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NIGER">Niger</a>, which, it is said, after running a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many leagues under a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> chain of mountains, rears up its head again, and mingles its streams with the waters of the lake Bornou in its course, from whence it washes the walls of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of this kingdom. The compilers of the Universal <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, however, are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that in these mountains the river Niger hath its source, because no river hath been traced to the eastward, except the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, which runs in a different course from north to south, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">White</a> river, on the western frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>, which is a branch of the Nile. The eastern and western parts of Bornou are inhabited by a people of a roving disposition, who live in tents, and have their women, children, and every thing else, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>; the word <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, or any idea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to it, being utterly unknown among them. They have neither <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, laws, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, nor any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of subordination; and hence they have been supposed by Cluverius to be the lineal descendents of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Garamantes, and this to have been the residence of that people. In these parts, the natives are almost to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> shepherds and husbandmen. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> they go naked, except a short apron before; but in winter they are warmly clothed with the softest sheep-skins, of which they also form their bedclothes; and indeed this is scarce a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> against the inclemency of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> at certain seasons of the year, when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> piercing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows from the northern mountains that chills the blood in proportion as the pores of the body have been opened by the scorching heats of summer. Baudrand and Draper affirm, that the natives are scarce superior in their understanding to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a>; not even having any names whereby to distinguish each other, except what they take from some personal defect or singularity; such as lean, fat, squinting, humpbacked, &c. In the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, however, it is acknowledged that they are something more civilized and polite, being many of them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>; but of these towns, or indeed of the kingdom in general, very little is known. BOROMÆUS. See BORROMÆUS.

BOROGNONE

Pages 37-37

a celebrated painter, whose true name was Giacomo Corte; but he is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Borognone, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> where he was born, about the year 1605. He was much admired and highly applauded for his admirable gusto and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> battles. He had for several years been conversant in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, was an officer of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, made the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> his school, and formed all his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> from what he had seen performed in the field. His style is roughly noble, full of fire and spirit, and there are a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> etched by his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he retired to the Jesuits convent at Rome, where he is said to have taken sanctuary to rid his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of an ill bargain he had got of a wife; but happily surviving her, he lived in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> till after the year 1675.

BOROMIO

Pages 38-38

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> depending on the republic of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRISONS">Grisons</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. It is bounded on the south by the state of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, on the east by the territory of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, and on the south and west by Caddeea. It is 15 miles over both ways; and is divided into five communities, viz. the town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BORMIO">Bormio</a>, the valley of Forbia, the Interior Valley, the Lower Valley, and the Valley of Luvino. Bormio is the only town in this district; and has a governor called called a podestà, sent by the Grisons to preside in civil and criminal affairs. It is seated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Addo and Isalacum, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. 10. N. Lat. 46. 45.

BORONDON

Pages 39-39

St, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, mentioned by some writers, particularly Linfchotten, in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the Canary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, as something supernatural. It is said to be about 100 leagues distant from Ferro, probably well, though no writer has pretended to lay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> its exact situation. Here it is affirmed several ships have touched by accident, and all agree in their relations of the state of the inhabitants and island. They affirm, that it is perpetually clothed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of wood, chiefly fruit-trees: that the valleys are in a perpetual state of verdure; and continually decked with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, the spontaneous productions of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> with corn and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, cultivated with great care by the inhabitants: that the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is so prolific as to raise <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities of corn for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>; and that the ships that call here never fail of meeting with refreshments of every kind. It is said to be peopled by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, who have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of their own, apparently combined of a variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> languages; for, say they, whoever understands the European tongues may make shift to hold conversation with this people. It is remarkable, that no ships, expressly sent upon this discovery, were ever fortunate enough to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in with the island of St Borondon, though the Spaniards have several times attempted it from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANARIES">Canaries</a>. Hence it has been called the marvellous island; and hence indeed we may conclude, either that it exists wholly in imagination, or at least that it is surrounded with such currents as infensibly carry ships out of their course, and prevent their meeting with it. Some writers affirm that it actually disappears upon certain occasions, and shifts its position: while others, with more appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, allege, that it is frequently overcast with thick and impenetrable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, which occasion the disappointment of all the adventurers who have gone in search of it.

BOROUGH

Pages 39-40

in its original Saxon borghe, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> borgh, is by some supposed to have been primarily meant of a tithing or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> consisting of ten families, who were bound and combined together as each others pledge. Afterwards, as Vertegan informs us, borough came to signify a town that had something of a wall or enclosure about it: so that all places which among our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, had the denomination borough, were one way or other fenced or fortified. But, in later times, the same appellation was also bestowed on several of the ville ingeniores, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of more than ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, though not walled. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Saxons, according to Spelman, gave the name burgh to those called, in other countries, cities. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> canons being made for removing the Borough episcopal fees from villages and small towns to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> cities, the name <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> became attributed to episcopal towns, and that of borough retained to all the rest; though these too had the appearance of cities, as being governed by their mayors, and having laws of their own making, and sending representatives to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and being fortified with a wall and castle, and the like. Borough, or burgh, is now particularly appropriated to such towns and villages as send burgesses or representatives to parliament. Boroughs are equally such, whether they be incorporate or not; there being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of our English boroughs not incorporated; and, on the contrary, several corporations that are not boroughs; e.g., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">Deal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENDAL">Kendal</a>, &c. Boroughs, in Scotland. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Boroughs, in Scotland, are corporations made for the advantage of trade, by charters granted by several of their kings; having the privilege of sending commissioners to represent them in parliament, besides other peculiar privileges. The royal boroughs are not only so many distinct corporations, but do also constitute one entire body, governed by, and accountable to, one general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, anciently called the court of four boroughs, held yearly to treat and determine concerning matters relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> advantage of all boroughs. The four boroughs which composed this court were, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, Stirling, Roxburgh, and Berwick; which two last falling into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the English, Linlithgow and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LANARK">Lanark</a> were put in their places; with a saving to the former whenever they should return to their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>. But this court not being sufficient to answer the necessities of the royal boroughs, they were all empowered under James III. in 1487, to send commissioners to a yearly convention of their own, which was then appointed to be held at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERKEITHING">Inverkeithing</a>, but is now held at Edinburgh, under the denomination of the convention of boroughs, vested with great power, and having for their object the benefit of trade, and the general <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the boroughs. Borough-Courts, are certain courts held in boroughs, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament: such are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>'s court, and court of hustings, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. Borough-English, a customary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of lands or tenements, in some ancient boroughs and copyhold manors, by which the youngest son, and not the eldest, succeeds to the burgage tenement on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father. For which Littleton gives this reason; because the younger son, by reason of his tender <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, is not so capable as the rest of his brethren to help himself. Other authors have indeed given a much stranger reason for this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the fee had anciently a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the seventh commandment with his tenant's wife on her wedding night; and that therefore the tenement descended, not to the eldest, but to the youngest son, who was more certainly the offspring of the tenant. But it cannot be proved that this custom ever prevailed in England, though it certainly did in Scotland, (under the name of mercebeta, or marcete), till abolished by Malcolm III. But perhaps a more rational account than either may be brought from the practice of the Tartars; among whom, according to Father Duhalde, this custom of descent to the youngest son also prevails. That <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> is composed totally of shepherds and herdsmen; and the elder sons, as soon as they are capable of leading a pastoral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, migrate from their father with a certain allotment of cattle, and go to seek a new habitation. The youngest son, therefore, who continues late with his father, is naturally the heir of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, the rest being already provided for. And thus we find, that among many other northern nations it was the custom for all the sons but one to migrate from the father, which one became his heir. So that possibly this custom, wherever it prevails, may be the remnant of that pastoral state of the ancient Britons and Germans which Caesar and Tacitus describe. Borough-head, or Head-borough, called also borough-holder, or burfholder, the chief <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of the decenna, or hundred, chosen to speak and act in behalf of the rest.

BOROUGHBRIDGE

Pages 40-40

a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> riding of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> in England, seated on the river Yore, over which there is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. The town is not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, but commodious, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. i. 15. N. Lat. 54° 10'.

BOROZAILE

Pages 40-40
or the zeal of the Ethiopians, a disease epidemic in the countries about the river Senegal. It principally affects the pudenda, but is different from the lues venerea. It owes its rise to excessive venery; in the men this distemper is called afab, and in women afflatatus. BORRACHIO. See CAOUTCHOUK. BORRAGE. See BORAGO, Botany Index.

BORRELLISTS

Pages 40-40

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, so denominated from their founder Borrel, a person of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Greek, and Latin tongues. They reject the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the sacraments, public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, and all other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> acts of worship. They assert, that all the Christian churches of the world have degenerated from the pure apostolical doctrines, because they have suffered the word of God, which is infallible, to be expounded, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather corrupted, by doctors who are not infallible. They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a very austere <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and employ a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of their goods in alms.

BORRICHIUS

Pages 40-40

one of the most learned men of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, the son of a Lutheran minister in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, was born in 1626. He applied himself to physic in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>, and began to practise during a most terrible <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> that made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> havoc in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. He travelled: but before his departure, in 1660, he was appointed professor in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>; and at his return discharged his duties with great fidelity, of which the works he published afford full <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>. He was raised to the office of counsellor in the supreme <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, in 1686; to that of counsellor of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, in 1689; and died of the operation for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, in 1690. He published, 1. Lingua pharmacopeorum. 2. Difficultates de poetica Graecis et Latinis. 3. De ortu et progressu chemiae; and several other works.

BORROMEUS

Pages 40-43
