ST <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">CHARLES</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>, and archbishop Borromeus, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>; a personage of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>, and whose sincere piety, simplicity of manners, and zeal for reformation, render him indeed a character equally interesting and instructive to the members of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. He was the son of Gilbert Borromeus <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARONA">Arona</a> and of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> of Medicis, and was born at the castle of Arona upon Lake Maggiore in the Milanese, in October 1538. When he was about 12 years old, Julius Caesar Borromeus resigned an abbacy to him of a considerable revenue, which was considered as an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> inheritance of the family; which Charles accepted, but applied the revenue wholly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. Having acquired a sufficient knowledge of the languages at Milan, he studied the civil and canon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>, where he lived like another <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a> in Sodom, preferring his innocence among a thousand <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> by which it was endangered. He received great advantage from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> and conversation of Francis Alciat, one of the most learned men of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, for whom he afterwards procured the purple. He would accept no new benefice but upon condition that he should be at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to apply the revenue to public uses. In the year 1554, Charles being then 16 years old, his father died, an event which brought him back to the castle of Arona; where, though he had an elder <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, Count Frederick, he was requested by the family to take upon him the management of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> affairs, to which at length he consented. After some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he returned again to his studies, which, in the year 1559, being then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> 21, he finished by a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, and took his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. The promotion of his uncle to the pontificate, by the name of Pius IV., which happened the year following, seemed to have very little effect upon him; but he was very soon made protonotary, and entrusted both with the public and privy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> state: he was also, at the same time, created cardinal deacon, and soon after archbishop of Milan. In obedience to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of his uncle the pope, he lived in great splendour, having a brilliant retinue and a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of domestics; yet his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> and humility were never brought into question. In order to render even his amusements useful, he established an academy of select and learned persons, as well <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> as laics, from among his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> and dependants, who were employed in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> which tended to inspire a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of virtue, and to form a just <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. Each of them was to write upon some chosen subject, either in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in prose, and to communicate to each other in frequent conferences the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of their studies. The works produced by this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> have been published in many volumes, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Novae Vaticanae, because these useful assemblies were held at the Vatican, and at night, after the bustle of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> was over. About this time Charles also formed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of founding a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> at Pavia, which should at the same time be a school of science and an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> from the vices and vanities of the world. In prosecution of this design, he raised a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> edifice upon the foundations of several houses which belonged to the family of Borromeus in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>; he obtained from the pope several benefices, which he attached to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; he provided it with all things necessary for the young scholars out of his own revenue; and he dedicated his Borromeus college to St. Justina virgin and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a>. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his only brother Frederick, his relations, his friends, and even the pope himself, advised him to change his state, to quit the church, and marry, that his family might not become extinct. Charles, however, contrary to this advice and the expectations of the world, received the priesthood, and addressed the pope in these terms; "Do not complain of me, Holy Father, for I have taken a spouse whom I love and on whom my wishes have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> fixed." From this time he became more fervent in exercises of piety and ecclesiastical knowledge: He perceived that some literati who had departed from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> had also corrupted the writings of some holy doctors of the church, and he thought he should render <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he could restore the genuine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>: He therefore employed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a> Statius, a Portuguese of great learning, in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, whom for that purpose he retained at Rome. To his zeal and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> also is owing the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of eight cardinals, still subsisting, to resolve doubts and obviate difficulties which should arise in explanations of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>. There was a very intimate friendship between Borromeus and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> Bartholomew des Martyrs archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a>, and author of a work entitled Stimulus Pannonum. This work falling into Borromeus's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> gave him an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> desire to become a preacher, as he was now convinced that preaching was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> duties of a prelate. An almost inconceivable multiplicity of business, ill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, a feeble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, and a difficult <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a>, were no insuperable obstacles to his design, yet he surmounted them all; and though his beginnings were weak, yet perseverance crowned them with success. Having obtained permission to visit his church, which the pope had hitherto refused as he found his presence necessary at Rome, he prepared to set out for Milan. He had before sent thither his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> Ormanetus, whose labours at first had not been unsuccessful, but who soon found oppositions so pertinacious and obstinate as put an end to his hopes: Borromeus therefore <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of going in person, and he was received with the most distinguished honours. He was, however, soon recalled to Rome, where many things made his presence necessary: the pope was gradually dying; and Charles arrived just time enough to administer to him the last sacraments. Pius IV. died on the 7th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1566, and 28 days afterwards Cardinal <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRINE">Alexandrine</a> mounted the papal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, and assumed the name of Pius V., the skill and diligence of Borromeus having contributed not a little to prevent the cabals of the conclave. As soon as this event had taken <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and all was quiet at Rome, Borromeus gave himself wholly up to the reformation of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, where the most flagitious irregularities were openly practised, having first made another <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> in his own family. He began by making pastoral visits in his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, where the canons were not distinguished for the purity of their manners. He soon restored proper decency and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> to divine service, by a variety of wise and necessary regulations: In conformity to the decrees of the council of Trent, he cleared the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of many pompous pompous tombs, rich ornaments, banners, arms, and in general of all the trophies with which the vanity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> had disfigured the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of God; and in order to give a sanction to his zeal by his example, he spared not the monuments of his nearest relations. Nor did his zeal stop here: he divided the nave of the church through its whole length into two parts, by strong thick planks, that the two sexes, being separated, might perform their devotions without any attention to each other, and with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> and recollection more suitable to the place. This pastoral care extended from the cathedral to the collegiate churches, and even to the fraternities or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of penitents, particularly that of St John the Baptist. The duty of this society was to attend criminals to the place of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, to assist, comfort, and prepare them for death; but the spirit of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> was now forgotten, and the wretches who were condemned to death were <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> dragged to execution like beasts, without any spiritual assistance or consolation. But the archbishop revived the original fervour of this order, in the exercise of their peculiar duty, and persuaded many of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and principal persons of the city to become members of a society appropriated to so eminent a branch of Christian charity. The reformation of the monasteries followed that of the churches, and the vigilance of the pastor soon extended itself from the city to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> round it, which abounded with irregularities that required his correction. The great abuses and irregularities which had overrun the church at this time arose principally from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the clergy; in order therefore to attack these evils at their root, Charles established seminaries, colleges, and communities, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of young persons intended for holy orders. He met with many difficulties, and much opposition in his endeavours to bring about a reformation of manners; but he prevailed against every obstacle by an inflexible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a>, tempered with great sweetness of manners. The governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, and many of the senators, were apprehensive that the cardinal's ordinances and proceedings would encroach upon the civil jurisdiction, and become inconsistent with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of his Catholic majesty, to whom the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Milan was then in subjection. And this was a fruitful source of remonstrances, representations, and complaints, which long troubled the courts of Rome and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>, and which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II., referred entirely to the decision of the pope. But Borromeus had a more formidable opposition to struggle with, that of several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> orders, particularly the Brothers of Humility. Three provosts of the society entered into a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> to cut him off; and one of their confederates, called Jerom Donat, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> was Farina, took upon him to carry the design into execution. For this purpose he mixed with the crowd that went into the archiepiscopal chapel, where the cardinal spent an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> every evening in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> with his domestics and other pious persons; and having watched his opportunity, he fired a harquebus at him, which was loaded with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> suited to the bore of the piece, and with a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of leaden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>. It is said that the ball struck him on the spinal bone, but fell <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> at his feet without doing any other damage than <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>- ing his rochet, and that one of the shot penetrated his clothes to the skin, and there stopped, without imprinting any wound, which was considered as a miracle, especially as the other shot tore away <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a wall, and went quite through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. In the year 1576, the city and diocese of Milan were visited by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, which swept away incredible numbers; and the behaviour of Borromeus, on this occasion, was truly Christian and heroic: He not only <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> on the spot, but he went about giving directions for accommodating the sick, and burying the dead, with a zeal and attention that were at once ardent and deliberate, minute and comprehensive; and his example stimulated others to join in the good work. He avoided no danger, and he spared no expense; nor did he content himself with establishing proper regulations in the city, but went out into all the neighbouring parishes where the contagion raged, distributing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to the poor, ordering proper accommodations for the sick, and punishing those, especially the clergy, who were remiss in the duties of their calling. Charles, notwithstanding the fatigue and perplexity which he suffered by thus executing his pastoral charge, abated nothing of the usual austerity of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, nor omitted any of his stated devotions; for, whatever approached to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> or magnificence, he considered as incompatible with the propriety of his character. It happened, that being once on a visit to the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a> at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, a very sumptuous entertainment was provided for him. Borromeus, though he had been used to content himself with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, yet sat down at the table, where however he ate but little, and gave sufficient intimation that he was much displeased with such ostentatious prodigality; but what was his surprise when he saw the table again covered with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESSERT">dessert</a>, consisting of whatever was most rare, exquisite, and costly! He immediately rose hastily from his seat, as if he had suddenly recollected some pressing business, and gave orders for his departure, notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, and the most earnest entreaties of the archbishop. "My <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>," said the cardinal, "if I should tarry here to-night, you would give me another such treat as that I have just seen, and the poor will then suffer another loss, great numbers of whom might have been fed with the superfluities that have been now set before us." The continual labours and austerities of Borromeus naturally shortened his life; he went to Vercal to put an end, if possible, to the divisions which threatened the most fatal consequences; and, when he was there, he received a message from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy, requesting his presence at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>. From Turin he retired to a place called the Sepulchre, on the mountain Varais, where he was seized with an intermittent fever, which scarce permitted him to return alive to Milan, where he arrived on the 3rd of November 1584, and died the next day. He was lamented by the city and the whole province with such marks of sincere sorrow as are rarely seen; and he was immediately worshipped as a saint without waiting for the pope's approbation. The pope, however, when he was told of it by Cardinal Baronius, gave directions that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> of the people should not be restrained, though Borromeus was not canonized till the 1st of November 1610, in the pontificate of Leo XI. Since that time many churches Borromeus, churches and chapels have been erected in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Borrowing; this saint, and many religious societies instituted and put under his protection. The foregoing particulars are extracted from an account of the life of Borromeus, written some years ago by Father Anthony Touron. Upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of this life with that written by Ribadeneira a Spanish Jesuit above a century ago, it appears that the improvement of knowledge has made a very striking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in this kind of biography. Ribadeneira, who lived in the midst of ignorance and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, did not suspect that the time was at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> when the incredible and ridiculous fables he recites could not be believed: his life of this saint therefore abounds with particulars which Touron has justly omitted. We are told that a miraculous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> was seen over the chamber of Borromeus's mother when she was in labour: That Borromeus, seeing two persons carried violently down a rapid river on their horses, and just ready to perish, caused their horses suddenly to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> with them out of the water, by giving them his benediction: That Octavian Varese, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of Milan, who was confined to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> by sickness, when Borromeus died became instantly well, by recommending himself to the saint's intercession. That a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Julius Bonacina was instantly cured of a disorder in her eye, which had taken away the sight of it, by performing an act of devotion in honour of this saint: That a count of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a> was instantly seized with a violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> upon speaking irreverently of Borromeus's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, but was cured upon confessing his fault. It would certainly be a work of infinite service to the Roman church, to new-write the lives of her saints in such a manner as can now be believed, since the lives already written might by that means be gradually superseded, which are a better antidote against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a> than the arguments of the best reasoner in the world.

BORROWING AND HIRING

Pages 43-43

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, are contracts by which a qualified <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> may be transferred to the hirer <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> borrower; in which there is only this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that hiring is always for a price or stipend, or additional recompense; borrowing is merely gratuitous. But the law in both <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> is the same. They are both contracts, whereby the possession and transient property is transferred for a particular <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, on condition and agreement to restore the goods so hired or borrowed, as soon as the time is expired, or the use performed, together with the price or stipend (in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of hiring) either expressly agreed upon by the parties, or left to be implied by law, according to the value of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. By this mutual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, the hirer or borrower gains a temporary property in the thing hired, accompanied with an implied condition to use it with moderation, and not to abuse it; and the owner or lender retains a reverification <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in the same, and acquires a new property in the price or reward. Thus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> hires or borrows a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, he has the possession and a qualified property therein during that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>; on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of which his qualified property determines, and the owner becomes (in case of hiring) entitled also to the premium or price for which the horse was hired. There is one <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of this price or reward the most usual of any, but concerning which many good and learned men have in former times very much perplexed themselves and other people, by raising doubts about Borrowing's legality in foro conscientiae. That is, when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a> on a contract to receive not only the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> sum again, but also an increase by way of compensation for the use, which is generally called interest by those who think it lawful, and usury by those who do not so. But as to this, see the article INTEREST. BORROWSTOWNESS. See BURROWSTOWNNESS.

BORSEHOLDER

Pages 43-43

among the Anglo-Saxons, one of the lowest magistrates, whose authority extended only over one free burgh, tithing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> decennary, consisting of ten families. Every freeman who wished to enjoy the protection of the laws, and not to be treated as a vagabond, was under the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of being admitted a member of the tithing where he and his family resided; and in order to obtain this admission, it was necessary for him to maintain a good reputation; because all the members of each tithing being mutual pledges and sureties for each other, and the whole tithing sureties to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> for the good behaviour of all its members, they were very cautious of admitting any into their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> who were of bad or doubtful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. Each tithing formed a little state or commonwealth within itself, and chose one of its most respectable members for its head, who was sometimes called the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDERMAN">alderman</a> of such a tithing or freeburgh, on account of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, but most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> borseholder, from the Saxon words borb, "a surety," and alder, "a head or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>." This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> had authority to call together the members of his tithing, to preside in their meetings, and to put their sentences in execution. The members of each tithing, with their tithing-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> or borseholder at their head, constituted a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, in which all the little controversies arising within the tithing were determined. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any dispute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difficulty or importance happened, or if either of the parties was not willing to submit to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> given in the tithing-court, the cause was referred or appealed to the next superior court, or court of the hundred.

BORSET

Pages 43-43
or Borsett, celebrated for its baths, a place about half a league from Aix-la-Chapelle in Germany. The abbey here is a very magnificent pile of building. It was formerly a monastery; but serves for a nunnery, whose abbess is a princess of the empire, and lady of Borset. The waters are warm, and of the nature of those of Aix-la-Chapelle; but they are only used as baths for the diphtheries in which the waters last mentioned are recommended, and also in dropsical and edematous cases. The waters are distinguished into the upper and lower springs. The former were found by Dr Simmons to raise the thermometer to 15°, the latter to only 127°. All the baths are supplied by the first. Dr Simmons observed that these waters were much less sulphurous than those of Aix-la-Chapelle, probably on account of their greater heat. He likewise found that they abounded much with selenites, which incrust the pipe through which the water passes, and likewise the sides of the bath. BORYSTHENES. See BORISTHENES.

BOS

Pages 43-44

John Baptist du, a celebrated author and member of the French academy, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUVAIS">Beauvais</a> in 1679, and finished his studies at the Sorbonne. In 1695, he was made one of the committee for foreign affairs. affairs under Mr Torez; and was afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with some important transactions in England, Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. At his return to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, he was handsomely preferred, made an abbé, and chosen perpetual secretary of the French academy. He was the author of several excellent works; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, 1. Critical reflections upon <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, 3 vols 12mo. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the four Gordians, confirmed and illustrated by medals. 3. A critical history of the establishment of the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> among the Gauls, 2 vols 4to, 4 vols 12mo. He died at Paris on the 23rd of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1742. Bos, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Janssen, an esteemed painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOIS_LE_DUC">Bois-le-Duc</a>. Having been carefully instructed in the art of painting by the artists of his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, he applied himself entirely to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> after <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and rendered himself very eminent for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of his colouring and the neatness of his handling. His favourite subjects were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, and curious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, which he usually represented as grouped, in glasses, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vases of crystal, half filled with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and gave them so lively a look of nature, that it seemed scarce possible to express them with greater truth or delicacy. It was frequent with this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> to represent the drops of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a> on the leaves of his objects, which he executed with an uncommon transparency; and embellished his subjects with butterflies, bees, wasps, and other insects, which Sandrart says, were superior to anything of that kind performed by his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> artists. He likewise painted portraits with very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success; and showed as much merit in that style as he did in his compositions of still <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He died in 1507. Bos, See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Bos, in Antiquity, was peculiarly used for an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, which was didrachmus, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to two drachms. It was so called as having on it the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of an ox, and chiefly obtained among the Athenians and Delians; being sometimes also struck of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. From this arose the phrase Bos in lingua, applied to those who had taken bribes to hold their tongue.

BOSA

Pages 44-44

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town in the western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, with a castle, a good port, and a bishop's see. It is seated on the river Bofa, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of an island of the same name; and has good <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> pits. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 30'. N. Lat. 40° 19'.

BOSCA

Pages 44-44

among painters, denotes a landscape representing much wood and trees.

BOSCAN

Pages 44-44

John, a Spanish poet of the 16th century, born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARCELONA">Barcelona</a>. He was the friend of Garcilaso de Viga, another Spanish poet. These two were the first who made any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> improvement in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and their pieces were printed together. Boscan, who died about the year 1542, principally succeeded in sonnets.

BOSCAWEN

Pages 44-44

Edward, a brave British <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son of Hugh late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> viscount <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALMOUTH">Falmouth</a>. Having early entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, he was, in 1740, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOREHAM">Shoreham</a>; and behaved with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> intrepidity as a volunteer under Admiral <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VERNON">Vernon</a>, Boscowen, at the taking of Porto Bello. At the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1740-1, he had the command of a party of seamen who resolutely attacked and took a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> of twenty-four pounders, though exposed to the fire of another fort of five guns. Lord Aubrey Beauclerk being killed at the attack of Boca-Chica, Captain Boscowen succeeded him in the command of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Frederic of 70 guns. In May 1742, he returned to England, and married Frances <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of William Glanville, Esq.; and the same year was elected representative for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRURO">Truro</a> in Cornwall. In 1744, he was made captain of the Dreadnought of 60 guns; and soon after he took the Medea, a French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> commanded by M. Hoquart, the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s ship taken in that war. May 3, 1747, he signalized himself under the admirals Anson and Warren, in an engagement with the French fleet off <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINISTERRE">Finisterre</a>, and was wounded in the shoulder with a musket <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>. Here M. Hoquart, who then commanded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAMOND">Diamond</a> of 56 guns, again became his prisoner; and all the French ships of war, which were ten in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, were taken. On the 15th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> he was made rear-admiral of the blue, and commander in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> forces employed on an expedition to the East Indies; and, on the 4th of November, sailed from St Helen's, with six ships of the line, five frigates, and 2000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. On the 29th of July 1748, he arrived at St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s, and soon after laid siege to Pondicherry; but the men growing sickly, and the monsoons being expected, the siege was raised, and Mr Boscowen showed himself as much the general as the admiral in his retreat. Soon after he had news of the peace, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MADRAS">Madras</a> was delivered up to him by the French. In April 1750, he arrived at St Helen's in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, and found that in his absence he had been appointed rear-admiral of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. He was the next year made one of the lords commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>, and chosen an elder <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the Trinity-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. In February 1755, he was appointed vice-admiral of the blue. On the 19th of April, failing in order to intercept a French squadron bound to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, he fell in with the Alcide and Leys of 64 guns each, which were both taken: on this occasion M. Hoquart became his prisoner a third <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and he returned to Spithead with his prizes and 1500 prisoners. In 1756, he was appointed vice-admiral of the white; and in 1758, admiral of the blue, and commander in chief of the expedition to Cape Breton; when, in conjunction with General <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMHERST">Amherst</a>, and a body of troops from New England, the important fortress of Louisbourg and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cape Breton was taken, for which he afterwards received the thanks of the house of commons. In 1759, being appointed to command in the Mediterranean, he arrived at Gibraltar, where hearing that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOULON">Toulon</a> fleet, under M. de la Clue, had passed the Straits, in order to join that at Brest, he got under sail, and on the 18th of August <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, pursued, and engaged the enemy. His ship, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAMUR">Namur</a> of 90 guns, losing her main-mast, he shifted his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> to the Newark; and, after a sharp engagement, took three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ships, and burnt two in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAGOS">Lagos</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, and the same year arrived at Spithead with his prizes and 2000 prisoners. On <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 8, 1760, he was appointed general

BOSCH

Pages 44-45
JACOB VANDEN, a painter of still life, was born at Amsterdam in 1636, and painted summer fruits of various kinds, peaches, pears, apples, plums, nectarines, and cherries, with extraordinary neatness of pencil. He painted all his objects after nature, and imitated every sort of fruit with so great truth and delicacy, with such natural and transparent colour, that they appeared delicious, and almost real. He died in 1676.

BOSCHAERTS

Pages 45-45

THOMAS WILLEBORTS, a celebrated painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERGEN_OP_ZOOM"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol0.html#article-BERGEN">Bergen</a>-op-zoom; and, like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> painters who flourished at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, began to draw, when very young, in the books that were intended for other studies. Preferring his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> to every thing else, he drew his own <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, by his resemblance in a looking-glass, so like, that those who <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> it were astonished. This he did before he had the least instruction from any one, and when he was only 12 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Upon this his parents sent him to a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, that he might follow the bent of his genius; but his first master being only an indifferent painter, and incapable of satisfying his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> desire of learning, he left him, and engaged himself with Gerard Segers; under whom, after four years practice, he proved a most accomplished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> being at that time the seat of arts, where there was a conflux of the most eminent painters, he thought it the fittest <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for his improvement; and there executed such a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of noble pieces as added greatly to the splendour of that wealthy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. In 1642, Henry Frederic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, and his son Prince William, employed him in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; in which he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> several years, and made those excellent pieces that are to be seen in that prince's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> and other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and painted portraits for most of the persons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> that were then living. He died in the flower of his age, in 1670.

BOSCO

Pages 45-45
or BOSCHI, a town of Italy, in the Milanese, seated on the river Orbe. E. Long. 9° 44'. N. Lat. 44° 53'.

BOSCOI

Pages 45-45
or Bosci, in ecclesiastical history, denotes a species or tribe of monks in Palestine, who fed on grass like the beasts of the fields. The word is Greek, βοσκειν, q. d. "grazers;" formed from βοσκω, παγω, "I feed." The Boscoi are ranked among the number of Adamites, not so much on account of their habit, as food. They took no care about provision; but when eating-time came, or any of them was hungry, went into the fields, with each his knife in his hand, and gathered and eat what he could find.

BOSCOVICH

Pages 45-63

ROGER <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">JOSEPH</a>, the founder of an original and sublime <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, deserves to be particularly noticed in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; but we have to regret that the materials from which our biographical memoir must be compiled, are insufficient to satisfy the curiosity concerning the literary habits, and the characteristic features of this very illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, indeed, as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, we are enabled to appreciate by perusing some of the immortal works which he has bequeathed us; but, for a knowledge of his moral character, disposition, and temporal concerns, we can only have recourse to the eulogies of his Bosovich friends. These are certainly entitled to much of our confidence; and when the names of M. de la Lande, M. Fabroni, Stay, and Zamagna are mentioned, we may be thought fastidious, in implying the least distrust of their testimony. It is our respect for the public and for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and it is our knowledge of the nature of eulogies, which have made us so. We have, therefore, endeavoured, rather to relate the incidents in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Bosovich, than to give a transcript of friendly <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a>; and yet perhaps it may be discovered, that our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> with eulogium, whilst its outlines are poorly defined. Bosovich was born on the 11th of May 1711, at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAGUSA">Ragusa</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Adriatic, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a small republic of the same name, under the protection of the Turks and the Venetians. We know so little of his parents, that we can only conjecture at their circumstances and capacity, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> which they gave to their son being liberal and judicious. It does not appear that our author gave any tokens of superior genius, till he was sent to learn <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> and philosophy in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of the Jesuits, who were at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> teachers in Ragusa, and throughout <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Amongst them, his docility and obedience could not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> unnoticed, but were sufficient to mark him as a likely subject for future eminence, and consequently to procure to him particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. In his 15th year, after he had gone through the ordinary course of education, and when it was necessary to determine his further pursuits, application was made to admit him into the order; and for the reasons we have mentioned, was readily complied with. This was agreeable to his own inclination, and proved the source of that distinction in learning to which he afterwards attained. The Jesuits, it is well known, had much <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> and authority to promote in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Rome; whither it was customary in them to send those members whom they knew to be qualified for that purpose, and those youths of whom they had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> expectations, for more instruction. As Bosovich was sent there in the year 1723, we may reasonably imagine he had profited much by his teachers, and was signalized for his abilities. This zeal in the cultivation of youth, which the Jesuits ever preserved, and which perhaps tended more to the preservation of their power than all their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> artifices, was attended with consequences the most beneficial to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>; and when we recollect how many and how great the geniuses were which it discovered, and fostered and brought to maturity, we are almost induced to believe that it counterbalanced all the ill effects of their order. Had this education been confined to some limited sphere; had it embraced the prattling doctrines of casuistry and the unwieldy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of cloistered <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> alone; unfortunate and melancholy for the world would have been this zeal: no refuge for the venial penitent, no security against boisterous fecundity would have remained; an unmannerly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETHARGY">lethargy</a> would have debauched the mind, and the moral and the intellectual world would have sunk to a dread <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a> of confusion. But the Jesuits knew well the benignant influence of literature, and the salutary elevation of science; they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> that wealth, and power, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, nour, followed philosophy; and that philosophy had driven famine, wretchedness, and vice, from their habitations. We dare not say that the interest and aggrandizement of their order were secondary considerations, but we <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> avow it as our <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the short reign of the Jesuits, and the objects at which they aimed, and above all the means which they employed, were more instructive, promised better, and effected more to humanity, than all the accumulated humility and sanctity of all the religious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. We have been led into this digression by the coincidence of certain considerations operating at the time on our minds. Bofcovich was of the order of Jesuits; that order is no more; its destruction took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in his life-time; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> for the delight and the instruction we have received from him and many others of the order; the present disposition among mankind to detract from its merits, to magnify its imperfections, and to confound it with the fanatical and enthusiastic groups of every persuasion which have disgraced the name and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. But to return; our author on his arrival in Rome, entered the novitiate of the order, where his studies wore a new aspect, but were still pursued with diligence. Christian morality, the rules and constitutions of the order, claimed his attention for two years; after which he was instructed in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, and became well versed in general literature, in a particular manner in Latin <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, which at that time was very much cultivated. From the noviciate he was sent to the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> and physics. It was in these sciences that his elevated genius and uncommon abilities shone forth so conspicuously, and procured to him the admiration of his superiors. In three years' time he was able to give private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> on mathematics; and was then exempted from a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, by which the novices were bound to teach Latin and the belles lettres for five years before they commenced the study of theology. This exemption was in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of his great predilection to the mathematics, of which he was soon afterwards made public professor. It would appear to us, that the science of theology, as it was then incultuated, had little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> for the mind of Bofcovich; for it is not likely that a mind intimately acquainted with truth, and accustomed to find her ever plain and unadulterated, could relish the retiring obscurities of philosophy, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the flimsy deceptions of a mystical religion; nor can we wonder, that during the four years in which he was constrained to the study, he should become more familiar with Leibnitz, Maclaurin, and Newton, than with Loyola, and Laynez, and Aquaviva. For the professorship of mathematics he was eminently qualified, as, besides a thorough knowledge of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> productions in the science, he had acquired a primitive severity of demonstration by studying the works of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> geometricians; and he conjoined withal an obliging accommodation of his own powers to the deficiencies of his pupils. It was for their benefit he at this time composed elementary treatises on <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">trigonometry</a>. But notwithstanding the arduous duties of his situation which he invariably fulfilled, he found time to instruct and enlighten more than boys; for about this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, he entertained some of those original notions which were destined to grow up into system, and one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> to astonish the whole world of science. These, as they grew, were strengthened by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> arguments in the public disputations, by anticipating obstructions, overcoming and removing them, and by mighty efforts in extending and applying them to the most remote and directive actions of the universe. The animating spirit of discovery and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> led him to consider every portion of physical science; and indeed so versatile and so vigorous was his mind, we would be at a loss to specify one portion, which, within a few years, it did not comprehend, elucidate, and advance. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of this we beg to present our readers with an enumeration of the principal subjects to which he turned his attention, and concerning which he published dissertations whilst he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the professorship. The transit of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; the spots in the sun; the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AURORA_BOREALIS"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">aurora</a> borealis; the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of spheric trigonometry; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a> to determine celestial objects; the ancient arguments for the rotundity of the earth; oscillating circles; on infinites and infinitely little quantities; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of bodies in unresisting spaces; the aberration of the fixed stars; the inequalities in terrestrial gravity; on <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>; on the limits of certainty in astronomical observations; on the solid of greatest attraction; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYCLOID">cycloid</a>; the logistic curve <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>; the vises vivae; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">comets</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>; the rainbow; the calculation of fractions; the centre of gravity; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>; the law of continuity; lenses and dioptrical telescopes; the objective micrometer; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISIBILITY">divisibility</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. Some of these are short, but all of them contain curious and valuable matter. It is only by perusing them we are able to discover the gradual progress of his mind; and to understand the manner in which he arrived at the theory of natural philosophy, which alone will render his name immortal. About this time a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for philosophical poetry was much prevalent amongst the learned, and some of our author's acquaintances had laboured in it with success. Of these we may mention Father Noceti who wrote on the rainbow and the aurora borealis, and the justly celebrated Benedict Stay, whose poems on the philosophy of Descartes, and on the more modern philosophy, are excellent examples of fine Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> and scientific <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>. Bofcovich published their works with annotations and supplements, in which a splendid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of information and learning is displayed. By such undertakings, the fame of our author was widely diffused, and he became an object of general admiration. The learned societies of many countries in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> conferred on him unfolicited honours, and several foreign princes invited him to their courts. His opinions on various subjects of civil <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, topography, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRODYNAMICS">hydrodynamics</a>, were asked and entertained by Pope Benedict XIV. John V. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, and others. These necessarily required his presence in different states, where he never failed to increase his reputation, and often terminated disputes which might otherwise have gone on to open warfare. He was employed to correct the maps of the papal dominions, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of the meridian passing passing through them. In this he was assisted by an English Jesuit, Christopher Maire. An account of their expedition was printed at Rome and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and is interspersed with some curious anecdotes, concerning the opinions which the peasants of the Apennines formed of them, and the operations which they had to perform; but it is valuable on account of the accurate detail which is given of their observations. In the year 1757, he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a> by the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a>, to reconcile some differences concerning the draining of a lake, in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Francis I. and that republic, were concerned. It was after he had succeeded in the object of his visit to that city, that he published there his "Theoria Philosophiae Naturalis" in 1758; and that he gained the esteem of the empress <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>. Another occasion for his mediating powers soon presented itself, and which more nearly interested him, as his native city of Ragusa required them. It had been suspected by the British <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, that some ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> were fitted out at that port for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the French, thereby infringing the neutrality. Such a suspicion having no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> foundation, alarmed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> of Ragusa, and required speedy removal, as the consequences of it might be extremely prejudicial to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. Bofcovich, who had often been successful in similar circumstances for other powers, appeared to them the most proper person for this purpose, and was accordingly intrusted with it. He repaired to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and here also effected the object of his mission with honour to himself. He visited the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, which received him with distinguishing marks of respect, and which he soon afterwards complimented with an excellent Latin poem on the solar and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> eclipses. This was in the year 1760, when Dr Johnson was in London. Mr Murphy speaks of an interview which took place between our author and Johnson; but in order to magnify the unruly powers of the tremendous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, he rather unhandsomely tells us of the easy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> with which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> might travel through Italy and France. We are unwilling to mention what effects on some minds may have been produced by the formidable society of a Johnson; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are a contempt of elegant simplicity and ingenuous ease, and an affected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> to repulsive pomp and authoritative ostentation, be our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> far from his influence, amid the peace and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of social life. Bofcovich was invited by the Royal Society to be of the party of their members sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, to observe the transit of Venus over the sun's disk, which happened in the year 1762. The nature of his embassy, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of returning home, however, prevented his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCEPTANCE">acceptance</a> of the invitation. Soon after his return, and when his embassy was fulfilled, he was appointed by the senate of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a> to the mathematical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>, and to superintend the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a> of the royal college of Brera. He continued in this situation for five years, when he was made professor of astronomy and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a> in the Palatine schools of Milan by the empress queen; who also requested him to continue his attention to the observatory. This he expected to be the most agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his life. Admired by the learned; beloved by his friends; having an adequate income, and a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> found and vigorous; he promised to himself, happy, because useful Bofcovich, days, in the tranquil cultivation of the sciences; but a cloud <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> impending now burst over his head, and these bright days never came. The mysterious regulation in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> constitution of the Jesuits, though it had attracted the keen curiosity of the world, had, for very substantial reasons never been explored; nay, such was the influence of the order over the minds of the most enlightened statesmen, that this impenetrable mystery was held sacred by the civil power in many countries, as if no danger could exist in what was not understood. But the rapid progress of science, and the gradual decay of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, required some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of security, and some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that it was ever necessary to conceal good intentions, and to cover virtuous principles with any other garb than what truth could bestow. These it is well known, the Jesuits either could not, or were unwilling to give; and they, therefore, justly incurred the suspicion of men. The most trivial circumstances would augment this suspicion, and the least deviation from rectitude in any of the order would serve to justify it; these were not wanting, and soon became invincible; the interest of the Jesuits rapidly declined for many years, and at last, in 1773, their order was totally abolished. No exemption from the edict for its downfall could be procured: all who held offices were dismissed; and Bofcovich sought refuge in the city of Paris. Thither indeed he was invited by the minister, (we believe Turgot) by whose means he was made one of the directors of optics for the sea service, and received a pension: but it does not seem that his situation was agreeable to him; for it is well known that the peculiar nature of his circumstances was the sole cause of his long residence in Paris. Whether his dislike arose from the envy of some of the French, his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRRITABILITY">irritability</a> of temper, or the incongruity of the prevailing manners with his own, we cannot determine: but it is reasonable to imagine, that the ruin of his order, and the subsidence of his own importance, would leave some indelible mark in his mind; and perhaps when he contemplated the apparent levity and the real skepticism of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he might be brought to fear that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a> or the downfall of the world was concomitant. Sentiments very opposite to those of the French, would thence naturally arise; morosity and discontent would invade him, and wished to revisit the scenes of his youth. Be all this, however, as it may, certain it is, he applied for leave of absence for two years, after he had resided in Paris for ten years: this he easily procured, and accordingly set out for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BASSANO">Bassano</a> in the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. At this place he published in five vols. quarto, a collection of the works which he had finished in Paris. This forms a body of optical and astronomical knowledge, well worthy the attention of the philosophical and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> cultivators of the sciences. It may be worth mentioning, that by proceeding on the principles contained in one of the dissertations in this collection, an amiable philosopher of our own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> (Dr. Robison) believed it possible to ascertain the motions of the earth, though the observer should be confined in a cellar; in prosecuting the subject, however, he Bosovich found that an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> into which Bosovich had fallen, concerning the aberration of light, undermined the principles on which he had erected such a wonderful but legitimate problem. The candid and very interesting acknowledgement of the error, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> disappointment in the discovery of it, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> made in the 3rd vol. of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> Transactions, is at once an evidence of his own liberality, and an undefeasible testimony to Bosovich's genius. We beg to recommend to our readers the perusal of the works which we have now mentioned; they would tend to form the mind to the true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of investigating the phenomena of nature, and will satisfactorily shew that this mode is always rewarded by discovery. The following is a pretty just account of their contents: A new <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for determining the refracting and diverging forces of diaphanous bodies; a demonstration of the fallacy of the Newtonian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> between light and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>; the algebraic formula regarding the focuses of lenses, and their applications for calculating the sphericity of those which are to be used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACHROMATIC">achromatic</a> telescopes; the corrections to be made in ocular lenses, and the error of the sphericity of certain glasses; the causes which hinder the exact union of the solar rays by means of the great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> glasses, and the determination of the loss arising from it; the method of determining the different velocities of light passing through different mediums by means of two dioptrical telescopes, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, the other of a new kind, containing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> between the objective glasses and the place of the image; a new kind of objective micrometers; the defects and inutility of a dioptrical telescope proposed and made at Paris, which gives two images of the same object, the one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>, the other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>, with two contrary motions of moveable objects; maladies haunting in the atmosphere, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIL">hail</a> of an extraordinary size, seen on the sun with the telescope, and resembling spots; the astronomical refractions, and various methods for determining them; various methods for determining the orbits of comets and of the new planet, with copious applications of these doctrines to other astronomical subjects, and still more generally to geometry and to the science of calculation; the errors, the rectifications, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of quadrants, of sextants, of astronomical sectors, of the meridian line, of telescopes called the instruments of transit, of the meridian, and of the parallactic machine; the trigonometrical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIFFERENTIAL">differential</a> formulae, which are of so much use in astronomy; the use of the micrometrical rhombus, extended to whatever oblique position; the error arising from refractions in using the astronomical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> for a sundial, and the correction to be made; the appearing and the disappearing of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>'s ring; the methods of determining the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a> of the sun by means of the spots, proposed formerly by the author, and now perfected; the greatest exactness possible in determining the length of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENDULUM">pendulum</a> oscillating every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of middle time by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of terrestrial and celestial gravity; a compend of astronomy for the use of the marine, containing the elements of the heavenly motions, and of the astronomical instruments, to be explained to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> in the course of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>; a method for determining the altitudes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> with the greatest exactness, by means of a gnomon alone, where other instruments are not to be had; the determination of the illuminated edge of the moon to be observed on the meridian; a method of using the retrograde return of Venus to the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, for determining the least certain elements of her orbit; a method for correcting the elements of a comet, of which the longitude of the node is given, and the inclination of the orbit has been found nearly; another method for the same purpose, and for finding the elliptical orbit, when the parabolic one does not agree with the observations; a method for correcting the elements of a planet by three observations; the projection of an orbit inclined in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the ecliptic; the projection of an orbit inclined in any other plane; the calculation of the aberration of the stars, arising from the successive propagation of light; some beautiful theorems belonging to triangles, which are of great use in astronomy, reduced to most simple demonstrations. After the publication of these works, our author left Baffano, and went to Rome to visit the companions of his youth. From Rome he proceeded to Milan, where he revised some of his own works, and prepared for publication the two last volumes of Stay's poems. In such occupations, and amidst friends whom equal misfortune and temporary separation had still more endeared, he had remained happy, and might perhaps have been still further useful to the world; but his leave of absence was now nearly expired, and his dislike to a residence in Paris was augmented by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> which his present abode afforded. He was too delicate to apply for more leave of absence; and though he was sensible of the gratitude which he owed to France, he could not reconcile it with the destruction of his own repose. About this time also he had several attacks of gout, but he would admit no medical aid. Under these distresses, and others which we have before mentioned, our illustrious author at last sunk: a melancholy depopulation seized on and subjugated his mind, so that for five months he remained perfectly fatuous; and an imposthume having burst in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, terminated his existence on the 13th of February 1787, in the 76th year of his age. The following inscription was composed by Benedict Stay, and engraved on marble by order of the senate of Ragusa, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of their useful citizen the illustrious Bosovich. Rogerio Nicolai F. Bosovichio, Summi Ingenii Viro, Philosopho Et Mathematico, Praestantissimo Scripторi Operum Egregiorum Res Phycicas Geometricas Astronomicas Plurimis Inventis Suis Auctas Continentium Celebriorum Europae Academiarum Socio Qui In Soc. Jesu Cum Esset Ac Rome Mathefim Profteretur Benedicto XIV. Mandante Multe Besides the works which we have mentioned, he wrote several others on various subjects, as, on the project of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> to Rome from Fiumicino to Maccarese; a third on two torrents in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERUGIA">Perugia</a>; a fourth on the bulwarks on the river Ponaro; a fifth on the river Sidone in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACENTIA">Placentia</a>; a sixth on the entrance into the sea of the Adige. He wrote other such works on the bulwarks of the Po; on the harbours of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIMINI">Rimini</a>, of Magna Vacca, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVONA">Savona</a>, besides others, almost all which were printed. He had likewise received a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> from Clement XIII. to visit the Pompin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, on the draining of which he drew up his opinion in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, to which he added further elucidations at the desire of Pius VI. We have spoken of Boscovich as the founder of a new system of natural philosophy, which has occupied much of the attention of the learned, and which alone will render the name of its author immortal. It becomes us therefore to give such a synopsis of it, as may satisfy the general reader, or induce the student to search for more information in the work from which we ourselves have derived it. In a subject so abstruse and remote from observation as many of the principles which we have to consider in this theory, much difficulty in investigation is to be expected, and perhaps the metaphorical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> which we are constrained to employ, will tend not a little to embarrass and mislead us.
