The constant addition of adventitious atoms to the interfaces in a solid body, as we have before mentioned, will cause vibrations, and will at last, by totally separating the atoms from the limits of cohesion and the sphere of the attractive power, render them susceptible of the influence of surrounding bodies, so that they leave each other, and combine with those which surround them. When caloric is the body added, the most general effect which results from its repeated and constant addition is evaporation. Now the particles of an evaporated fluid will recombine if the supersubstantial caloric which holds them together be withdrawn, provided the bodies with which they unite do not attract them more powerfully than they do each other. But it is possible that such an addition will in certain cases strengthen the combination of a solid, i.e., that fluidity will not always be the consequence of insinuating atoms into the vacant spaces, for it is possible to specify circumstances, in which a body already fluid, may be rendered solid by interposing amongst its particles, the particles of another fluid. When the adventitious atoms are removed, one of two consequences will occur, either the atoms of a solid which has been rendered fluid by such insinuation, will be left within their spheres of attraction, and consequently will enter into limits of cohesion, and form a solid again, or they may be left beyond these spheres, so as not to enter into limits of cohesion, but to form a loose uncombined pulverulent substance. It may happen that in the latter case, the particles being separated from each other beyond their spheres of attraction, will enter into combinations with other bodies, of whose influence they are now susceptible. We have instances of both of these in the fusion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>: sometimes on cooling these form again into solids; others, having their atoms too far separated from each other, cannot unite, but combine with other bodies, (generally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a>) and form powders which retain no characteristics of metals; and some combine with other metals constituting alloys. Vol. IV. Part I. We recommend the prosecution of this subject to the philosophical chemist; and though we encounter the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of vanity, we cannot help flattering ourselves with having pointed out a mode by which, though nothing should be discovered, yet to resolve some apparently unconnected phenomena into one general principle, and hence to abridge the labour of acquiring the science of chemistry, and to facilitate the application of it to the practical purposes of life. We are of opinion that the facts in chemistry are now so numerous, as to require a generalizing spirit to reduce them into some kind of order, to shew their connexion in the chain of nature, and to derive from them by induction, certain principles which may be employed in the synthetic process. Indeed without such it will soon be found that no ordinary memory can retain what may be useful, but certainly is elegant in the art, and that a great body of evidence is insufficient to enforce conviction, if it be budded together in chaotic confusion: pillars and porticoes and carved <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> may be collected, and may astonish us by their grandeur; but unless they be methodized, connected, and combined, our astonishment will resemble that which we feel, when we contemplate the preposterous structure of some natural monster, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> are individually elegant, but serve by their elegance to magnify the error of their position. We do not wish to depreciate the merits of modern chemists, but we must confess, they appear to us more scrupulous about ascertaining the few grains of earth in some cockle shell, than anxious to erect a temple to their science, and are themselves too much elevated by the discovery of a semi-metal, to be concerned about the deities which preside. What we have said may be thought mere <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLAMATION">declamation</a>, if we do not accompany it with some example of the employment of such a generalizing spirit; we know not how far it may become us to do so, but as the consideration of the theory of Boscovich, in which we have been engaged, has naturally led us to those phenomena which seem best qualified to admit of its application, and as therefore, in some sort resulting from, or connected with our subject, we shall attempt to give a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> specimen of it. It is well known to chemists, that although certain individual or single bodies of the saline class be very soluble in water, the compounds formed of them are very insoluble in that fluid, i.e., that though <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a> singly very soluble in water, the neutral salts formed by them are very insoluble; and that many varieties in the degrees of solubility are to be met with in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> bodies or neutral salts, which are contrary to what we should expect from reasoning on the varieties of these degrees, in the simple or elementary bodies which compose them. For example, the sulphuric acid is very soluble in water, and so is the vegetable alkali or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTASH">potash</a>; but the sulphate of potash, which is a compound of these, is so difficult of solution, that 16 times its own weight of water, at the temperature of 60°, is required to effect it. The acetate of potash affords another example, though not so remarkable, requiring only about 10 times its own weight of water at the same temperature. Indeed, there are many instances of a compound or neutral <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> being less soluble than either the alkali or the acid which enter into its composition; but in those we have mentioned, the difference is so great as to have merited much attention, though as far as we know, Boscovich's there has not been assigned a reason for it. Now we apprehend the reason to be, that as both the simple bodies have an attraction for water, or that as there is an attraction between water and these two bodies, the degree of attraction will be equal to the difference only of the separate attractions between water and the bodies individually; or, in other words, the attraction between water and one of the bodies will be lessened by the attraction between water and the other body, so that the difference only of these two will influence. Now, in certain cases, this difference will be equal to nothing, when the attractions are equal; but in every case, it is evident, it will be less than the greater of the attractions, and, of consequence, the solubility of the compound will be less than that of the simple bodies which compose it. Now this consequence is not affected by the absolute solubility of the simple bodies, but by their solubility in respect to each other, i.e., relative alone; therefore, the compound of simple bodies, which themselves are highly soluble, may be no more soluble than the compound of simple bodies, which themselves are very little soluble. The principle is universal. Other consequences will result, which are not only curious, but, in our opinion important; and we do not in the least hesitate to assert, that the principle may be applied to determine a priori the degrees of solubility of neutral salts, provided we are sufficiently acquainted with the relative solubility of the simple bodies which compose them. One consequence will be, that a compound formed of a very soluble and a very insoluble simple body will be nearly, or quite, as soluble as the former, feeling that the attraction between it and water will be little or not at all diminished by the attraction between the other very insoluble body and water. As a proof of this, we may take the instance of the sulphate of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNESIA">magnesia</a>, which is soluble in its own weight of water at temperature 60°: Now in this case, the magnesia is soluble to a very small amount only; but the acid, it is well known, is so to a great degree; even the small solubility of the magnesia, however, does in a certain degree impair the solubility of the compound. The same is true of the nitrat and muriat of magnesia; and, did our limits permit, we might adduce very many examples of the same; we might shew, that the compounds of very soluble acids with the metallic oxys are soluble, if these oxys are not so; but if they are, the solubility of the compound is impaired: and we might also apply the principle to bodies soluble in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCOHOL">alcohol</a> and other menstrua, where it will be found to hold. But we leave the prosecution of the subject to our chemical readers, conferring, however, that we have found exceptions to its universality, which as yet we have not been able to reconcile. Perhaps, a principle still more general, and higher in the order of events, may influence or modify this which we have specified; it may be connected with some of those varieties in the composition of forces, which may take place in the insensible distances, changing the limits of cohesion, and modifying the position and the action of the atoms of matter. We have ventured far in the exposition we have given; did we persevere, there might be imputed to us temerity. We have attempted to apply Boscovich's theory to several Bosovich's several other chemical phenomena, particularly those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTIVE">elective</a> attraction and dissolving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a>; but though our success has been somewhat flattering, we have not been able hitherto to collect and arrange our principles and results, so as to present them properly to the public. At some future stage of this work, however, such may be in our power, when we hope to convince our readers, that the theory is sufficiently accommodated to that object, and that it will assist us in deducing principles more general, than any yet received in chemical science. It is now time for us to conclude our account of the theory of Bosovich; and in so doing, it becomes us to recommend to our readers, that they endeavour to form a just and an adequate opinion of its merits, of the objects which it has in view, and of the means which it employs to accomplish them. Considered in respect to itself only, as the production of a great and an enlightened mind, no labour to comprehend it can be in vain or worthless, and no one can comprehend it without receiving the most elevated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; but there is another inducement for us to effect this purpose, different from any we have yet mentioned: we mean the tendency it will have to modify, and to subvert, many of the leading doctrines in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a> of the day. Nor ought this to alarm any of our readers, for if these doctrines be true and legitimate, they will be paramount to all objections, and the improvements made in every other science will serve to confirm them; but if they are not so, surely the sooner they are subverted the better it will be for science and for us all; at all events, an inquiry into them is rational, and it may do good. This, however, we dare not now propose to ourselves, and will therefore recommend our readers to peruse the Essays on Perception, by Professors Reid and Stewart, where they will find sentiments which derive most of their validity from some of the Bosovichian principles. They are sentiments in which we have the honour to agree with these true philosophers; though it is somewhat mortifying to us to confess, that they have convinced us that the phenomenon of which they treat is inexplicable. It is indeed very mortifying to humanity to be convinced, that for many, very many centuries, our forefathers have been unceasingly attempting to explain phenomena intellectual and material by a nullity, on principles which do not exist; but it would be still more mortifying to find, that though there is ground for such convictions, men calling themselves philosophers should persevere steadfastly in the same invariable course of error and absurdity. In our own days, a light, clear and authoritative, has arisen to direct and to animate us in the search after truth; it is our own faults if we shut our eyes against its splendour, and suffer the interior man to be dark and unenlightened. Of this light the theory of Bosovich forms a part: it has succeeded and surpassed that of Newton; it will be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> of a greater than either; it professes to conduct us to the interior veil of the temple of nature; but it has failed in this very sublime attempt, failed, however, only after it has conducted us beyond Descartes, Leibnitz, and Newton.

BOSEA

Pages 63-65
GOLDEN-ROD TREE. See Botany Index.** **BOSHIES-MEN,** a species of Hottentots, so called, according to Dr Sparman, from their dwelling in woody or mountainous places. They are sworn enemies to a pastoral life. Some of their maxims are, to live on hunting and plunder, and never to keep any animal alive for the space of one night. By these means they render themselves odious to the rest of the inhabitants of the Cape; and are pursued and exterminated like the wild beasts, whose manners they have assumed. Others of them again are kept alive, and made slaves of. Their weapons are poisoned arrows, which shot out of a small bow will fly to the distance of 200 paces, and will hit a mark with a tolerable degree of certainty at the distance of 50 or even 100 paces. From this distance they can by stealth, as it were, convey death to the game they hunt for food, as well as to their foes, and even to so large and tremendous a beast as the lion; this noble animal thus falling by a weapon which perhaps it despised, or even did not take notice of. The Hottentot, in the mean time, concealed and safe in his ambush, is absolutely certain of the operation of his poison, which he always culls of the most virulent kind; and it is said he has only to wait a few minutes in order to see the wild beast languish and die. The dwellings of these foes to a pastoral life are generally not more agreeable than their maxims and manners. Like the wild beasts, bushes and cliffs in rocks by turns serve them instead of houses; and some of them are said to be far worse than beasts, that their foil has been found close by their habitations. A great many of them are entirely naked; but such as have been able to procure the skin of any sort of animal, great or small, cover their bodies with it from the shoulders downwards as far as it will reach, wearing it till it falls off their backs in rags. As ignorant of agriculture as apes and monkeys, like them they are obliged to wander about over hills and dales after certain wild roots, berries, and plants (which they eat raw), in order to sustain a life that this miserable food would soon extinguish and destroy were they used to better fare. Their table, however, is sometimes composed of several other dishes, among which may be reckoned the larvae of insects, or that kind of caterpillars from which butterflies are generated; and in like manner a sort of white ants (the termites), grasshoppers, snakes, and some sorts of spiders. With all these changes of diet, the Boshies-man is nevertheless frequently in want, and famished to such a degree as to waste almost to a shadow. "It was with no small astonishment (says Dr Sparman), that I for the first time saw in Lange Kloof a lad belonging to this race of men with his face, arms, legs, and body, so monstrously small and withered, that I could not have been induced to suppose but that he had been brought to that state by the fever that was epidemic in those parts, had I not seen him at the same time run like a lapwing. It required but a few weeks to bring one of these starvelings to a thriving state, and even to make him fat; their stomachs being strong enough to digest the great quantity of food with which they are crammed, as they may rather be said to bolt than eat. It sometimes happens indeed that they cannot long retain what they have taken in; but this circumstance, it is said, does not hinder them from beginning again upon a new score." "The capture of slaves from among this race of men..." is by no means difficult; and is effected (Dr Sparman informs us) in the following manner. "Several farmers that are in want of servants join together and take a journey to that part of the country where the Boshies-men live. They themselves, as well as their Lego-Hottentots, or else such Boshies-men as have been caught some time before, and have been trained up to fidelity in their service, endeavour to spy out where the wild Boshies-men have their haunts. This is best discovered by the smoke of their fires. They are found in societies from 10 to 15 and 100, reckoning great and small together. Notwithstanding this, the farmers will venture in a dark night to set upon them with six or eight people, which they contrive to do by previously stationing themselves at some distance round about the kraal. They then give the alarm by firing a gun or two. By this means there is such a conflagration spread over the whole body of these savages, that it is only the most bold and intelligent among them that have the courage to break through the circle and steal off. These captors are glad enough to get rid of at so easy a rate; being better pleased with those that are stupid, timorous, and struck with amazement, and who consequently allow themselves to be taken and carried into bondage. They are however, at first treated by gentle methods; that is, the victors intermix the fairest promises with their threats, and endeavour, if possible, to throtl some of the larger kinds of game for their prisoners, such as buffaloes, sea-cows, and the like. Such agreeable baits, together with a little tobacco, soon induce them, continually cockered and feasted as they are, to go with a tolerable degree of cheerfulness to the colonist's place of abode. There this luxurious junketing upon meat and fat is exchanged for more moderate portions, consisting for the most part of butter-milk, frumenty, and hasty-pudding. This diet, nevertheless, makes the Boshies-man fat in a few weeks. However, he soon finds his good living embittered by the maudering and grumbling of his master and mistresses. The words t'guazeri and t'gaunath, which perhaps are best translated by those of "young sorcerer" and "imp," are expressions which he must frequently put up with, and sometimes a few curses and blows into the bargain; and this for neglect, remissness, or idleness: which last failure, if it cannot be said to be born with him, is however in a manner naturalized in him. So that, both by nature and custom detesting all manner of labour, and now from his greater corpulency becoming still more slothful, and having besides been used to a wandering life subject to no control, he most sensibly feels the want of his liberty. No wonder, then, that he generally endeavours to regain it by making his escape: but what is really a subject for wonder is, that when one of these poor devils runs away from his service, or more properly bondage, he never takes with him anything that does not belong to him. This is an instance of moderation in the savages towards their tyrants which is universally attested, and at the same time praised and admired by the colonists themselves; which, however, I cannot easily reconcile with what I have learned of the human heart." Is it in consequence of their fearing to meet with harder usage in case they should be retaken? This far, however, is certain, that none of this species of Hottentots are much given to violence or revenge. Free from many wants and desires that torment the rest of mankind, they are little, if at all, addicted to thieving, if we except brandy, victuals, and tobacco. It is not improbable likewise, that the advantages accruing from a theft may be overlooked by them, when their thoughts are taken up with regaining their liberty, the greatest of all treasures. It is necessary to observe here, that some of the Hottentots or Boshies-men, who are thus forced into the service of the colonists, live in small societies peaceably and quietly in desert tracts, where the colonists cannot easily come at them, and are sometimes in the possession of a few cows. These people probably originate from Boshies-men who have run away from the colonists service. "I must confess (continues our author), that the Boshies-men in some hutbandmen's service are treated in the gentlest manner, and perhaps even without ever having a harsh word given them; live very well with regard to provisions; are well clad, relatively to their condition in life; and are very comfortably lodged, in comparison of what others are, in their own straw cottages. The chief of their benefits perhaps consists in tending a herd of cattle or flock of sheep during the heat of the day, when they have an opportunity of getting into a gentle state of intoxication by smoking tobacco; a state which excites in them sensations of as agreeable a nature as the frenzy produced by spirituous liquors and opium seems to afford to many others, who are never at ease but when they can procure to themselves this delicious pleasure. And yet, though they may thus agreeably pass away the otherwise tedious hours of their lives in smoking and sleep, they nevertheless generally run away. The colonists wonder at this, as a procedure entirely devoid of reason; without perceiving, that in so doing they suppose the Hottentots not endowed with a desire, which has its immediate foundation in nature, and which is common to the human race, and even to most brute animals, viz. an earnest longing after their birthplace and families, and especially after their liberty. "The slave benefits, that violent outrage to the natural rights of mankind, always in itself a crime, and which leads to all manner of misdemeanors and wickedness, is exercised by the colonists in general with a cruelty towards the nation of Boshies-men which merits the abhorrence of every one; though I have been told that they pique themselves upon it; and not only is the capture of those Hottentots considered by them merely as a party of pleasure, but in cold blood they destroy the bands which nature has knit between husbands and their wives and children. Not content, for instance, with having torn an unhappy woman from the embraces of her husband, her only protection and comfort, they endeavour all they can, and that chiefly at night, to deprive her likewise of her infants; for it has been observed, that the mothers can seldom persuade themselves to flee from their tender offspring. The amiable tenderness of the mother, which perhaps glows with a more lively flame in the breast of this poor heathen than in those of her Christian tyrants, is the very circumstance laid hold on by their persecutors in order to rivet the chains of this wretched female so much the faster. There are some mothers, however, that let themselves free, when they have lost all hopes of saving their children. After having made their escape, they sometimes keep secretly about the neighbourhood, in hopes of finding some opportunity of recovering their infants again."

BOSNIA

Pages 65-65

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, seated between Slavonia and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>. It belongs entirely to the Turks; but they were on the point of being expelled from it by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, when the Spaniards invaded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and obliged the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> to conclude the peace of Passarowitz in 1718, by which he gave up Bosnia to the Turks. It is 200 miles in length, and 75 in breadth. It is a barren <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and but little cultivated: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> revenue arising chiefly from the silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> there are falcons, which are held in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem.

BOSNIA SERAGIO

Pages 65-65

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Bosnia. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 18° 57'. N. Lat. 44° 40'.

BOSPHORUS

Pages 65-65
or Bosporus, in Geography, a long and narrow sea, which it is supposed a bullock may swim over. In a more general sense, it is a long narrow sea running in between two lands, or separating two continents, and by which two seas, or a gulf and a sea, are made to communicate with each other: In which sense, bosporus amounts to the same with what we otherwise call an arm of the sea, channel, or strait; the Italians, faro; the Latins, fretum; and the French, pas, manche. The word is Greek, βοσπόρος, formed from βοσκειν, "bullock," and πέρας, "passage." The name bosporus, is chiefly confined to two straits in the Mediterranean sea, viz. the bosporus of Thrace, commonly called the straits of Constantinople, or channel of the "xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black sea; and the Cimmerian or Scythian bosporus, so called, it seems, from its resemblance to the Thracian; now more commonly the straits of Kapha, or Kieferler, from two cities standing on it. The origin of the name is better agreed on than the reason why it was first given to the Thracian bosporus. Nymphius tells us, on the authority of Accarion, that the Phrygians, desiring to pass the Thracian strait, built a vessel, on whose prow was the figure of a bullock; and which was hence called βοσκειν, "bullock;" and served them for a ferry-boat. Dionysius, Vallerius Flaccus, Callimachus, Apollodorus, Martial, &c., say, that it, being transformed into a cow by Juno, passed this strait swimming, which hence was called bosporus. Arrian tells us, that the Phrygians were enjoined by the oracle, to follow the rout which a bullock should mark out to them; and that, upon stirring one up, it jumped into the sea to avoid their pursuit, and swam over this strait. Others say, that an ox, tormented by a gad-fly, threw itself in, and swam over; and others, that anciently the inhabitants of these coasts, when they would pass over, joined little boats together, and had them drawn over by bullocks, &c.

BOSQUETS

Pages 65-65

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, groves so called from boquete, an Italian word which signifies a little wood. They are compartments in gardens formed by branches of trees disposed either regularly in rows, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wildly and irregularly, according to the fancy of the owner. A boquet is either a plot of ground enclosed with palisadoes of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a>-beam, the middle of it being filled with tall trees, as elm or the like, the tops of which make a tuft or plume; or it consists of only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> trees, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-chestnut, elm, &c. The ground should be kept very smooth and rolled, or else covered with grass, after the manner of green plots. In <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> boquets, care should be taken to mix the trees which produce their leaves of different shapes, and various shades of green, and hoary or mealy leaves, so as to afford an agreeable prospect. Boquets are only proper for spacious gardens, and require a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> expense to keep them up.

BOSSAGE

Pages 65-65

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used for any <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> that has a projection, and is laid rough in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, to be afterwards carved into <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDINGS">mouldings</a>, capitals, coats of arms, &c. Bossage is also that which is otherwise called rustic-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; and consists of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> which advance beyond the naked <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the building, by reason of indentures or channels left in the joinings. These are chiefly used in the corners of edifices, and thence called rustic quoins. The cavities or indentures are sometimes round, sometimes chain-framed, or bevelled, sometimes in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> form, sometimes enclosed with a cavetto, and sometimes with a listel.

BOSSINEY

Pages 65-65
or BOSS CASTLE, a town of Cornwall, in England, which sends two members to parliament. W. Long. 5° 0'. N. Lat. 50° 40'.

BOSSU

Pages 65-65

RENE LE, born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1631, was admitted a canon regular in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of St Genevieve, in 1649; and after a year's probation, took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>. He taught polite literature with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success in several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses for 12 years, when he gave up the talk for retirement. He then published a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> between the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and those of Des Cartes, with a view to reconcile them; which was but indifferently received. His next treatise was on epic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, which Boileau declared one of the best compositions on that subject in the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and which produced a great friendship between them. He died in 1680, and left a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of MSS. which are kept in the abbey of St John de Chartres.

BOSSUET

Pages 65-65

JAMES BENIGNE, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a>, was born at Dijon, on the 27th of September, 1627. He distinguished himself by his preaching, and the zeal he discovered in his endeavours to bring over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> of France to the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; by his opposition to quietism; and by his numerous writings both in French and Latin, which have been collected together, and printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 17 vols 4to. This famous divine died at Paris, in 1704, aged 77.

BOSSUPT

a town of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Brabant. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 30'. N. Lat. 50° 52'.

BOSSUS

Pages 65-65

MATTHEW, distinguished by his virtue and his learning, was born in 1427. He devoted himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> state in 1451, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of regular canons of Lateran, and afterwards taught <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>. His orations, his sermons, and his letters, have been often printed. He also wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of an apology for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHALARIS">Phalaris</a>, and other works. He died at Padua in 1502, aged 75.

BOSTANGIS

Pages 65-66

in the Turkish affairs, persons employed in the garden of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERAGLIO">seraglio</a>, out of whose <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> are collected those that are to row in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Signior's brigantines, when he has a mind to divert himself with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> upon the canal. They who row on the left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> are only capable of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> employments in the gardens; but they who row on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hand may be promoted to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of boftangi-bachi, who has the general intendency of all the grand signior's gardens, and commands above 10,000 boftangis.

BOSTON

Pages 66-66

a corporation town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a> in England, which sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It is commodiously seated on both sides the river Witham, over which it has a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>; and, being near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, enjoys a good trade. It has a spacious market-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and the largest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> without crosis aisles in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, the fleepole of which serves for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>-mark to sailors. Bofton is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARONY">barony</a> in the Irby family. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 15. N. Lat. 53. 3. Boston, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of New England in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, built in 1630, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of about four miles in circumference, at the bottom of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASSACHUSETTS">Massachusetts</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, in a very convenient situation for trade. The following is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of this capital before the commencement of the late American <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. "The town stands in W. Long. 71. 5. N. Lat. 42. 24. about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> miles from the mouth of the bay. At the entrance of this bay are several small rocks which appear above <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and upwards of a dozen of small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, some of which are inhabited. There is but one safe channel to approach the harbour; and that so narrow, that two ships can hardly sail through abreast; but within the harbour there is room for 500 sail to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> in a good depth of water. On one of the islands of the bay stands Fort William, the most regular fortress in British America. This castle is defended by 100 guns, 20 of which lie on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the water, so that it is scarce possible for an enemy to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the castle. To prevent surprise, they have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> placed on one of the rocks, at two leagues distance, from whence they make signals to the castle when any ships come near it. Boftonworth. There is also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> of guns at each end of the town. At the bottom of the bay is a noble pier near 2000 feet in length; along which on the north side extends a row of warehouses for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>; and to this pier ships of the greatest burden may come and unload without the help of boats. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the town lies round the harbour in the form of a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> beyond it rising gradually and affording a delightful prospect. The neck of land which joins the peninsula to the continent is but 40 yards over; which situation, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> properly improved, might render the town impregnable on the land side. Bofton contains only about 18,000 inhabitants. They were more numerous 50 years ago; but the surprising increase of Newburyport, Salem, Marblehead, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Ann, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARTMOUTH">Dartmouth</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Nantucket, checked the growth and trade of the capital. The trade of Bofton, however, was so considerable, that, in 1768, 1300 sail entered and cleared at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> there. The predominant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> is the Independent; though there are other persuasions, and ten churches serve for them all, but the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDEPENDENTS">Independents</a> have six." Bofton has frequently suffered by fire, but the houses that were thus destroyed have always been rebuilt to advantage. The late American war began here by the attack at Bunker's-hill, when many brave men lost their lives."

BOSWORTH

Pages 66-66

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a> in England, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 24. N. Lat. 52. 25. It has a lofty situation on a hill, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> about it is fertile in corn and grass. It is memorable for the decisive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought near it between Richard III. and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a>, afterwards Henry VII., wherein the former lost his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>.

BOTALLUS

Pages 66-68

LEONARD, physician to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Alençon, and to Henry III., was born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTI">Asti</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>. He introduced at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> the practice of frequent letting of blood; which was condemned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>; but soon after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> it came into practice with all the physicians. He published several books in physic and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>; and the best edition of his works is that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 1660, octavo. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> Is that science which arranges, distinguishes, and names all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vegetables, to enable us to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> their properties and uses. Vegetables consist of an innumerable succession of individuals which it is impossible to examine, and would be useless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it were possible. It is therefore necessary to diminish the labour by forming them into groups or classes, that the same name may apply to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of individuals. Now certain individual plants have so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> a resemblance to others in their flower, fruit, leaves, and general appearance, that almost every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> at first sight would give them the same name. Thus every man who has seen the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> daisy once, and knows its name, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> probably apply the same name without mistake to every other individual of the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. This forms the first step in botany, or what is called arranging and naming plants according to their species. Nor is it only the first, but the easiest step in botany. It is also the most important; for all the individuals of the same species must in similar circumstances possess the same qualities. For example, we have no reason to doubt that each individual plant of common <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HEMLOCK">hemlock</a>, or of foxglove, possesses the same medical qualities, though from their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of growth these qualities may differ in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. It is therefore the individuals of the species alone that are useful; and the whole value of any arrangement consists in enabling the botanist to distinguish and name the individuals, with the greatest ease and accuracy. If the number of species were small, definitions, or descriptions Elements. scriptions of them would alone be sufficient; but as they amount perhaps to 40,000 or 50,000 or more, to search for every single species amid such a multitude would be a task for which neither <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> nor human <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> would be sufficient. To shorten the labour, it has been found very expedient to arrange plants into various divisions; first into some very general divisions which may reduce them into a small compass, then to subdivide these general divisions into others less comprehensive, and these into others, till we arrive at the particular species which we are in search of. Thus the arrangement descends from a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of all plants to every particular species. Many plans of this kind have been attempted by various botanists, but the arrangement of the celebrated Linnæus is incomparably the most ingenious, most accurate, as well as the simplest and easiest. That illustrious botanist divided all plants into classes, the classes into orders, the orders into genera, and the genera into species. The orders too, and the species, when numerous, he frequently subdivided into sections. Objections have been made to the arrangement of Linnæus, because it admits divisions which do not appear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>. But such persons, though distinguished botanists, seem to us to have misunderstood the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and intention of that arrangement. It is not, and ought not to be, its object to give what has been called a natural arrangement; for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> does not classify her productions. She places before us innumerable individuals, and leaves us to classify them according to the purpose which we have in view. If nature had formed plants into classes, orders, and genera, the botanist would have nothing to do but to study these. But in none of her works has nature done this. Classification is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of man; and it is necessary for man merely on account of the limited nature of the faculties of his mind. Classification enables us to accomplish by several steps or operations what we cannot accomplish by one. But were our faculties much more exalted, were our penetration much more acute, and our memories perfectly retentive; could we at once survey all the qualities of objects, discern their relations to one another, and retain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of these accurately, we should have no occasion to generalize at all. As generalization or classification is necessary to aid our limited faculties, the best classification is that which leads us without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, and by the easiest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, to the particular object which we have occasion to investigate. The arrangement of Linnæus is therefore the best: It is, however, not so perfect in some of its parts as it may yet be rendered. This is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in some of the genera which are distinguished by marks that are too minute. But when we consider the indefatigable mind of that illustrious man, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a> in which he found botany, and the beautiful arrangement which he gave to it, we may justly enroll the name of Linnæus in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, and Newton, and Locke. A botanical system is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a> by which a person who has studied the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of the science may find out the name of every plant which he meets with. This dictionary has been much enlarged by the labours of the great many eminent botanists of the present <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. We shall therefore point out the method of consulting it, after giving a very concise view of the principles upon which it is founded. We will give a concise view, because we think most or perhaps all the elementary books of this science tend to confound and disgust beginners by physiological definitions, and by the multiplicity of terms which they require to be studied at the very first outset. Their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> as if a teacher of Latin was to require his pupils first to make themselves masters of a Latin dictionary before he allowed them to translate. Our plan is to require of a beginner no more elementary knowledge than what is sufficient to enable him to consult the system as he would do a dictionary. The meaning of the rest of the botanical terms we think can best be learned by having recourse to an explanation in an alphabetical form, as they occur in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>. This we intend to add to the present article. And we wish sincerely that every man who publishes a system of botany would do the same; for we have strong reasons to believe that different writers use the same words in different senses from one another. Linnæus, indeed, has defined his botanical terms; but in his two works, *Deliciæ Plantarum* and *Philosophia Botanica*, he sometimes defines the same word differently. Now we ought to know which of his definitions succeeding botanists have adopted. Besides almost every botanist introduces terms of his own which we shall look for in vain in the definitions of Linnæus. **ELEMENTS OF BOTANY.** The parts of a plant which it is necessary for the young botanist first to know, are the flower, and fruit. These include <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>; the calyx, corolla, stamen, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISTIL">pistil</a>, pericarp or seed-vessel, seed and receptacle. We will describe these in the order which will make them most easily distinguished. 1. The corolla, which in common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is called the flower, and in fruit-trees the blossom, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> which is most beautifully coloured, which is of the finest texture, and is often odorous. It is to be found of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, except green, a hue which it very seldom attains. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, as in the blossoms of the cherry, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> as in the primrose and ranunculus or buttercup, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> as in the rose, blue as in the violet. It is sometimes of one piece, and sometimes divided into distinct pieces, called petals. When the corolla consists of one petal, the outer or upper part which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> is named the limb or border; and the lower part which is narrow and hollow, by which it is fixed, is called the tube. When the corolla consists of more than one petal, the lower part is called a claw, and the upper lamina. In the corolla it is necessary to attend to its form, its divisions, the number of its petals, its colour and the part to which it is attached. See Plate XCV. Fig. 11. a corolla of one petal: a, the tube; b, the laminae. Fig. 13. a corolla of more than one petal: a, the claw; b, the laminae. 2. The calyx is situated on the outside of the corolla, and enclosing it <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> at the base. It is generally Generally of a greenish colour and of a coarser texture than the corolla. It consists of one part, or of two, three, &c., and is then said to be one-leaved, two-leaved, three-leaved, many-leaved. The calyx is of various shapes, tubular, globular, inflated, &c. There are seven species of calyx, perianth, involucre, glume, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTHER">anther</a>, (pathe, calyptra, and volva. For explanation of these consult the vocabulary and Plate XCV. Fig. 18, a, the calyx. 3. The pistil, or pistils, commonly appear in the centre of the corolla, from which they rise like so many columns. There are from one to twelve in the same flower, and sometimes more. A pistil consists of three parts, the stigma, the style, and the germen. 1. The stigma is the highest part of the pistil; which is sometimes globular, sometimes cleft, sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-shaped, &c. 2. The style is the pillar or thread which supports the stigma. 3. The germen is the pedicel or base of the pistil, most commonly of a roundish or globular shape; but sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and slender. Sometimes there are several germens together. See Plate XCV. fig. 12, c, the stigma; b, the style; a, the germen. 4. The filaments, which resemble threads or pillars, usually stand between the corolla and the pistil, are placed in regular order round the pistils, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> with the petals. They are in number on one flower from one to several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>. But it is not necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> them when they are more than twenty. A filament consists of two parts, the anther and the filament. 1. The anther is the summit of the filament, containing a mealy or powdery substance called pollen, and is generally of a different colour from the filament. They are of different forms, globular, horned, &c. 2. The filaments are the threads or pillars which support the anthers. The filaments are attached to the corolla, to the calyx, to the receptacle, or to the style. See Plate XCV. fig. 18. Filaments marked by e, e, e, e, e, e. 5. The pericarp, or seed-vessel, is the case or covering of the seed, and is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> part of the germen come to maturity. It is of various shapes; globular, as in the poppy; long, as in the pod of the common garden or field <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>: it is pulpy with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> in the middle, as in the plum; pulpy, containing seeds enclosed in a case, as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>; juicy, and containing seeds which have only an external case, as the currant and gooseberry. There are eight species of pericarp; <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPSULE">capsule</a>, silique, legume, follicle, drupe, pome, berry, and strobile. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of these will be given in the vocabulary. Consult also Plate XCV. fig. 23. to 30. 6. The seeds are so well known, that they require no description in the elements of the science. 7. The receptacle is a point, line, or broad base, to which some or all of the six parts now described are attached. When it is the base of all these parts, it is called the receptacle of the fructification. When the calyx, corolla, and stamens only are attached to it, it is called the receptacle of the flower. When the germens together with the pistil only is fixed to it, it is called the receptacle of the fruit. It is called proper when only one flower with its fruit is inserted into it. It is called common when many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are attached to it, as in the common daisies, dandelion. See Plate XCV. Elements: Fig. 13, c, a proper receptacle. Fig. 9, 10, a common receptacle. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">Attention</a> to the receptacle is most necessary chiefly in classes 11th, 13th, and 19th. Besides these seven, which are called the parts of fructification, because when they exist together, they are supposed necessary for producing proper fruit, there is another part which Linnaeus calls the nectary, that requires attention, as it is the foundation of some genera. It is difficult for beginners to distinguish it, as it varies much in its appearance, and is not very discernible in a great many species. It is sometimes the name of a small gland; sometimes of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> or a number of scales; sometimes of a cup; sometimes of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a> or spur on the corolla, as in larkspur and violet; sometimes of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a> or excavation. In short, it appears to be a name for any singular or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> appearance of any of the parts of the flower. In all accurate and perspicuous systems, it is so well described that it can be easily found out. If this be done the name may be admitted, but if not it must <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to ambiguity and want of precision.

BOTT'S

Pages 408-409

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>**, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> which can be produced and nourished only in the intestines of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. It is there alone they can enjoy the proper temperature of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and receive the nourishment necessary for them. See *Oestrus, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>*. Besides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> worms which have been observed in the bodies of horses, there are also short ones.—By these are to be understood what we call *botts*. All authors, both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, who have treated of the diseases of horses, have taken notice of these worms; but M. Vallifnieri is the first who has traced them to the last stage of their transformation, and has seen them change into a hairy kind of fly like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRONE">drone</a>. The flies from which these botts are produced inhabit the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and do not come near houses, at least not near those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>; and therefore horses are never liable to have the worms (*i.e.*, botts) in their bodies, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they have been kept in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, especially in a town, during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> and autumn. It is in the former of these seasons, and perhaps too in the beginning of the latter, that the females of these flies apply themselves to the anus of horses, and endeavour to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> admittance, in order there to deposit their eggs, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> perhaps their worms. The precise instant of their entrance <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> scarce admit of an eye-witness, but by the merest chance; yet M. Vallifnieri says, that Dr Gaspari had attained this very uncommon sight. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> (he tells us) was one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> looking at his mares in the field; and from being very quiet, he observed, that on a sudden they became very restless, and ran about in great agitation, prancing, plunging, and kicking, with violent motions of their tails. He concluded, that these extraordinary effects were produced by some fly buzzing about them, and endeavouring to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> upon the anus of one of them; but the fly not being able to succeed, he observed it to go off with less noise than before, towards a mare that was feeding at a distance from the rest; and now the fly taking a more effectual method to obtain its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, passed under the tail of the mare, and so made its way to the anus. Here at first it occasioned only an itching, by which the intestine was protruded with an increasing aperture of the anus; the fly taking the advantage of this, penetrated further, and secured itself in the fold of the intestine:—this effected, it was in a situation proper for laying its eggs. Soon after this, the mare became very violent, running about, prancing, and kicking, and throwing herself on the ground; in short, was not quiet, nor returned to feeding, till after a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. The fly then, we see, can find means of depositing its eggs, or perhaps its worm (*i.e.*, botts), in the fundament of the horse; which once effected, it has done all that is necessary for them. If these bott-worms are not hatched when first deposited in the horse, but are then only eggs, it will not be long before it happens, from the nutritive heat they there receive. These bott-worms soon make their way into the intestines of the horse: they occupy such parts of this region as are to them most convenient; and sometimes (as we shall see presently) they penetrate even to the stomach. All the hazard they appear to be exposed to, is that of being carried away from the places they have fixed on by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCREMENT">excrement</a>, which may seem likely to drive all before it. But <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> has provided for all things; and when we shall have further described these bott-worms, it will seem that they are able to maintain their situation, and to remain in the body of the horse, as long as they please. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when these bott-worms are of themselves disinclined to leave this their habitation, it being no longer convenient for them after the purposes of their growth are answered. Their transformation to a fly must be performed out of the horse's body: and accordingly, when the time of their transformation draws near, they approach towards the anus of the horse; and then leave him of their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a>, or with the excrement, with which they then suffer themselves to be carried along. According to M. de Reaumur's observations, the bott-worms have two unequal claws, by which they are enabled to remain in the intestines of the horse in opposition to all efforts of the excrement to force them out.—These claws are a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, differently disposed from those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> anchors, but contrived to produce the same effect. Besides these two claws, nature has given them a very great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of triangular spines or bristles, very sufficient to arm them against the coats of the intestines, and to resist the force employed to drive them towards the anus, provided the head be directed towards the stomach of the horse. It will be asked, no doubt, if these bott-worms are not not dangerous to horses?—The mares which afforded M. de Reaumur, for several years, those on which he made his observations, did not appear to be less in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> than those which had none; but it may sometimes happen, that they are in so great a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> in the body of the horse as to prove fatal to him. M. Vallifshieri supposes these bot-worms to have been the cause of an epidemical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> that destroyed a great many horses about <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a> in the year 1713. The observations communicated to him by Dr Gaffari sufficiently confirm his supposition. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, upon dissecting some horses that died of this distemper, found in their stomachs a surprising quantity of short worms; of which to give us some idea, he compares them to the kernels of a pomegranate opened: each of these, by gnawing on the coat of the stomach, had made itself a kind of cellule therein, each of which would easily contain a grain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> wheat. It is easy to imagine by this means the stomach must be reduced to a wretched condition; the outer membranes were inflamed, and the inner ones ulcerated and corrupted; a very small quantity of these worms were found in the small intestines, and only a few in the larger, to which last they were found affixed, but had not corroded them. It is only perhaps when these bot-worms are in great numbers, and thereby incommoding each other in the intestines of the horse, that they make their way towards the stomach; and indeed a very few flies must be enough to overflow the inside of a horse, provided they should deposit all their eggs, and such should all be animated, M. Vallifshieri having counted 700 and odd in the body of one single fly. When one of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOTS">bots</a> has left the anus of the horse, it falls on the ground; and immediately seeks out for some <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of safety, where it may retire, to prepare for the last stage of its transformation, by which it is to become a fly. And now by degrees the skin hardens and thickens; and at length forms a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> shell or cocoon, the form of which scarcely differs from that of the worm. It is first of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, which changes into chestnut; and at length, by the addition of gradual and successive shades of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, the shell is rendered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. The worm or bot, before it passes into a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a>, is of the form of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>; it remains in this form much longer than worms of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-fly kind. M. de Reaumur met with worms that retained this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> five or six days: as yet, one can perceive no traces of the legs, wings, and head of the nymph. Hence he first learned, that those bot-worms do not become nymphs immediately upon their first change; but that, in order to become flies, they must undergo one change more than caterpillars ordinarily do to become butterflies.—For the cure of horses troubled with bots, see Farriery Index.

BOTTLE

Pages 407-407

a small vessel proper to contain liquors, made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, glass, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. The word is formed from butellus, or botellus, used in barbarous Latin writers, for a lesser vessel of wine; being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of bota, which denoted a butt or cask of that liquor. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Jewish bottles were casks made of goats or other wild beasts' skins, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> on the inside, well sewed and pitched together; an aperture in one of the animal's paws serving for the mouth of the vessel. Glass-bottles are better for cider than those of stone. Foul glass-bottles are cured by rolling sand or small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> in them; muffle bottles, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> them. See Glass. Bottles are chiefly made of thick coarse glass; though there are likewise bottles of boiled leather made and sold by the cask-makers. Fine glass-bottles covered with straw or wicker, are called flasks, or betters. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the glass has been sometimes found to affect the liquor in the bottle. Dr Percival cautions against the practice of cleaning of wine bottles with leaden shot. It frequently happens (he thinks), through inattention, that some of the little pellets are left behind; and when wine or beer is again poured into the bottles, this mineral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> slowly dissolve, and impregnate those vinous liquors with its deleterious qualities. The sweetness which is sometimes perceived in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> port wine may arise from this cause, when such an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADULTERATION">adulteration</a> is neither designed nor suspected.—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTASH">Potash</a> is recommended for cleansing bottles: a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> will clean two groats.

BOTTLING

Pages 407-407

the operation of putting up liquors in bottles corked, to keep, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a>, and improve. The writers on good husbandry give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> rules concerning the bottling of beer, cider, and the like. The virtues of Spaw, Pyrmount, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCARBOROUGH">Scarborough</a>, and other waters, depend on their being well bottled and corked, otherwise they lose both their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and smell. To preserve them, it is necessary the bottles be filled up to the mouth, that all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> may be excluded, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> enemy of bottled liquors. The cork is also further secured by a cement. Some improve their bottled beer, by putting crystals of tartar, and wine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> malt spirits, and others, by putting <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> boiled up with the essence of some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a>, and cloves, into each bottle. Cyder requires special precautions in the bottling; being more apt to fly, and burst the bottle, than other liquors. The best way to secure them, is to have the liquor thoroughly fine before it be bottled. For want of this, some leave the bottles open a while, or open them after two or three days bottling to give them vent. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> one bottle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a>, through <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, it is best to give them all vent, and cork them up again. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">Mean</a> cyder is apter to break the bottles than rich. Some soak the corks in scalding <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, to render them more pliant and serviceable. Another particular to be observed is, to lay the bottles so as that the liquor may always keep the cork wet and swelled. Something also depends on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the bottles are set, which ought to be such as exposes them as little as possible to the alterations and impressions of the air: the ground is better for this purpose than a frame; sand better than the bare ground; and a running water, or a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> often changed, best of all. To hasten the ripening of bottled liquors, they are sometimes set in a warm place, or even exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, when a few days <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> bring them to maturity.

BOTTOM

Pages 407-407

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>, is used to denote as well the channel of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and harbours, as the body <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HULL">hull</a> of a ship. Thus, in the former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, we say, a gravelly bottom, clayey bottom, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> bottom, &c. and in the latter sense, a British bottom, a Dutch bottom, &c. By statute, certain commodities imported in foreign bottoms pay a duty called petty customs, over and above what they are liable to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> imported in British bottoms.

BOTTOMRY

Pages 407-408

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, (a practice which originally arose from permitting the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of a ship in a foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to hypothecate the ship in order to raise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to refit), is in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a mortgage of a ship; when the owner takes up money to enable him to carry on his voyage, and pledges the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEEL">keel</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bottom of the ship (pars pro toto) as a security for the repayment. In which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it is understood, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the ship be lost, the lender loses also his whole money; but if it return in safety, then he shall receive back his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>, and also the premium or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> agreed upon, however it may exceed the legal rate of interest. And this is allowed to be a valid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> in all trading nations, for the benefit of commerce, and by reason of the extraordinary hazard run by the lender. And in this case, the ship and tackle, if brought home, are answerable (as well as the person of the borrower) for the money <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a>. But if the loan is not upon the vessel, but upon the goods and merchandise, which must necessarily be sold or exchanged in the course of the voyage, then only the borrower, personally, is bound to answer the contract; who therefore, in this case, is said to take up the money at respondentia. These terms are also applied to contracts for the repayment of money borrowed, not on the ship and goods only, but on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> hazard of the voyage itself; when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> lends a merchant 100l. to be employed in a beneficial trade, with condition to be repaid with extraordinary interest, in case such a voyage be safely performed; which kind of agreement, is sometimes called fennius nauticum, and sometimes njura maritima. But as this gave an opening for furious and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a> contracts, especially upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> voyages, it was enacted by the statute 19 Geo. II. c. 37; that all monies lent on bottomry, or at respondentia, on vessels bound to or from the East Indies, shall be expressly lent only upon the ship, or upon the merchandise; that the lender shall have the benefit of salvage; and that if the borrower has not on board effects to the value of the sum borrowed, he shall be responsible to the lender for so much of the principal as hath not been laid out, with legal interest and all other charges, though the ship and merchandise be totally lost. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOTTOMY">BOTTOMY</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> bottomy, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, terminates... Bottrigaro, nates at each end in three buds, knots, or buttons, resembling, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, the three-leaved gras; on which account Segoing, in his *Tresor Héraldique*, terms it *croix treffle*. It is the badge of the order of St Maurice. See *Heraldry Plates*.

BOTTRIGARO

Pages 408-408

Hercule**, a person eminently skilled in the science of music, though not a musician by profession. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>; and appears, from several letters to him that have been printed, to have had the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a>. He published several controversial pieces on the subject of music. It seems that he entertained strong prejudices in favour of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> music; and that he attempted, as Vincentine and others had done, to introduce the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHROMATIC">chromatic</a> genius into practice, but with no better success than had attended the endeavours of others. He corrected Gogavino's Latin version of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> in numberless instances; and that to so good a purpose, that Dr Wallis has in general conformed to it in that translation of the same author which he gave to the world many years after. He also translated into Italian *Boetius de Musica*, and as much of Plutarch and Macrobius as relates to music: besides this, he made annotations upon Aristozenus, Franchinus, Spataro, Vicentino, Zarlinio, and Galilei; and, in short, on almost every musical treatise he could lay his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> on, as appears by the copies which were once his own, and are now repotted in many <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Of Bottrigaro's works it is said, that they contain greater proofs of his learning and skill in music, than of his abilities as a writer, his style being remarkably inelegant: nevertheless, he affected the character of a poet; and there is extant a collection of poems by him, in 8vo, printed in 1557. Walther represents him as an able mathematician, and a collector of rarities; and says that he was possessed of a cabinet, which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Ferdinand II. had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> desire to purchase. He died in 1609.

BOTWAR

Pages 409-409

a town of Germany, in the circle of Swabia, and subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Württemberg. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 15. N. Lat. 49. 0.

BOTZENBURG

Pages 409-409
