a town of Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Mecklenburg. It had a castle, which was destroyed by the Danes in 1202. It is seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, and the vessels that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> by are obliged to pay a considerable toll. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. 48. N. Lat. 53. 34.

BOUCHAIN

Pages 409-409

a fortified town of the French No. Bouchaintherlands, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Hainault. It is divided into two parts by the river Scheld. It was taken by the French in 1676; and by the allies under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a> in 1711, which was the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> achievement of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> general; but the following year it was retaken by the French. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 15. N. Lat. 50. 17. BOUCHE <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, the privilege of having meat and drink at court foot-free. The word is also written bouge, bouge, and budge; it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> French, where it signifies mouth.—The French still <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the phrase, Avoir bouche à la cour; that is, to have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> or diet at court. This privilege is sometimes only extended to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, beer, and wine; it was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> anciently in use, as well in the houses of noblemen as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s court. Thomas <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a> retained Sir John de Ewre, to serve him with ten men at arms in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, allowing them bouge of court, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a> of hay and oats, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-hoes and nails. Sir Hugh Merrill had the same privilege for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, on condition of serving King Edward II.

BOUCHET

Pages 409-409

JOHN, a French poet and historian, flourished in the 16th century. The most considerable of his writings are the Annals of Aquitaine, and his Chapelet des Princes.

BOUDRY

Pages 409-409

a small town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Neuchâtel, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a chatelainry of the same name. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 5. N. Lat. 47. 11.

BOUFLERS

Pages 409-410
LEWIS FRANCIS, DUKE OF, a peer and marshal of France, and a general of distinguished reputation, was the son of Francis count of Boufflers. He was born in the year 1644, and entering early into the army, was raised in 1669 to the rank of colonel of dragoons, and in the conquest of Lorraine, served under Marshal Crequi. In the war against Holland he served under the celebrated Turenne, and frequently distinguished himself for his skill and bravery; and when that general was killed, in 1675, he commanded the rear-ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard during the retreat of the French army. After performing various military services in Germany, in Flanders, and on the frontiers of Spain, he gradually rose in rank as well as in reputation. In 1690, he was created general of the army of the Moselle. In the following year, he acted as lieutenant-general, under the king in person; and while he invested Mons was wounded in an attack on that place. He conducted the bombardment of Liège, although it was defended by a superior enemy, and he forced the allied generals to abandon Luxemburg. He was entrusted with the command of the covering army, against King William, at the siege of Namur; and for this and many other important services, he was raised in 1693 to the high rank of marshal of France. In 1694, he was appointed governor of French Flanders, and of the town of Lille. By a skilful manoeuvre he threw himself into Namur, in 1695, and held out for sixty-three days, against the combined armies of the allies under King William. Having agreed to a capitulation, he was arrested prisoner of war. war, because the French had not performed the stipulated terms on which the garrison had surrendered; and when he remonstrated that the garrison should have been retained rather than himself, he received a fine compliment, by being answered, that he was estimated at 10,000 men. In the conferences which were held with the earl of Portland, and which terminated in the peace of Rylwick, he had a principal share. During the following war, when Lille was again threatened, in 1708, with a siege by the duke of Marlborough and Prince Eugene, Boufflers was appointed to the command, and made a very obstinate resistance of four months. His magnanimity was not less remarkable than his military conduct; for when a partisan represented to him that it would not be difficult to kill Prince Eugene, he was told by the marshal, that he might expect a great reward for taking him prisoner, but the severest punishment if anything were attempted against his life. He was rewarded and honoured by the king for his defence of Lille, as if he had been victorious. When the affairs of France were threatened with the most urgent danger, though a senior officer to Villars, he made an offer to serve under that general, and was with him at the battle of Malplaquet. Here he again displayed his military skill, by conducting the retreat, so that he lost neither cannon nor prisoners. He died at Fontainbleau in the year 1711, at the age of 68, and left the character of a true patriot, as well as of a great commander. Madame de Maintenon, said of him, "that his heart was the last part that died." His conduct was uninfluenced by private interest, and superior to court intrigue. When he was ordered to take upon him the defence of Lille, and permitted to have the choice of his lieutenants, he waited not to arrange or regulate his private affairs, or even to take leave of his family, but flew to the place, and carried with him only two officers, one taken from the Bataille, and another who had been in disgrace; preferring merit obscured in the shades of retirement, to the gaudy flutterer in the sunshine of court favour.

BOUGENT

Pages 410-410

WILLIAM HYACINTH, a famous Jesuit, first taught <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAEN">Caen</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEVERS">Nevers</a>, and afterwards settled at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, where he employed himself in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> several works; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which were, 1. A collection of physical observations, extracted from the best authors. 2. A <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the wars and negotiations which preceded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Westphalia. 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>, a philosophical amusement on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of beasts, &c. He died in 1743.

BOUGET

Pages 419-419

Dom John, an ingenious French antiquary, was born at the village of Beaumains near Falaise, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Seze, in 1724. He was educated at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>-school at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAEN">Caen</a>, whence he was removed to that university, and pursued his studies with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> diligence and success till 1745, when he became a Benedictine monk of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of St Martin de Seze. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after this, he was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> claustral of the said abbey, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> five years in that office, when he was nominated prior of Tiron en Perche: whence being translated to the abbey of St Stephen at Caen, in the capacity of sub-prior, he managed the temporalities of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> during two years, as he did their spiritualities for one year longer; after which, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the house, he resigned his office. His superiors, sensible of his merit and learning, removed him thence to the abbey of Bec, where he resided till 1764. He was elected an honorary member of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of Antiquaries of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, Jan. 10, 1765; in which year he returned to the abbey of St Stephen at Caen, where he continued to the time of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> offices, to which he was promoted on account of his great abilities, enabled him not only to pursue his favourite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and antiquities of some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> Benedictine abbeys in Normandy, but likewise gave him access to all their charters, deeds, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>-books, &c., &c. These he examined with great care, and left behind him in MS. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and accurate accounts of the abbeys of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> de Jumiges, St Stephen, and the Holy Trinity at Caen (founded by William the Conqueror and his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> Matilda), and a very particular history of the abbey of Bec. These were all written in French. The "History of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Abbey of Bec" (which he presented to Dr Ducarel in 1764) is only an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of his larger <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> abbey (which hath produced several archbishops of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> and other illustrious prelates of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>) is frequently mentioned by our old historians. The death of our worthy Benedictine (which happened on New Year's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> 1776) was occasioned by his unfortunate neglect of a hurt he got in his leg by falling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three steps in going from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> to the cloister of the abbey of St Stephen at Caen, being deceived by the ambiguous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of a glimmering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> that was placed in the passage. He lived universally esteemed, and died sincerely regretted by all those who were acquainted with him; and was buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the said abbey, Jan. 3, 1776.

BOUGH

Pages 410-410

denotes much the same with branch.—Green boughs anciently made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a> of altars and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, especially on festival occasions. Oaken boughs were offered to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>; those of laurel, to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>; of olive, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>; myrtle, to Venus; ivy, to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>; pine, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">Pan</a>; and cypresses to Pluto. Some make them the primitive food of mankind before acorns were invented.

BOUGIE

Pages 410-410

in the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, signifies a wax <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>, and is applied to a machine which (as the wax candle formerly was) is introduced into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-URETHRA">urethra</a> for removing obstructions there. Monf. Daran, a French surgeon, lately boasted of his introducing them as an improvement in his art, and acquired considerable profit by making and selling them. Scultetus, about Bouhours, the middle of the 17th century, used bougies in dicales of the urethra, and Monf. Daran, probably took the hint from him. Different compositions have been used, and generally <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of them. Riverius made a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> as follows: R. ol. oliv. &c. iv. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">ceres</a> citrin. ib. ii. minii & ceruss. &c. Ib. is tereb. venet. & rez. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALB">alb</a>. &c. iii m. Whether the bougies are made up of this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, they must be of different sizes, from the bigness of a knitting <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> to that of a goose quill. They are made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> rags, spread with a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, and then rolled up as follows. Having spread any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the linen rag with the composition that is chosen for the purpose, cut it into slips from six to ten inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and from half an inch to an inch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>: then dexterously roll them on a glazed tile into the form of a wax candle: and as the end of the bougie that is to be entered first into the urethra should be somewhat smaller than the rest, it would be as well to cut the slips a little tapering. It should also be observed, that when the bougies are rolled up, that side must be outward on which the plaster is spread. Monf. Daran, and some others, attributed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of their bougies to the composition they made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in forming them. Mr Sharp apprehended, that as much of their efficacy was owing to the composition they made on the affected part, as to any other principle; and Mr Aiken very justly says, As it is evident that bougies of very different compositions succeed equally well in curing the same disorders in the urethra, it is plain that they do not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> by means of any peculiar qualities in their composition, but by means of some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to them all. This must be their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> form and texture, therefore their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of action must be simple compression. The efficacy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> compression in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of constriction is well known, from the use of sponge tents for widening parts that are straitened by cicatrices; and admitting obstructions in the urethra to be from a constriction formed by cicatrized ulcers, or a projection of the spongy substance of the urethra into the canal, we may easily conceive, that a gentle <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> compression <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> overcome the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. We may also readily account for the inferior efficacy of metallic and whalebone bougies, from their not having the property of swelling with moisture, and therefore not making to equal a compression. As to bougies procuring a discharge of matter, there is no doubt but the mechanical stimulus of a foreign body in such a tender part, though free from disease, must produce it in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; and that this will be varied according to the chemically irritating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the composition, and the irritable state of the urethra: but it seems an absurdity to apply a topic, made uniform throughout, to the whole length of a canal, with a view of producing extraordinary effects upon a particular part of it, by means of some powerful quality in the ingredients. As to that part of the bougie which was in contact with the diseased part, being particularly covered with matter; this circumstance is probably owing to the greater irritation of that part of the urethra where the disorder is, than any other.

BOUHOURS

Pages 410-411

DOMINIC, a celebrated French critic, Bouillon, tic, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1628; and has been by some considered as a proper person to succeed Malherbe, who died about that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. He was entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of Jesuits at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 16; and was appointed to read lectures upon polite literature in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Clermont at Paris, where he had studied; but he was incessantly attacked with the headache, that he could not pursue the destined task. He afterwards undertook the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of two sons of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Longueville, which he discharged with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause. The duke had such a regard for Bouhours, that he would needs die in his arms; and the "Account of the pious and Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>" of this great personage was the first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which Bouhours gave the public. He was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUNKIRK">Dunkirk</a> to the Popish refugees from England; and in the midst of his missionary occupations, found means to compose and publish books. Among these were, Entretiens d'Arifte et d'Eugene, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> "Dialogues between Ariftus and Eugenius," a work of a critical <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and concerning the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. His book was printed no less than five times at Paris, twice at Grenoble, at Lyons, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, &c., and embroiled him in quarrels with a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of censors, with Menage in particular, who, however, lived in friendship with our author before and after. The fame of this piece, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> he took in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> it, recommended Bouhours so effectually to the celebrated minister Colbert, that he trusted him with the education of his son the marquis of Seguelai. He wrote afterwards several other works; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of which are, 1. Remarks and doubts upon the French language. 2. Dialogues upon the art of thinking well in works of genius. 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of St Ignatius. 4. The art of pleasing in conversation. 5. The life of St Francis Xavier, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> of the Indies and of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>. This last work was translated from the French into English by Mr Dryden, and published at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in the year 1668, with a dedication prefixed to James II.'s <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>.

BOUILLON

Pages 411-411

a town of France, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same name, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Luxemburg, with a fortified castle, which is seated on a rock that is almost inaccessible. The French took it in 1676; upon which it was given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Bouillon. This duchy is a sovereignty, independent of France; and in 1792, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> granted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> d'Auvergne, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, his license to accept the succession to the said duchy, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, only son of the reigning duke, without issue <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a>, pursuant to a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of his serene highness, in 1791, "at the desire, and with the express and formal consent of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>." Accordingly, Captain d'Auvergne has since assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of prince of Bouillon. In May 1794 this town was taken by storm, by General Beaulieu, after defeating a considerable body of republicans, and given up to pillage; 1200 French were killed, and 300 taken prisoners. It is seated near the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, 12 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEDAN">Sedan</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 20. N. Lat. 49. 45. Bouillon, in the manege, a lump <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> excrescence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> that grows either upon or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> by the frith, in much that the frith thouts out, just like a lump of flesh, and makes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> halt; and this is called the fleb blowing upon the frith. Manege horses, that never wet their feet, are subject to these excrescences, which make them very lam. See Frush. BOVINA affectio, a distemper of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, caused by a worm lodging between the skin and the flesh, and perforating the same. This distemper is not mentioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks, and is but little known in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.

BOULAINVILLIERS

Pages 411-411

Henry de, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> of St Saife, and an eminent French writer, was descended from a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and noble family, and born at St Saife in 1658. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> was among the fathers of the oratory; where he discovered from his infancy those uncommon abilities for which he was afterwards distinguished. He applied himself principally to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; and his performances in this way are numerous, and considerable. He was the author of a history of the Arabians; fourteen letters upon the ancient parliaments of France; a history of France to the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> VIII.; the state of France, with historical <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> concerning the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Hugh Capet, "written (says M. Montesquieu) with a simplicity and honest freedom worthy of that ancient family from which their author was descended. M. Boulainvilliers died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1722; and after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was published his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Mahomet.

BOULANGER

Pages 411-412

Nicholas Anthony, a very singular Frenchman, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1722, and died there in 1759, aged only 37. During his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, he is said to have come out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUVAIS">Beauvais</a> almost as ignorant as he entered into it; but struggling hard against his unaptitudes to learn, he at length overcame it. At seventeen, he began to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>; and in three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four years made such a progress, as to be useful to the baron of Thiers, whom he accompanied to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of engineer. Afterwards he had the supervision of the highways and bridges; and he executed several public works in Champagne, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, and Lorraine. The author of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, in the Dictionnaire des Hommes célèbres, writes, that in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> a terrible spirit discovered itself in him, which he himself did not suspect before; and this was, it seems, the spirit of "thinking philosophically." In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, directing and changing the courses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and in breaking up and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> over the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a multitude of different substances, which (he thought) evinced the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity of it, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of revolutions which it must have undergone. From the revolutions in the globe, he passed to the changes that must have happened in the manners of men, in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>, in governments, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and he formed many conjectures upon all these. To be farther satisfied, he wanted to know what, in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of ages, had been said upon these particulars; and Boulanger that he might be informed from the fountain head, he learned first Latin and then Greek. Not yet content, he plunged into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Syriac, Chaldaic, and Arabic; and acquired so immense an erudition, that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had lived, he would have been one of the most learned men in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, as we have observed, prematurely took him off. His works are, 1. *Traité du Désertisme Oriental*, 2 vols 12mo; a very bold <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; but not so bold and licentious as, 2. *L'Antiquité desville*, 3 vols 12mo. This was posthumous. 3. He furnished to the *Encyclopédie* the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Delage, Corveé, and Société. 4. He left behind him in MS. a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, which may be regarded as a concordance in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. As a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, he is said to have been of a sweet, calm, and engaging temper; which, however, it is very difficult to reconcile with the dark, impetuous, ardent spirit, that appears to have actuated him as a writer. **Boulanger**, John, an engraver, who flourished towards the end of the last century, was a native of France. His first manner of engraving appears to have been copied, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, from that of Francis de Poilly; but soon after he adopted one of his own, which, though not original, he however greatly improved: He finished the faces, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and all the naked parts of his figures, very neatly with dots instead of strokes, or strokes and dots. The effect is singular enough, and by no means unpleasing: only, in some few instances, he has opposed the coarse graving of his draperies, and back-ground, so violently to the neater work of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, that the outline of the latter is thereby rendered hard, and the general appearance of it flat and chalky. This style of engraving has been carried to its greatest perfection in the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, particularly in England. He did not draw the naked parts of his figures correctly, or with fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. His draperies are apt to be heavy, and the folds not well marked. However, his best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> possess much merit, and are deservedly held in great esteem. **Boulay**, César, was born at St Ellier, a village of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a> in France; and became professor of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> at the college of Navarre, regester, rector, and historiographer of the university of Paris. He died in 1678, after having published several works. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of them are, *A History of the University of Paris*, in Latin, 6 vols folio; and the *<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">Treasure</a> of Roman Antiquities*, in 1 vol. folio. **Boulcolaca**, among the modern Greeks, denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECTRE">spectre</a> of some wicked person who died excommunicated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>, reanimated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>, and causing great disturbance among the people; of which many strange stories are told. The word is Greek, and is sometimes written βουκολακας, boulkolakos; and supposed to be derived from βυργας, or βυργα, "mud," and λακας, a "ditch," on account of the filthiness of the sight. **Boulder-wall**, a kind of wall built of round flints or pebbles, laid in strong <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, and used where the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> has a beach <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> up, or where there are plenty of flints. **<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BOULETTE">Boulette</a>**, in the manege. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> is called boulette, when the fetlock, or pattern-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> forward, and out of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> situation, whether through violent riding, or by reason of being too short-jointed, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the least fatigue <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> bring it. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOULOGNE">Boulogne</a>**, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a>, painter to the French Boulogne <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, and professor of the academy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, distinguished himself by his art; and died at Paris in 1674, aged 65. There are three of his pictures in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Notre Dame.—He left two sons who were admired for their skill in painting. The elder, who is well known under the name of Bon Boullon, was first instructed by his father; after which we went to perfect himself in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and for that purpose the king allowed him a pension; at his return, he was made professor of the academy of painting. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. employed him in adorning several of his palaces; and there are a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his pictures at Paris. His talents for copying the pictures of the great Italian masters were so very extraordinary, that he frequently deceived the greatest judges. He died in 1717.—Lewis Boullon, his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, after being also instructed by his father, gained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> of painting at 18 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; upon which he obtained the king's pension. He set out for Italy at his brother's return, and acquired great skill in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> and colouring. At his return to Paris he was much employed; and at length became <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the academy of painting, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the order of St Michael, and first painter to the king. Louis XIV. allowed him several pensions, and raised him and his posterity to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. He embellished the church of the Invalids, the chapel of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>, &c. **Boullon**, Bon de, a painter of some eminence, was born at Paris in 1649. From his father Louis de Boulogne he learned the first principles of the art; but went to Rome in order to perfect himself from the works of the best masters. He abode in Italy five years. He excelled in history and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a>. His talents for copying the pictures of the great Italian painters were so very extraordinary, that he frequently deceived the greatest judges. He died at Paris in 1717, aged 68. **Boulogne**, Louis de, born at Paris in 1654, was the younger brother of the preceding; and like him learned from his father the first principles of painting, and afterwards went to Rome to complete his studies. His works, on his return, were so much esteemed, that Louis XIV. honoured him with the order of St Michael, and, after the death of Antony Coppell, appointed him his principal painter. He chiefly excelled in historical and allegorical subjects. He died at Paris in 1734, aged 80 years. **Boulogne**, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sea-port town of Picardy in France, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Boulognois, now called the department of the Straits of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a>, with a harbour, and formerly a bishop's see. It is divided into two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>; the higher, and the lower. The former is strong both by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and art; and the latter is only surrounded with a single wall. The harbour has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> for the safety of shipping, which at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> prevents it from being choked up. The lower town is inhabited by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, and has three large streets, one of which leads to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> town, and the other two run in a line on the side of the river. It is situated at the mouth of the river Lianeuse, and 14 miles south of Calais. E. Long, 1. 42. N. Lat. 50. 42. **Boulognois**, a territory of France, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Picardy, about 30 miles in length and 20 in breadth. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town is Boulogne, and the chief trade

BOULTER

Pages 412-413

Dr Hugh, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, of reputable and wealthy parents. He was educated at Merchant-taylors school; and, before the Revolution, was from thence admitted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a> of Christ-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, he was chosen a demy of Magdalen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> with Mr Addison and Dr Wilcox. From the merit and learning of the persons elected, this was <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called by Dr Hough, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the college, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> election. He afterwards became fellow of the same college; in which station he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the university till he was invited to London by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Hodges, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> secretary of state, in the year 1709, who made him his chaplain, and recommended him to Dr Tenison archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>; but his first preferments were owing to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Sunderland, by whose <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> and influence he was promoted to the parsonage of St Olave in Southwark, and the archdeaconry of Surry. Here he continued discharging very faithfully and diligently every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his pastoral office, till he was recommended to attend George I. as his chaplain when he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a> in 1719. He had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to teach <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Frederic the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; and by his conduct he so won the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s favour, that he promoted him to the deanery of Christ-church, and the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, in the same year. As he was visiting his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> five years afterwards, he received a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from the secretary of state, acquainting him that his majesty had nominated him to the archbishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMAGH">Armagh</a> and primacy of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. This honour he would gladly have declined; and desired the secretary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> his good offices with his majesty to excuse him from accepting it. Ireland happened to be at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, occasioned by Wood's ruinous project; and the ministry thought that the bishop would greatly contribute to quench it by his judgment, moderation, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>. The king therefore laid his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> commands upon him; to which he submitted, but with some reluctance. As soon as he had taken possession of the primacy, he began to consider that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in which his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, as his own; and to promote its true interest with the greatest zeal and affluency. Accordingly, in innumerable instances, he exerted himself in the noblest acts of beneficence and public spirit. In seasons of the greatest scarcity, he was more than once instrumental in preventing a famine which threatened that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. On one of these occasions he distributed vast quantities of corn throughout the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, for which the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons passed a vote of public thanks; and at another time 2500 persons were fed at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>-house in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, every morning, and as many every evening, for a considerable time together, mostly at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a>'s expense. When schemes were proposed for the advantage of the country, he encouraged and promoted them not only with his counsel but his purse. He had great compassion for the poor clergy of his diocese, who were disabled from giving their children a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>; and he maintained several of the children of such in the university. He erected four houses at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROGHEDA">Drogheda</a> for the reception of clergymen's widows, and purchased an estate for the endowment of them. His charities for augmenting small livings and buying glebes amounted to upwards of 30,000l. besides what he devised by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> for the like purposes in England. In short, the instances he gave of his generosity and benevolence of heart, his virtue, his piety, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, are almost innumerable, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of his life is his noblest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a>. This excellent prelate died at London, on the 2d of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1742, and was interred in Westminster-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, where a beautiful monument of finely polished marble is erected to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>.

BOULTINE

Pages 413-413

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> which workmen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for a moulding, the convexity of which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> one-fourth of a circle; being the member just below the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLINTH">plinth</a> in the Tuscan and Doric <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>.

BOULUKE

Pages 413-413

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> orders of the Turks, a body of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANIZARIES">janizaries</a>, with an officer in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a> at their head, sent upon some particular enterprise; they are selected out of the body for this, and as soon as the business is over, are received again into their former companies.

BOUM SOLIS STABULA

Pages 413-413

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the territory of Mylae, so called: A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on the east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>; remarkable for its fertility and rich pastures (Theophratus); and hence arose the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of the oxen of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> feeding there (Scholiast on Apollonius). Pliny and Seneca say, that something like dung is thrown out on the coast of Mylae and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MESSANA">Messana</a>, which gave rise to the fable of the oxen of the sun being stalled there; and at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> the inhabitants affirm the same thing (Cluverius).

BOUNCE

Pages 413-413

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, the English name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of squalus. See SQUALUS.

BOUND

Pages 413-413

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">Dancing</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> from one foot to the other; by which it differs from a hop, where the spring is from one foot to the same. It also differs from a half coupsie, as in the latter the body always bears on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, either on one foot <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the other; whereas, in the bound, it is thrown quite from the floor. Bound-Bailiffs, are sheriffs officers for executing of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>. The sheriffs being answerable for their misdemeanors, the bailiffs are usually bound in a bond for the due execution of their office; and thence are called bound-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people have corrupted into a much more homely appellation. BOUNDS OF LANDS. See ABUTTALS.

BOUNTY

Pages 413-415

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, a premium paid by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> to the exporters of certain British commodities, as sail-cloth, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>-stockings, fish, corn, &c. The happy influence which bounties have on trade and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> is well known; nor can there be a more convincing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the good intentions of the government under which we live, than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care that is taken to give all possible encouragement to those who shall establish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> improve any hazardous branch of trade. All undertakings, in respect either to mercantile enterprises, or in the establishment of manufactures, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> weak and feeble in their beginnings; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> unsuccessful, Survey of either sink entirely, or at least are seldom revived in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Accidents of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> are not only destructive to private persons, but exceedingly detrimental to the public <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. On this principle, more especially especially since trade, for which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> designed us, hath been attended to, such attempts have been thought deserving, and have been favoured with public support. This in former times usually flowed from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, in the form of letters-patent, charters, or other grants of privileges, which, however requisite they might be, were notwithstanding very frequently objects of censure. If such as obtained them failed in their endeavours, they were reputed projectors; if, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, they succeeded, they were considered as monopolizers. Corporations, which imply the uniting certain individuals into a body, that they may thereby become more useful to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>, are created by the crown. Many of these were formed for promoting trade; and, according to the old system of our government, were necessary and useful. On the same principle, privileges were granted to private persons, on a suggestion, that what was immediately of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to them would terminate in public utility. These also did good in bringing in many arts and manufactures; though, in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, tending to private interest more than public emolument, they were liable to legal correction. In later times, and in concerns of moment, a much better method has been adopted, as often as it hath been found practicable, by rejecting private or particular interest, and proposing the designed advantages to such as should perform the stipulations on which they are granted. These bounties, as they are paid by the public, so they are solely calculated for the benefit of the public. They are sometimes given to encourage industry and application in raising a necessary commodity; which was intended by the bounty on exporting corn. The intention of this bounty was to encourage <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> hath been, that we now grow more than twice as much as we did at the establishment of the bounty; we even consume twice as much <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> as we then grew; yet in A.D. 1697, we exported a fifteenth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of what we grew, of late years a twenty-ninth part only. The bounty on this twenty-ninth part amounted to somewhat more than 50,000l., and the produce to more than 400,000l. It is evident that all this is so much clear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. But this is far from being all that we have annually gained. For if our cultivation is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, as indeed it is, then the rent of lands, the subsistence of working <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, the profits of the tradesmen supplying them with utensils, clothes, the value of horses employed, &c. must all be taken into the account. Besides this, we must add the freight (amounting to half the bounty), to make the idea of the advantages complete. Sometimes bounties are given with a view to promote manufactures, as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of those made of silk. Many laws are to be found in our statute books in favour of the silk manufacture, made with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and propriety, for the encouragement and support of many thousands of industrious persons employed therein. By statute 8 Geo. I. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 15, § 1, a bounty was given on the due <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of ribbons and stuffs, of silk only, of three shillings upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; silk, and ribbons of silk, mixed with gold and silver, four shillings a-pound; on silk gloves, silk stockings, silk fringes, silk laces, and sewing silk, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> and threepence a-pound; on stuffs of silk and grommet yarn, eightpence a-pound; on silks mixed with inkle or cotton, one shilling; on stuffs of silk mixed with worsted, sixpence a-pound, for three years; and, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> of their utility, these were <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> by subsequent statutes. Sometimes bounties are given to support a new manufacture against foreigners already in possession of it, as in making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and fail-cloth. The promoting of the manufacture of British fail-cloth was undoubtedly a very important national object, as the consumption was very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and of consequence the purchase of it from foreigners a heavy expense on the public. Many methods were therefore devised, and countenanced by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, both here and in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, for introducing and encouraging our own in preference to that of strangers, more especially in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>. By stat. 12 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, cap. 16, § 2, a bounty was given of one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> per ell on all that was exported for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, and continued by subsequent statutes. By 4 Geo. II. cap. 27, § 4, an additional bounty of another penny an ell is granted. These bounties were to be paid out of an additional duty on imported fail-cloth. By the same statute every ship built in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, or in the plantations, is, under the penalty of 50l., to be furnished with a complete <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of fails of British manufacture. The amount of these bounties mark the progress of the manufacture, which is also affixed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> on which the payment is assigned. The assistance, however, are never bestowed but on mature deliberation, in virtue of strong proofs, and with a moral certainty of a national benefit. The great intention of bounties is to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the British trader on such ground as to render his commerce beneficial to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. In order to this, some profit must accrue to himself, otherwise he would not embark therein; but this, whatever it be, must prove inconsiderable in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of what results to the public. For if, by the help of such a bounty, one or many traders export to the value of 1000, 10,000, or 100,000 pounds worth of commodities or manufactures, whatever his or their profit or loss (for the latter, through avidity and overloading the market, sometimes happens) may be, the nation gains the 1000l., 10,000l., or 100,000l.; which was the object of the legislature in granting the bounty. Upon this consideration, that the entire produce of what is exported accrues to the nation, the legislature, when an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of circumstances required it, have made no scruple of augmenting a bounty; as in the case of refined <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> exported, from three to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> shillings per hundred weight. In like manner, the original bounty of one pound per ton in favour of vessels employed in the whale-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> hath been doubled, and many new regulations made, in order to render this fishery more advantageous to the public. As a bounty is given on malt when allowed to be exported, so an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> of 30 shillings per ton hath been granted on all British made malt-spirits when exported, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> benefit to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, manufactures, and commerce. It is indeed true, that on whatever account, or to whatever amount, this reward is given, the public seem to pay, and private persons seem to receive. But these private persons receive it as the hire from the public for performing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> which otherwise they would not perform, the benefit of which accrues to the public, and who can therefore very well afford to pay that reward in reality, which, as we have stated it, the on- ly seems to do. For, looking a little closer, we cannot help observing, that the bounty is paid to individuals, who, as such, make a part of the public. But the commodities or manufactures exported are sold to foreigners, and the whole produce of them, be it what it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, comes into the purview of the public. By attending to this self-evident doctrine, every reasonable and public-spirited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> will be easily reconciled to bounties; and the three following considerations will be sufficient to obviate the most common objections that have been made to the practice of giving them. 1. That no bounty can be desired but on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> of national utility, which always deserves notice, and cannot be mistaken. It must likewise be alleged and proved, that this is the only means whereby the national benefit can be attained. 2. The sums issued on this account not only show the clear expense of the bounty, but also indicate the profit gained by the public; for as the one cannot exist without the other, that amount must be the incontestable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> of both. 3. It must be remembered (and of this too some instances might be given), that if bounties should be improperly bestowed, they will of course prove ineffectual, and after a few fruitless trials will remain unclaimed, and consequently produce no expense. There is indeed another objection which hath been made against the giving of bounties. This is grounded on the frauds to which they are supposed to be liable; and particularly the relanding of the goods on which the bounty hath been paid, and thereby deceiving and cheating the public. But whoever peruses the laws made on this head, and attentively considers the numerous precautions taken to fix every circumstance relative to the obtaining the bounty, the checks on the shipping of goods, the securities taken for their due exportation, the certificates required to ascertain their being actually delivered and sold in a foreign market, must be convinced, that to discharge all those securities, in case of an intended fraud, is a thing very difficult, if not impossible. To these remarks we may add, that bounties are usually granted only for a limited <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and then expire; are always liable to be suspended; and of course can never be the cause of any great national loss. There is no doubt that, exclusive of frauds, the immoderate thirst of gain may tempt interested men to aim at converting what was calculated for public benefit to its detriment, for their own private advantage. Thus, on a prospect of short crops in other countries, men may take <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, but directly against the spirit, of the law, to send so much of our corn abroad as to endanger a famine at home. For this the wisdom of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> provides, not barely by suspending the bounty, but by prohibiting exportation and opening the ports for foreign supplies. We cannot with any shadow of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> ascribe scarcity to the bounty on the exportation. If this was the case, suspensions would be frequent, whereas there have been but five in a course of 70 years. If the bounty had any share, the larger the exportation, the greater would be the scarcity. In A.D. 1750 we exported more than one fifth of our growth of wheat, which was notwithstanding but at four shillings per bushel; whereas a century before, A.D. 1650, when we had neither bounty nor exportation, wheat was at nine shillings and sixpence per bushel. The causes of scarcity are unkindly fea- fons; which though <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> policy cannot prevent, yet their sad effects have been evidently lessened by our increased growth, since the taking place of bounty and exportation. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Anne's Bounty, for augmenting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> livings under 50l. per annum, confits of the produce of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and tenths, after the charges and pensions payable out of the same are defrayed. A corporation for management of the same was settled, &c. in 1704. See Augmentation.

BOURBON

Pages 415-418
or Mascarenhas, Isle of, an island in the Indian ocean, lying on the east of Madagascar, in E. Long. 58° 30'. S. Lat. 21° 23'. This island has no port, and is in some places inaccessible. Its length and breadth have not been well determined; but the circumference, according to the account of a person who resided there some time, is about 57 leagues. It is for the most part mountainous, but in some places there are very beautiful and fertile plains. In the south part of the island there is a burning mountain, which has thrown out vast quantities of bitumen, sulphur, and other combustible materials; neither does it cease throwing them out still, so that the country about it is useless, and is called by the inhabitants pays brûlé, that is, burnt land. The shore is high and rocky all round; but though on this account it hath no ports, there are several good roads, particularly one on the west, and another on the north-east. As to its form, this island is irregular, so that it is difficult to judge from the maps whether it is round or long. The air is equally pleasant and wholesome, inasmuch that the people live to a great age without feeling either infirmities or diseases. This is occasioned by the hurricanes, of which they have one or two every year. These purge and cleanse the air so as to render it highly salubrious; the certainty of which is thus distinguished, that when they fail of making their annual visits, as sometimes they do, diseases and death find an entrance into the island, which otherwise would soon be overstocked with inhabitants. The climate is hot, but not to such a degree as might be expected from its situation, the breezes from the mountains being constant and very refreshing. The tops of these mountains are in winter covered with snow; which, melting in the summer, furnishes abundance of rivers and rivulets, with which the country is plentifully watered: so that the soil, though not very deep, is wonderfully fruitful, producing Turkey corn and rice twice a-year, and the latter in great abundance. Most sorts of cattle are found here, good in their kind, and are very cheap; wild goats and wild hogs are found in the woods and on the tops of the mountains; here also are vast quantities of wild fowl of different kinds, fish, and land tortoises, affording at once the most delicate and wholesome food. As to fruits, they have bananas, oranges, citrons, tamarinds, and other kinds; neither does it want valuable commodities, particularly ebony, cotton, white pepper, gum benzoin, aloes, and tobacco; all excellent in their kind, when compared with those of other countries. This island is also happy in its deficiencies; for no animals that are venomous are to be found therein, and only two sorts that are disagreeable to the sight, viz. spiders of the size of a pigeon's egg, which weave nets of a surprising strength, reckoned by some capable of being treated to as to become as valuable- luable as silk; and bats of a most enormous size, which are not only skinned and eaten, but esteemed also the greatest delicacy that they have. The island of Bourbon was discovered by the Portuguese in 1545, as appears by a date inscribed by them upon a pillar when they first landed; but when the French settled in Madagascar, this island was totally desolate. Three Frenchmen being banished thither, and left there for three years, made such a report of it at their return as surprized their countrymen. They lived most of that time upon pork; and though they were in a manner naked, yet they affirmed that they never had the least pain or sickness whatever. This tempted one Anthony Taureau to go over thither in 1654, accompanied by seven French and six negroes, who carried with them the cattle from which the island has been stocked ever since. The first thing they did was to erect the arms of France, by order of M. Falcourt who was governor of Madagascar, and to bestow upon the island a new name. Then they set up huts, and laid out gardens, in which they cultivated melons, different sorts of roots, and tobacco; but just as the last became ripe, the whole plantation was destroyed by a hurricane. The French, however, went to work again; and having some acquaintance with the climate, succeeded better, and added aloes to the rest of their plantations; but receiving no succour from Madagascar, and being tired of living by themselves in the ille de Bourbon, they very readily embraced the offer of an English captain, and in the year 1658 embarked for Madras. When the last great blow was given to the French at Madagascar by the natives, who surprized and cut them off in one night, there escaped as many men as, with their wives, who were natives, filled two canoes; and these being driven by the wind on the ille de Bourbon, were the next set of people who inhabited it. This last colony, for want of an opportunity to remove, were constrained to cultivate this new country of theirs, and to remain in it. It was not long before a further stock of inhabitants arrived. A pirate that had been committing depredations in the Indies, returning to Europe, ran ashore and was split to pieces upon the rocks, so that the crew were forced to join themselves to the former inhabitants; and as they had on board their vessel a great many Indian women whom they had made prisoners, they lived with them, and in process of time had a numerous posterity. As East India ships touched frequently here, when too late to double the Cape, many of the sailors, for the sake of the women, deferred at the time of their departure, and staying behind became planters in the ille de Bourbon. As the place grew more populous, the people naturally became more civilized, and desirous of living in a more commodious manner; which induced them to build small vessels, that in these they might sometimes make a trip to Madagascar, in order to purchase slaves, whom they employed in their plantations to cultivate aloes, tobacco, and other things, with which they drove a small trade, when ships of any nation anchored in their roads for the sake of refreshments. In this situation they were, when the French East India company put in their claim; and assuming the property of the island, lent thither five or six families and a governor. At first the inhabitants expected to reap some benefit from their new masters; but finding very little, and thinking the governor took too much upon him, they revolted at the instigation of a priest, seized their governor and put him into a dungeon, where he died of hunger and grief. For this some of the ring-leaders were punished, a kind of fort was erected, some guns placed on it, and the French flag kept flying; but in other respects, so little care was taken, that till within these 40 years, the island was in no state of defense. The number of inhabitants in the year 1717 was computed at 2000; viz. 900 free, and 1100 slaves. Amongst these people the usual distinction of whites and blacks entirely fails: for even the free are of different colours; and a French writer affirms us, that he saw in a church one family, consisting of five generations, of all complexions. The eldest was a female, 108 years of age, of a brown black, like the Indians of Madagascar; her daughter, a mulatto; her grand-daughter, a mestizo; her great-grand-daughter, of a dusky yellow; her daughter again, of an olive colour; and the daughter of this last, as fair as any English girl of the same age. These people are, generally speaking, of a gentle quiet disposition, very industrious, and submissive enough to authority, provided it is exercised with a tolerable degree of equity and decency; for otherwise the whole of them are apt to rise in rebellion at once; and the slaves have so little reason to complain of their masters, that they are always on the same side. The island is divided into four quarters. The first is that of St Paul, which is the largest and best peopled: their houses are built at the foot of a steep mountain, on both sides of a fresh water lake. As for the plantations, they are on the top of a mountain, which they ascend by a very rough and troublesome passage. On the summit there is a spacious plain, a great part of which is divided into plantations of rice, tobacco, corn, sugar, and fruits. The quarter of St Dennis lies seven leagues from that of St Paul, towards the east, and there the governor resides. It is not so well peopled as the former; but the country is more pleasant, and the situation better. At two leagues distance, proceeding along the sea-coast, is the quarter of St Mary's, which is but thinly peopled. The last and most fertile quarter is that of St Sannah, which is at the distance of four leagues from St Dennis. The road between these two quarters is tolerable, though part of it has been cut with much difficulty through a wood; but the passage from St Dennis to St Paul is only by sea. When the present company of India became, by their perpetual establishment, possessed of the island of Bourbon, they began to improve it exceedingly; raising new forts and batteries, so as to render it in a manner inaccessible; and importing coffee-trees from Arabia; which have succeeded so well, that it is believed they produce an eighth, according to some a fifth, part as much coffee as is raised in the kingdom of Yemen in Arabia, and it is likewise held next in goodness to that. In 1763, the population amounted to 4627 white people, and 15,149 blacks; the cattle consisted of 8702 beefeves, 4084 sheep, 7405 goats, and 7619 hogs. Upon an extent of 125,909 acres of cultivated land, they gathered as much coffee as would feed their slaves, 1,135,000 pounds weight of corn, 844,100 pounds of rice, Bourbon rice, 2,879,100 pounds of maize, and 2,535,100 pounds of coffee; which last the company bought up at about 3d. per pound. In 1743, Admiral Bocawen appeared before this island with a British fleet; but found it well fortified both by nature and art, that he was obliged, after some cannonading to very little purpose, to pursue his voyage. Bourbon, Nicholas, a famous Latin poet in the 16th century, was a native of Vendeuvre near Langres, and the son of a wealthy man who was master of several forges. Margaret de Valois appointed him preceptor to her daughter Jane d'Albert of Navarre, the mother of King Henry IV. At length he retired to Conde, where he had a benefice, and died about the year 1550. He wrote eight books of Epigrams; and a poem on the forge, which he has entitled Ferraria. He had great knowledge of antiquity and of the Greek language. Erasmus praises his Epigrams. Bourbon, Nicholas, a celebrated Greek and Latin poet, was nephew of the preceding. He taught rhetoric in several colleges of Paris; and the cardinal de Perron caused him to be nominated professor of eloquence in the Royal College: he was also canon of Langres, and one of the 40 of the French academy. At length he retired to the fathers of the oratory, where he died in 1644, aged 70. He is esteemed one of the greatest Latin poets France has produced. His poems were printed at Paris in 1630. Bourbon-Lancy, a town of France, in the department of Saone and Loire. It is remarkable for its castle and baths; and there is a large marble pavement, called the great bath, which is a work of the Romans. It is seated near the river Loire, in E. Long. 3° 46'. N. Lat. 46° 37'. Bourbon L'Archeboul, a town of France, in the department of Allier, remarkable for its baths, which are exceedingly hot. E. Long. 3° 28'. N. Lat. 46° 35'. Family of Bourbon, the late royal family of France. Henry IV. in 1589, though of the 10th generation, was the nearest heir, and succeeded Henry III. (the last of the Valois race), whose brother Francis II. married Mary queen of Scots, and both died without issue. Louis XVI. was the 5th king of this family in succession. This family also mounted the throne of Spain in 1700, by Philip V., grandson to Louis XIV., which was the occasion of the long and bloody war that ended in the peace of Utrecht. A branch of the Spanish family likewise mounted the throne of the two Sicilies in 1734. These three branches, entered into a treaty offensive and defensive in 1761, which goes by the name of the family-complot. Bourbonne-le-Bains, a town of France, in Champagne, and in the Bailligny, famous for its hot baths. E. Long. 5° 45'. N. Lat. 47° 54'. Bourbonnois, a province of France, with the title of a duchy; bounded on the north, by Nivernois and Berry; on the west, by Berry and a small part of Upper Marche; on the south, by Auvergne; and on the east, by Burgundy and Forez. It abounds in corn, fruits, pastures, wood, game, and wine. Its principal town is Moulins; and the rivers are the Loire, the Allier, and the Cher. Bourbourg, a town in French Flanders, whose fortifications are demolished. It is seated on a canal that goes to Dunkirk, in E. Long. 2° 15'. N. Lat. Bourchies 50° 55'. Bourchier, John, lord Bemars, grandson and heir of a lord of the same name, who was descended from Thomas of Woodstock, duke of Gloucester, and had been knight of the garter, and constable of Windsor-castle. Under Edward IV., our lord John was created a knight of the Bath, at the marriage of the duke of York second son of Edward IV., and was first known by quelling an insurrection in Cornwall and Devonshire, raised by Michael Joseph a blacksmith, in 1495, which recommended him to the favour of Henry VII. He was a captain of the pioneers at the siege of Therouanne, under Henry VIII., by whom he was made chancellor of the exchequer for life, lieutenant of Calais and the Marches, appointed to conduct the lady Mary the king's sister into France on her marriage with Louis XII., and had the extraordinary happiness of continuing in favour with Henry VIII. for the space of 18 years. He died at Calais in 1532, aged 63. He translated, by King Henry's command, Froissart's Chronicle; which was printed in 1523, by Richard Pynson, the scholar of Caxton, and the fifth on the list of English printers. His other works were a whimsical medley of translations from French, Spanish, and Italian novels, which seem to have been the mode then, as they were afterwards in the reign of Charles II. These were: The Life of Sir Arthur, an Armorican knight; The famous exploits of Sir Hugh Bourdeaux; Marcus Aurelius; and, The cattle of love. He composed also a book of the duties of the inhabitants of Calais; and a comedy entitled Ite in Vineam, which is mentioned in none of our catalogues of English plays. Anthony Wood says it was usually acted at Calais after vespers.
