Bourdaloue, Lewis, a celebrated preacher among the Jesuits, and one of the greatest orators France has produced, was born at Bourges on the 20th of August 1632. After having preached at Provence, he in 1669 went to Paris; and there met with such applause, that the king resolved to hear him; on which he was sent for to court, and frequently preached before Louis XIV. He afflicted the sick, visited the prisoners and hospitals, and was very liberal in giving alms. He died at Paris on the 13th of May 1704. The best edition of his sermons is in octavo. Bordeaux, an ancient, large, handsome, and rich town of France, in the department of Gironde, is the capital of Guienne, and an archbishop's see; has an university and an academy of arts and sciences. It is built in the form of a bow, of which the river Garonne is the string. This river is bordered by a large quay, and the water rises four yards at full tide, for which reason the largest vessels can come up to it very readily. The castle called the Trompe is seated at the entrance of the quay, and the river runs round its walls. Most of the great streets lead to the quay. The town has 12 gates; and near another castle are fine walks under several rows of trees. The ancient city of Bordeaux, though considerable in point of size, was ill built, badly paved, dangerous, without policy or any of those municipal regulations indispensably requisite to render a city splendid or elegant. It has entirely changed its appearance within these last thirty years. The public edifices are very noble, and all the streets newly built are regular and handsome. The quays are... four miles in length, and the river itself is considerably broader than the Thames at London bridge. On the opposite side, a range of hills covered with woods, vineyards, churches, and villas, extends beyond the view. Almost in the centre of the town is a fine equestrian statue in bronze erected to Louis XV. in 1743, with the following inscription: Ludovicus quindecimus Sepe victori, semper pacificatoris; Suos omnes, quam latè regnum patet, Paterno pectori gerentis; Suorum in animis penitus habitanit. The beauty of the river Garonne, and the fertility of the adjoining country, were probably the causes which induced the Romans to lay the foundations of this city. The ruins of a very large amphitheatre yet remain, constructed under the emperor Gallienus; it is of brick, as are most of the edifices of that period, when the empire was verging to its fall, and the arts began rapidly to decline. During the irruptions of the barbarous nations, and particularly in those which the Normans repeatedly made, Bordeaux was ravaged, burnt, and almost entirely destroyed. It only began to recover again under Henry II. of England, who having united it to the crown by his marriage with Eleanor of Aquitaine, rebuilt it, and made it a principal object of his policy to restore the city again to the lustre from which it had fallen. The Black Prince received all Guienne, Gascony, and many inferior provinces, in full sovereignty from his father Edward III. He brought his royal captive, John king of France, to this city, after the battle of Poictiers in 1356; and held his court and residence here during eleven years. His exalted character, his uninterrupted feats of good fortune, his victories, his modesty, his affability, and his munificence, drew strangers to Bordeaux from every part of Europe; but all this splendour soon disappeared. He lived to experience the ingratitude of Peter the Cruel, to whom he had restored the kingdom of Castile; he became a prey to distempers in the vigour of life; he saw his dominions reunited again in many of their branches to the crown of France, by Charles V.; he lost his eldest son Edward, a prince of the highest expectations; and at length, overcome with sorrow at this last affliction, he quitted Bordeaux, and re-embarked for England, there to expire a memorable example of the hasty revolution of human greatness! In 1453, Charles VII. king of France, re-entered the city, and subjected the whole province of Guienne, which had been near three centuries under the English government. Conscious of the importance of such a conquest, he ordered the Chateau Trompette to be built to defend the passage of the river; and Louis the XIV. afterwards employed the celebrated Vauban to erect a new fortress in the modern style of military architecture, on the same spot.—Madame de Maintenon, whom fortune seemed to have chosen as the object of her extreme rigour and extreme bounty, was removed from the prisons of Niort in Poitou, where she was born, with her father the Baron d'Aubigne, to this castle, where she used to play with the daughter of the turnkey, in the greatest indigence. Bourdeaux prefers few remains of antiquity. The cathedral appears to be very old, and has suffered considerably from the effects of time. The unfortunate duke of Guienne, brother to Bourdelet Louis the XI. who was poisoned in 1473, lies buried before the high altar. The adjacent country, more particularly the Pays de Medoc, which produces the finest claret, is exceedingly pleasant, and at the season of the vintage forms one of the most delicious landscapes in the world. W. Long. o. 39. N. Lat. 44° 50'.

BOURDELOT

Pages 418-418

JOHN, a learned French critic, who lived at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the 16th and beginning of the 17th centuries. He distinguished himself by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> notes on Lucian, Petronius, and Heliodorus; by an Universal <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>; Commentaries on Juvenal; a Treatise on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">Etymology</a> of French words; and by some other works which were never published.—There was also an Abbé Bourdelot, his sister's son, who changed his name from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Michon to oblige his uncle. He was a celebrated physician at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, who gained <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation by a Treatise on the Viper, and other works. He died in 1685.

BOURDINES

Pages 418-418

a town of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAMUR">Namur</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. o. N. Lat. 50° 35'.

BOURDON

Pages 418-418

SEBASTIAN, a famous painter, born at Montpelier, in 1619. He studied <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years at Rome; and acquired such a reputation, that at his return to France he had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of being the first who was made rector of the academy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. He succeeded better in his landscapes than in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>-painting. His pieces are seldom finished; and those that are so, are not always the finest. He once laid a wager with a friend, that he should paint 12 heads after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and as big as the life, in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. He won it; and these are said not to be the worst things he ever did. His most considerable pieces are, The gallery of M. de Bretonvilliers, in the aisle of Notre Dame; and, The seven works of mercy, which he etched by himself. But the most esteemed of all his performances is, The martyrdom of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, drawn for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Notre Dame; It is kept as one of the choicest rarities of that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>. Bourdon was a Calvinist; much valued and respected, however, in a Popish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, because his life and manners were good. We have also by this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of etchings; which are executed in a bold masterly style, and much more finished than those we generally meet with from the point of the painter. They are justly held in the highest estimation by the generality of the collectors. He died in 1673, aged 54.

BOURG

Pages 418-418

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAYENNE">Cayenne</a>, a French colony on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUIANA">Guiana</a>, in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 52°. o. N. Lat. 5°. o. BOURG-en-Bresse, a town in France, and capital of Bresse, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>. It is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a>, almost in the centre of Bresse, in E. Long. 4° 19'. N. Lat. 46° 13'. BOURG-sur-Mer, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of France in Guienne, and in the Bourdelois, with a tolerable good harbour: seated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DORDOGNE">Dordogne</a> and Garonne, in W. Long. 3° 35'. N. Lat. 45°. o.

BOURGES

Pages 418-419

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of France, in the department of Cher, and formerly an archbishop's see, with a famous university. The archbishop assumes the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> title of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">Patriarch</a> of the Aquitaine, and enjoys the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of primacy with regard to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBI">Albi</a>. It is seated between two small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, the Everse and the Orron, upon a hill that has a gentle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to these rivers, by which it is almost surrounded, for there is but one avenue to it by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, which is that of Port Bourbonnoux. It stands upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of ground; but one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it is without houses; and the rest is but thinly peopled with gentlemen, students, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, the whole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of souls amounting only to about 1800. They have no manner of trade but for their own necessaries. It is divided into the old and new town. The walls of the old are almost entire, and the new town is almost as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as the old. There are several churches, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, and nunneries. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, dedicated to St Stephen, is a fine old Gothic structure: it is seated in the highest part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and on each side of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> are two handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> towers. The new one, which is built in the room of one which fell down, is almost 200 feet high. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURBON">Bourbon</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> is the largest in the city, where there was formerly an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, and now a market. There is a fine walk from St Michael's gate into the fields, and three alleys, formed by four ranks of trees, the middlemost of which is spacious; besides which, there is a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> mall. The university is famous for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. This city stands almost in the centre of France. E. Long. 2° 30'. N. Lat. 47° 10'.

BOURGET

Pages 419-419

a town of Savoy, subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, seated at the southern extremity of a lake of the same name. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 55'. N. Lat. 45° 45'.

BOURGOGNE

Pages 419-419
or Burgundy, as it is called; a considerable province of France with the title of a duchy. It is 130 miles in length, and 75 in breadth. It is bounded on the east, by the Franche Comté; on the west, by Bourbonnois and Nivernois; on the south, by Lyonnais; and on the north by Champagne. It is very fertile in corn and fruit, and produces excellent wine. It is watered by the rivers Seine, Dehune, Bresinse, Armançon, Ouche, Souzon, Tille, and Saône. There are four mineral springs at Apoigny, Primeau, Bourbon-Lancy, and St Reine. The first are obscure, and the two last in high reputation. In the canton of Brefle, there are two subterranean lakes which often overflow in times of the greatest drought, and lay a large tract of ground under water: one of them has no apparent spring or opening; and yet in a dry season, it throws out water enough to overflow the meadow-land near it. The grottoes or caves of Arcy are seated about 18 miles from Auxerre, and over them is foil about 10 feet deep. The entrance into these cavities is 200 paces long, but narrow. There are arches which form several vaults, from whence drops clear water, which turns into a brilliant hard stone. Twenty paces from the entrance is a lake, which seems to be formed by that part of the water that will not petrify. The height of these vaults is not above eight feet. About 80 paces from the entrance there is a kind of hall, with a coffee-coloured ceiling, wherein there are a thousand odd figures, which have a very agreeable effect. Dijon is the capital town.

BOURGUIGNONS

Pages 419-420
or Burgundians, one of the northern nations who overran the Roman empire, and settled in Gaul. They were of a great stature, and very warlike; for which reason the emperor Valentinian the Great engaged them in his service against the Germans. They lived in tents which were close to each other, that they might the more readily unite in arms on any unforeseen attack. These conjunctions of tents, they called burgi; and they were to them what towns are to us. Sidonius Apollinaris tells us, that they wore long hair, took great pleasure in singing, and were fond of praise for their vocal talents. He adds, that they ate great quantities; and anointed their hair with butter, deeming that unction very ornamental. Their crown was at first elective, and the authority of their kings expired with their successors. They were not only accountable for their own misconduct, but likewise for the calamities of nature, and the caprice of fortune. They Bourignon were deposed if they had lost a battle; if they succeeded ill in any enterprise; or if, in short, any great event had not corresponded with the hopes of the public. They were not more favourably treated in case of a bad harvest or vintage, or if any epidemical distemper had ravaged the state. At first they were governed by many kings, and benden was the title of the royal dignity. But in latter times they were subject to one sovereign; and they grew humane and civilized, especially when Christianity was propagated in their country. Before that epocha, their religion was much the same with that of the other northern nations. The had many priests, the chief of whom was distinguished by the name of jinifru. He was perpetual, and they paid him great respect and veneration.

BOURIGNON

Pages 420-420

ANTONIETTA, a famous enthusiastic preacher and pretended prophetess, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LILLE">Lille</a> in 1616. At her birth she was so deformed, that it was debated some days in the family whether it was not proper to stifle her as a monster; but her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a> diminishing, she was spared; and afterwards attained such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, that she had her admirers. From her childhood to her old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> she had an extraordinary turn of mind. She set up for a reformer, and published a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of books filled with very singular notions; the most remarkable of which are entitled The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of the World, and the testimony of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">Truth</a>. She was an enemy to reason and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, which she maintained ought to give <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to the illumination of divine <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>; and affected, that whenever any one was born again by embracing her doctrine, he felt the pains and throws of a woman in labour. Of her pretended visions and revelations we shall give one instance as a sample. In one of her ecstasies she <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> in the same form in which he appeared before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, and the manner in which he was capable of procreating other men, since he himself possessed in himself the principles of both sexes*. Nay the pretended it was told her that he had carried this procreating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> so far as to produce the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ. "The first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> (says she), whom Adam brought forth without any concurrent assistance in his glorified state, was chosen by God to be the throne of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">Divinity</a>; the organ and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> by which God would communicate himself externally to men: This is Chiff the first born united to human nature, both God and man." Besides these and such like extravagancies, she had other forbidding qualities: her temper was morose and peevish, and was the extremely avaricious and greedy of amassing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>. She drest like a hermit, and traveled to France, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, England, and Scotland. In the last she made a strong party, and some thousand sectarians, known by the name of Bourignonists. She died at Franeker in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Frise, October 30th 1680. Her works have been printed in 18 vols octavo.

BOURN

Pages 420-420

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, in England, seated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 17. N. Lat. 52. 40. It is a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, has a good market for corn and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, and is noted for the coronation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Edmund.

BOURNE

Pages 420-420
or BURN, an appellation anciently given to all little brooks or rivulets, and still used in the same sense in Scotland and in the north of England.

BOURO

Pages 420-420

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean, between the Moluccas and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELEBES">Celebes</a>. It is well cultivated; and is now subject to the Dutch, who have built a fortress here. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in it are exceeding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on one side is uncommonly deep. It produces nutmegs and cloves, as well as cocoa and banana trees; besides many vegetables introduced by the Dutch. It is about 50 miles in circumference. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 129. S. Lat. 4. 30.

BOUTANT

Pages 420-420
or ARCH-BOUTANT, in architecture, an arch, or part of an arch, abutting against the reins of a vault to prevent its giving way. A Pillar Boutant, is a large chain or pile of stone, made to support a wall, terrace, or vault. BOUTÉ, in the manege. A horse is called bouté when his legs are in a straight line from the knee to the coronet: short-jointed horses are apt to be bouté, and on the other hand long-jointed horses are not.

BOUTON

Pages 420-420

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean, about 12 miles distant from the south-east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the island of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACASSAR">Macassar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELEBES">Celebes</a>. The inhabitants are small but well shaped, and of a dark olive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town is Callafjung, which is about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on the top of a small hill, and round it a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> wall. The houses are not built upon the ground, but on posts. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the inhabitants is Mahometanism. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 122. 30. S. Lat. 4. 30.

BOUTS RIMES

Pages 420-420

a popular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in the French <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>; signifying certain rhymes, disposed in order, and given to a poet together with a subject, to be filled up with verses ending in the same words, and the same order. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the bouts-rimes is owing to one Du <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a>, a poet, in the year 1649. In fixing the bouts, it is usual to choose such as seem the remotest, and have the least connection. Some good authors fancy that these rhymes are of all others the easiest, that they assist the invention, and furnish the most new thoughts of all others. Sarrafin has a poem on the defeat of the bouts-rimes. The academy of Lanternists at Thoulouse have contributed towards keeping in countenance the bouts-times, by proposing each year a set of fourteen, to be filled upon the glories of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> monarch; the victorious sonnet to be rewarded with a fine medal.—An influence hereof may be given in the following one, filled up by P. Commire. Tout est grand dans le roi, l'aspect seul de son buste Rend nos fiers ennemis plus froids que des glaçons, Et Guillaume n'attend que le temps des moissons, Pour se voir succomber sous un bras si robuste, Qu'on ne nous vante plus les <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> d'Auguste; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> de bien regner lui ferait des leçons; Horace en vain l'égale aux dieux dans ses chansons: Moins que mon héros il eut sage et juife, &c.

BOUVILLON

Pages 420-420

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Luxemburg in the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 0. N. Lat. 49. 55.

BOVEY COAL

Pages 409-409

an inflammable fossil found in England, France, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, &c. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> brownish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and of a laminar structure. It is composed of wood, penetrated by petrol or bitumen; and frequently contains pyrites, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, and vitriol.

BOVINES

Pages 411-411

a small town of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAMUR">Namur</a>, seated on the river Maëse <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Meuse, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 50. N. Lat. 49. 45.

BOVINIO

Pages 411-411

an episcopal town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPITANATA">Capitanata</a>, seated at the foot of the Apennine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16. 15. N. Lat. 41. 17.

BOVIUM

Pages 411-411

(Itinerary); a town of the Silures, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, fifteen miles to the south of Isca Silurum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAERLEON">Caerleon</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONMOUTHSHIRE">Monmouthshire</a>: now called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COWBRIDGE">Cowbridge</a>; according to Baudrand, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANGOR">Bangor</a> in Carnarvonshire.

BOW

Pages 420-422

(arcus), a weapon of offence made of wood, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, which, after being strongly bent, by means of a string fastened to its two ends, in returning to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state throws out an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> force. It is also called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>-bow, by way of distinction from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-bow or arbalist. The bow is the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, and the most universal of of all weapons. It has been found to obtain among the most barbarous and remote people, and who had the least <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the rest of mankind. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the bow and arrow was first abolished in France under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XII. in 1481, and in their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> were introduced the Swiss arms, that is, the halberd, pike, and broadsword. The long-bow was formerly in great vogue in England; most of our victories in France were acquired by it; and many laws were made to regulate and encourage its use. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> under Henry VIII. complain "of the disuse of the long-bow, heretofore the safeguard and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and the dread and terror of its enemies." 33 Hen. VIII. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 6. The art of using bows is called <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHERY">archery</a>, and those practised therein, archers, or bowmen. See Archery. The strength of a bow may be calculated on this principle, that its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, i.e., the power whereby it restores itself on its natural position, is always proportionate to the distance or space it is removed therefrom. The most barbarous nations often excel in the fabric of the particular things which they have the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> for in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> offices of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. The Laplanders, who support themselves almost entirely by hunting, have an art of making bows, which we, in these improved parts of the world, have never arrived at. Their bow is made of two pieces of tough and strong wood, shaved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the same size, and flattened on each side; the two flat sides of the pieces are brought closely and evenly together, and then joined by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a> made of the skins of perch, which they have in great plenty, and of which they make a glue superior in strength to any which we have. The two pieces, when once united in this manner, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> never separate, and the bow is of much more force to expel the arrow, than it could possibly have been under the same dimensions <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> made of only one piece. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, the bow-string, called τεξίσις, was made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and hence also called ιχνευμα; though <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s bow-strings are frequently made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> cut into small thongs; whence τεξίσις βούνος. The uppermost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the bow, to which the string was fastened, was called κορώνη, being <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> made of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, and the last thing towards finishing the bow. The Grecian bows were frequently beautified with gold or silver; whence we have mention of aurei arcus; and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> is called Ἀργυρόπτερος. But the matter of which they were ordinarily composed, seems to have been wood; though they were anciently, Scythian-like, made of horn, as appears from that of Pandarus in Homer, Iliad. 2. v. 105. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the bow is usually ascribed to Apollo, and was communicated to the primitive inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, who are said to have been the first of mortals who undertook the use of bows and arrows. And hence, even in later ages, the Cretan bows were famous, and preferred by the Greeks to all others. Some, however, rather choose to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> Perseus, the son of Perleus, with the invention of the bow; while others ascribe it to Scythes, son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, and progenitor to the Scythians, who were excellent at this art, and by many reputed the first masters of it. From them it was derived to the Grecians, some of whose ancient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> were instructed by the Scythians in the use of the bow, which in those days passed for a most princely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. It was first introduced into the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The Indians still retain the bow. In the repository of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> we see a West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> bow two yards long. The Scythian bow was famous for its incurvation, which distinguished it from the bows of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and other nations; being so great as to form an half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a>; whence the shepherd in Athenaeus, being to describe the letters in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a>'s name, and expressing each of them by some apposite resemblance, compares the third to the Scythian bow; meaning not the more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> character Σ, but the ancient Κ, which is semicircular, and bears the third place in ΘΗΣΕΥΣ. Gros-Bow, is also called arbalest or arbaltes; which word is derived from arbaliata, e.i. arcubalista, "a bow with a fling." The arbalest consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> bow, let in a shaft of wood, furnished with a string and a trigger; and is bent with a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> fitted for that purpose. It serves to throw bullets, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> arrows, darts, &c. The ancients had large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> for throwing many arrows at once, called arbalests or barbette. Bow, is also an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, for taking the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a>; consisting of a large <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of 90° graduated, a thank or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, a side vane, a sight vane, and an horizon vane. It is now out of use. Bow, among builders, a beam of wood or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, with three long screws that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> a lathe of wood or steel to any arch; chiefly used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> draughts of ships and projections of the sphere, or wherever it is requisite to draw large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>. Bow, in Music, a small machine, which, being drawn over the strings of a musical instrument, makes it resound. It is composed of a small stick, to which are fastened 80 or 100 horse hairs, and a screw which serves to give these hairs a proper tension. In order that the bow may touch the strings briskly, it is usual to rub the hairs with rosin. The ancients do not appear to have been acquainted with bows of hair: in lieu thereof they touched their instruments with a plectrum; over which our bows have great advantage, for giving long and short sounds, and other modifications which a plectrum cannot produce. Bow, among artificers, an instrument so called from its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; in use among gunsmiths, locksmiths, watchmakers, &c., for making a drill go. Among turners it is the name of that pole fixed to the ceiling, to which they fasten the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> that whirls round the piece to be turned. Bow, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a> in England, 188 miles west from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and a little to the west of Crediton, has a weekly market, and two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> in the year. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a> is commonly kept here. Bows of a Saddle, are two pieces of wood laid archwise to receive the upper part of a horse's back, to give the saddle its due form, and to keep it tight. The fore-bow which sustains the pommel, is composed of the withers, the breasts, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> or toes, and the coking. The hind-bow bears the torsequin or quilted roll. The bows are covered with finewax, that is, with bulls pizzles beaten, and so run all over the bows to make them stronger. Then they are strengthened with bands Bow of iron to keep them tight: and on the lower side are nailed on the saddle-straps, with which they make fast the girths. Bow, Epaule, in Ship <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, the rounding part of a ship's side forward, beginning at the place where the planks arch inwards; and terminated where they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, at the stem or prow. It is proved by a variety of experiments, that a ship with a narrow bow is much better calculated for sailing swiftly, than one with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> bow; but is not so well fitted for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> sea, into which she always pitches or plunges her fore-part very deep, for want of sufficient breadth to repel the volume of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> which she so easily divides in her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. The former of these is called by seamen a lean, and the other a bluff bow. "The bow which meets with the least resistance in a direct course, not only meets with the least resistance in oblique courses, but also has the additional <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of driving the least to leeward; which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> advantage gained by forming the bow so as to give it that figure which will be least resisted in moving through any medium." On the Bow, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>, an arch of the horizon comprehended between some distant object and that point of the compass which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> a-head, or to which the ship's stern is directed. This phrase is equally applicable when the object is beheld from the ship, or discovered by trigonometrical calculation: As, We <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a fleet at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> three points on the starboard-bow: that is, three points from that part of the horizon which is right a-head, towards the right-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. See the article Bearing. Bow-dye, a kind of scarlet <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, superior to madder; but inferior to the true scarlet grain for fixedness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. It was brought into England, and first practised at the village of Bow, near London, by Kephler, a Dutchman, in the year 1643. Bow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, in the sea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, a frame or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> or junks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a>, used to be laid out at the bows, stems, and sides of ships, to preserve them from great flukes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>, chiefly when they fail in high <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> or south latitudes. Bow-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>, or Bow-wheel, an engine for catching fish, chiefly lobsters and craw-fish, made of two round wicker baskets, pointed at the end, one of which is thrust into the other; at the mouth is a little rim, four or five inches broad, somewhat bent inwards. It is also used for catching sparrows. Bow-legged, or Bandy-legged. Some children are bow-legged from their birth; others become so from setting them on their feet too early. The tibia of some is crooked; the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> of others are distorted; from a fault in the ankle, the feet of some are turned inwards. These are called varus; and in others, who are called valgus, they are turned outwards. The best method of preventing these disorders in weakly children is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> them duly, but not violently, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> or toying them about in one's arms; and not setting them much upon their feet, at least not without properly supporting them: if the disorder attends at the birth, or increases after it is begun, apply emollients, then apply boots of strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, wood, &c. so as gradually to dispose the crooked legs to a proper form; or other instruments may be used instead of boots, which, when not too costly, are usually to be preferred. Slighter instances of these disorders yield to careful nursing, without instruments. Bow Line, or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOWLING">Bowling</a>, a rope fastened near the middle of the leech, or perpendicular edge of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> sails, by three or four subordinate parts called bridles. It is only used when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> is so unfavourable that the sails must be all braced sideways, or close hauled to the wind: in this situation the bow-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> are employed to keep the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a> edges of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> sails tight, forward, and steady, without which they would always be shivering, and rendered incapable of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. To check the bow-line is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLACKEN">slacken</a> it, when the wind becomes large. Bow Pieces, are the pieces of ordnance at the bow of a ship. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">Rain</a>-Bow. See Rain-Bow. Bow-Bearer, an inferior officer of the forest, who is sworn to make <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> of all trespasses against venison, and to attach offenders.

BOWER

Pages 422-422

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> under <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVERT">covert</a> of trees, differing only from an arbour, as being round <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and made with a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOME">dome</a> or ceiling at top; whereas the arbour is always built <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and arched. Bower, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, the name of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> carried at the bow of a ship. There are generally two bowers, called first and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and little, or best and small bower. See Anchor.

BOWESS

Pages 422-422
or Bowet, in Falconry; a young hawk, when he draws any thing out of her nest, and covets to clamber on the boughs.

BOWLER-STONES

Pages 422-422

small <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of a roundish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and no determinate size, found on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shore, and on banks <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather channels of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>.

BOWLING

Pages 422-423

the art of playing at bowls.—This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> is practised either in open places, as barns and bowling-greens, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in cloe-bowling-alleys. The skill of bowling depends much on a knowledge of the ground, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> choice of a bowl suitable to it: for cloe alleys, the flat bowl; for green fowards plain and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, the bowl as round as a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> is preferred. The terms used in bowling are, to bowl wide, which is when the bias does not hold, or is not strong enough; narrow, when it is too strong, or holds too much; finely bowled, is when the ground is well chosen, and the bowl passes near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>, even though it goes much beyond it: bowling through, or a yard over, is done in order to move the block; an over-bowl, that which goes beyond it; a bowl laid at band, is that put <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> within the gamester's reach, to be in the way of the next bowler, and hinder his having the advantage of the best ground; bowling at length, neither bowling through nor short; a dead length, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> or exact one; throwing or flinging, is discharging a bowl with a strength purposely too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> for a length, in order to carry off either the block or some near bowl; bowl-room, or milling-room, is when a bowl has free passage, without striking on any other; get off, is when a bowl being being narrow, is wanted to be wider; bowl left at block, that nearest the block: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> or bowl, is to win it by bowling nearer, without stirring either the bowl or block; a bowl is said to rub, when it meets with some obstacle in the ground, which retards its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, and weakens its force; it is gone, when far beyond the block. Block signifies a little bowl laid for a mark, also called a jack. Mark, is a proper bowling distance, not under so many yards; and being at least a yard and a half from the edge of the green. Ground, a bag or handkerchief laid down to mark where a bowl is to go. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">Lead</a>, the advantage of throwing the block, and bowling first. Cast, is one left bowl at an end. End, a <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a>, or when all the bowls are out. The game, or up, is five casts or left bowls. Bowling-Green, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, a kind of parterre in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>, laid with fine turf, requiring to be frequently mowed, laid out in compartments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> figures, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DWARF">dwarf</a>-trees and other decorations. Bowling-greens are of English origin, but have been adopted by the French and Italians, who have them only for ornament; being unacquainted with or not fancying the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, on account of which they were first made in England. Bowling-Bridles, are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> by which the bow-line is fastened to the leech of the sail.

BOWSE

Pages 423-423

in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, signifies as much as to hale <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pull. Thus <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOWLING">bowling</a> upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TACK">tack</a>, is hauling upon a tack. Bowse away, that is, Pull away all together.

BOWSPRIT

Pages 423-423
or BOLTSPRIT, a kind of mast, resting floppewise on the head of the main stern, and having its lower end fastened to the partners of the foremast, and farther supported by the fore stay. It carries the sprit-sail, sprit-top-sail, and jack-staff; and its length is usually the same with that of the foremast.

BOWYER

Pages 423-425

WILLIAM, the most learned printer of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Friars in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 17, 1609. His father, whose name also was William, had been eminent in the same profession; and his maternal grandfather (<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Dawes) was employed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> the celebrated Polyglott <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">bible</a> of Bishop Walton. At a proper age, he was placed for grammatical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> under the care of Mr <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a> Bonwicke, a nonjuring clergyman of known piety and learning, who then lived at Headly, near Leatherhead in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>. Here Mr Bowyer made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advances in literature, and a firm <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> commenced between him and his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. On the 30th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1713, the whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the elder Mr Bowyer was destroyed by fire; on which occasion Mr Bonwicke generously undertook the education of his pupil for one year. In 1716, young Mr Bowyer was admitted a fellow at St John's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where Dr Robert Jenkin was at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> master. He <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> at the college of Cambridge under the tuition of the reverend Dr John Newcomb till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1722, during which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he probably took his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of bachelor of arts; and it appears that he was desirous of obtaining a fellowship, though it is not certain that he ever stood a candidate for that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. Soon after this he had an opportunity of repaying the kindness which Mr Bonwicke had shown him, by officiating some time after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in the capacity of a schoolmaster for the benefit of his family. Mr Bowyer now entered into the printing business along with his father. One of the first books which received the benefit of his correction was the complete edition of Selden in three volumes folio by Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Wilkins. This edition was begun in 1722, and finished in 1726; and Mr Bowyer's great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to it appeared in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up an epitome of Selden de Synedris, as he read the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>-sheets. In 1727, he drew up an excellent sketch of William Baxter's Glossary of the Roman Antiquities. This was called "A view of a book entitled Reliquia Baxteriana." In a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to a friend. A single sheet 8vo. By this first public proof of Mr Bowyer's abilities, Dr Wotton and Mr Clarke were highly pleased; but as it was never published, and very few copies printed, it is very seldom found with the glossary. In 1727 Mr Bowyer lost his mother; on which occasion he received a letter of consolation from Mr Chishull the learned editor of the Antiquitates Anglicanae. In October 1728 he married Miss Ann Prudom, his mother's niece, a very accomplished lady, by whom he had two sons, William and Thomas; the former of whom died an infant, and the latter survived his father. In 1729 Mr Bowyer published a curious treatise, entitled, "A Pattern for young Students in the University; set forth in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Ambrose Bonwicke, sometime scholar of St John's College, Cambridge:" but though this treatise was generally ascribed to Mr Bowyer, it was in reality the production of Mr Ambrose Bonwicke the elder. About this time it appears, that Mr Bowyer had written a pamphlet against the Separatists, though neither the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> nor the occasion of it are now remembered. The same year, through the friendship of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> Hon. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a> Onslow, he was appointed printer of the votes of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons; which office he held, under three successive speakers, for near fifty years. In 1731 Mr Bowyer published, and, it is believed, translated Voltaire's Life of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> XII. This year also his wife died; on which occasion his friends Mr Clarke and Mr Chishull wrote him very affectionate and Christian letters. He remained a widower till 1747, when he married a very benevolent and worthy woman, Mrs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">Bill</a>, by whom he had no children. In 1733 he published a piece in two sheets 4to, entitled, "The Beau and the Academic;" being a translation from a Latin poem recited that year at the Sheldonian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>; and in 1736 he was admitted into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of Antiquarians, where he became an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and useful member. In 1737 Mr Bowyer lost his father; and on this occasion Mr Clarke again addressed to him a letter of consolation. In 1742 our author published a translation of Trapp's Latin Lectures on <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, in which he was assisted by Mr Clarke, though the latter had a contemptible <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the performance. In 1749, Mr Bowyer, along with Dr Burton, was virulently attacked by Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> in a piece entitled Elogium famae inferiens Jacobi Ettenensis five Gigantis: <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, "The praises of Jack Eaton, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Jack the Giant."—This abuse was probably occasioned by Mr Bowyer's having hinted in conversation some doubts concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>'s skill in Latin. Our author drew up some strictures in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, which he intended to insert at the conclusion of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to Montesquieu's Reflections; but by Dr Clarke's advice, they they were omitted. In 1750, a prefatory critical dil- feration and some notes were annexed by our author to Kutter's Treatise De usu verborum mediorum; a new edition of which, with farther improvements, ap- peared in 1773. He wrote likewise about the same time a Latin preface to Leedes's Veteres poetarum, &c.—Being soon after employed to print an edition of Col. Bladen's translation of Caesar's Commentaries, that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> received considerable improvements from Mr Bowyer's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, with the addition of such notes in it as are signed Tyrocr. In the subsequent editions of this work, though printed by another person during our author's lifetime, the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIGNATURE">signature</a>, though contrary to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECORUM">decorum</a>, and even to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, was still retained. In 1751, he wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> preface to Montefiore's "Re- flections on the rise and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the Roman Empire;" translated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> between Sylla and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>; made several corrections to the work from the Baron's " Spirit of Laws;" and improved it with his own notes. A new edition, with many new notes, was printed in 1759. In 1751 he also published the first translation that ever was made of Rousseau's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARADOXI">paradoxi</a>- cal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORATION">oration</a>, which gained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> at the academy of Dijon in 1750; and which first announced that singular genius to the attention and admiration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. On the publication of the third edition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORRERY">Orrery</a>'s " Remarks on the Life and Writings of Dr Swift," in 1752, Mr Bowyer wrote and printed, but never pub- lished, "Two Letters from Dr Bentley in the Shades below, to Lord Orrery in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">Land</a> of thick darkness." The notes signed B, in the ninth quarto volume of Swift's works, are extracted from these letters. In 1753, he endeavoured to allay the ferment occasioned by the Jew bill; with which view he published, in quarto, "Remarks on the speech made in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>- <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, on the bill for permitting persons professing the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> to be naturalized, so far as proph- ecies are supposed to be affected by it." This little tract was written with spirit, and well received by those who were superior to narrow prejudices. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was to show, that whatever <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> reasons might be alleged against the bill, Christianity was in no danger of being prejudiced by the intended protection promised to the Jews. The same year some of Mr Bowyer's notes were annexed to Bishop Clatton's translation of "A Journal from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a> to Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SINAI">Sinai</a> and back again."—In 1754, Mr Bowyer, with a view of lessening his fatigue, entered into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a> with a relation; but some disagreement arising, the connection was dissolved in three years. On the death of Mr Richardson in 1761, Mr Bowyer succeeded him as printer to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Society, through the favour of the late <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of Macclesfield; and, under the friend- ship of five successive presidents, enjoyed that office till his death. In 1763, Mr Bowyer published an excellent edition of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, in two vols. 12mo. It ap- peared under the following title: Novum Testamentum Graecum; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> fidem Graecorum folum Codicum MSS. nunc primum impressum, adiungantur Joanne Jacobo Weiffenius, justa Selectione Jo. Alberti Bengelii divulgata; et nova interpretatione sapientium illustrata. Accedere in altero volumine, Emendationes conjecturales virorum doc- torum undecunque collectae. This fold with great rapid- ity; the Conjectural Emendations were well received by the learned, and are thought to be a valuable work. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> and fellows of Harvard college in Cam- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> expressed their approbation of this edition in very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> terms. In a letter to Mr Bowyer, written in the year 1767, "This work (say they), though small in bulk, we esteem as a rich <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of sacred learning, and of more value than many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> volumes of the commentators." A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition of the Con- jectures on the New Testament, with very considerable enlargements, was separately published, in one vol. 8vo, in 1772. Bishop Warburton having censured a pas- sage in the former edition, Mr Bowyer sent him a copy of this book, with a conciliatory letter. Dr <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>- burton's Divine Legation had received very consider- able advantage from Mr Bowyer's corrections; and this even in an edition which was necessarily given to another press. In 1761 he was employed to print his Lordship's Doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a>. A second edition be- ing soon wanted, and Mr Bowyer not having been in- trusted with the care of it, he prepared a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of let- ters to the bishop in his own defence; of which, to- gether with a few he had formerly received from that great writer, he afterwards printed twelve copies, of which ten have since been destroyed. However, there is the best authority for asserting, that notwithstanding any little alterations which happened, Dr War- burton always retained a sincere regard for our au- thor. In 1765, at the request of Thomas Hollis, Esq., Mr Bowyer wrote a short Latin preface to Dr Wallis's Grammatica Linguae Anglicane. He wrote also a large English preface for the same work, which, however, still remains unprinted. In 1766 he entered into partnership with Mr Nichols, who had been train- ed by him to the profession, and had for several years assisted him in the management of his business. The same year, Mr Bowyer wrote an excellent Latin pre- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> to Joannis Harduii, Jesuitae, ad Centuram Scrip- turae veterum Prologomena. Juxta Autographum. In 1767 he was appointed to print the journals of the house of lords and the rolls of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. This year he printed Mr Clarke's excellent and learned work on "The Connection of the Roman, Saxon, and English Coins;" and wrote some notes upon it, which are interspersed throughout the volume with those of the author. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> of the Dissertation on the Roman leprechaun was likewise Mr Bowyer's production; and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a>, which is an uncommonly good one, was drawn up by him entirely. In January 1771 Mr Bowyer lost his second wife, and again received a letter of consolation from his old friend Mr Clarke, who had sent him one almost forty years before on a similar occasion. In the Philoso- phical Transactions for this year was printed a very inge- nious "Inquiry into the Value of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek and Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">Money</a>," by the late Matthew Raper, Esq. But his opinions not coinciding with those of Mr Bowyer, he printed a small pamphlet, entitled, "Remarks, occasioned by a late Dissertation on the Greek and Roman money." In 1773 three little tracts were published by him, under the title of "Se- lect Discourses. 1. Of the correspondence of the He- brew months with the Julian, from the Latin of Pro- fessor Michaelis. 2. Of the Sabbatical years, from the same. 3. Of the years of jubilee, from an anonymous writer in Mason's Histoire Critique de la Republique <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOWYERS">Bowyers</a>, des Lettres." In 1774 he corrected a new edition of Schrevelius's Greek Lexicon; to which he has added a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of words, distinguished by an asterisk, which he himself had collected in the course of his studies. Considerable additions, still in manuscript, were made by him to the lexicons of Hederic and Buxtorf, the Latin ones of Faber and Littleton, and the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a> of Bailey; and he left behind him many other proofs of his critical skill in the learned languages. In 1774 was published, "The Origin of Printing," in two essays. 1. The substance of Dr Middleton's Dissertation on the Origin of Printing in England. 2. Mr Meereman's Account of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">Invention</a> of the Art at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAARLEM">Haarlem</a>, and its progress to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>, with occasional Remarks, and an Appendix." The original idea of this valuable tract was Mr Bowyer's, but it was completed by Mr Nichols. Although our author, during the last ten years of his life, had been afflicted with the palsy and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, he not only preserved a remarkable cheerfulness of temper, but was enabled to support the labour of almost incessant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>; and he regularly corrected the learned works, especially the Greek books, which came from his press. This he continued to do till within a few weeks of his death, which happened in November 1777, when he had nearly completed his 78th year. For more than half a century Mr Bowyer was unrivalled as a learned printer; and many of the most masterly productions of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> have come from his press. To his literary and professional abilities he added an excellent moral character; and he was particularly distinguished by his inflexible probity, and an uncommon alacrity in relieving the necessitous.

BOWYERS

Pages 425-425

artificers whose business is to make bows: in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, bowyers stand distinguished from fletchers, who make arrows. The bowyers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> was incorporated in 1622: and consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, two wardens, twelve assistants, and 30 on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHERY">ARCHERY</a>.

BOX

Pages 425-425

in its most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> acceptation, denotes a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEST">chest</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> coffer for holding things. Dice-Box, a narrow deep casket, channelled within, wherein the dice are shaken and thrown. This answers to what the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> called fritillus; whence, crepitantes fritillae; and, in Seneca, resonantia fritillo. The same author uses also concurre fritillum, figuratively, for playing.—Besides the fritillus, the Romans, for greater security, had another kind of dice-box called pyrgus, wugae, and sometimes turrícula. It was placed immovable in the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, being perforated or open at both ends, and likewise channelled within; over the top was placed a kind of funnel, into which the dice were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> out upon the fritillus; whence descending, they fell through the bottom on the table; by which all practising on them with the fingers was effectually prevented. For want of some contrivance of this kind, our sharpers have opportunities of playing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> tricks with the box, as palming, topping, flabbing, &c. Box, is also used for an uncertain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>: thus a box of quicksilver contains from one to two hundred <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; a box of prunellas only 14 pounds; a box of rings for keys, two groats, &c. Box-Tree. See Buxus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. African Box. See Myrsine, Botany Index.

BOXERS

Pages 425-425

a kind of athletæ, who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> contend for victory with their fists. Boxers amount to the same with what among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were called pugiles. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> boxers battled with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> force and fury, infomuch as to dash out each other's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, and often kill each other. The strange disfigurements these boxers underwent were such that they frequently could not be known, and rendered them the subject of many railleries. In the Greek anthology there are four epigrams of the poet Lucilius, and one of Lucian, wherein their disfigurements are pleasantly enough exposed. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOXING">BOXING</a>.

BOXHORNIUS

Pages 425-425

MARC ZUERIUS, a learned critic born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERGEN_OP_ZOOM"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol0.html#article-BERGEN">Bergen</a>-op-Zoom in 1612, was professor of eloquence at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, and at length of politics and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> in the room of Heinsius. He published, 1. Theatrum urbium Hollandiae. 2. Scriptores historici Auguṣtæ, cum notis. 3. Poetæ satyrici minores, cum comment. 4. Notes on Justin, Tacitus; and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of other works. He died in 1653, aged 41.

BOXING

Pages 425-426

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of fighting with the fists, either naked <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or leaden <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> grasped in them: in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, boxing coincides with the pugilatus of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and what on our amphitheatres is sometimes called <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of manhood. When the champions had επίμαχοι, or balls, whether of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> or stone, it was properly denominated επίμαχος. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> boxing differed from the pugna caelum, in which the combatants had leathern thongs on their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and balls to offend their antagonists; though this distinction is frequently overlooked, and fighting with the caelus ranked as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the bufines of pugiles. We may distinguish three <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of boxing; viz. where both the head and hands were naked; where the hands were armed and the head naked; and where the head was covered with a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, called amphiodes, and the hands also furnished with the caelus. Boxing is an ancient exercise, having been in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in the heroic ages. Those who prepared themselves for it, used all the means that could be contrived to render themselves fat and fleshy, that they might be better able to endure blows: whence corpulent men or women were usually called pugiles, according to Terence: Siqua efl habitoor paulo, pugilem efse aiunt. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times this art has been in a manner appropriated by the English. About half a century ago it formed as regular an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> as we now see at any of the places of public amusement, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a> alone excepted. It was encouraged by the first ranks of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, patronized by the first subjects in the realm, and tolerated by the magistrates. Before the establishment of Broughton's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, a booth was erected at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOTTENHAM">Tottenham</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a>, in which the proprietor, Mr George Taylor, invited the professors of the art to display their skill, and the public to be present at its exhibition. The bruisers then had the reward due to their prowess, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the entrance-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, which sometimes was 100l. or 150l. The general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of sharing was for two thirds to go to the winning champion, while the remaining third was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of the loser; though sometimes by an express agreement of the parties, the conqueror and the vanquished shared alike. The nobility and gentry having complained of the inconveniences sustained at Taylor's Booth, prevailed on Mr Broughton, who was then... then rising into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> as the first builder in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, to build a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> better adapted for such exhibitions. This was accordingly done in 1742, principally by subscription, behind <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> was called Broughton's New Amphitheatre; and, besides the stage for the combatants, had seats corresponding to the boxes, pit, and galleries, much in the same manner with those at Astley's. After a course of years, however, these exhibitions became gradually less patronized and frequented, owing probably to the refinement of our manners. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> ago, indeed, they seemed to be revived, and very considerably engaged the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the public; but a fatal illuse which attended one of them, brought the practice again into disrepute. One of the combatants was killed on the spot. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> highness the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> was present, and declared that he would have some settlement made on the nearest relation of the deceased, but that, on account of the dreadful example he had then witnessed, he would never more either see or patronize another stage-fight. Boxing, among sailors, is used to denote the rehearsing the several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the compass in their proper order. Boxing is also used for the tapping of a tree to make it yield its juice. The boxing of maple is performed by making a hole with an axe or chisel into the side of the tree about a foot from the ground; out of it flows a liquor of which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> is made.

BOXTEHUDE

Pages 426-426

a town of Germany, in the circle of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, subject to the Danes. It is seated on the rivulet Eife, which falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 35', N. Lat. 53° 40'.

BOXTEL

Pages 426-426

a town in Dutch Brabant, with sluices seated on the river Bommel. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 15'. N. Lat. 51° 30'.

BOYAR

Pages 426-426

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEE">grandee</a> of Russia and Transylvania.
