Beccan says, that the boyars are the upper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>; and adds, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CZAR">Czar</a> of Muscovy, in his diplomas, names the boyars before the waywodes. See Waywode.

BOYAU

Pages 426-426

in Fortification, a ditch covered with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a>, which serves as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between two trenches. It runs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the works of the body of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and serves as a line of contravallation, not only to hinder the fallies of the besieged, but also to secure the miners. But when it is a particular cut that runs from the trenches to cover some spot of ground, it is drawn so as not to be enfiladed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> scoured by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> from the town.

BOYD

Pages 426-426

Mark Alexander, an extraordinary genius, was son of Robert Boyd, who was eldest son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> Boyd of Pinkhill, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Boyd. He was born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a> on the 13th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1562, and came into the world with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>. He learned the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of the Latin and Greek languages at Glasgow under two grammarians; but was of so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and untractable a spirit, that they despaired of ever making him a scholar. Having quarrelled with his masters, he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> them both, burnt his books, and forswore learning. While he was yet a youth, he followed the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and did his utmost to push his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> there; but the fervour of his temper soon precipitated him into quarrels, from which he came off with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and safety, though frequently at the hazard of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He, with the approbation of his friends, went to serve in the French <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and carried his little patrimony with him, which he soon dissipated at play. He was shortly after routed by that emulation which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> minds, and applied himself to letters with unremitting ardour, till he became one of the most consummate scholars of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He is said to have translated Caesar's Commentaries into Greek in the style of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, and to have written many Latin poems which were little inferior to the first productions of the Augustan age. He also left several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> on philological, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a>, and historical subjects, in Latin and French, which languages were as familiar to him as his native tongue. He could with facility dictate to three amanuenses at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, in different languages, and on different subjects. He was also one of the best Scottish poets of the age. To all this we must add, that his personal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and accomplishments were equal to his mental superiority. He died at Pinkhill in Scotland, in 1601. The following works, which are all that have been printed, were published in the Deliciæ Poetarum Scotorum; Amstel. 1637, 12mo. 1. Epigrammatæ, lib. ii. 2. Hieroidum Epistle XIV. lib. ii. 3. Hymni XIV.

BOYER

Pages 426-426
Abel, a well-known glossographer and historiographer, born at Caëres in France, in 1664. Upon the revocation of the edict of Nantes, he went first to Geneva, then to Franeker, where he finished his studies; and came finally to England, where he applied himself to assiduously to the study of the English language, and made so great a proficiency therein, that he became an author of considerable note in it, being employed in the writing of several periodical and political works. He was for many years concerned in a newspaper called the Post-boy, of which he had the principal management. He likewise published a monthly work entitled the Political State of Great Britain. He wrote a life of Queen Anne in folio, which is esteemed a very good chronicle of that period of the English history. But what has rendered him the most known, and has most firmly established his reputation, are the excellent Dictionary and Grammar of the French language, which he compiled, and which are still reckoned the best in their kind. He also wrote, or rather translated from the French of M. de Racine, the tragedy of Iphigenia, which he published under the title of The Victim. It was performed with success at the theatre of Drury-lane, and is far from being a bad play. Nor can there perhaps be a stronger instance of the abilities of its author, than success in such an attempt; since writing with any degree of correctness or elegance, even in prose, in a foreign language, is an excellence not very frequently attained; but to proceed so far in the perfection of it as to be even tolerable in poetry, and more especially in that of the drama, in which the diction and manner of expression require a peculiar dignity and force, and in a language so difficult to attain the perfect command of as the English, is what has been very seldom accomplished. He died in 1729. Boyer, in Navigation, a kind of Flemish sloop, or small vessel of burden, having a boltspirit, a cante at each end, and a tall mast; chiefly fit for the navigation of rivers, and in many of its parts resembling a smack.

BOYES

Pages 426-427

idolatrous priests among the savages of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLORIDA">Florida</a>. Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> attends a particular idol, and the natives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> themselves to the priest of that idol to which they intend to pay their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. The idol is invoked in hymns, and his usual offering is the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>.

BOYLE

Pages 427-435

Roger, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORRERY">Orrery</a>, younger <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the former, and the fifth son of Richard, styled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> earl of Cork, was born April 25, 1621; and by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of his father with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> Faulkland, raised to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Baron Broghill, when only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years old. He was educated at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, where he soon distinguished himself as an early and promising genius. He afterwards made the tour of France and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and at his return afflitted his father in opposing the rebellious Irish, in which he behaved with all the spirit of a young, and all the deference of an old, officer. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, he retired to Marston in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>, and hid himself in the privacy of a cloister retirement; but being at length ashamed to fit the tame spectator of all the mischief that appeared round him, he resolved to attempt something in favour of the king; and under the pretence of going to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPA">Spa</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, he determined to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> the seas, and apply himself to King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> to raise what forces he could in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in order to restore his majesty, and recover his own estate. To this purpose, he prevailed on the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a> to procure a licence for his going to the Spa; and having raised a considerable sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, came up to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> to prosecute his voyage; but he had not been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> in town when he received a message from Cromwell, who was then general of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>'s forces, that he intended to wait upon him. The lord Broghill was surprized at this message, having never had the least acquaintance with Cromwell; and desired the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> to let the general know, that he would wait upon his excellency. But while he was waiting the return of the messenger, Cromwell entered the room; and after mutual civilities had passed between them, told him in few words, that the committee of state were apprised of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of going over and applying to Charles Stuart for a commission to raise forces in Ireland; and that they were determined to make an example of him, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he himself had not diverted them from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>. The lord Broghill interrupted him, by affirming him that the intelligence which the committee had received was false; and that he neither was in a capacity nor had any inclination to raise disturbances in Ireland: but Cromwell, instead of making any reply, drew some papers out of his pocket, which were the copies of several letters which the lord Broghill had sent to those persons in whom he most confided, and put them into his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. The lord Broghill, upon the perusal of these papers, finding it to no purpose to dissemble any longer, asked his excellency's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> for what he had said, returned him his humble thanks for his protection against the committee, and intreated his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> how to behave in such a delicate conjuncture. Cromwell told him, that though till this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he had been a stranger to his person, he was not so to his merit and character; he had heard how gallantly his lordship had behaved in the Irish wars; and therefore, since he was named lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of Ireland, and the reducing that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> was now become his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, he had obtained obtained leave of the committee to offer his lordship the command of a general officer, if he would serve in that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and he should have no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> engagements imposed upon him, nor be obliged to draw his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> against any but the Irish rebels. The lord Broghill was infinitely surprised at so generous and unexpected an offer. He <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> himself at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, by all the rules of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, to serve against the Irish, whose rebellion and barbarities were equally detested by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> party and the parliament. He desired, however, some time to consider of what had been proposed to him. But Cromwell briskly told him, that he must come to some resolution that very instant: that he himself was returning to the committee, who were still sitting; and if his lordship rejected their offer, they had determined to send him to the tower. Upon this, the lord Broghill, finding that his liberty and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> were in the utmost danger, gave his word and honour that he would faithfully serve him against the Irish rebels: on which Cromwell once more assured him, that the conditions which he had made with him should be punctually observed; and then ordered him to repair to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, adding, that he himself would soon follow him into Ireland. Lord Broghill, therefore, having settled the business of his command, went over into that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; where, by his conduct and intrepidity, he performed many important services, and fully justified the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> Cromwell had conceived of him. By his own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> he now raised a gallant troop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, consisting chiefly of gentlemen attached to him by personal friendship; which corps was soon increased to a complete regiment of 1500 men. These he led into the field against the Irish rebels; and was speedily joined by Cromwell, who placed the highest confidence in his new ally, and found him of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to the interest of the commonwealth. Among other considerable exploits performed by Lord Broghill, the following deserves to be particularly mentioned. Whilst Cromwell laid siege to Clonmel, Broghill being detached to disperse a body of 5000 men who had assembled to relieve the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, he, with 2000 horse and dragoons, came up with the enemy at Macrooms on the 10th of May 1650; and, without waiting for the arrival of his foot, immediately attacked and routed them, making their general prisoner. Then proceeding to the castle of Carrigdohid, he sent a summons to the garrison to surrender before the arrival of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERING">battering</a> cannon, otherwise they were to expect no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. His own <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> was surprised at this summons, as knowing he had not one piece of heavy cannon: but Broghill had ordered the trunks of several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> trees to be drawn at a distance by his baggage horses; which the besieged perceiving, and judging from the slowness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> that the guns must be of a vast bore, immediately capitulated. He afterwards relieved Cromwell himself at Clonmel, where that great commander happened to be so dangerously situated, that he confessed, nothing but the reasonable relief afforded him by Lord Broghill could have saved him from destruction. When Ireton sat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> before <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMERICK">Limerick</a>, he gave Broghill 600 foot and 400 horse, with orders to prevent Lord Muskerry's joining the pope's nuncio, who had got together a body of 8000 men, and was determined to attempt the relief of Limerick. Muskerry was at the head of 1000 horse and dragoons, and about 2000 foot: notwithstanding which, Lord Broghill fell resolutely upon him. The Irish, having the advantage of the ground and numbers, would have conquered, but for a stratagem of Lord Broghill. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> he desired those about him to repeat what he said; and then cried out as loud as he could, "They run, they run." The first line of the Irish looked round to see if their rear broke; and the rear seeing the faces of their friends, and hearing the shouts of the enemy, imagined that the first line was routed, and fled. The taking of Limerick, which put an end to the war in Ireland, was the consequence of this defeat. When Cromwell became protector, he sent for Lord Broghill, merely to take his advice occasionally. And we are told, that, not long after his coming to England, he formed a project for engaging Cromwell to restore the old <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. The basis of the scheme was to be a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> between the king (Charles II.) and the protector's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>. As his lordship maintained a secret correspondence with the exiled monarch and his friends, it was imagined that he was beforehand pretty sure that Charles was not adverse to the scheme, or he would not have ventured to have proposed it seriously to Cromwell; who at first seemed to think it not unfeasible. He soon changed his mind, however, and told Broghill that he thought his project impracticable: "For (said he) Charles can never forgive me the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father." In fine, the business came to nothing, although his lordship had engaged Cromwell's wife and daughter in the scheme; but he never durst let the protector know that he had previously treated with Charles about it. On the death of the protector, Lord Broghill <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> attached to his son Richard, till, when he saw that the honesty and good-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of that worthy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> would infallibly render him a prey to his many enemies, he did not think it advisable to sink with a man that he could not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a>. The dark <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> of anarchy seemed now to be hovering over the British <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. Lord Broghill saw the storm gathering, and he deemed it prudent to retire to his command in Ireland, where he shortly after had the satisfaction of seeing things take a turn extremely favourable to the design he had long been a well-wisher to, viz. that of the king's restoration. In this great event Lord Broghill was not a little instrumental; and, in consideration of his eminent services in this respect, Charles created him earl of Orrery by letters-patent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> September 5, 1660. He was soon after made one of the lords justices of Ireland; and his conduct, while at the head of affairs in that kingdom, was such as greatly added to the general esteem in which his character was held before. His lordship's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and toilsome course of life at length brought upon him some diseases and infirmities which gave him much pain and uneasiness; and a fever which fell into his feet, joined to the gout with which he was often afflicted, abated much of that vigour which he had shown in the early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his life: but his industry and application were still the same, and bent to the same purposes; as appears from his letters, which show at once a capacity, and an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to business, which do honour to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and may serve as an example to this. Notwithstanding Notwithstanding his infirmities, on the king's desiring to see his lordship in England, he went over in 1665. He found the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> in some disorder; where his majesty was on the point of removing the great earl of Clarendon, lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>; and there was also a great misunderstanding between the two royal brothers. Lord Orrery undertook to reconcile the king with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>; which he effected by prevailing on the latter to ask his majesty's pardon for some steps he had taken in support of the lord chancellor. On his return to Ireland, he found himself called to a new <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of action. The Dutch war was then at its height; and the French, in confederacy with the Hollanders, were endeavouring to stir up the allies of rebellion in Ireland. The duke de Beauport, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> of France, had formed a scheme for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> upon Ireland; but this was rendered abortive by the extraordinary diligence, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> skill, and prudent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, of Lord Orrery. But in midst of all his labours, a dispute arose, founded on a mutual jealousy of each other's greatness, betwixt him and his old friend the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a>, then lord lieutenant; the bad effects of which were soon felt by both disputants, who resorted to England to defend their respective interests and pretensions, both having been attacked by secret enemies who sagaciously many things to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>. This quarrel, though of a private beginning, became at last of a public nature; and producing first an attempt to frame an impeachment against the duke of Ormond, occasioned in the end, by the way of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, an actual impeachment against the earl of Orrery. He defended himself, however, so well against a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of high crimes, and even of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> itself, that the prosecution came to nothing. He nevertheless lost his public employments; but not the king's favour; he still came frequently to court, and sometimes to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. After this revolution in his affairs, he made several voyages to and from Ireland; was often consulted by his majesty on affairs of the utmost consequence; and on all occasions gave his opinion and advice with the freedom of an honest plain-dealing man and a sincere friend; which the king always found him, and respected him accordingly. In 1678, being attacked more cruelly than ever by his old enemy the gout, he made his last voyage to England for advice in the medical way. But his disorder was beyond the power of medicine; and having in his last illness given the strongest proofs of Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, manly courage, and rational fortitude, he breathed his last on the 16th of October 1679, in the 59th year of his age. His lordship wrote, 1. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled "The Art of War." 2. Parthenilla, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>, in one volume folio. 3. Several poems. 4. Dramatic pieces, two volumes. 5. State-tracts, in one volume folio, &c. Mr Walpole, speaking of this nobleman, says, he never made a bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> but as a poet. As a soldier, his bravery was distinguished, his stratagems remarkable. As a statesman, it is sufficient to say, that he had the confidence of Cromwell. As a man, he was grateful, and would have supported the son of his friend; but, like Cicero and Richelieu, he could not be content without being a poet; though he was ill qualified, his writings of that kind being flat and trivial. Boyle, Robert, one of the greatest philosophers as well as best men that our own or indeed any other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> has produced, was the seventh son and the 14th child of Richard earl of Cork, and born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LISMORE">Lismore</a> in the province of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a> in Ireland, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 25, 1626-7. Before he went to school, he was taught to write a very fair <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and to speak French and Latin, by one of the earl's chaplains, and a Frenchman that he kept in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. In the year 1635, his father sent him over to England, in order to be educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETON">Eton</a> school, under Sir Henry Wotton, who was the earl of Cork's old friend and acquaintance. Here he soon discovered a force of understanding which promised great things, and a disposition to cultivate and improve it to the utmost. While he remained at Eton, there were several very extraordinary accidents that befell him, of which he has given us an account; and three of which were very near proving fatal to him. The first was, the sudden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the chamber where he was lodged, when himself was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>; when, besides the danger he run of being crushed to pieces, he had certainly been choked with the dust during the time he lay under the rubbish, if he had not had presence of mind enough to have wrapped his head up in the sheet, which gave him an opportunity of breathing without hazard. A little after this, he had been crushed to pieces by a starting horse that rose up suddenly, and threw himself backwards, if he had not happily disengaged his feet from the stirrups, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> himself from his back before he fell. A third accident proceeded from the carelessness of an apothecary's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, who, by mistaking the phials, brought him a strong vomit instead of a cooling julep. He remained at Eton, upon the whole, between three and four years; and then his father carried him to his own seat at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STALBRIDGE">Stalbridge</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>, where he remained for some time under the care of one of his chaplains who was the parson of the place. In 1638, he attended his father to London; and remained with him at the Savoy, till his brother Mr Francis Boyle espoused Mrs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> Killigrew; and then, towards the end of October, within four days after the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, the two brothers, Francis and Robert, were sent abroad upon their travels, under the care of Mr Marcomb. They embarked at Rye in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, and from thence proceeded to Dieppe in Normandy; then they travelled by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a>, so to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and from thence to Lyons; from which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> they continued their journey to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, where his governor had a family; and there the two gentlemen pursued their studies without interruption. Mr Boyle, during his stay here, resumed his acquaintance with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, or at least with the elements of that science, of which he had before gained some knowledge. For he tells us in his own <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a>, that while he was at Eton, and afflicted with an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGUE">ague</a>, before he was ten years old, by way of diverting his melancholy, they made him read Amadis de <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, and other romantic books, which produced such a restlessness in him, that he was obliged to apply himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUBE">cube</a> roots, and to the more laborious operations of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>, in order to fix and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the volatile operations of his fancy. In September 1641, he quitted Geneva, after having spent 21 months in that city; and passing through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> Switzerland and the country of the Grifons, entered <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a>. Then, taking his route through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERGAMO">Bergamo</a>, Brescia, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>, he arrived at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>; where having made a short stay, he returned to the continent, and spent the winter at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>. Here he employed his spare hours in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> in Italian, and the works of the celebrated astronomer Galileo, who died in a village near this city during Mr Boyle's residence in it. It was at Florence that he acquired the Italian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; which he understood perfectly, though he never spoke it so fluently as the French. Of this indeed he was such a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, that as occasion required he passed for a native of that country in more places than one during his travels. About the end of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1642, he began his journey from Florence to Rome, which took up but five days. He surveyed the numerous curiosities of that city; among which, he tells us, "he had the fortune to see Pope Urban VIII. at chapel, with the cardinals, who, feverishly appearing mighty princes, in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> looked like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> friars." He visited the adjacent villages which had anything curious or antique belonging to them; and had probably made a longer stay, had not the heats disagreed with his brother. He returned to Florence; from thence to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a>; and so by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>: then passing through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Nice, he crossed the sea to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIBES">Antibes</a>, where he fell into danger from refusing to honour the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRUCIFIX">crucifix</a>: from thence he went to Marigues by land. He was in that city, in May 1642, when he received his father's letters, which informed him that the rebellion had broken out in Ireland, and how difficultly he had procured the 250l. then remitted to them in order to help them home. They never received this money; and were obliged to go to Geneva with their governor Marcombes, who supplied them with as much at least as carried them thither. They continued there a considerable time, without either advice or supplies from England; upon which Marcombes was obliged to take up some jewels upon his own credit, which were afterwards disposed of with as little loss as might be; and with the money thus raised, they continued their journey for England, where they arrived in the year 1644. On their arrival, Mr Boyle found his father dead; and though the earl had made an ample provision for him, by leaving him his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> of Stalbridge in England, as well as other considerable estates in Ireland, yet it was some time before he could receive any money. However, he procured protections for his estates in both kingdoms from the powers then in being; from which he also obtained leave to go over to France for a short space, probably to settle accounts with his governor Mr Marcombes. In March 1646, he retired to his manor at Stalbridge, where he resided for the most part till May 1650. He made excursions sometimes to London, sometimes to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; and in February 1647, he went over to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>: but he made no considerable stay anywhere. During his retirement at Stalbridge, he applied himself with incredible industry to studies of various kinds, to those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> in particular. He omitted no opportunity of obtaining the acquaintance of persons distinguished for parts and learning; to whom he was in every respect a ready, useful, generous assistant, and with whom he held a constant correspondence. He was also one of the first members of that small but learned body of men which, when all academical studies were interrupted by the civil wars, seceded themselves about the year 1645; and held private meetings, first in London, afterwards at Oxford, for the sake of canvassing subjects of natural knowledge upon that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of experiment which Lord <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> had delineated. They styled themselves then The philosophic college; and, after the Restoration, when they were incorporated, and distinguished openly, they took the name of the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> of 1654, he put in execution a design he had formed for some time of residing at Oxford, where he chose to live in the house of one Mr Croft, an apothecary, rather than in a college, for the sake of his health, and because he had more room to make experiments. Oxford was indeed the only place at that time in England where Mr Boyle could have lived with much satisfaction; for here he found himself surrounded with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of learned friends, such as Wilkins, Wallis, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">Ward</a>, Willis, Wren, &c., suited exactly to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and who had resorted thither for the same reasons that he had done, the philosophical society being now removed from London to Oxford. It was during his residence here that he improved that admirable engine the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>; and by numerous experiments was enabled to discover several qualities of the air, so as to lay a foundation for a complete <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>. He was not, however, satisfied with this; but laboured incessantly in collecting and digesting, chiefly from his own experiments, the materials requisite for this purpose. He declared against the philosophy of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, as having in it more words than things; promising much, and performing little; and giving the inventions of men for indubitable proofs, instead of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> upon observation and experiment. He was so zealous for, and so careful about, this true method of learning by experiment, that though the Cartesian philosophy then made a great noise in the world, yet he would never be persuaded to read the works of Des Cartes, for fear he should be amused and led away by plausible accounts of things founded on conjecture, and merely hypothetical. But philosophy, and inquiries into nature, though they engaged his attention deeply, did not occupy it entirely; since we find that he still continued to pursue critical and theological studies. In these he had the affluence of some great men, particularly Dr Edward Pocock, Mr Thomas Hyde, and Mr Samuel Clarke, all of great eminence for their skill in the oriental languages. He had also a strict intimacy with Dr Thomas Barlow, at that time head keeper of the Bodleian library, and afterwards bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, a man of various and extensive learning. In the year 1659, Mr Boyle, being acquainted with the unhappy circumstances of the learned Sanderston, afterwards bishop of Lincoln, who had lost all his preferments on account of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the royal party, conferred upon him an honorary stipend of 50l. a-year. This stipend was given as an encouragement to that excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of reasoning to apply himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> of "Cates of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">Conscience</a>;" and accordingly Boyle. ingly he printed his lectures *De obligatione conscientiae*, which he read at Oxford in 1647, and dedicated them to his friend and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>. Upon the restoration of Charles II. Mr Boyle was treated with great civility and respect by the king, as well as by the two great ministers the lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> Southampton and the lord chancellor Clarendon. He was solicited by the latter to enter into holy orders, not only out of regard to him and his family, but chiefly with a view to serve the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> itself; for Mr Boyle's noble family, his distinguished learning, and, above all, his unblemished reputation, induced Lord Clarendon to think that any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> preferments he might attain would be worthily discharged, so as to do honour to the clergy, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the established <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>. Mr Boyle considered all this with due attention: but, to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> these, he reflected, that, in the situation of life in which he was, whatever he wrote with respect to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> would have to much the greater <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> as coming from a layman: since he well knew that the irreligious fortified themselves against all that the clergy could offer, by supposing, and saying, that it was their trade, and that they were paid for it. He considered likewise, that, in point of fortune and character, he needed no accretions; and indeed he never had any appetite for either. He chose, therefore, to pursue his philosophical studies in such a manner as might be most effectual for the support of religion; and began to communicate to the world the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of these studies. The first of these was printed at Oxford in 1662, in 8vo, under the title of, 1. New experiments, phylico-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a>, touching the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of the air and its effects. 2. Seraphic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>; or some motives and incentives to the love of God, pathetically discoursed of in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to a friend. 3. Certain physiological essays and other tracts, 1661, 4to. 4. Sceptical chemist, 1662, 8vo; a very curious and excellent work, reprinted about the year 1679, 8vo, with the addition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> experiments and notes about the producibleness of chemical principles. In the year 1663, the Royal Society being incorporated by King Charles II. Mr Boyle was appointed one of the council; and as he might be justly reckoned among the founders of that learned body, so he continued one of the most useful and industrious of its members during the whole course of his life. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1663, he published, 5. Considerations touching the usefulness of experimental natural philosophy, 4to. 6. Experiments and considerations upon colours; to which was added a letter, containing Observations on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> that shines in the dark, 1663, 8vo. This treatise is full of curious and useful remarks on the hitherto unexplained doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and colours; in which he shows great judgment, accuracy, and penetration; and may be said to have led the way to that mighty genius the great Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, who has since let that point in the clearest and most convincing light. 7. Considerations on the style of the Holy Scriptures, 1663, 8vo. It was an extract from a larger work, entitled, "An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Scripture;" which was afterwards published by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Pett, a friend of Mr Boyle's. In 1664, he was elected into the company of the royal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>; and was all this year taken up in the prosecution of various good designs, which probably was the reason why he did not send abroad any treaties either of religion or philosophy. The year following, came forth, 8. Occasional reflections upon several subjects; whereto is prefixed a discourse about such kind of thoughts, 1665, 8vo. This piece is addressed to Sophronia, under whose name he concealed that of his beloved sister the viscountess of Ranelagh. The thoughts themselves are on a vast variety of subjects, written many years before; some indeed upon trivial occasions, but all with great accuracy of language, much <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, more learning, and in a wonderful strain of moral and pious reflection. Yet this exposed him to the only severe censure that ever was passed upon him; and that too from no less a man than the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a> Swift, who, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> these discourses, wrote A pious meditation upon a broomstick, in the style of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> Mr Boyle. But as his noble relation the late Lord Orrery has said, "To what a height must the spirit of sarcasm arise in an author, who could prevail on himself to ridicule so good a man as Mr Boyle? The sword of wit, like the scythe of time, cuts down friend and foe, and attacks every object that lies in its way. But, sharp and irresistible as the edge of it may be, Mr Boyle <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> always remain invulnerable." The same year, he published an important work, entitled, 9. New experiments and observations upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, 1665, 8vo. In the year 1666, he published, 10. Hydrological paradoxes made out by new experiments, for the most part physical and easy, in 8vo. 11. The origin of forms and qualities, according to the corpuscular philosophy, illustrated by considerations and experiments. This treatise did great honour to Mr Boyle, whether we consider the quickness of his wit, the depth of his judgment, or his indefatigable pains in searching after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. We must not forget to observe, that, both in this and the former year, he communicated to his friend Mr Oldenburgh, who was secretary to the Royal Society, several curious and excellent short treatises of his own, upon a great variety of subjects, and others transmitted to him by his learned friends both at home and abroad, which are printed and preserved in the Philosophical Transactions. In the year 1668, Mr Boyle resolved to settle in London for life: and removed for that purpose to the house of his sister, the lady Ranelagh, in Pall-Mall. This was to the infinite benefit of the learned in general, and particularly to the advantage of the Royal Society, to whom he gave great and continual assistance, as the several pieces communicated to them from time to time, and printed in their Transactions, do abundantly testify. Those who applied to him, either to desire his help, or to communicate to him any new discoveries in science, he had his set hours for receiving; otherwise it is easy to conceive that he would have had very little of his time for himself. But, besides these, he kept a very extensive correspondence with persons of the greatest figure, and most famous for learning, in all parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In the year 1669, he published, 12. A continuation of new experiments touching the weight and spring of the air; to which is added, A discourse of the atmospheres of different bodies: and the same year he revised and made many additions to several of his former tracts, some of which... which were now translated into Latin, in order to gratify the curious abroad. 13. Tracts about the comical qualities of things; comical suspicions; the temperature of the subterranean regions; the bottom of the sea: to which is prefixed an introduction to the history of particular qualities. This book occasioned much speculation, as it seemed to contain a vast <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of knowledge which had never been communicated to the world before; and this too grounded upon actual experiments, and arguments justly drawn from them, instead of that notional and conjectural philosophy which in the beginning of the 17th century had been so much in fashion. In the year 1671, he published, 14. Considerations on the usefulness of experimental and natural philosophy; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> part, 4to. And, 15. A collection of tracts upon several useful and important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of practical philosophy, 4to. Both of which works were received as new and valuable gifts to the learned world. 16. An essay about the origin and virtues of gems, 1672, 8vo. 17. A collection of tracts upon the relation between <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> and air; and several other useful and curious subjects: besides furnishing, in this and the former year, a great number of short dissertations upon a vast variety of topics, addressed to the Royal Society, and inserted in their Transactions. 18. Essays on the strange subtilty, great efficacy, and determinate nature, of effluvia; to which were added a variety of experiments on other subjects; 1673, 8vo. 19. A collection of tracts upon the saltness of the sea, the moisture of the air, the natural and preternatural state of bodies; to which is prefixed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> concerning cold; 1674, 8vo. 20. The excellency of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> compared with philosophy, 1673, 8vo. This discourse was written in the year 1665, while Mr Boyle, to avoid the great <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> which then raged in London, was forced to go from place to place in the country, and had little or no opportunity of consulting his books. It contains a great number of curious and useful, as well as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> and natural, observations. 21. A collection of tracts containing suspicions about hidden qualities of the air; with an appendix touching celestial magnets; animadversions upon Mr Hobbes's problem about a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a>; a discourse of the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> and suction; 1674, 8vo. 22. Some considerations about the reconcileable benefits of reason and religion. By T. E. a layman. To which is annexed a discourse about the possibility of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>. By Mr Boyle, 1675, 8vo. The reader must be informed, that both these pieces were of his writing; only he thought fit to mark the former with the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> letters of his name. Among other papers that he communicated this year to the Royal Society, there were two connected into one discourse: the first was entitled, An experimental discourse of quicksilver growing hot with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>: the other related to the same subject; and both of them contained discoveries of the utmost importance. In the year 1676, he published, 23. Experiments and notes about the mechanical origin or production of particular qualities, in several discourses on a great variety of subjects, and among the rest on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a>. In 1678, he communicated to Mr Hooke a short memorial of some observations made upon an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> substance that shines without any preceding illumination; which that gentleman thought fit to publish in his Lettiones Cutlerianae. 24. Historical account of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a> of gold made by an anti-elixir. This made a great noise both at home and abroad, and is looked upon as one of the most remarkable pieces that ever fell from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a>; since the facts contained in it would have been esteemed incredible, if they had been related by a man of less integrity and piety than Mr Boyle. The regard which the great Newton had for Mr Boyle, appears from a very curious letter, which the former wrote to him, at the latter end of this year, for the sake of laying before him his sentiments of that etherial medium, which he afterwards considered in his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a> as the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVITATION">gravitation</a>. This letter is to be found in the life of our author by the reverend Dr Birch. In the year 1680, Mr Boyle published, 25. The aerial noctiluca; or some new phenomena, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of a factitious self-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> substance, 8vo. This year the Royal Society, as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the just <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of his great worth, and of the constant and particular services which through a course of many years he had done them, made choice of him for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>; but he being extremely, and, as he says, peculiarly tender in point of oaths, declined the honour done him, by a letter addressed to "his much respected friend Mr Robert Hooke, professor of mathematics at Gresham college." 26. Discourse of things above reason; inquiring, whether a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> should admit any such; 1681, 8vo. 27. New experiments and observations upon the icy noctiluca: to which is added a chemical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARADOX">paradox</a>, grounded upon new experiments, making it probable that chemical principles are transmutable, so that out of one of them others may be produced: 1682, 8vo. 28. A continuation of new experiments, physic-mechanical, touching the spring and weight of the air, and their effects; 1682, 8vo. In 1683, he published nothing but a short letter to Dr Beale, in relation to the making of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> out of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. In 1684, he published two very confidential works, viz. 29. Memoirs for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural history</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> blood, especially the spirit of that liquor, 8vo; and, 30. Experiments and considerations about the porosity of bodies, &c. In 1685, Mr Boyle obliged the world with, 31. Short memoirs for the natural experimental history of mineral waters, with directions as to the several methods of trying them; including abundance of new and useful remarks, as well as several curious experiments. 32. An essay on the great effects of even languid and unheeded motion; whereunto is annexed an experimental discourse of some hitherto little regarded causes of the salubrity and infalibility of the air and its effects. None of his treaties, it is said, were ever received with greater or more general applause than this. 33. Of the reconcileable benefits of specific medicines to the corporeal philosophy; to which is annexed a discourse about the advantages of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of simple medicines; 8vo. Besides these philosophical tracts, he gave the world the same year, an excellent theological one, 34. Of the high veneration man's intellect owes to God, peculiarly for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and power, 8vo. At the entrance of the succeeding year, came abroad his, 35. Free inquiry into the vulgarly received notion of nature; a piece which was then, and will always be, greatly admired by those who have a true zeal and relish for pure religion and philosophy. In 1687, he published, 36. The martyrdom of Theodora and Diodymus; a work he had drawn up in his youth. 37. A disquisition about the final causes of natural things; wherein it is inquired, whether, and (if at all) with what caution, a naturalist should admit them; with an appendix about vitiated light; 1688, 8vo. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of May this year, our author, though very unwilling, was constrained to make his complaint to the public, of some inconveniences under which he had long laboured; and this he did by an advertisement, about "the loss of many of his writings addressed to J. W., to be communicated to those of his friends that are virtuosi; which may serve as a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to most of his mutilated and unfinished writings." He complains in this advertisement of the treatment he had met with from plagiarists both at home and abroad; and though it might have been difficult in any other man to have done so without incurring the imputation of self-conceit and vanity, yet Mr. Boyle's manner is such as only to raise in us a higher esteem and admiration of him. This advertisement is inserted at length in his life by Birch. He began now to find that his health and strength, notwithstanding all his care and caution, gradually declined, as he observes in a letter to M. le Clerc, dated May 30, 1689; which put him upon using every possible method of husbanding his remaining time for the benefit of the learned. It was with this view that he no longer communicated particular discourses, or new discoveries, to the Royal Society; because this could not be done without withdrawing his thoughts from talks which he thought of still greater importance. It was the more steadily to attend to these, that he resigned his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of governor of the corporation for propagating the gospel in New England; nay, he went so far as to signify to the world that he could no longer receive visits as usual, in an advertisement which begins in the following manner: "Mr. Boyle finds himself obliged to intimate to those of his friends and acquaintance, that are wont to do him the honour and favour of visiting him, 1. That he has by some unlucky accidents, namely, by his servant's breaking a bottle of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of vitriol over a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEST">chest</a> which contained his papers, had many of his writings corroded here and there, or otherwise impaired, that, without help himself fill up the lacunae out of his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, they will not be intelligible. 2. That his age and sicknesses have for a good while admonished him to put his scattered and partly defaced writings into some kind of order, that they may not remain quite useless. And, 3. That his skilful and friendly physician, Sir Edmund King, seconded by Mr. Boyle's best friends, has pressingly advised him against speaking daily with so many persons as are wont to visit him, representing it as what cannot but waste his spirits, &c. He ordered likewise a board to be placed over his door, with an inscription signifying when he did, and when he did not, receive visits." Among the other great works, which by this means he gained time to finish, there is great reason to believe, that one was a collection of elaborate processes in chemistry; concerning which he wrote a letter to a friend, which is still extant; wherein we read, that Boyle "he left it as a kind of hermetic legacy to the studious disciples of that art." Besides these papers committed to the care of one whom he esteemed his friend, he left very many behind him at his death, relating to chemistry; which, as appears by a letter directed to one of his executors, he desired might be inspected by three physicians whom he named, and that some of the most valuable might be preserved. In the meantime, Mr. Boyle published some other works before his death; as, 38. Medicina Hydrostatica; or, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYDROSTATICS">Hydrostatics</a> applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a>, showing how, by the weight that divers bodies used in physics have in water, one may discover whether they be genuine or adulterated. To which is subjoined a previous hydrostatical way of estimating ores, 1690, 8vo. 39. The Christian virtuoso; showing, that, by being addicted to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">experimental philosophy</a>, a man is rather assisted than indisposed to be a good Christian. To which are subjoined, 1. A discourse about the distinction that represents some things as above reason, but not contrary to reason. 2. The first chapters of a discourse entitled Greatness of mind promoted by Christianity. The last work which he published himself, was in the spring of 1691; and is entitled, 40. Experimenta et Observations Physice: wherein are briefly treated of several subjects relating to natural philosophy in an experimental way. To which is added a small collection of strange reports, 8vo. About the entrance of the summer, he began to feel such an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in his health as induced him to think of settling his affairs; and accordingly, on the 18th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, he signed and sealed his last will, to which he afterwards added several codicils. In October, his distemper increased; and on the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1691, he departed this life, in the 65th year of his age. He was buried in St. Martin's church in the Fields, Westminster, on the 7th of January following; and his funeral sermon was preached by Dr. Gilbert Burnet, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>. The bishop made choice upon this occasion of a text very apposite to the subject; namely, "For God giveth to a man that is good in his sight, wisdom, knowledge, and joy." After explaining the meaning of the words, he applied the doctrine to the honourable person deceased; of whom, he tells us, he was the better able to give a character from the many happy hours he had spent in conversation with him, in the course of 29 years. He gives a large account of Mr. Boyle's sincere and unaffected piety; and more especially of his zeal for the Christian religion, without having any narrow notions concerning it, or mistaking, as so many do, a bigotted heat in favour of a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, for that zeal which is an ornament of a true Christian. He mentions as a proof of this, his noble foundation for lectures in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the gospel against infidels of all sorts; the effects of which have been conspicuous in the many volumes of excellent discourses which have been published in consequence of that noble and pious foundation. He was at the charge of the translation and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> into the Malayan tongue, which he sent over all the East Indies. He gave a noble reward to him that translated Grotius's incomparable book "Of the truth of the Christian religion" into Arabic; and was at the charge of a whole impression, which he took care should... should be dispersed in all the countries where that language was understood. He was resolved to have carried on the impression of the New Testament in the Turkish language; but the company thought it became them to be the doers of it, and so suffered him only to give a large share towards it. He was at 100l. charge in the edition of the Irish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">bible</a>, which he ordered to be distributed in Ireland; and he contributed liberally to the impression of the Welsh bible. He gave, during his life, 300l to advance the design of propagating the Christian religion in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; and as soon as he heard that the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> Company were entertaining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> for the like design in the east, he sent 100l. for a beginning, as an example, but intended to carry it much farther when it should be set on foot to purpose. In other respects his charities were so bountiful and extensive, that they amounted, as this prelate tells us, from his own knowledge, to upwards of 1000l. a-year. But as our limits will not allow us to follow the bishop in the copious and eloquent account he has given of this great man's abilities, we must therefore content ourselves with adding the short eulogium by the celebrated physician, philosopher, and chemist, Dr Herman Boerhaave; who, after having declared Lord Bacon to be the father of experimental philosophy, affirms, that "Mr Boyle, the ornament of his age and country, succeeded to the genius and inquiries of the great chancellor Verulam. Which (says he) of all Mr Boyle's writings shall I recommend? All of them. To him we owe the secrets of fire, air, water, animals, vegetables, foils: so that from his works may be deduced the whole system of natural knowledge." The reader perhaps may here be pleased to know, that Mr Boyle was born the same year in which Lord Bacon died. As to the person of this great man, we are told, that he was tall, but slender; and his countenance <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> and emaciated. His constitution was so tender and delicate, that he had divers sorts of cloaks to put on when he went abroad, according to the temperature of the air; and in this he governed himself by his thermometer. He escaped indeed the small-pox; but for almost forty years he laboured under such feeble-ness of body, and such lowness of strength and spirits, that it was astonishing how he could read, meditate, make experiments, and write, as he did. He had likewise a weakness of his eyes; which made him very tender of them, and extremely apprehensive of such distempers as might affect them. He imagined likewise, that if sickness should confine him to his bed, it might raise the pains of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> which might be above his strength to support; so that he feared his last minutes should be too hard for him. This was the ground of all the caution and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> with which he was observed to live; but as to life itself, he had that just indifference for it which became a philosopher and a Christian. However, his sight began to grow dim not above four hours before he died; and when death came upon him, he had not been above three hours in bed before it made an end of him, with so little pain that the flame appeared to go out merely for want of oil to maintain it. Mr Boyle was never married; but Mr Evelyn was assured, that he courted the beautiful and ingenious daughter of Cary earl of Monmouth, and that to this pallion was owing his "Seraphic Love." In the memorandum of Mr Boyle's life set down by Bishop Burnet, it is remarked that he abstained from marriage, at first out of policy, afterwards more philosophically; and we find by a letter of Dr John Wallis to him, dated at Oxford, July 17th, 1669, that he had an overture made him with respect to the Lady <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HASTINGS">Hastings</a>, sister to the earl of Huntingdon. But it does not appear from any of his papers, that he had ever entertained the least thoughts of that kind; nay, there is a letter of his, wrote when he was young, to the Lady Barrymore his niece, who had informed him of a report that he was actually married, which almost shows that he never did. The letter is written with great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>, and in the true spirit of gallantry; and is a clear proof, that though Mr Boyle did not choose to marry, yet it was no philanthropic cynical humour which restrained him from it. It is impossible to entertain the reader better than by prefacing him with that part of it which concerns the point in question. "It is high time for me to hasten the payment of the thanks I owe your ladyship for the joy you are pleased to wish me, and of which that with possibly gives me more than the occasion of it would. You have certainly reason, madam, to suspend your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of a marriage, celebrated by no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> but Fame, and made unknown to the suppos'd bridegroom. I may possibly ere long give you a fit of the spleen upon this theme; but at present it were incongruous to blend such pure rillery, as I ever rate of matrimony and amours with, among things I am so serious in as those this scribble pretends you. I shall therefore only tell you, that the little gentleman and I are still at the old defiance. You have carried away too many of the perfections of your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a> to leave enough in this country for reducing to stubborn a heart as mine; whose conquest were a task of so much difficulty, and so little worth it, that the latter <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> is always likely to deter any that hath <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and merit enough to overcome the former. But though this untamed heart be thus insensible to the thing itself called love; it is yet very acceivable to things very near of kin to that pallion; and esteem, friendship, respect, and even admiration, are things that their proper objects fail not proportionably to exact of me, and consequently are qualities which in their highest degrees are really and constantly paid my lady Barrymore by her most obliged humble servant, and affectionate uncle, Robert Boyle." We shall conclude this account of Mr Boyle with the mention of his posthumous works, which are as follow. 1. "The general History of the air deigned and begun. 2. "General heads for the natural history of a country, great or small; drawn out for the use of travellers and navigators." 3. "A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> of the honourable Robert Boyle's, deposited with the secretaries of the Royal Society, October 14th, 1680, and opened since his death; being an account of his making the phosphorus, September 30th, 1680." Printed in the Philosophical Transactions. 4. "An account of a way of examining waters, as to freckles or saltness." 5. "A free discourse against customary swearing, and a dissuasive from cursing," 1695, 8vo. 6. "Medicinal experiments, or a collection of choice remedies, chiefly simple and easily prepared, useful in families, and fit for the service of the country people. The third and last volume," volume, published from the author's original manuscript; whereunto is added several useful notes explanatory of the same," 1698, 12mo. Beautiful editions of all his works have been printed at London, in 5 volumes folio, and 6 volumes 4to. Boyle, Charles, earl of Orrery in Ireland, and baron of Mahton in the county of Somerset, was the second son of Roger the second earl of Orrery, and was born in August 1679. He was educated at Christ-church in Oxford, and soon distinguished himself by his learning and abilities. Like the first earl of Orrery, he was an author, a soldier, and a statesman. He translated the life of Lyander from the Greek of Plutarch; and published a new edition of the epistles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHALARIS">Phalaris</a>, which engaged him in a literary dispute, in which he defended the genuineness of these epistles against Dr Bentley. He was three times member for the town of Huntingdon; but his elder brother, Lionel earl of Orrery dying on the 23rd of August 1703 without issue, he succeeded to that title; and, entering into the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s service, had a regiment given him, when he behaved with such bravery, that in 1709 he was raised to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>-general, and sworn one of her majesty's <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy council</a>. At the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of the wood, he gave the strongest proofs of his intrepid courage, remaining at the head of his regiment in the warmest part of the action, till the victory was complete, which, as it was one of the most glorious, so it was the dearest bought, of any of that war. His lordship had the honour of being appointed the queen's envoy to the states of Brabant and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>; and having honourably discharged the trust, was raised to the dignity of a British peer, by the title of Lord Boyle, baron of Mahton in Somersetshire. He enjoyed several other additional honours in the reign of King George I.; but having the misfortune to fall under the suspicion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, his lordship was committed to the tower; he was, however, at length, admitted to bail; and nothing being found that could be esteemed a sufficient ground for a prosecution, he was discharged. His lordship died after a flight indisposition, on the 21st of August 1731. To his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>, Mr Atterbury, he probably owed a good part of that fine relish he had for the writings of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. He made these his constant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, and expressed a high contempt, says Budgell, for the greater part of our modern wits and authors. He was delighted with the company of two sorts of persons; either such as were really geniuses of the first rank, who had fine understandings, strong judgments, and true tastes; or such as had a few foibles, and an eye of ridicule in them, which served to make him laugh. He would rally these in so agreeable, and yet in so tender a manner, that, though it diverted himself and others, it was never offensive to the person rallied. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> which was invented by him, and bears his name, representing the solar system according to the sentiments of the new astronomers, is an undeniable proof of his mechanic genius. His lordship had also a turn for medicine; which led him not only to buy and read whatever was published on that subject, but also to employ his friends to send him accounts of herbs and drugs in foreign countries. Boyle, John, earl of Cork and Orrery, a nobleman distinguished by his learning and genius, was the only son of Charles earl of Orrery, and was born on the 2nd of January 1707. He was educated at Christ church college in Oxford; but, as he himself declares, early disappointments, indifferent health, and many untoward accidents, rendered him fond of retirement, and of improving his talents for polite literature and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>; of which last art he gave several excellent specimens. He also wrote a translation of Pliny the Younger's letter, with various notes, for the service of his eldest son the Lord Boyle, in two volumes, 4to. This was first published in 1751. The year following, he published the Life of Dean Swift, in several letters, addressed to his second son <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a> Boyle; and afterwards printed Memoirs of Robert Cary earl of Monmouth, a manuscript presented to him by a relation, with explanatory notes. He died in 1762. Boyle's Lectures, a course of eight sermons or lectures preached annually, set on foot by the honourable Robert Boyle, Esq.; by a codicil annexed to his will in 1691; whose design, as expressed by the instigator, is, to prove the truth of the Christian religion against infidels, without descending to any controversies among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; and to answer new difficulties, scruples, &c. For the support of this lecture he assigned the rent of his house in Crooked-lane to some learned divine within the bills of mortality, to be elected for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> not exceeding three years, by the late Archbishop Tennison and others. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> proving precarious, the salary was ill paid; to remedy which inconveniences, the said archbishop procured a yearly stipend of 50l. for ever, to be paid quarterly, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> on a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BRILL">Brill</a> in the county of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUCKS">Bucks</a>. To this appointment we are indebted for many elaborate defences both of natural and revealed religion.

BOYNE

Pages 435-435

a river in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, which rises in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN_S_COUNTY"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>, and runs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRIM">Trim</a> and Cavan, falling at last into the Irish channel a little below <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROGHEDA">Drogheda</a>. It is memorable for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought on its banks between James II., and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> William III., in which the former was defeated.

BOYSE

Pages 435-437

Boys, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Bois, John, one of the translators of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> in the reign of James I., was son of William Bois, rector of Weft Stowe, near St Edmundsbury, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, and born at Nettlestead in Suffolk on the 3rd of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1560. He was taught the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of learning by his father; and his capacity was such, that at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of five years he read the Bible in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>. He went afterwards to Hadley school; and at 14 was admitted of St John's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where he distinguished himself by his skill in Greek.
