Happening to have the small-pox when he was elected fellow, he, to preserve his seniority, caused himself to be carried in blankets to be admitted. He applied himself for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of medicine; but, fancying himself affected with every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> he read of, he quitted that science. He was ten years <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> Greek lecturer in his college, and read every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. He voluntarily read a Greek lecture for some years at four in the morning, in his own chamber, which was frequented by many of the fellows. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father, he succeeded him in the rectory of Weft Stowe. At the age of 36, he married the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Mr <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLT">Holt</a>, rector of Boxworth, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGESHIRE">Cambridgeshire</a>; whom he succeeded in that living, October 13, 1596. On his quitting the university, the college gave him His young wife, who was bequeathed to him with the living, which was an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOWSON">advowson</a>, proving a bad economit, and he himself being wholly addicted to his studies, he soon became so much involved in debt, that he was obliged to sell his choice collection of books, consisting of almost every Greek author then extant. When a new translation of the Bible was by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. directed to be made, Mr Bois was elected one of the Cambridge translators. He performed not only his own, but also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> assigned to another, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation; though with no profit, for he had no allowance but his commons. He was also one of the six who met at Stationers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">Hall</a> to revile the whole; which talk they went through in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> months, having each from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of stationers, during that time 30s. a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. He afterwards assisted Sir Henry Saville in publishing the works of St Chrysostom. In 1615, Dr Lancelot Andrews, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>, bestowed on him, unasked, a prebend in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. He died on the 14th of January 1643, in the 84th year of his age. He left a great many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> behind him, particularly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> on almost all the books of the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>.—When he was a young student at Cambridge, he received from the learned Dr Whitaker three rules for avoiding those dilemmas which usually attend a sedentary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, to which he adhered with equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> and success. The first was, To study always standing; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, Never to study in a window; and the third, Never to go to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> with his feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. Boyle, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, a late eminent dissenting minister in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, much respected not only for learning and abilities, but his extensive <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and undefiled piety. During his ministerial <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> at Dublin, he published many sermons which compose several folio volumes, a few poems, and other tracts; but what chiefly distinguished him as a writer, was the controversy he carried on with Dr King, archbishop of Dublin, and author of the Origin of Evil, concerning the office of a scriptural bishop. This controverted point was managed on both sides with great force of argument and calmness of temper. The bishop asserted, that the episcopal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of jurisdiction had its foundation in the New Testament: Mr Boyle, consistent with his principles, denied that any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> superiority appeared there, with the greatest candour and good manners. He was father to Boyle, Samuel, the poet, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> remarkable for the fineness of his genius, the loveliness of his manners, and the wretchedness of his life. He was born in 1708, and received the rudiments of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in a private school in Dublin. When he was but 18 years old, his father, who probably intended him for the ministry, sent him to the university of Glasgow, that he might finish his education there. He had not been a year at the university, when he fell in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with the daughter of a tradesman in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and was imprudent enough to interrupt his education by marrying her before he had entered into his 20th year. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> extravagance of his temper soon exposed him to want; and as he had now the additional charge of a wife, his reduced circumstances obliged him to quit the university, and go over with his wife (who also carried a sister with her) to Dublin, where they relied on the old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> for support. Young Boyle was of all men the furthest removed from a gentleman; he had no graces of person, and fewer still of conversation. Never were three people of more libertine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> than young Boyle, his wife, and sister-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; yet the two ladies wore such a mask of decency before the old gentleman, that his fondness was never abated. The estate his father possessed in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> was sold to discharge his debts; and when the old man lay in his last sickness, he was entirely supported by presents from his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a>, and buried at their expense. We have no further account of Mr Boyle, till we find him soon after his father's death at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. At this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> his poetical genius raised him many friends, and some patrons of very great eminence. He published a volume of poems in 1731, to which are subjoined The Tablature of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEBES">Cebes</a>, and A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a> upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">Liberty</a>, inserted in the Dublin Journal 1726; and by these he obtained a very great reputation. They are addressed to the countess of Eglinton. This amiable lady was the patroness of all men of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, and greatly distinguished Mr Boyle while he resided in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Upon the death of the viscountess Stormont, Mr Boyle wrote an elegy, which was very much applauded by her ladyship's relations. This elegy he entitled The Tears of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>, as the deceased lady was a woman of the most refined <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> in the sciences, and a great admirer of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Stormont was so much pleased with this mark of esteem paid to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of his lady, that he ordered a very handsome present to be given to Mr Boyle by his attorney at Edinburgh. The notice which lady Eglinton and the lord Stormont took of our poet, recommended him likewise to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> to the duchess of Gordon; who was so solicitous to raise him above <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, that she employed her <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in procuring the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of a place for him. She gave him a letter, which he was next day to deliver to one of the commissioners of the customs at Edinburgh. It happened that he was then some miles distant from the city; and, the morning on which he was to have rode to town with her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>'s letter of recommendation proved to be rainy. This slender circumstance was enough to discourage Boyle, who never looked beyond the present moment; he declined going to town on account of the rainy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; and while he let slip the opportunity, the place was bestowed upon another, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> declared he kept for some time vacant in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of seeing a person recommended by the duchess of Gordon. Boyle at last having defeated all the kind intentions of his patrons towards him, fell into contempt and poverty, which obliged him to quit Edinburgh. He communicated his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of going to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> to the duchess of Gordon; who, having still a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of his poetical abilities, gave him a letter of recommendation to Mr Pope, and obtained another for him to Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> King the lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of England. Lord Stormont recommended him to the solicitor-general his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, and many other persons of the first fashion. Upon receiving these letters, he, with great caution, quitted Edinburgh, regretted by none but his creditors. Upon his arrival in London, he went to Twickenham, in order to deliver the duchess of Gordon's letter to Mr Pope; but that gentleman not being at home, Mr Boyle never gave himself the trouble to repeat his visit. He wrote poems; but those, though excellent in their kind, were lost to the world, by being introduced with no advantage. He had so strong a propensity to grovelling, that his acquaintance were generally of such a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> as could be of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to him; and those in higher life he addressed by letters, not having sufficient confidence or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> familiarly with them. Thus unfit to support himself in the world, he was exposed to a variety of distresses, from which he could invent no means of extricating himself but by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> mendicant letters. It <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear amazing, that this man, of so abject a spirit, was voluptuous and luxurious; he had no taste for any thing elegant, and yet was to the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> expensive. Can it be believed, that often when he had received but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">guinea</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a supplicating letter, he would go into a tavern, order a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> to be prepared, drink of the richest wines, and spend all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> that had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> been given him in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, without having any one to participate the regale with him, and while his wife and child were starving at home? It was about the year 1740, that Mr Boyle, reduced to the last extremity of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> wretchedness, had not a shirt, a coat, or any kind of apparel, to put on; the sheets in which he lay were carried to the pawn-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROKER">broker</a>'s, and he was obliged to be confined to his bed with no other covering than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLANKET">blanket</a>. He had little support but what he got by writing letters to his friends in the most abject style; but was perhaps ashamed to let this instance of his distress be known, which probably was the occasion of his remaining six weeks in that situation. During this time he had some employment in writing verses for the Magazines; and whoever had seen him in his study, must have thought the object singular enough: he sat up in bed with the blanket wrapped about him, through which he had cut a hole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> enough to admit his arm, and, placing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> upon his knee, scribbled in the best manner he could the verses he was obliged to make: whatever he got by those, or any other of his begging letters, was but just sufficient for the preservation of life. And perhaps he would have remained much longer in this distressful state, had not a compassionate gentleman, upon hearing this circumstance related, ordered his clothes to be taken out of pawn, and enabled him to appear again abroad. About the year 1745, Mr Boyle's wife died. He was then at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">Reading</a>, and pretended much concern when he heard of her death. His business at Reading was to compile a Review of the most material transactions at home and abroad during the last <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>: in which he has included a short account of the late rebellion. Upon his return from Reading, his behaviour was more decent than it had ever been before; and there were some hopes that a reformation, though late, would be wrought upon him. He was employed by a bookseller to translate Fenelon on the Existence of God; during which time he married a second wife, a woman in low circumstances, but well enough adapted to his taste. He began now to live with more regard to his character, and supported a better appearance than usual; but while his circumstances were mending, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> appetites losing ground, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> visibly declined. He had the satisfaction, while in this lingering illness, to observe a poem of his, entitled The Deity, recommended by two eminent writers, the ingenious Mr Fielding, and the reverend Mr James Harvey author of The Meditations. Mr Boyle's mind was often religiously disposed; he frequently talked upon that subject, and probably suffered a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> from the remorse of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>. The early impressions of his good education were never entirely obliterated; and his whole life was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> struggle between his will and reason, as he was always violating his duty to the one, while he fell under the subjection of the other. It was in consequence of this war in his mind, that he wrote a beautiful poem called The Recantation. In May 1749, he died in obscure lodgings near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOE">Shoe</a>-lane; but in sentiments, there is the greatest reason to believe, very different from those in which he had spent the greatest part of his life. An old acquaintance of his endeavoured to collect money to defray the expenses of his funeral, so that the scandal of being buried by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> might be avoided; but in vain: the remains of this son of the muse were, with very little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, hurried away by the parish officers. Never was a life spent with less grace than that of Mr Boyle, and never were such distinguished abilities given to less purpose. His genius was not confined to poetry only: he had a taste for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, music, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>; with the latter of which he was very well acquainted. His poetical pieces, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> collected, would make five moderate volumes. Many of them are scattered in The Gentleman's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>, marked with the letter Y, and Alceus. Two volumes were published in London. An ode of his in the manner of Spenser, entitled The Olive, was addressed to Sir Robert Walpole, which procured him a present of ten guineas. He translated a poem from the High Dutch of Van Haren, in praise of peace, upon the conclusion of that made at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle; but the poem which procured him the greatest reputation was that upon the attributes of the Deity. He was employed by Mr Ogle to translate some of Chaucer's tales into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> English, which he performed with great spirit, and received at the rate of three pence a line for his trouble. Mr Ogle published a complete edition of that old poet's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> Tales modernized; and Mr Boyle's name is put to such tales as were done by him. In 1743, Mr Boyle published, without his name, an ode on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Dettingen, entitled <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBION">Albion</a>'s Triumph.

BOZOLA

Pages 437-437

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a territory of the same name, and subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10° 25'. N. Lat. 45° 9'. B QUADRO, Quadrato, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Durale, in music, called by the French b quarré, from its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> ||. This is what we call B <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> or sharp, in distinction to B mol or flat. See FLAT and SHARP. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the flat b be placed before a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> in the thorough <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a>, it intimates, that its third is to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>; and if placed with any cypher over a note in the bass, as b 6, or b 5, &c., it denotes, that the fifth or sixth thereto are to be flat. But if the quadro || be placed over any note, or with a cypher, in the thorough bass, it has the contrary effect; for thereby the note or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> thereof is raised to its natural order.

BRABANCIONES

Pages 437-437

in middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers, a kind of Netherland foldery, infamous for rapine, being lit-

BRABANT

Pages 437-438

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the province of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> and the duchy of Guelderland; on the east, by the same duchy and the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a>; on the south, by the province of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAMUR">Namur</a> and Hainault; and on the west, by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>. It is divided into Dutch Brabant and Austrian Brabant; watered by several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, of which the Scheld, the Ruppel, and the Dommel, are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is very fertile; and it contains 26 fortified <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>.

BRABEUTES

Pages 438-438
or BRABEUTA, in Antiquity, an officer among the Greeks, who presided at public games, and decided controversies that happened among the antagonists in the gymnastic exercises. The number of brabeute was not fixed; sometimes there was only one, but more commonly they amounted to nine or ten. BRACCiano, a town of St Peter's patrimony, about 12 miles north of Rome, situated on the west side of a lake to which it gives name. E. Long. 13° N. Lat. 42°.

BRACCIOLINI

Pages 438-438

Francis, an Italian poet, a native of Pistoia, and the friend of Pope Urban VIII. He was born about the year 1566. Removing to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, he was admitted into the academy there, and devoted himself to literature. At Rome he entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Maffeo Barberini, with whom he afterwards went to France. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Clement VIII., he returned to his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and for some years prosecuted his studies in retirement. When his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> Barberini was elected pope, under the name of Urban VIII., Bracciolini repaired to Rome, where he was well received, and made secretary to the pope's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, Cardinal Antonio. He had also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> conferred on him of taking a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> from the arms of the Barberini family, which were Bees; and thenceforth he was known by the name of Bracciolini dell' Api. He resided in Rome during the whole of that pontificate, frequenting the most illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a>, and listened to with general applause, but, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, censured for his fond aversion. He returned at length to his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, where he died in the year 1645. Bracciolini was a copious writer. There is scarcely any <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, epic, dramatic, pastoral, lyric, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLESQUE">burlesque</a>, which he did not attempt. He is principally noted for his mock-heroic poem, entitled Seberno degli Dei, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> of the heathen <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, and which disputes priority of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> with Tasso's Seccia Rapi. In merit, indeed, its inferiority is acknowledged, yet it obtained considerable applause. Of his serious heroic poems, the most celebrated is the Croce Racquifata," which by some is placed next to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> works of Ariosto and Tasso, but not without a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>. He celebrated the elevation of his patron Urban VIII. in a poem of twenty-three books, which shows with what facility he could write verses. His dramatic pastoral entitled L'Amoroso Sdegno, is accounted one of the best productions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which it was written; and some of his tragedies met with much applause, particularly his Evandro. BRACE is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> taken for a couple <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a>, and applied by huntsmen to several beasts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, as a brace of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUCKS">bucks</a>, foxes, hares, &c.

BRACE

Pages 438-438

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>, a crooked line enclosing a passage, as in a triplet.

BRACELET

Pages 438-438

an ornament worn on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WRIST">wrist</a>, much used among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>: it was made of different materials, and in different fashions, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the wearer. The word is French, bracelet; which Menage derives further from braceletum, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of bracele, a word occurring in writers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a> age; all formed from the Latin brachium, arm. It amounts to the same with what was called by the ancients, armilla, brachiale, occabus; in the middle age, boza, bauga, armipatba. Bracelets are much worn by the savages of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, who are so excessively fond of them, as to give the richest commodities, and even their fathers, wives, and children, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> for those made of no richer materials than shells, glass-beads, and the like. They form also, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> civilized countries, a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ornaments of the ladies. BRACHLÆUS, the name of a muscle. See Anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles. Coraco-BRACHIALIS. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BRACES

Pages 438-438

in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> belonging to all the yards of a ship, except the mizen, two to each yard, reeved through blocks that are fastened to pennants, seized to the yard-arms. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is either to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> the yards. Hence to brace the yard, is to bring it to either side. All braces come aftward on; as, the main brace comes to the poop, the main-top-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> brace comes to the mizen-top and thence to the main-throats; the fore and fore-top-fall braces come <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by the main and main-top-fall stays, and so of the rest. But the mizen-bowline serves to brace to the yard, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-jack braces are brought forwards to the main-throats, when the ship falls <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. BRACES of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COACH">Coach</a>, thick straps of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> on which it hangs.

BRACHMINS

Pages 438-439
or Brachmans, a branch of the ancient Gymnosophists, or philosophers of India, remarkable for the severity of their lives and manners. See the article Gymnosophists. Some say they derive their name from the patriarch Abraham, whom they call in their language Brachma, or Brama. Others deduce it from the name of their god Brachma; which some again take to be the same with Abraham: whence Poitier calls them Abrachmanes. F. Thomafin Brachygra. F. Thomassin derives the word from the Hebrew barach, to fly or escape; because the Brachmans retire into the country and live in deserts. The same author gives us another derivation, viz. from the Hebrew barach (bene- diction, oracle), to blest or pray; in regard this is their principal occupation.—The Greeks ascribe to them the doctrine of the immortality of the soul, and certain no- tions concerning the nature of the Supreme Being and future rewards and punishments. To this species of knowledge the Brachmans added an infinite number of religious observances, which were adopted by Pytha- goras in his school; such as fasting, prayer, silence, and contemplation. They were looked upon as the friends of the gods, because they affected to pay them so much regard; and as the protectors of mankind, because they paid them no regard at all. No bounds were therefore set to the respect and gratitude that were shown them: princes themselves did not scruple to consult these re- cluses upon any critical conjuncture, from a supposition, no doubt, that they were inspired; since it was impos- sible to imagine that they had the advantages of expe- rience. We can scarcely, however, deny, that there might be among them some men of real virtue, whose minds relished the pure and ingenious delights of study and science; and who, by nobly raising their thoughts to the contemplation of the First Being, must have had more powerful incitements to render them- selves worthy of his care, and none to justify them in deceiving and tyrannizing over their fellow-creatures. There appear still some remains of the ancient brach- mans in the east, under the denomination of Bramins. See Bramins.

BRACHYLOGY

Pages 439-439

(from βραχύς and λόγος "ex- pression"), in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, the expressing anything in the most concise manner. This, so far as consistent with periphrasis, is a virtue and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of style; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> ob- scurely be the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, which is often the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, it becomes a blemish and inexcusable defect.—Quintilian gives an instance of brachylogy from Sallust: "Mitridates corpore ingenti perinde armatus;" "Mitridates, as it were, armed with the huge size of his stature."

BRACHYPTERA

Pages 439-439

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by Willoughby, to denote those hawks which have their wings so short as not to reach to the end of the tail. Of this kind are the goshawk, sparrow-hawk, &c.

BRACHYPYRENA

Pages 439-439

in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of fossils, a genus of lepidoptera, with a short roundish nucleus. See Septarie.

BRACHYTELOSTYLA

Pages 439-439

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, the name by which Dr Hill calls those crystals which are composed of a short hexangular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> terminated at each end by an hexangular <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>. See Crystal.

BRACKET

Pages 439-439

among carpenters, &c., a kind of wooden stay, serving to support shelves and the like.

BRACKETS

Pages 439-439

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNNERY">Gunnery</a>, are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a> of the car- riage of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>: they are made of strong planks of wood, of almost a semicircular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and bound round with thick <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> plates; they are fixed to the beds by four bolts, which are called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>-bolts; they rise up on each side of the mortar, and serve to keep her at any elevation by means of some strong iron bolts, called bracket-bolts, which go through these cheeks <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> brac- kets.

BRACKLAW

Pages 439-439

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of that name, which is the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Podolia; it is also called Lower Podolia, and is of greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> than Upper Podolia, but is more defoliate, on account of the neighbourhood of the Tartars.

BRACKLEY

Pages 439-439

a borough-town in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTON">Northampton</a>- shire, in England, seated on the edge of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, next Buckinghamshire, on a branch of the river Ouse. It is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> corporation-town, containing two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-churches; is governed by a mayor and al- dermen; and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It had formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, which is turned into a free school. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 15. N. Lat. 52. 0.

BRACKTON

Pages 439-439

Henry, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of Eng- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> in the reign of Henry III. was probably a native of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of laws, and was made one of the itinerant judges about the year 1244. Ten years after he became chief justice, and had the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> assigned him for his town residence, during the minority of that nobleman. He is said to have filled this important office with singular reputation during 20 years. When he died is not known; probably it was in the reign of Edward I. He wrote De legibus et consuetudinibus Angliae, which is one of the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, and also most methodical books on our laws. His method is copied from Justi- nian. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was printed at London in 1569, fol- io; and in 1640, 4to. The first is very incorrect.

BRACTEA

Pages 439-439

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a thin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> plate of any folium florale, ranged by Linnaeus among the fulcrum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. These floral leaves differ in shape and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, from the other folia of the plant; are generally situated on the pedunculus, and often so near the corolla as to be easily mistaken for the calyx; than which, however, the bracteae are generally more permanent. Examples of the floral leaves are seen in the tilia, fumaria bul- <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOSA">bosa</a>, lavandula, and horminum.

BRACTEARIA

Pages 439-439

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a genus of talc, composed of small plates in form of spangles, each plate either being very thin, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fissile into very thin ones. Of this genus there are a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, called from their different colours, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MICA">mica</a> aurea, or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>-glim- mer; and mica argentea, silver-glimmer, or cats-filiver, &c.

BRADFIELD

Pages 439-439

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> in England, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 30. N. Lat. 51. 14.

BRADFORD

Pages 439-440

John, a divine, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a> to the re- formation, Bradford formation, was born in the former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the reign of Henry VIII. at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>. Being a remarkable penman and accountant, he became secretary to Sir John <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARRINGTON">Harrington</a>, who was several times employed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry, and his successor Edward VI., as paymaster to the troops abroad. Bradford at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was a gay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and to support his extravagance made free with the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; but being at last unable to support the reflection of his guilt, he determined to make restitution, and actually repaid the money. Quitting his employment of secretary, about the year 1547, he took chambers in the inner temple, and for some time studied the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; but finding himself an inclination to preach the gospel, in the following year he removed to Catharine-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where he applied with such uncommon affluence to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, that in a much shorter time than usual he was admitted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts, and soon after made fellow of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>-hall. Bishop Ridley, who, in 1550, was translated to the see of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, charmed with Bradford's application and zeal, now sent for him to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, ordained and appointed him his chaplain. In 1553, he was also made chaplain to Edward VI., during which time he became one of the most popular preachers in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Such a reformer was too dangerous to be suffered in the succeeding reign. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> was hardly in possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, before Bradford's persecutions began. He was first confined in the tower for sedition, where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> a year and a half; during which time he wrote several epistles that were dispersed in various parts of the kingdom. He was afterwards removed to other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a>, and at last brought to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> before that infernal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> in which Gardiner sat as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> inquisitor, where he defended his principles to the last, in contempt of their utmost power. They condemned him to the flames; and he was accordingly burnt alive in Smithfield, on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1, 1555. His works are: 1. Seventy-two letters, written to various people, whilst the author was in prison; printed in Bishop Cordell's collection. 2. Ten letters, printed in Fox's acts and monuments. 3. Complaint of verity, 1559, 8vo. 4. Three examinations before the commissioners, and his private talk with the priests, with the original of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, 1561, octavo. 5. Two notable sermons, 1574, octavo, 1631. 6. Godly meditations and prayers, 1614, 24to. 7. Treatise of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a>, 1622. With several translations and other pieces.

BRADFORTH

Pages 440-440

a town in the west of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, seated on a branch of the river <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIRE">Aire</a>, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 35'. N. Lat. 53° 40'.

BRADLEY

Pages 440-441

Dr James, a famous English astronomer, was the third son of William and Jane Bradley, and was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHERBORNE">Sherborne</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a> in the year 1692. He was educated for the university at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Leach by Mr Egles and Mr Brice, who kept a boarding-school there; and from North Leach he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. His friends intended him for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and his studies were regulated with that view; and as soon as he was of sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> to receive holy orders, the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a>, who had conceived a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem for him, gave him the living of Bridgwater, and soon after he was inducted to that of Welford in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEMBROKESHIRE">Pembrokeshire</a>. But notwithstanding these advantages, from which he might <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> himself still further advancement in the church, he at length resigned his livings, that he might be wholly at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to pursue his favourite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and particularly <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. He was nephew to Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">Pound</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who is well known in the learned world by many excellent observations, and who would have enriched it with more, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the journals of his voyages had not been burnt at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULO">Pulo</a> Condore, when the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was set on fire, and the English who were settled there cruelly massacred, Mr Pound himself very narrowly escaping with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. With this gentleman, Mr Bradley passed all the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that he could spare from the duties of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>; and perhaps he sometimes trespassed upon them: he was then sufficiently acquainted with the mathematics to improve by Mr Pound's conversation; yet it does not appear that, in this study, he had any preceptor but his genius, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any assistant but his labour. It may be easily imagined, that the example and conversation of Mr Pound did not render Bradley more fond of his profession than he was before; he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, however, as yet to fulfil the duties of it, though at this time he had made such observations as laid the foundation of those discoveries which afterwards distinguished him as one of the greatest astronomers of his age. Though these observations were made as it were by stealth, they gained him at first the notice, and then the friendship, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> Macclesfield, Mr Newton, afterwards Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a>, Mr Halley, and many other members of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, into which he was soon elected a member. About the same time, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of Savilian professor of astronomy became vacant by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the celebrated Dr Keil; and Mr Bradley was elected to succeed him on the 1st of October 1721, being then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> 29 years old; and his colleague was Mr Halley, who was professor of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> on the same foundation. Bradley, upon his being elected into this professorship, gave up both his livings, and with great joy quitted a situation in which his duty was directly opposite to his inclination. From this time, he applied himself wholly to the study of his favourite science; and in the year 1727 he published his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the aberration of the fixed stars, which is allowed to be one of the most useful and ingenious discoveries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> astronomy. Three years after this discovery, by which Mr Bradley acquired very great reputation, he was appointed lecturer in astronomy and physics, at the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> of Oxford. He pursued his studies with equal application and delight; and in the course of his observations, which were innumerable, he discovered that the inclination of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH_S"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>'s axis upon the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the ecliptic was not always the same, but that it varied backwards and forwards some seconds, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of these variations was <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years. This period seemed altogether unaccountable, as it could not be supposed to have anything in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with the revolution of the earth, which is performed in one year. Mr Bradley, however, discovered the cause of this phenomenon in the Newtonian system of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a>. He published this discovery in 1737, so that in the space of about ten years he communicated to the world two of the finest discoveries in modern astronomy, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> forever make a memorable epocha in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of that science. Mr Bradley always preserved the esteem and friendship of Mr Halley; who, being worn out by age and infirmities, thought he could do nothing farther for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of astronomy, than procure for Mr Bradley the place of regius professor of astronomy at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>, which he had pollied himself many years with the greatest reputation. With this view, he wrote many letters, which have been since found among Mr Bradley's papers, desiring his permission to apply for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of the reverence of it to him, and even offering to resign in his favour, if it should be thought necessary: but before Mr Halley could bring this kind project to bear, he died. Mr Bradley, however, obtained the place afterwards, by the favour and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Lord Macclesfield, who was afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the Royal Society. As soon as the appointment of Mr Bradley to this place was known, the university of Oxford sent him a diploma creating him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. The appointment of astronomer at Greenwich placed Mr Bradley in his proper element, and he pursued his observations with unwearied diligence. However numerous the collection of astronomical instruments at the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a> at Greenwich, it was impossible that such an observer as Dr Bradley should not desire to increase them, as well to answer those particular views, as in general to make observations with greater exactness. In the year 1748, therefore, he took the opportunity of the annual visit made by the Royal Society to the observatory, in order to examine the instruments and receive the professor's observations for the year, to represent so strongly the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of repairing the old instruments, and purchasing new, that the society thought proper to represent it to his majesty, and his majesty gave them 100l. for that purpose. This sum was laid out under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of Dr Bradley, who, with the assistance of the late celebrated Mr Graham and Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">Bird</a>, furnished the observatory with as complete a collection of astronomical instruments, as the most skilful and diligent observer could desire. Dr Bradley, furnished with such assistance, pursued his observations with new assiduity, an incredible <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of which were found after his death, and put into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Royal Society. It has been already observed, that when Dr Bradley was elected to the professor's chair at Oxford, he gave up his two livings, which were at such a distance, that he could not possibly fulfil the duties of them himself; but it happened that after he was settled at Greenwich the living of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> became vacant, which is very considerable, and which was offered to him, as he was upon the spot to perform the duty, and had the claim of uncommon merit to the reward. This living, however, Dr Bradley, very greatly to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, refused, fearing the duties of the astronomer would too much interfere with those of the divine. His majesty, however, hearing of the refusal, was so pleased with it, that he granted him a pension of 250l. a-year in consideration of his great abilities and knowledge in astronomy and other branches of the mathematics, which had procured so much advantage to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, as is particularly mentioned in the grant which is dated the 15th of February 1752. Dr Bradley, about the same time, was admitted into the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of the Royal Society. In the year 1748, he was admitted a member of the royal academy of sciences and belles lettres of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, upon the death of M. Crevier, first physician to his Catholic majesty; in the year 1752, a member of the imperial academy at Petersburg; and in 1757, of that instituted at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>. Dr Bradley was still indefatigable in his observations, and whatever honour he received became an incitement to obtain new distinction; his corporeal abilities, however, at length declined, though his intellectual suffered no abatement. In the year 1760, he became extremely weak and infirm; and towards the end of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1762, he was attacked with a total suppression of urine, caused by an inflammation of the reins, which on the 12th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> following put an end to his life, in the 70th year of his age. He was buried at Mitchin-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPTON">Hampton</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> with his mother and his wife. In the year 1744, he married Susannah Peach, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of a gentleman of that name in Gloucestershire, by whom he had only one daughter. As to his character, he was remarkable for a placid and gentle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, very uncommon in persons of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> temper and robust <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. It was still more remarkable, that, with this untroubled equanimity of temper, he was compassionate and liberal in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. Although he was a good speaker, and possessed the rare but happy art of expressing his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> with the utmost precision and perspicuity, yet no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was a greater lover of silence, for he never spoke but when he thought it absolutely necessary. He did indeed think it necessary to speak when he had a fair opportunity to communicate any useful knowledge in his own way; and he encouraged those that attended his lectures to ask him questions, by the exactness with which he answered, and the care he took to adapt himself to every capacity. He was not more inclined to write than to speak, for he has published very little; he had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> diffidence, which made him always afraid that his works should injure his character; and therefore suppressed many, which probably were well worthy of the public <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. He was even known, as it were, in spite of himself; and, in spite of himself, he was known much, and consequently much esteemed. He was acquainted with many of the first persons in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, persons eminent as well for their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> as their abilities; he was honoured by all men of learning in general; and there was not an astronomer of any eminence in the world with whom he had not a literary correspondence. Upon the whole, it may be said of Dr Bradley, that no man cultivated great talents with more success, or had a better claim to be ranked among the greatest astronomers of his age.

BRADNINCH

Pages 441-441

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, once a confident <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, but some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> ago totally destroyed by fire. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 35. N. Lat. 50. 45.

BRADS

Pages 441-441

among artificers, a kind of nails used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, which have no spreading heads as other nails have. They are distinguished by ironmongers by fix names; as joiner's brads, flooring-brads, battens-brads, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a>-brads, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> heads, &c. Joiners-brads are for hard wainscot; battens-brads are for soft wainscot; bill-brads are used when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> is laid in haste, or for shallow <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOISTS">joists</a> subject to warp. See Nail.

BRADSHAW

Pages 441-442

Henry, a Benedictine monk, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, about the middle of the 15th century. Discovering an early propensity to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and literature, he was received while a boy into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of St Werberg in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>; and having there imbibed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, he was afterwards sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, in the suburbs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where for a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he studied <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> with the novices of his order, and then returned to his convent at Chester; here, in the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he applied himself chiefly to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and wrote several books. He died in the year 1513, the fifth of Henry VIII. His <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> is not inferior to that of any of his contemporaries. His works are, 1. De antiquitate et magnificentia urbis Celfriae. 2. Chronicon. 3. The life of the glorious virgin of St Werberg. Printed Lond. 1521, 4to, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. The life of St Werberg makes only part of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; for it contains also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Mercia, life of St Etheldreda, the life of St Sexburga, the foundation and history of Chester, and the chronicles of some kings. Possibly this work may include the two first. Bishop Tanner says, that he wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a> in English verse, extracted from Bede, Malmesbury, Geraldus, and others. Probably this is the chronicle above mentioned.

BRADWARDIN

Pages 442-442

Thomas, archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, was born at Hartfield in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the 13th century. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERTON">Merton</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; and acquired the reputation of a profound scholar, a skilful mathematician, and consummate divine. Authors are not agreed as to his first preferences. Pitt says he was professor of divinity at Oxford. They agree, however, in asserting, that from being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, he became a courtier and confessor to Edward III., whom he constantly attended during his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with France, afflicting that victorious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> with his advice, animating the troops, and fervently praying for their success. After his return from the war, he was made prebendary of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, and afterwards archbishop of Canterbury. He died at Lambeth in the year 1349, forty days after his consecration: and was buried in St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANSELM">Anselm</a>'s chapel, near the south wall. His works are, 1. De causa Dei, printed at London, 1618, published by J. H. Savile. 2. De geometria <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a>, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1495, 1512, 1530. 3. De arithmetica practica, Paris, 1502, 1512. 4. De proportionibus, Paris, 1495. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, 1505, folio. 5. De quadratura circuli, Paris, 1495, folio.

BRADY

Pages 442-442

Nicholas, an excellent divine and poet, born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANDON">Bandon</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cork, October 28th 1659. He studied at Westminster-school, and afterwards at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. He was a zealous promoter of the Revolution; and, in 1690, when the troubles broke out in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, by his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> with McCarty, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James's general, he thrice prevented the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of the town of Bandon. Having quitted several preferments in Ireland, he settled in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where he was successively promoted to several livings; and at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was rector of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CLAPHAM">Clapham</a>, minister of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a>, and chaplain to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a>'s troop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-guards. He wrote <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the new version of the Psalms, now sung in many churches in England and Ireland; the Æneids of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, in 4 vols; and 3 vols of sermons. He died May 20th 1726.

BRADYPUS

Pages 442-442
or Sloth, a genus of quadrupeds, belonging to the order of bruta. See Mammalia Index.

BRAE-MAR

Pages 442-442

a mountainous territory of Scotland, in the shire of Aberdeen, where the last <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Mar began to raise a rebellion in 1715. It is 27 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Aberdeen. BRAE-Murray, a mountainous and woody tract of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, lying in the shires of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ELGIN">Elgin</a> and Nairn in Scotland.

BRAG

Pages 442-442

an ingenious and pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, where as many may partake as the cards <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> supply; the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> dealing three to each person at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> up the last card all round. This done, each gambler puts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> three stakes, one for each card.—The first stake is won by the best card turned up in the dealing round; beginning from the ace, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNAVE">knave</a>, and so downwards. When cards of the same value are turned up to two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more of the gamblers, the eldest hand gains; but it is to be observed, that the ace of diamonds wins, to whatever hand it be turned up.—The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> stake is won by what is called the brag, which consists in one of the gamblers challenging the rest to produce cards equal to his: Now it is to be observed, that a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of aces is the best brag, a pair of kings the next, and so on; and a pair of any four wins the stake from the most valuable single card. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> consists the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> diversion of the game; for, by the artful management of the looks, gestures, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, it frequently happens, that a pair of fives, treys, or even duces, out-brags a much higher pair, and even some pairs <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>, to the no small merriment of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. The knave of clubs is here a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> favourite, making a pair with any other card in hand, and with any other two cards a pair royal.—The third stake is won by the person who first makes up the cards in his hand one and thirty; each dignified card going for ten, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> from the pack, as usual in this game.

BRAGA

Pages 442-442

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Entre-montes-ho-duro, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, situated on the river Cavado, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 40'. N. Lat. 41° 20'.

BRAGANZA

Pages 442-442

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same name. It is seated on an eminence, by a brook called Farsenca; and is divided into two parts, the old city and the town. The former is upon an eminence, and fortified with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> wall. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> next the town has five battions, but no ditch; the citadel is on the opposite side joined to the wall. The town is in a plain, and defended by a fort with four bastions. It is seated near the river Sabor, on the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a>, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 15'. N. Lat. 41° 27'.

BRAGGOT

Pages 442-442

a kind of drink made of malt, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and spices, much used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>.

BRAHE

Pages 442-443

Tycho, a celebrated astronomer, descended of an illustrious family originally of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> but settled at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, was born <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 14, 1546, at BRAHE at Knudstorp in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Schonen. He was taught Latin when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years old, and studied five years under private tutors. His father dying, his uncle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a> him, in April 1559, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> eclipse of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> on the 21st of August 1560, happening at the precise <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the astronomers had foretold, he began to look upon <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> as something divine; and purchasing the tables of Stadius, gained some notion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>. In 1562, he was sent by his uncle to Leipzig to study <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; but astronomy wholly engrossed his thoughts, and in purchasing books on that science he employed all his pocket-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. Having procured a small celestial globe, he was wont to wait till his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> was gone to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>, in order to examine the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a> and learn their names; and when the sky was clear, he spent whole nights in viewing the stars. In 1565, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> arising between Brahe and a Danish nobleman, they fought, and the former had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his nose cut off; which defect he so artfully supplied with one made of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, that it was not perceivable. It was about this time that he began to apply to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, proposing nothing less than to obtain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER_S_STONE"><a class="xref" hre</a>f="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. In 1571, he returned to Denmark; and was favoured by his mother's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, Steno Belle, a lover of learning, with a convenient <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> at his castle of Herritzvad near Knudstorp, for making his observations, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LABORATORY">laboratory</a>. His marrying a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> girl, beneath his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, occasioned such a violent quarrel between him and his relations, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> was obliged to interpose to reconcile them. In 1574, by his majesty's command, he read lectures upon the theory of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">comets</a> at Copenhagen. The year following he began his travels through Germany, and proceeded as far as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>; he then resolved to remove his family, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>; but Frederic II. king of Denmark being informed of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, and unwilling to lose a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> that was capable of being such an ornament to his country, promised to enable him to pursue his studies, to bestow upon him for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Huen in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">Sound</a>, to erect an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a> and laboratory there, and to defray all the expenses necessary for carrying on his designs. Tycho Brahe readily embraced this proposal; and accordingly the first stone of the observatory was laid August 8, 1576. The king also gave him a pension of 2000 crowns out of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, a fee in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, and a canonry of Rofhild, which brought him in 1000 more. James VI. of Scotland, afterwards raised to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of England, going to Denmark in order to marry the princess <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, paid a visit to our author in his retirement at Uraniaburg, made him several presents, and with his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> wrote a copy of verses in his praise; but, soon after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of King Frederic, he was deprived of his pension, fee, and canonry; upon which, finding himself incapable of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the expenses of his observatory, he went to Copenhagen, whither he brought some of his instruments, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his astronomical observations in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, till Valkendorf, chamberlain to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> of Christian IV. commanded him by the king's order to discontinue them. He then removed his family to Rotstock, and afterwards to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>, in order to solicit Henry Ranzou to introduce him to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>; and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> complying with his request, he was received by the emperor at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a> with the utmost civility and respect. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> gave him a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, till he could procure one for him more fit for astronomical observations; assigned him a pension of 3000 crowns; and promised upon the first opportunity, a fee for him and his descendants; but he did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> enjoy this happy situation; for, upon the 24th of October 1601, he died of a retention of urine, in the 55th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and was interred in a very magnificent manner in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> at Prague, where a noble monument was erected to him.—His skill in astronomy is universally known, and he is famed for being the inventor of a new system, which he endeavoured, though without success, to establish upon the ruins of that of Copernicus. He was very credulous with regard to judicial astrology and presages. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> he met an old woman when he went out of doors, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a hare upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> on a journey, he used to turn back immediately, being persuaded that it was a bad <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>. When he lived at Uraniaburg, he had at his house a madman, whom he placed at his feet at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and fed himself. As he imagined that everything spoken by mad persons prefigured something, he carefully observed all that this man said; and because it sometimes proved true, he imagined it might always be depended on. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> trifle put him in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>; and against persons of the first rank, with whom it was his duty to keep on good terms, he openly discovered his resentment. He was very apt to rally others, but highly provoked if the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> was taken with himself. His principal works are, 1. Progymnasmata astronomiae. 2. De mundi ætheris recentioribus phænomenis. 3. Epistolæ rerum astronomiarum liber. BRAHMA. See BRAHA.

BRAIDALBIN

Pages 443-444

a district of <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-PERTHSHIRE">Perthshire</a> in Scotland, stretching 32 miles from east to west, and 13 where broadest from south to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>.
