It is a mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, lying among the Grampian hills, supposed to be the country anciently known by the name of Allannach; whence the Highlanders to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> call themselves Allinich. It is bounded on the west by Lochaber, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORN">Lorn</a>, and Knapdale; on the north and east, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Lochaber and part of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHOL">Athol</a>; and on the south by Strathern and Monteith. It produces plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle; is inhabited by Highlanders said to be the most ferocious in all Scotland; and gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to a branch of the Campbell family, which is possessed of a noble and magnificent seat in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>. Much <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> is cultivated here. Some years ago, when premiums were given for the greatest crops, from 70 to 120 hogheads of linseed were annually sown, each peck yielding two <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of dressed flax; and when the yarn fold highest, 2000l. worth has been sold out of the country. Oats and potatoes are the other crops. Oats yield from four to six fold at the most, often less; bear from eight to ten, at an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> six. The corn raised seldom suffices the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants, so they are often obliged to have recourse to importation. From their potatoes some have distilled a very strong spirit, which has been found cheaper than what is distilled from any grain. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STARCH">Starch</a> is also made from them; and, in some places, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. Corcur, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the lichen omphaloides, is an article of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities have been scraped from the rocks, and exported for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the dyers, at the price of 1s. or 16d. per <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. A good many sheep are reared here, and much <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> is sent out of the country. There are few horses raised in this country; such as feed on the tops of the higher hills are often afflicted with a distemper that <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> proves fatal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a remedy is not applied within 24 hours. It attacks them in the months of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> and August, usually after a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, or before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a> rises in the morning. An universal swelling spreads over the body; the remedy is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, chafing, or any other method that promotes urine and perspiration. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> this evil to a certain animal that scatters its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a> over the grass; but, more probably, it arises from some noxious vegetable, hitherto unobserved. Before the year 1745, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Braidalbin was obliged to keep a constant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> for the protection of his valuable cattle, or to retain spies among the thieves, having too much spirit to submit to pay an infamous tax, called blackmail, to the plundering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>-tans, as the price of their safety.

BRAIL

Pages 444-444
or BRAILS, in a ship, are small ropes made use of to furl the sails across; they belong only to the two courses and the mizen-sail; they are reeved through the blocks, seized on each side the ties, and come down before the sail, being at the very skirt thereof fastened to the cringles; their use is, when the sail is furled across, to haul up its bunt, that it may the more easily be taken up or let fall. Hale up the brails, or brail up the sail; that is, Hale up the sail, in order to be furled or bound close to the yard.

BRAILLOW

Pages 444-444

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Podolia, seated on the river Bog, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 29° 0'. N. Lat. 43° 50'.

BRAIN

Pages 444-444

in Anatomy, is that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, soft, whitish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, enclosed in the cranium <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> skull; wherein all the organs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> terminate, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> is supposed principally to reside. See ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BRAINE LE COMTE

Pages 444-444

a town of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Hainault. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 11'. N. Lat. 50° 35'.

BRAINTREE

Pages 444-444

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> in England, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 30'. N. Lat. 51° 50'.

BRAKE

Pages 444-444

denotes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> fern, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it grows.—Also a sharp bit or snaffle for horses; and a baker's kneading-trough.—Also an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> to bruise <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>. See FLAX DRESSING.

BRAKEL

Pages 444-444

a town of Germany, in the circle of Westphalia, and in the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADERBORN">Paderborn</a>, seated on the rivulet Brught, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 8'. N. Lat. 51° 46'.

BRAMA

Pages 444-444

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of cyprinus. See CYPRINUS.

BRAMANT

Pages 444-444

a town of Savoy, in the valley of Maurich, seated on the river Arck, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 15'. N. Lat. 45° 0'.

BRAMBER

Pages 444-444

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a> in England, formerly of some account, but has neither market nor fair; however, it sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 15'. N. Lat. 50° 50'.

BRAMBLE

Pages 444-444
or Brambling, in Ornithology, the trivial name of a species of Fringilla.

BRAMER

Pages 444-444

LEONARD, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>-painter, was born at Delft in 1596; but learned the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> in the school of Rembrandt, and imitated the manner of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in small. In the 18th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> he went to Rome for his improvement; but although he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> for some years, and acquired somewhat in his style rather more graceful than Rembrandt, yet he could never divest himself of the Flemish gout. Pittiglione. He had a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>; his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> is generally good, and in some of his compositions truly noble. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> is delicate, and his colouring very peculiar in the tints, being also remarkably thin in many parts, so as barely to cover the panel; yet, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> skill in the management of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIARO_SCURO">chiaro-scuro</a>, his colouring is bright, bold, and full of lustre; particularly in the vases, which he was fond of introducing in every subject that could admit them, as he knew how to give them a rich and fine relievo. He had accustomed himself to paint with a very thin body of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, especially in the browns and shadowy parts, in order to give his pictures a greater transparency. At <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, and other cities of Italy, as well as at Rome, he left many proofs of his extraordinary merit, which rendered his name deservedly famous; and his works are rarely to be met with out of Italy, where he painted most; but whenever they are to be purchased they are bought at considerable prices, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are entire and undamaged. One of the most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> pictures of Bramer is the Raising of Lazarus, in which there is a charming opposition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and shadow; and another is the Denial of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>: They are both painted in his best manner; they are bright, transparent, and finely penciled, and are still preserved at Rome. Likewise at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Ryfwick, there are several valuable paintings by this master; in which the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> and execution are highly commendable. But none of his works can be more admired than a small <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> representing the story of Pyramus and Thisbe.

BRAMHALL

Pages 444-445

DR. JOHN, archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMAGH">Armagh</a>, was born of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family at Pontefract in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, about the year 1593. He was invited over to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> Wentworth; and soon after obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>-deaconry of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEATH">Meath</a>, the best in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. In 1634, he was made bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONDONDERRY">Londonderry</a>, which see he improved very much; but the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> he did to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Ireland, was by getting, with the deputy's affiance, several acts passed for abolishing fee-farms, recovering impropriations, &c., by which, and by other means, he regained to the church in the space of four years £30,000, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> £40,000 a-year. In the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a> he prevailed upon the church of Ireland to unite in the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> with the church of England, by adopting the 39 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> BRA Bramins, cles of that church; and would willingly have introduced the English canons, but could only prevail on their accepting such as they deemed proper. Articles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> were exhibited against him in the Irish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UXBRIDGE">Uxbridge</a> in 1644, the English parliament made it a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRELIMINARY">preliminary</a> article, that Bishop Bramhall, with Archbishop Laud, and others, should be excepted from the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>. He went abroad; but on the restoration was appointed archbishop of Armagh, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> and metropolitan of all Ireland, and was chosen speaker of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of lords. He died in 1663; and was the author of several works, which are collected in one vol. folio.

BRAMINS

Pages 445-445

the name of the priests among the idolatrous Indians; the successors of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Brahmins. See the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> BRACHMANS. Their name is formed from Brama, their particular deity. They are found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>, Malabar, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, Coromandel, and most other eastern nations anywhere civilized; but their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> seat is in Indofian*, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Mogul's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. They have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> peculiar to themselves, which they call Shanjchrit; in which they have several ancient books, written, as is alleged, by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> prophet Brahma; as the Shaftram, which is their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">bible</a>; and Porane, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> which they esteem sacred, and pretend to have been dictated by God himself. There are several orders of Bramins. Those who mix in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> are for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> very corrupt in their morals: they believe that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of the Ganges <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> wash away all their crimes; and, as they are not subject to any civil jurisdiction, live without either restraint or virtue, excepting that character of compassion and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> which is so <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> found in the mild <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. The others, who live abstracted from the world, are either weak-minded men or enthusiasts; and abandon themselves to laziness, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>. We find in their disputes the very same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> that occur in the writings of our most celebrated metaphysicians; such as, substance, accident, priority, posteriority, immutability, indivisibility, &c. Their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, which was anciently of the allegorical and moral kind, hath degenerated into a heap of extravagant and obscene superstitions, owing to their having realized those fictions which were intended merely as so many symbols and emblems. Were it possible to obtain a sight of their sacred books, the only remains there are of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> antiquities, we might in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> be enabled to remove the veil that envelopes those numerous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a>; but the following story will show how little reason there is to hope that we shall ever be intrusted with such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Mahmoud Akbar had an inclination to make himself acquainted with the principles of all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> sects throughout his extensive provinces. Having discarded the superstitious notions with which he had been prepossessed by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in the Mahometan <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, he resolved to judge for himself. It was easy for him to be acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of those systems that are formed upon the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of making profestes; but he found himself disappointed in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> when he came to treat with the Indians, who will not admit any person whatever to the participation of their mysteries. Neither the authority nor promises of Akbar could prevail with the Bramins to disclose the tenets of their religion; he was therefore obliged to have recourse to artifice. The stratagem he made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of was to cause a boy, of the name of Feizi, to be committed to the care of these priests, as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> orphan of the sacerdotal line, who alone could be initiated into the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. Feizi, having received the proper instructions for the part he was to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, was conveyed privately to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENARES">Benares</a>, the seat of knowledge in Indofian; he was received into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of a learned Bramin, who educated him with the same care as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had been his own son. After the youth had spent ten years in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, Akbar was desirous of recalling him: but he was struck with the charms of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of his preceptor. The women of the sacerdotal tribe are looked upon as the greatest beauties in Indofian. The old Bramin laid no restraint upon that growing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> of the two lovers: he was fond of Feizi, who had gained his affection by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> and docility; and offered him his daughter in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. The young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, divided between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>, resolved to conceal the fraud no longer; and falling at the feet of the Bramin, discovered the imposture and asked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> for his offence. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, without reproaching him in the least, seized a poignard, which hung at his girdle, and was going to plunge it in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, if Feizi had not prevented him by taking hold of his arm. The young man used every means to pacify him, and declared himself ready to do anything to expiate his treachery. The Bramin, bursting into tears, promised to pardon him on condition that he should swear never to translate the Bedac or sacred volumes, or disclose to any person whatever the symbol of the Bramin creed. Feizi readily promised all that the Bramin required: how far he kept his word is not known; but the sacred books of the Indians have never been translated by him, or any one else, to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. As the Bramins are the only persons who understand the language of the sacred books, their comments on the text are the same as those that have ever been made on religious books; all the maxims which fancy, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, passion, or false zeal can suggest, are to be found in these volumes. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> SHAFTAH and VEDAM. They own a supreme God, who created Brama, and gave him a power to create the world. They have also their subaltern deities, their pagods or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and idols, whom they fan to defend from flies, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> before them. They also hold a feast in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, considered as the source of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, whereby all nature is fecundified. Their pagods or temples consist of three parts. The first is a vaulted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, supported on <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> columns: it lies open, and all persons, without distinction, are allowed to enter into it. It is adorned with symbolical figures made of wood, as elephants, oxen, and horses. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> part is open in the daytime, and shut at night. It is filled with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROTESQUE">grotesque</a> and monstrous figures, as men with many heads and arms. The third, which is a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCEL">chancel</a>, is kept always shut, with a very strong gate. In this is placed the statue of the deity to whom the pagod is dedicated. A great num-

BRANCH

Pages 445-446

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, an arm of a tree, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> which, sprouting out from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, helps to form the head or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> thereof. Branches do not <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> surface of the trunk, but are profoundly rooted therein, so as not only to penetrate into the cortical, but also the woody substance, and even the pith. The constituent parts therefore of a branch are the same as of the trunk, viz. skin, bark, wood, and pith. See the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">Plants</a>. Branches of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDLE">Bridle</a>, in the manege, are two pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> bended, which, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between the one and the other, bear the bit-mouth, the crofs-chains, and the curb; so that on one end they answer to the head-stall, and on the other to the reins, in order to keep the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s head in subjection. With regard to their form and structure, branches are either straight, in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISTIL">pistil</a>, for young horses to form their mouth; or after the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a> of France's fashion, proper for a horse that carries his head well. Some are in form of a gigot or leg, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> prevent horses from carrying too low; some are in form of a bent knee, contrived for horses that arm themselves against the operation of the bit; and others after the French fashion, which is hardly above \( \frac{1}{4} \) of an inch at the sevile hole, and kneed \( 1\frac{1}{2} \) inch at the jarret or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAM">ham</a>. It is to be observed, 1. That the farther the branch is from the horse's neck, the more effect it will have. 2. That short branches, ceteris paribus, are ruder, and their effects more sudden, than those of longer. 3. That the branch is to be proportioned to the length of a horse's neck; and one may sooner err in choosing one too short than too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. Branches of Ogives, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> of Gothic vaults. These arches, traversing from one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> to another diagonal-wise, form a crois between the other arches, which make the sides of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, of which the arches are diagonal. Branch-Stand, with falconers, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to signify the making a hawk <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> from tree to tree, till the dog <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>.

BRANCHER

Pages 446-446

among sportsmen, a young hawk, newly taken out of the nest, that can hop from bough to bough.

BRANCHIAE

Pages 446-446
or GILLS, in the anatomy of fishes, the parts corresponding to the lungs of land-animals. All fishes except the cetaceous ones, and the pteromyzum, which have lungs, are furnished with these organs of respiration. See Anatomy Index. BRANCHIDÆ, in Grecian antiquity, priests of the temple of Apollo, which was at Didymus in Ionia, a province of Lesser Asia, towards the Aegean sea, upon the frontiers of Caria. They opened to Xerxes the temple of Apollo, the riches whereof he took away. After which, thinking it unsafe to stay in Greece, they fled to Sogdiana, on the other side of the Caspian sea, upon the frontiers of Persia, where they built a city, called by their own name: but they did not escape the punishment of their crime; for Alexander the Great having conquered Darius king of Persia, and being informed of their treachery, put them all to the sword, and razed their city, thus punishing the impiety of the fathers in their posterity.

BRANCHIOSTEGLI

Pages 446-447

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to express one of the general classes of fishes; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are, that the rays of the fins are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONY">bony</a> Bony substance, but these fish have no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> officula at the branchiae, as the malacopterygious and acanthopterygious fishes all have.

BRANCHON

Pages 447-447

a town of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAMUR">Namur</a>, seated on the river Meuse. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 40'. N. Lat. 50° 32'. BRAND <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, Dimanche des Brandons, in French <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, denotes the first Sunday in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>; which is thus called on account of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> practice in the Lyonnais, where the peasants, in the night of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, walked about their orchards, gardens, &c., with torches lighted, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fire-brands in their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; in which plight they visited every tree, and adorning themselves to them one after another, threatened, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they did not bear fruit well the ensuing season, they should be cut <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the ground and burnt. This is evidently a relic of Paganism; the like of which was practised by the ancient idolaters in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of February; hence called Februarius, à februaendo.

BRANDEIS

Pages 447-447

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14° 25'. N. Lat. 50° 15'.

BRANDENBURG

Pages 447-448

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the marquifate of that name, situated on the river Havel, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13°. N. Lat. 52°. 25′. It is divided into the old and new town, and was anciently the see of a bishop. The mountain in the neighbourhood called Marienberg, is planted with vines. Here is a small colony of French Calvinists, with a manufacture of cloth, fustian, and canvas; and a pretty good trade is carried on by Havel. The fort here looks like a suburb, and contains a riding school, with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> also of the members of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> which fill subfifts, and is composed of a Lutheran provost, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, senior, subfiorior, and three other canons, reside in it. They are distinguished by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> enamelled with violet, terminating in eight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>; and have a considerable estate. Near the town is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> lake.

BRANDEUM

Pages 448-448

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> veil put over the tombs of the apostles St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> and St Paul, and left there for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; by which it is supposed to acquire a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of sanctity, so as to be worshipped as a relic; and for that purpose frequently sent by the pope as a present to some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, Brandeum amounts to the same with what was otherwife called sanctuarium, judarium, orarium, and velum. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of brandea was introduced as a means of diffusing and propagating the virtues and influences of relics, without moving, or any way impairing, the substance of them; the translation of relics in early days being forbidden.

BRANDING

Pages 448-448

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> inflicted by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> on various offences, by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> with a hot-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, after the offender hath been once admitted to benefit of clergy.

BRANDON

Pages 448-448

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a> in England, seated on a little river Ouse, over which it has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, and a ferry at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a>'s distance: whence it is divided into Brandon, and Brandon ferry; which last has the most business, because commodities are brought thither from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> gives the British <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> to the family of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a> in Scotland. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o°. 55′. N. Lat. 52°. 30′.

BRANDRITH

Pages 448-448

among builders, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rail about the mouth of a well.

BRANDT

Pages 448-448

GERARD, a learned divine of the reformed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1626, and was successively minister in several places of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>. He wrote some works which are esteemed, particularly the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the reformation of the Netherlands, 4 vols. 4to; and The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Ruyter; both written in the Flemish tongue. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a> in 1685.

BRANDY

Pages 448-448

a spirituous and inflammable liquor, extracted from wine and other liquors by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>. See Distillation. Wine-brandy, made in France, is esteemed the best in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. They make it wherever they make wine, and for that purpose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> wine that is pricked rather than good wine. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> brandies for foreign trade, and those accounted best, are the brandies of Bordeaux, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COGNAC">Cognac</a>, Charenton, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Rhe, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Blafois, Poitou, Touraine, Anjou, Nantz, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, and Champagne.

BRANK

Pages 448-448

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used in some parts of Scotland, and in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, for correcting scolding women. It is a sort of head-piece, which opens and encloses the head of the impatient, while an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, sharp as a chisel, enters the mouth, and subdues the more dreadful weapon within. Thus harnessed, the offender is led in triumph through the streets. Dr Plott, in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Staffordshire, has favoured the world with a minute <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the instrument*, which Page 380. is there called a scolding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a>; and tells us, he looks Tab. 32. upon it "as much to be preferred to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCKING">ducking</a>-stool, which not only endangers the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of the party, but also gives the tongue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> betwixt every dip; to neither of which this is at all liable."

BRANLIN

Pages 448-448

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of salmon, with several transverse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> streaks, resembling the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of so many fingers.

BRANNODUNUM

Pages 448-448

with a garrison of the Equites Dalmatiae, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, on the Sinus Metaris; now Brancester, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, on the Waffes.

BRANOGNIUM

Pages 448-448
or BRANONIUM, a town of the Coritani, a people in the heart of Britain: from the distances of the Itinerary, Camden supposes it to be Worcester.

BRANSKA

Pages 448-448

a town of Transylvania, situated on the river Marish. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 23°. 15′. N. Lat. 46°. 0′.

BRASIDA

Pages 449-449

an anniversary solemnity at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Brasidas, a Lacedemonian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, famous for his achievements at Methone, Pylos, and Amphipolis. It was celebrated with sacrifices and games, wherein none were permitted to attend but free-born Spartans. Whoever neglected to be present at the solemnity was fined.

BRASIDAS

Pages 448-449

BRASIDAS, a celebrated general of the Lacedemonians, about 424 years before the birth of Christ. He defeated the Athenians by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, took many places, and rendered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> formidable to all the neighbouring states. He conquered the Athenians on their attempting to surprise Amphipolis, but died of the wounds he received in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">ATTICA</a> and LACEDEMON.

BRASIL

Pages 449-451

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, being the easternmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of that continent, lying between the equinoctial line and the tropic of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPRICORN">capricorn</a>. It is about 1560 miles in length, and 1000 in breadth; but, measuring along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, it is 2000 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and is bordered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> that open from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time, and form good harbours where vessels may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in safety. It was accidentally discovered by the Portuguese in 1500. Emmanuel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> had equipped a squadron of 13 sail, carrying 1200 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> and sailors destined for the East Indies, under the conduct of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Alvarez Cabral. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, quitting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a> on the 9th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1500, struck out to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to avoid the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, and steered his course southward, that he might the more easily turn the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope, which projects a good way into the ocean. On the 24th of April, he got sight of the continent of South America, which he judged to be a large <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> at some distance from the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COASTING">Coasting</a> along for some time, he ventured to send a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> on shore; and was astonished to observe the inhabitants entirely different from the Africans in features, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>. It was found, however, impracticable to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> upon any of the Indians, who retired with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> celerity to the mountains on the approach of the Portuguese; yet, as the sailors had discovered a good harbour, the admiral thought proper to come to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, and called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> Puerto Seguro. Next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> he sent another boat on shore, and had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> to lay hold on two of the natives, whom he clothed and treated kindly, and then dismissed, to make a proper report to their countrymen. The stratagem had the desired effect. The Indians, having heard the relation of the prisoners, immediately crowded to the shore, singing, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, and sounding horns of different kinds; which induced Cabral to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and take solemn possession in the name of his Portuguese majesty. As soon as the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Lisbon had ordered a survey to be taken of the harbours, bays, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>, and was convinced that the country afforded neither <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> nor silver, they held it in such contempt, that they sent thither none but condemned criminals and abandoned women. Two ships were sent every year from Portugal, to carry the refuse of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> to this new world, and to bring home parrots and woods for the dyers and cabinet-makers. Ginger was afterwards added; but soon after prohibited, left it should interfere with the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of the same article from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. In 1548, the Jews, many of whom had taken refuge in Portugal, beginning to be persecuted by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>, were stripped of their possessions, and banished to Brazil. Here, however, they were not entirely forsaken. Many of them found kind relations and faithful friends; others, who were known to be men of probity and understanding, obtained <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> in advance from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> of different nations with whom they had formerly had transactions. By the affluence of some enterprising men, they were enabled to cultivate <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> canes, which they first procured from the island of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADEIRA">Madeira</a>. Sugar, which till then had been used only in medicine, became an article of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>. Princes and great men were all eager to procure themselves this new <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>. This circumstance proved favourable to Brazil, and enabled it to extend its sugar plantations. The court of Lisbon, notwithstanding its prejudices, began to be sensible, that a colony might be beneficial to the mother country, without producing gold <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> silver; and this settlement, which had been wholly left to the capricious management of the colonists, was now thought to deserve some kind of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; and accordingly Thomas de Souza was sent thither, in 1549, to regulate and superintend it. This able governor began by reducing these men, who had always lived in a state of anarchy, into proper subordination, and bringing their scattered plantations closer together; after which he applied himself to acquire some information respecting the natives, with whom he knew he must be incessantly engaged either in traffic or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. This it was no easy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to accomplish. Brazil was full of small nations, some of which inhabited the forests, and others lived in the plains and along the rivers. Some had settled habitations; but the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of them led a roving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and most of them had no intercourse with each other. It is not to be supposed that such a people would be at all disposed to submit to the yoke which the Portuguese wanted to put upon them on their arrival. At first they only declined all intercourse with these strangers; but finding themselves pursued in order to be made slaves, and to be employed in the labours of the field, they took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> and devour all the Europeans they could seize upon. The friends and relations of the savages that were taken prisoners also ventured to make frequent attempts to rescue them, and were sometimes successful: so that the Portuguese were forced to attend to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> employments of labour and war. Souza did not bring a sufficient number of forces to change the situation of affairs. Indeed, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> San Salvador, he gave a centre to the colony; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of settling, extending, and making it really useful to the mother-country, was reserved for the Jesuits who attended him. These men, who for their arts of insinuation and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> have been equalled by none, dispersed themselves among the Indians. When any of the missionaries were murdered, they were immediately replaced by others; and seeming to be inspired only with sentiments of peace and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, the Indians, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time, grew not only familiar but passionately fond of them. As the missionaires were too few in number to transact all the business themselves, they frequently deputed some of the most intelligent Indians in their stead. These men having distributed hatchets, knives, and looking-glasses, among the savages they met met with, represented the Portuguese as a harmless, humane, and good sort of people. The prosperity of the colony of Brazil, which was visible to all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, excited the envy of the French, Spaniards, and Dutch successively. The latter, indeed, bid farewell to the conquest of the whole. Their admiral Henry Lonk arrived, in the beginning of the year 1639, with 46 men of war, on the coast of Fernando de Noronha, one of the largest and best fortified captainships of these parts. He reduced it after several obstinate engagements, in which he was always victorious. The troops he left behind subdued the captainships of Temaraca, Pareiba, and Rio Grande, in the years 1633, 1634, and 1635. These, as well as Fernando de Noronha, furnished annually a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of sugar, a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of wood for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>, and other commodities. The Hollander was so elated with the acquisition of this wealth, which flowed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> instead of Lisbon, that they determined to conquer all the Brazils, and intruded Maurice of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a> with the conduct of this enterprise. That general reached the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his destination in the beginning of the year 1637. He found the soldiers so well disciplined, the commanders such experienced men, and so much readiness in all to engage, that he directly took the field. He was successively opposed by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBUQUERQUE">Albuquerque</a>, Banjola, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Rocca de Borgia, and the Brazilian Cameron, the idol of his people, passionately fond of the Portuguese, brave, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, cunning, and who wanted no qualification necessary for a general, but to have learned the art of war under able commanders. These several chiefs exerted their utmost efforts to defend the possessions that were under their protection; but their endeavours proved ineffectual. The Dutch seized upon the captainships of Siara, Sereipipe, and the greater part of that of Bahia. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> of the 15 provinces which composed the colony had already submitted to them, and they flattered themselves that one or two campaigns would make them masters of the rest of their enemies possessions in that part of America; when they were suddenly checked by the revolution happening on the banishment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> IV., and placing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRAGANZA">Braganza</a> on the throne. After this, the Portuguese recovering their spirits, soon drove the Dutch out of Brazil, and have <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> masters of it ever since. The country of Brazil is divided into the following provinces, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIA">Paria</a>, Maragnano, Siara, Rio Grande, Pareiba, Tamaraca, Fernando de Noronha, Sereipipe, Bahia, Porto Seguro, Espirito Santo, Rio de Janeiro, Angra, St Vincent, and Del Rey. See these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. The first aspect of the country from the sea is rather unfavourable, as it appears <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, rough, and unequal; but, on a more narrow inspection, nothing can be more delightful, the eminences being covered with woods, and the valleys and savannahs with the most refreshing verdure. In so vast a tract of land, it cannot be imagined that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found at all equal, or the seasons uniform. The northern provinces are subject to heavy rains and variable winds, like other countries under the same parallels. Tornadoes, storms, and the utmost fury of the elements, wreak their vengeance here; while the southerly regions are blest with all the comforts which a fine fertile <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and temperate climate can afford. In some of the provinces, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the climate is thought to prove favourable to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of a great variety of poisonous reptiles: some of which, as the liboy or redback snake, are said to extend to the length of 30 feet, and to be two or three yards in circumference. The rattlesnake and other reptiles of the same kind, grow likewise to an enormous size; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> called ibilaboca is affirmed to be 7 yards long, and half a yard in circumference, possessed too of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a> instantaneously fatal to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. Here also are scorpions, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANT">ant</a>-bears, tygers or mandillos, porcupines, janoweras, and an animal called tapiraffe, which is the production of a bull and an ass, having a great resemblance to both. No country on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> affords a greater number of beautiful birds, nor variety of the most exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> commodities are Brazil-wood, ebony, dyeing woods, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBERGRIS">ambergris</a>, rosin, balsams, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, sweetmeats, sugar, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, gold, diamonds, beautiful pebbles, crystal, emeralds, jasper, and other precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; in all which the Portuguese carry on such an amazing trade, as may justly be reputed the support, and indeed the vital fountain, of the mother country. The gold and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> are but a recent discovery: they are first opened in the year 1681; and have since yielded above five millions <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> annually, of which sum a fifth belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. So plentiful are diamonds in this country, that the court of Portugal hath found it necessary to refrain their importation, to prevent too great a diminution of their value. They are neither so hard nor so clear as those of the East Indies, nor do they sparkle so much, but they are whiter. The Brazilian diamonds are sold ten per cent. cheaper than the Oriental ones, supposing the weights to be equal. The largest diamond in the world was sent from Brazil to the king of Portugal. It weighs 1680 carats, or 12 ounces; and has been valued at £6,787,500. Some skilful lapidaries, however, are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that this supposed diamond is only a topaz; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> a very great abatement must be made in its value. The crown revenue arising from this colony amounts to two millions sterling in gold, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> some late writers, besides the duties and customs on merchandise imported from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. This indeed is more than a fifth of the precious metal produced by the mines; but, every other consequent advantage considered, it probably does not much exceed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. The excellent confluence of people to the Brazil colonies, as well from other countries as from Portugal, not only enlarges the imports of gold, but, what is of infinitely more importance to Europe in general, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of this hemisphere; of which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> are the following. Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> sends woollen manufactures; such as fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> medley cloths, fine Spanish cloths, fcarlet and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cloths; ferges, duroys, druggets, sagathies, falloons, camlets, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a> stuffs; black <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLCHESTER">Colchester</a> baize; say's, and perpetuans called long ell's; <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, stockings, and gloves. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, Germany, and France, chiefly export fine hollands, bone-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, and fine thread; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> manufactures, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> tin, and other articles, are also sent from different countries. Besides the particulars already specified, England likewise trades with Portugal, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the Brazils, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and bras, wrought and unwrought <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEWTER">pewter</a>, and all kinds of hardware; all which articles have so enlarged the Portuguese trade, that, instead of 12 ships usually employed in the Brazil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, there are now never fewer. Brazil-wood fewer than 100 sail of large vessels constantly going and returning to those colonies. To all this may be added the vast slave-trade carried on with the coast of Africa for the use of the Brazil colonies; which, we may believe, employs a great number of shipping, from the multitude of slaves that are annually transported. Indeed the commerce of Brazil alone is sufficient to raise Portugal to a considerable height of naval power, as it maintains a constant nursery of seamen; yet a certain infatuation in the policy of the country has prevented that effect, even amidst all these extraordinary advantages. All the ships in this trade, being under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, have their appointed seasons of going and returning, under convoy of a certain number of men of war; nor can a single ship clear out or go, except with the fleet, but by a special license from the king, which is seldom granted; though it is easily determined, that such restrictions can prove no way beneficial to the general commerce, though possibly the crown revenue may be better guarded thereby. The fleets sail in the following order, and at the following stated periods: That to Rio de Janeiro sets sail in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>; the fleet to Bahia, or the Bay of All Saints, in February; and the third fleet, to Fernambucca, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of March. Brazil-Wood, or Brazil-wood, an American wood of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and very heavy. It is denominated variously, according to the places from whence it is brought: Thus we have brasil of Fernambucca, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, Lamon, &c. For its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, &c. see Cæsalpinia, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Brasilietto, the same with Brazil-wood. Braslaw, a considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, in Lithuania, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILNA">Wilna</a>, with a castle. It is seated on a small lake, in E. Long. 17° 5'. N. Lat. 55° 45'.

BRASS

Pages 451-452
or, as the French call it, yellow copper, is a fictitious metal, composed of copper and zinc. See Chemistry Index. The first formation of bras, as we are assured by scripture, was prior to the flood, and discovered even in the seventh generation from Adam*. But the use of it was not, as is generally believed, and the Arundelian marbles assert, previous to the knowledge of iron. They were both first known in the same generation, and first wrought by the same discoverer. And the knowledge of them must have been equally carried over the world afterwards, with the spreading of the colonies of the Noachidae. An acquaintance with the one or the other was absolutely necessary to the existence of the colonists; the clearing away of the woods about their settlements, and the erection of houses for their habitation. The ancient Britons, though acquainted from the remotest periods with the use of both these metals, remained long ignorant that they were to be obtained in the island. Before this discovery they imported all their iron and bras from the continent. And when they had at length detected the former in their own hills, and had ceased to introduce it, they continued to receive the latter. Their want of the metal remained, and no mines of it were opened in the island. In the earliest ages whose manners have been delineated by history, we find the weapons of their warriors invariably framed of this fictitious metal; and the most authentic of all the profane records of antiquity, the A- * Gen. iv. rundelian marbles, for that reason, mistakenly date the first discovery of iron a couple of centuries below the Trojan war. Every military nation, as such, is naturally studious of brightness in its arms; and the Britons, particularly, gloried in the neatness of theirs. For this reason the nations of the world still fabricated their arms of bras, even long after the Arundelian era for the discovery of iron; and the Britons continued to import it from the continent, though they had found iron to be a native of the country, and could have supplied themselves with a sufficient quantity of it. Mr Whitaker supposes, that when the Britons deprived their iron and bras from the continent, they purchased the latter at an easier expense than the former. The Gauls had many large bras works carried on in the kingdom, but seem to have had but few iron forges within it. And this would naturally induce the Belgae to be less diligent in their inquiry after the veins of copper and calamine at home, than for the courses of iron ore; though the one was equally discoverable in the island as the other, and lay equally within the Belgic regions of it. Bras being thus cheaper than iron, they necessarily formed with it some domestic as well as military implements. Such were common among the Gauls; and such were familiar to the Britons, either imported into the island, as some actually were, or manufactured within it, as others also assuredly were. The Britons had certainly bras foundries erected among them, and minted money, and fabricated weapons of bras. In this condition of the works, the Romans entered the island. And seeing so great a demand among the natives for this article, they would speedily instruct them to discover the materials of it among themselves. This must unavoidably have resulted from the conquest of the Romans. The power of surprising their new subjects with so unexpected a discovery would naturally stimulate the pride of the Roman intellect; and the desire of obliging themselves with so cheap a supply of that useful metal, stationary as they were in that kingdom, would also equally actuate the selfishness of the Roman bras. The veins of copper and calamine would be easily found out by an experienced inquirer after them; and the former metal is therefore distinguished among the Welsh, only by the Roman appellation of cyprium, koppr or copper. And many foundries of bras appear to have been established in the island. Some had been erected before, one perhaps within the confines of every kingdom, and probably in the vicinity of every capital. One at least would be necessary, in order to supply the armory of the principality; and one perhaps was sufficient for most of the British states. But several appear now to have been settled in every kingdom, and one perhaps near every stationary town. Two have been discovered in the fingle county of Essex, and within a narrow portion of it, at Fifield and Danbury. And a third was placed upon Easterly Moor in Yorkshire, 12 miles to the north-west of York, and in the neighbourhood of Harrow or Aldborough. Corinthian Brass, famous in antiquity, is a mixture of gold, silver, and copper. L. Mummius having sacked and burnt the city of Corinth, 146 years before Christ, it is said this metal was formed from the immense quantities of gold, silver, and copper, wherewith that city abounded, thus melted and run together by the violence of the conflagration. Brass, in the glass trade.—Thrice calcined brass is a preparation which serves the glaziers to give many very beautiful colours to their metal. The manner of preparing it is this: Place thin plates of brass on tiles on the feet of the furnace near the ocelli; let it stand to be calcined there for four days, and it will become a black powder sticking together in lumps. Powder this, sift it fine, and recalcine it four or five days more; it will not then stick together, but remain a loose powder, of a rufflet colour. This is to be calcined a third time in the same manner; but great care must be taken in the third calcination, that it be not overdone nor underdone: the way to be certain when it is right is, to try it several times in glasses while melting. If it makes it, when well purified, to swell, boil, and rise, it is properly calcined; if not, it requires longer time. This makes, according to the different proportions in which it is used, a sea-green, an emerald-green, or a turcoise colour. Brass, by long calcination alone, and without any mixture, affords a fine blue or green colour for glasses; but they have a method of calcining it also with powdered brimstone, so as to make it afford a red, a yellow, or a chalcedony colour, according to the quantity and other variations in using it. The method of making the calcination is this: Cut thin plates of brass into small pieces with shears, and lay them stratum super stratum, with alternate beds of powdered sulphur, in a crucible; calcine this for 24 hours in a strong fire; then powder and sift the whole; and finally expose this powder upon tiles for 12 days to a reverberating furnace; at the end of this time powder it fine, and keep it for use. The glass-makers have also a method of procuring a red powder from brass, by a more simple calcination, which serves them for many colours. The method of preparing it is this: They put small and thin plates of brass into the arches of the glass furnaces, and leave them there till they are sufficiently calcined, which the heat in that place, not being enough to melt them, does in great perfection. The calcined matter powdered, is of a dusky red, and requires no farther preparation. Brass-Colour, one prepared by the braziers and colour-men to imitate brass. There are two sorts of it; the red brass or bronze, and the yellow or gilt brass: the latter is made only of copper-filings, the smallest and brightest that can be found; with the former they mix some red ochre, finely pulverized; they are both used with varnish.—In order to make a fine brass that will not take any rust or verdigris, it must be dried with a chafing-dish of coals as soon as it is applied.—The finest brass-colour is made with powder brass imported from Germany, diluted into a varnish, made and used after the following manner: The varnish is composed of one pound four ounces of spirit of wine, two ounces of gum-lac, and two ounces of sandarac; these two last drugs are pulverized separately, and afterwards put to dissolve in spirit of wine, taking care to fill the bottle but half full. The varnish being made, you mix such quantity as you please of it with the pulverized brass, and apply it with a small brush to what you would brass over. But you must not mix too much at once, because the varnish being very apt to dry, you would not have time to employ it all soon enough; it is therefore better to make the mixture at several times. After this manner they brass over figures of platter, which look as well as if they were of cast brass. Brass-Leaf is made of copper, beaten out into very thin plates, and afterwards rendered yellow. The German artists, particularly those of Nuremberg and Augsburg, are said to possess the best method of giving to these thin plates of copper a fine yellow colour like gold, by simply exposing them to the fumes of zinc, without any real mixture of it with the metal. These plates are cut into little pieces, and then beaten out fine like leaves of gold; after which they are put into books of coarse paper, and sold at a low price for the vulgar kinds of gilding. The pairings or shreds of these very thin yellow leaves being well ground on a marble plate, are reduced to a powder similar to gold; which serves to cover, by means of gum-water, or some other glutinous fluid, the surface of various mouldings or pieces of curious workmanship, giving them the appearance of real bronze, and even of fine gold, at a very trifling expense, because the gold colour of this metallic powder may be easily raised and improved by flaring it on a wide earthen basin over a slow fire. Brass-Lumps, a common name given by miners to the globular pyrites. See Pyrites, Mineralogy Index.

BRASSAW

Pages 452-452
or Cronstadt, a strong town of Transilvania in Burezland; seated on the river Buxel, in E. Long. 22. 35. N. Lat. 46. 30. BRASSE. A species of Perca. See Ichthyology Index.

BRASSICA

Pages 452-457

cabbage, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, for the classification of which see Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. But as many of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of this genus are of considerable importance as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of food, we shall here lay before our readers a more particular account of their uses and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of culture under the names known to practical gardeners. The species called campestris grows naturally on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shore near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a>, has a perennial branching stalk, and in this it differs from all the other species. In very severe winters, when the other sorts are destroyed, this is a necessary plant, for the most severe frosts do not injure it. The flower-talks grow from the end of the branches, and spread out horizontally; but those which arise from the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> grow erect, and seldom put out branches. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAULIFLOWER">cauliflower</a> has been much more improved in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> than in any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In France they rarely have cauliflowers till Michaelmas, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> has been often supplied with them from Britain. In many parts of Germany there were none of them cultivated till within a few years past, and most parts of Europe are supplied with seeds from Britain. That which is generally known by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cole-seed is much cultivated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>, and some other parts of England, for its seed, from which rape-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> is drawn; and it hath also been cultivated of late years, in other places, for feeding of cattle, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advantage. The cole-feed, when cultivated for feeding of cattle, should be sown about the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>. The ground for this should be prepared for it in the same manner as for turnips. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of seeds for an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> is from six to eight pounds; and as the price of the feed is not great, so it is better to allow eight eight pounds; so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the plants are too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> in any part they may be easily thinned when the ground is hoed, which must be performed in the same manner as is practiced for turnips, with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> only, of leaving them much nearer together; for as they have <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> roots and slender stalks, so they do not require near so much room. These plants should have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> hoeing about five or six weeks after the first, which, if well performed in dry <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> entirely destroy the weeds, so they will require no farther culture. Where there is not an immediate want of food, these plants had better be kept as a reserve for hard weather, or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> feed, when there may be a scarcity of other green food. If the heads are cut off, and the stalks left in the ground, they will float again early in the spring, and produce a good second crop in April; which may be either fed off, or permitted to run to seed, as is the practice where this is cultivated for the seeds; but if the first is fed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, there should be care taken that the cattle do not destroy their stems, or pull them out of the ground. As this plant is so hardy as not to be destroyed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROST">frost</a>, so it is of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in hard winters for feeding of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EWES">ewes</a>; for when the ground is so hard frozen as that turnips cannot be taken up, these plants may be cut off for a constant supply. This will afford late food after the turnips are run to seed; and if it is afterwards permitted to stand for seed, one acre will produce as much as, at a moderate computation, will fell for five pounds, clear of charges. Partridges, pheasants, turkeys, and most other fowl, are very fond of this plant; so that wherever it is cultivated, if there are any birds in the neighbourhood, they will constantly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> among these plants. The seeds of this plant are sown in gardens for winter and spring salads, this being one of the small salad herbs. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, flat, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>-sided cabbages, are chiefly cultivated for autumn and winter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. The seeds of these sorts must be sown the beginning or middle of April, in beds of good fresh <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; and when the young plants have about eight leaves, they should be pricked out into shady borders, about three or four inches <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, that they may acquire strength, and to prevent their growing long stalked. About the middle of June you must transplant them out, where they are to remain. If they are planted for a full crop in a clear spot of ground, the distance from row to row should be three feet and a half, and in the rows two feet and a half aifter: if the season should prove dry when they are transplanted out, you must <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> them every other evening until they have taken fresh root; and afterwards, as the plants advance in height, you should draw the earth about the stems with a hoe, which will keep the earth moist about their roots, and greatly strengthen the plants.
