These cabbages will some of them be fit for use soon after Michaelmas, and will continue until the end of February, if they are not destroyed by bad weather; to prevent which, the gardeners near <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> pull up their cabbages in November, and trench their ground up in ridges, laying their cabbages against their ridges as close as possible on one side, burying their stems in the ground; in this manner they let them remain till after Christmas, when they cut them for the market; and although the outer part of the cabbage be decayed (as is often the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in very wet or hard winters), yet, if the cabbages were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and hard when laid, the inside will remain <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>. The Russian cabbage was formerly in much greater esteem than at present, it being now only to be found in particular gentlemen's gardens, who cultivate it for their own use. This must be sown late in the spring of the year, and managed as those before directed, with this difference only, that they must be sooner planted out, and must have an open clear spot of ground, and require much less distance every way, for it is but a very small hard cabbage. This sort will not continue long before they will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> and run up to seed. The early and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-loaf cabbages are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> sown for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> use, and are what the gardeners about London commonly call Michaelmas cabbages. The season for sowing of these is about the end of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, or beginning of August, in an open spot of ground; and when the plants have got eight leaves, you must prick them into beds at about three or four inches distance every way, that the plants may grow strong and short stalked; and toward the end of October you should plant them out: the distance that these require is, three feet row from row, and two feet and a half aifter in the rows. The ground must be kept clean from weeds, and the earth drawn up about your cabbage plants. In May, if your plants were of the early kind, they will turn in their leaves for cabbaging; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the gardeners near London, in order to obtain them a little sooner, tie in their leaves close with a slender offer twig to blanch their middle; by which means, they have them at least a fortnight sooner than they could have if they were left untied. The early cabbage being the first, we should choose to plant the fewer of them, and a greater quantity of the sugar-loaf kind, which comes after them; for the early kind will not supply the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> long, generally cabbaging apace when they begin, and as soon grow hard and burst open; but the sugar-loaf kind is longer before it comes, and is as slow in its cabbaging; and being of a hollow kind, will continue for a good long time. The sugar-loaf kind may be planted out in February, and will succeed as well as if planted earlier; with this difference only, that they will be later before they cabbage. You should also reserve some plants of the early kind in some well-sheltered spot of ground, to supply your plantation, in case of a defect; for in mild winters many of the plants are apt to run to seed, especially when their seeds are sown too early, and in severe winters they are often destroyed. The Savoy cabbages are propagated for winter use, as being generally esteemed the better when pinched by the frosts; these must be sown about the end of April, and treated after the manner as was directed for the common white cabbage; with this difference that these may be planted at a closer distance than those; two feet and a half square will be sufficient. These are always much better when planted in an open situation, which is clear from trees and hedges; for in clove places they are very subject to be eaten almost up by caterpillars and other <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a>, especially if the autumn prove dry. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROCCOLI">broccoli</a> may also be treated in the same manner, but need not be planted above one foot aifter in the rows, and the rows two feet distance; these are ne- ver eaten till the frost hath rendered them tender; for otherwise they are tough and bitter. The seeds of the broccoli (of which there are several kinds, viz. the Roman or purple, the Neapolitan or white, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> broccoli, with some others, but the Roman is preferred to them all), should be sown about the latter end of May, or beginning of June, and when the plants are grown to have eight leaves, transplant them into beds (as was directed for the common cabbage); and toward the latter end of July they will be fit to plant out, which should be done into some well-sheltered spot of ground, but not under the drip of trees: the distance there require is about a foot and a half in the rows, and two feet row from row. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in which they should be planted ought to be rather <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> than heavy: if your plants succeed well (as there will be little reason to doubt, unless the winter prove extremely hard), they will begin to throw their small heads, which are somewhat like a cauliflower, but of a purple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, about the end of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, and will continue eatable till the middle of April. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> or black broccoli is by many persons greatly esteemed, though it doth not deserve a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the kitchen-garden where the Roman broccoli can be obtained, which is much sweeter, and will continue longer in season: indeed, the brown sort is much harder, so that it will thrive in the coldest situations, where the Roman broccoli is sometimes destroyed in very hard winters. The brown sort should be sown in the middle of May, and managed as hath been directed for the common cabbage, and should be planted at the same distance, which is about two feet and a half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURLONG">furlong</a>. This will grow very tall, so should have the earth drawn up to their stems as they advance in height. This doth not form heads so perfect as the Roman broccoli; the stems and hearts of the plants are the parts which are eaten. The Roman broccoli (if well managed) will have large heads, which appear in the centre of the plants like clutters of buds. These heads should be cut before they run up to feed, with about four or five inches of the stem; the skin of the stems should be stripped off before they are boiled. After the first heads are cut off, there will be a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of side-shoots produced from the stems, which will have small heads to them, but are full as well flavoured as the large. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> broccoli hath white heads very like those of the cauliflower, and eats so like it as not to be distinguished from it.—Besides this first crop of broccoli (which is usually sown in the end of May), it will be proper to sow another crop the beginning of July, which will come in to supply the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> the latter end of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> and the beginning of April; and being very young, will be extremely tender and sweet. In order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> good seeds of this kind of broccoli, you should reserve a few of the largest heads of the first crop, which should be let remain to run up to seed, and all the under shoots should be constantly stripped off, leaving only the main stem to flower and seed. If this be duly observed, and no other sort of cabbage permitted to seed near them, the seeds will be as good as those procured from abroad, and the sort may be preserved in perfection many years. The turnip-rooted cabbage was formerly more cultivated in Britain than at present; for since other sorts have been introduced which are much better flavoured, this sort has been neglected. There are some persons who esteem this kind for soups, but it is too strong for most palates; and is seldom good but in hard winters, which will render it tender and less strong. At the end of June the plants should be transplanted out where they are to remain, allowing them two feet distance every way, observing to water them until they have taken root; and as their stems advance, the earth should be drawn up to them with a hoe, which will preserve a moisture about their roots, and prevent their stems from drying and growing woody, so that the plants will grow more freely; but it should not be drawn very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, for as it is the globular part of the stalk which is eaten, so that should not be covered. In winter they will be fit for use, when they should be cut off, and the stalks pulled out of the ground and thrown away, being good for nothing after the stems are cut off. As food for cattle, however, the cultivation of this species deserves particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> Index. The curled colewort or Siberian broccoli is now more generally esteemed than the former, being extremely hardy, so is never injured by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, but is always sweeter in severe winters than in mild seasons. This may be propagated by sowing of the seeds the beginning of July; and when the plants are strong enough for transplanting, they should be planted in rows about a foot and a half a furlong, and ten inches distance in the rows. These will be fit for use after Christmas, and continue good until April, so that they are very useful in a family. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULE">mule</a> cabbage. This may be propagated in the same manner as the common cabbage, and should be allowed the same distance: it will be fit for use in October, November, and December; but, if the winter proves hard, these will be destroyed much sooner than the common sort. The common colewort or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a> kale, is now almost lost near London, where their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are usually supplied with cabbage plants instead of them. The best method to cultivate this plant in the fields is, to sow the seeds about the beginning of July, choosing a moist soil, which will bring up the plants in about ten days or a fortnight; the quantity of seed for an acre of land is <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> pounds: when the plants have got five or six leaves they should be hoed, as is practised for turnips, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> down all the weeds from amongst the plants, and also thinning the plants where they are too thick; but they should be kept thicker than turnips, because they are more in danger of being destroyed by the fly: this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> should be performed in dry weather, that the weeds may be killed. About six weeks after, the plants should have a second hoeing, which, if carefully performed in dry weather, will entirely destroy the weeds, and make the ground clean, so that they will require no farther culture: in the spring they may be either drawn up and carried out to feed the cattle, or they may be turned in to feed upon them as they stand; but the former method is to be preferred, because there will be little waste; whereas, when the cattle are turned in amongst the plants, they will <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a> down and destroy more than they eat, especially if they are not fenced off by hurdles. The two last sorts of cabbages are varieties fit for a botanic garden, but are plants of no use. They are annual Brassicas, annual plants, and perish when they have perfected their seeds. The best method to save the seeds of all the sorts of cabbages is, about the end of November you should make choice of some of your best cabbages, which you should pull up, and carry to some shed or other covered place, where you should hang them up for three or four days by their stalks, that the water may drain from between their leaves; then plant them in some border near a hedge or pile, quite down to the middle of the cabbage, leaving only the upper part of the cabbage above ground, observing to raise the earth above it, so that it may stand a little above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the ground; especially if the ground is wet, they will require to be raised pretty much above the surface. If the winter should prove very hard, you must lay a little straw or pease haulm lightly upon them, to secure them from the frost, taking it off as soon as the weather proves mild, least by keeping them too close they should rot. In the spring of the year these cabbages will shoot out strongly, and divide into a great number of small branches: you must therefore support their stems, to prevent their being broken off by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>; and if the weather should be very hot and dry when they are in flower, you should refresh them with water once a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> all over the branches, which will greatly promote their feeding, and preserve them from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILDEW">mildew</a>. When the pods begin to change brown, you will do well to cut off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> part of every shoot with the pods, which will strengthen your seeds; for it is generally observed, that those seeds which grow near the top of the shoots, are very subject to run to seed before they cabbage; so that by this there will be no loss, but a great advantage. When your seeds begin to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a>, you must be particularly careful that the birds do not destroy it, for they are very fond of these seeds. The best method to prevent this, is to get a quantity of birdlime, and dawb over a parcel of slender twigs, which should be fastened at each end to stronger sticks, and placed near the upper part of the seed in different places, so that the birds may alight upon them, by which means they will be fastened thereto; where you must let them remain, if they cannot get off themselves; and although there should not above two or three birds be caught, yet it will sufficiently terrify the rest, that they will not come to that place again for a considerable time after. When your seed is fully ripe, you must cut it off; and after drying, thrash it out, and preserve it in bags for use. But in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> of cabbages for seed, it will be proper never to plant more than one sort in a place, or near one another: for example, never plant red and white cabbages near each other, nor Savoy with white or red cabbages; for they will, by the commixture of their effluvia, produce a mixture of kinds: and it is said to be owing to this neglect, that the gardeners rarely save any good red cabbage seed in Britain, but are obliged to procure fresh seeds from abroad; as supposing the soil or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of Britain alters them from red to white, and of a mixed kind betwixt both; whereas, if they should plant red cabbages by themselves for seeds, and not suffer any other to be near them, they might continue the kind as good in Britain as in any other part of the world. Cauliflowers have of late years been so far improved in Britain, as to exceed in goodness and magnitude what are produced in most parts of Europe, and by the skill of the gardener are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for several months together; but the most common season for the great crops is in May, June, and July. Having procured a parcel of good seed, you must sow it about the 21st of August, upon an old cucumber or melon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>, fitting a little earth over the seeds, about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an inch thick; and if the weather should prove extremely hot and dry, you should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> the beds with mats, to prevent the earth from drying too fast, and give it gentle waterings as you may see occasion. In about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>'s time after sowing, your plants will be fit to prick out: you should therefore put some fresh earth upon your cucumber or melon beds; or where these are not to be had, some beds should be made with a little new dung, which should be trodden down close, to prevent the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> from getting through it; but it should not be hot dung, which would be hurtful to the plants at this season, especially if it proves hot; into this bed you should prick your young plants at about two inches square, observing to shade and water them at first planting; but do not water them too much after they are growing, nor suffer them to receive too much <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> if the season should prove wet, which would be apt to make them black blanched, as the gardeners <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> it, which is no less than a rottenness in their stems, and is the destruction of the plants so affected. In this bed they should continue till about the 30th of October, when they must be removed into the place where they are to remain during the winter season; which, for the first sowing, is commonly under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> glasses, to have early cauliflowers, and these should be of an early kind: but in order to have a succession during the season, you should be provided with another more late kind, which should be sown four or five days after the other, and managed as was directed for them. In order to have very early cauliflowers, you should make choice of a good rich spot of ground that is well defended from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, east, and west winds, with hedges, pales, or walls; but the first are to be preferred, if made with reeds, because the winds will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> dead in these, and not reverberate as by pales or walls. This ground should be well trenched, burying therein a good quantity of rotten dung; then level your ground, and if it be naturally a wet soil, you should raise it up in beds about two feet and a half, or three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and four inches above the level of the ground; but if your ground is moderately dry, you need not raise it at all: then plant your plants, allowing about two feet six inches distance from glass to glass in the rows, always putting two good plants under each glass, which may be at about four inches from each other; and if you <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> them for a full crop, they may be three feet and a half row from row: but if you intend to make ridges for cucumbers between the rows of cauliflower plants (as is generally practised by the gardeners near London), you must then make your rows about eight feet asunder; and the ground between the rows of cauliflowers may be planted with cabbage plants, to be drawn off for coleworts in the spring. When you have planted your plants, if the ground is very dry, you should give them a little water, and then let your glasses over them, which may remain quite close down over them, till till they have taken root, which will be in about a week or ten days time, unless there should be a kindly shower of rain; in which case you may set off the glases, that the plants may receive the benefit of it; and in about ten days after planting, you should be provided with a parcel of forked sticks or bricks, with which you should raise your glases about three or four inches on the side toward the south, that your plants may have free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>; in this manner your glases should remain over the plants night and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, unless in frothy weather, when you should set them down as close as possible; or if the weather should prove very warm, which many times happens in November, and sometimes in December, in this case you should keep your glases off in the day-time, and put them on only in the night, lest, by keeping the glases over them too much, you should draw them into flower at that season; which is many times the case in mild winters, especially if unskillfully managed. Toward the latter end of February, if the weather proves mild, you should prepare another good spot of ground to remove some of the plants into, from under the glases, which should be well dugged and trenched (as before): then set off your glases; and, after making choice of one of the most promising plants under each glas, which should remain, take away the other plant, by raising it up with a trowel, &c., so as to preserve as much earth to the root as possible; but take care not to disturb or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> the roots of the plants which remain. Then plant the plants which you have taken out at the distance before directed, viz. if for a full crop, three feet and a half, row from row; but if for ridges of cucumbers between them, eight feet, and two feet four inches distance in the rows: then, with a small hoe, draw the earth up to the stems of the plants which were left under the glases, taking great care not to let the earth fall into their hearts; and set your glases over them again, raising your props an inch or two higher than before, to give them more air, observing to take them off whenever there may be some gentle showers, which will greatly refresh the plants. In a little time after, if you find your plants grow so fast as to fill the glases with their leaves, you should then slightly dig about the plants, and raise the ground about them in a bed broad enough for the glases to stand, about four inches high, which will give your plants a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of room, by raising the glases so much higher when they are set over them; and by this means they might be kept covered until April, which otherwise they could not, without prejudice to the leaves of the plants; and this is a great advantage to them, for many times we have returns of severe frosts at the latter end of March, which prove very hurtful to these plants, if exposed thereto, especially after having been nursed up under glases. After you have finished your beds, you may set your glases over your plants again, observing to raise your props pretty high, especially if the weather be mild, that they may have free air to strengthen them; and in mild soft weather set off your glases, as also in gentle showers of rain; and now you must begin to harden them by degrees to endure the open air; however, it is advisable to let your glases remain over them as long as possible, if the nights should be frothy, which will greatly forward your plants; but you must not let your glases remain upon them in very hot sunshine, especially if their leaves press against the sides of the glases; for it hath often been observed in such <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, that the moisture which hath risen from the ground, together with the perspiration of the plants, which by the glases remaining over them hath been detained upon the leaves of the plants, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> hath shone hot upon the sides of the glases, have acquired such a powerful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> from the beams thereof, as to scald all their larger leaves, to the no small prejudice of the plants: nay, sometimes large quantities of plants have been so affected therewith, as never to be worth anything after. If your plants have succeeded well, toward the end of April some of them will begin to fruit: you must therefore look over them carefully every other day, and when you see the flower plainly appear, you must break down some of the inner leaves over it to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> it from the sun, which would make the flower <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> and unsightly if exposed thereto; and when you find your flower at its full bigness (which you may know by its outside parting as if it would run), you must then draw it out of the ground, and not cut them off, leaving the stalk in the ground, as is by some practised; and if they are designed for present use, you may cut them out of their leaves; but if designed to keep, you should preserve their leaves about them, and put them into a cool place; the best time for pulling them is in a morning, before the sun hath exhaled the moisture; for cauliflowers pulled in the heat of the day, lose that firmness which they naturally have, and become tough. But to return to our second crop (the plants being raised and manured as was directed for the early crop, until the end of October), you must then prepare some beds, either to be covered with glass-frames, or arched over with hoops, to be covered with mats, &c. These beds should have some dung laid at the bottom, about six inches or a foot thick, according to the size of your plants; for if they are small, the bed should be thicker of dung to bring them forward, and so vice versa; this dung should be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> down close with a fork, in order to prevent the worms from finding their way through it; then lay some good fresh earth about four or five inches thick thereon, in which you should plant your plants about two inches and a half square, observing to shade and water them until they have taken new root: but you must not keep your coverings close, for the warmth of the dung will occasion a large damp in the bed, which, if pent in, will greatly injure the plants. When your plants have taken root, you must give them as much free open air as possible, by keeping the glases off in the day-time as much as the weather will permit; and in the night, or at such times as the glases require to be kept on, raise them up with props to let in fresh air, unless in frothy weather; at which time the glases should be covered with mats, straw, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAT">peat</a>-haulm, &c., but this is not to be done but in very hard frosts; you must also observe to guard them against great rain, which in winter time is very hurtful to them, but in mild weather, if the glases are kept on, they should be propped to admit fresh air; and if the under leaves grow yellow and decay, be sure to pick them off: for if the weather should prove very bad in winter, so that you should be obliged to keep them close covered for two or three days together, as it sometimes happens, these decayed leaves will render the inclosed air very noxious; and the plants perishing pretty much at that time, are often destroyed in vast quantities. In the beginning of February, if the weather be mild, you must begin to harden your plants by degrees, that they may be prepared for transplantation: the ground where you intend to plant your cauliflowers out (which should be quite open from trees, &c. and rather moist than dry), having been well dugged and dug, should be fown with radishes a week or fortnight before you intend to plant out your cauliflowers; the sowing of radishes is particularly mentioned, because if there are not some radishes amongst them, and the month of May should prove hot and dry, as it sometimes happens, the fly will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> your cauliflowers, and eat their leaves full of holes, to their prejudice, and sometimes their destruction; whereas, if there are radishes upon the spot, the flies will take to them, and never meddle with the cauliflowers so long as they last: indeed, the gardeners near London mix spinach with their radish-feed, and so have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> crop; which is an advantage where ground is dear, or where persons are straitened for room; otherwise it is very well to have only one crop amongst the cauliflowers, that the ground may be cleared in time. Your ground being ready and the season good, about the middle of February you may begin to plant out your cauliflowers; the distance which is generally allowed by the gardeners near London (who plant other crops between their cauliflowers to succed them, as cucumbers for pickling, and winter cabbages (is every other row four feet and a half apart, and the intermediate rows two feet and a half, and two feet two inches distance in the rows; so that in the later end of May or beginning of June (when the radishes and spinach are cleared off), they put in seeds of cucumbers for pickling, in the middle of the wide rows, at three feet and a half apart; and in the narrow rows plant cabbages for winter use, at two feet two inches distance, so that these stand each of them exactly in the middle of the square between four cauliflower plants; and these after the cauliflowers are gone off, will have full room to grow, and the crop be hereby continued in a succession through the whole season. There are many people who are very fond of watering cauliflower plants in summer; but the gardeners near London have almost wholly laid aside this practice, as finding a deal of trouble and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> to little purpose; for if the ground be very dry as not to produce tolerable good cauliflowers without water, it seldom happens that watering of them makes them much better; and when once they have been watered, if it is not constantly continued, it had been much better for them if they never had any; as also, if it be given them in the middle of the day, it rather helps to leal them: so that, upon the whole, if care be taken to keep the earth drawn up to their stems, and clear them from every thing that grows near them, that they may have free open air, you will find that they will succeed better without than with water, where any of these cautions are not strictly observed. But in order to have a third crop of cauliflowers, you should make a slender hot-bed in February, in which you should sow the seeds, covering them a quarter of an inch thick with light mould, and covering the bed with glass-frames. When the plants are come up, and have grown four or five leaves, you should prepare another hot-bed to prick them into, which may be about two inches square; and in the beginning of April harden them by degrees, to fit them for transplanting, which should be done the middle of that month, at the distance directed for the second crop, and must be managed accordingly: these (if the soil is moist where they are planted, or the season cool and moist) will produce good cauliflowers about a month after the second crop is gone, whereby their season will be greatly prolonged. There is also a fourth crop of cauliflowers, which is raised by sowing the seed about the 23rd of May; and being transplanted, as hath been before directed, will produce good cauliflowers in a kindly season and good soil after Michaelmas, and continue through October and November, and if the season permit often a great part of December. All the species of cabbage are supposed to be hard of digestion, to afford little nourishment, and to produce flatulencies, though probably on no very good foundation. They tend strongly to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>, and run into this state sooner than almost any other vegetable; when putrefied, their smell is likewise the most offensive, greatly resembling that of putrefied animal substances. A decoction of them is said to loosen the belly. Of all these plants cauliflower is reckoned the easiest of digestion. The white is the most fetid, and the red most emollient or laxative; a decoction of this last is recommended for softening acrimonious humours in some disorders of the breath, and in hoarsenesses. The red cabbage is chiefly used for pickling. In some countries they <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> the white cabbage when full grown in the autumn, and thus preserve it all winter. The Germans cut them to pieces, and, along with some aromatic herbs and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, press them close down in a tub where they soon ferment, and are eaten under the name of Sour-croft. See that article.

BRASSICAVIT

Pages 457-457
or BRACHICAVIT, in the manege, is a horse whose fore-legs are naturally bended archwise: being so called by way of distinction from an arched horse whose legs are bowed by hard labour.

BRAULS

Pages 457-457
Indian cloths with blue and white stripes. They are otherwise called turbants, because they serve to cover those ornaments of the head, particularly on the coast of Africa.

BRAUNA

Pages 457-457

a town of Germany, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, seated on the river Inn. It has a strong fortress: notwithstanding, it was taken by the Austrians in 1743. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. 3. N. Lat. 48. 10.

BRAUNSBERG

Pages 457-457

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, in Regia <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, with a very commodious harbour, and belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Prussia. It is seated near the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 20. 0. N. Lat. 54. 15.

BRAUNSFIELD

Pages 457-457

a town of Germany, in the circle of the Upper <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Solmes, with a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> castle. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 32. N. Lat. 50. 22.

BRAURONIA

Pages 458-458

in Grecian antiquity, a festival in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, surnamed Brauronia, from its having been observed at Brauron, an Athenian borough. This festival was celebrated once in five years, being managed by ten men, called in Greek [ιεροποιοι]. The victim offered in sacrifice was a goat, and it was customary for certain men to sing one of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s Iliads. The most remarkable persons at this solemnity were young virgins, habited in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> gowns, and consecrated to Diana. It was unlawful for any of them to be above ten <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> under five years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

BRAVO

Pages 457-458

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> de Verd <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, remarkable for its excellent wines, and inhabited by Portuguese. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and consists of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which look like pyramids. It abounds in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn, gourds, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> melons, potatoes, horses, asses, and hogs. There is also plenty of fish on the the coast, and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> produces <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-petre. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 25° 35' N. Lat. 14° 0'. Bravo, a town of Africa, on the coast of Ajan, with a pretty good harbour. It is an independent <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and is about 80 miles distant from Magadoxo. E. Long. 41° 35' N. Lat. 1° 0'.

BRAWN

Pages 458-458

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of a boar soused <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pickled: for which end the boar should be old; because the older he is, the more horny <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> the brawn be.—The method of preparing brawn is as follows: The boar being killed, it is the flitches only, without the legs, that are made brawn; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of which are to be taken out, and then the flesh sprinkled with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and laid in a tray, that the blood may drain off: Then it is to be salted a little, and rolled up as hard as possible. The length of the collar of brawn should be as much as one side of the boar will bear, so that when rolled up it will be <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> or ten inches diameter. The collar being thus rolled up, is to be boiled in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> kettle, till it is so tender, that you can run a straw through it; then set it by till it is thorough <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and put it into the following pickle. To every gallon of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, put a handful or two of salt, and as much wheaten bran: Boil them together, then drain the bran as clear as you can from the liquor; and when the liquor is quite cold, put the brawn into it.

BRAY

Pages 458-458

Sir Reginald, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> and politician, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son of Sir Richard Bray, one of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VI. Sir Reginald was instrumental in the advancement of King Henry VII. to the throne of England; and was greatly in favour with that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, who bestowed honours and wealth upon him. His skill in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> appears from Henry VII.'s chapel at Westminster, and the chapel of St George at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>, as he had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> concern and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of the former, and the finishing and bringing to perfection the latter, to which he was also a liberal benefactor. In the middle of the south aisle of the above chapel is a spacious chapel built by him, and still called by his name. He died in 1501; and was interred in the above chapel, probably under the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> where lies Dr <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATERLAND">Waterland</a>; for, on opening the vault for that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, who died in 1740, a leaden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> form was found, which, by other appearances, was judged to be that of Sir Reginald, and was, by order of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, immediately arched over. Bray, Dr Thomas, an eminent, learned, and pious divine, was born at Marton, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>, in the year 1656, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. He was at length presented to the vicarage of Over-Whitacre, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a>; and in 1690, to the rectory of Sheldon, where he composed his Catechetical Lectures; which procured him such reputation, that Dr Compton, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, pitched upon him as a proper person to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> the infant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARYLAND">Maryland</a>, and establish it upon a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> foundation, and for that purpose he was invested with the office of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a>. He now engaged in several noble undertakings. He procured sums to be raised for purchasing small <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> ministers in the several parts of our plantations; and the better to promote this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, he published two books; one entitled Bibliotheca parochialis, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a scheme of such theological and other heads as seem requisite to be perused or occasionally consulted by the clergy, together with a catalogue of books which may be profitably read on each of those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>; the other, Apologetical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and excellency considered. He endeavoured to get a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> established for the propagation of the gospel, especially among the uncultivated Indians; and by his means a patent was obtained for erecting the corporation called The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> for the propagation of the gospel. He, by his industry, procured relief for prisoners; and formed the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> for the society for the reformation of manners, charity-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, &c. He wrote, 1. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARTYROLOGY">Martyrology</a>, or papal usurpation in one volume folio; 2. Diclorium missionarium; and other works. This excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> died in 1730, aged 73. Bray, a port town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WICKLOW">Wicklow</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>, seated on St George's channel, eight miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 16' N. Lat. 53° 8'. Bray sur <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, a town of France, in Champagne, and in Senonais, on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIE">Brie</a>. E. Long. 2° 15' N. Lat. 48° 35'.

BRAYLE

Pages 458-458

among fowlersmen, a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> slit to put upon the hawk's wing, to tie it up.

BRAZED

Pages 458-458

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> serving to describe three chevrons, one clasping another.

BRAZEN

Pages 458-458

something consisting of bras, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> formed out of it. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">BRASS</a>. Brazen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">Age</a>. See AGE. Brazen Dijb, among miners, is the standard by which the other dikes are gauged, and is kept in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZEN_SEA">Brazen <a </a>class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, in Jewish antiquity, one of the sacred utensils in the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>. It was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> in the plain of Jordan, and removed from thence into the inner <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the temple; where it was placed upon 12 oxen, three of which looked towards each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the world. It was ten cubits from the one brim to the other, five cubits in height, and 30 cubits in circumference, and contained 3000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. The brim of it was perfectly round, and so it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the two upper cubits; but below the brim, in the three lower cubits, it was <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. It was a handbreadth thick, and the brim was wrought like the brim of a cup, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of lilies. About the body of this huge vessel there were two borders of engravings, being the heads of oxen in demi-relief; out of which some supposeth the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> flowed, and that they were made as cocks and conveyances for that purpose.—This brazen or molten sea, was designed for the priests to wash themselves in before they performed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the temple. The supply of water was through a pipe out of the well Etam; though some are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that it was constantly supplied with water by the Gibonites.

BRAZIER

Pages 458-459

BRAZIER, an artificer who makes and deals in all kinds of brafs <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>. This trade, as exercised in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, may be reckoned a branch of the smithery, though they seldom keep forges, except for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRAZING">brazing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> foldering, and tinning the infides of their vessels, which they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> up chiefly out of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and brafs prepared rough to their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. They confift of a working <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, and a shop-keeping part, which latter many carry on to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, dealing as well in all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, as copper and brafs goods for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> furniture; and lately have fallen much into selling what is called French plate, made of a fort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> metal, silvered and polished to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> that the eye cannot soon distinguish it from real silver. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">BRAZIL</a>. See Brasil.

BRAZING

Pages 459-459

the foldering <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> joining two pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> together by means of thin plates of brafs, melted between the pieces that are to be joined. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> be very fine, as when two leaves of a broken fan are to be brazed together, they cover it with pulverized <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a>, melted with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, that it may incorporate with the brafs powder, which is added to it: The piece is then exposed to the fire without touching the coals, and heated till the brafs is seen to run. Brazing is also the joining two pieces of iron together by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> them hot, the one upon the other, which is used for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pieces by farriers, &c.

BRAZZA

Pages 459-459

a town and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, opposite to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPALATRO">Spalatro</a>, and subject to Venice. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 28°. N. Lat. 43°.

BREACH

Pages 459-459

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a>, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rupture in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a fence or enclosure, whether owing to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> or violence.—Inundations, or overflows of lands, are frequently owing to breaches in the dikes or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> banks. Dagenham breach is famous; it was made in 1797, by a failure of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> wall in a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tide. The force wherewith it burst in upon the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> tore up a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> channel or passage for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> 100 yards wide, and in some places 20 feet deep, by which a multitude of subterraneous trees that had been buried many ages before were laid bare. Breach, in Fortification, a gape made in any part of the works of a town by the cannon or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of the besiegers, in order to make an attack upon the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. To make the attack more difficult, the besieged few the breach with crow feet, or flop it with chevaux de frise.—A practicable breach, is that where the men may mount and make a lodgment, and ought to be 15 or 20 fathoms wide. The besiegers make their way to it, by covering themselves with gabions, earthbags, &c. Breach, in a legal fence, is where a person breaks through the condition of a bond or covenant; on an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> upon which, the breach must be assigned: And this assignment must not be general, but particular, as, in an action of covenant for not repairing houses, it ought to be assigned particularly what is the want of reparation: and in such certain manner, that the defendant may take an issue.

BREAD

Pages 459-466

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of dough kneaded and baked in an oven. See Baker, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKING">Baking</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARM">Barm</a>. The grains of all vegetables are almost entirely composed of substances very proper for the nourishment of animals; and amongst grains those which contain a farinaceous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> are the most agreeable and most nutritious. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a> who appears to be designed by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> to eat of all substances which are capable of nourishing him, and still more of vegetables than animals, has, from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> immemorial, and in all parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, used farinaceous grains as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> basis of his food: but as these grains cannot be without difficulty eaten by men in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state, this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and intelligent animal has gradually found means not only to extract the farinaceous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, that is, the only nutritive part of these grains, but also to prepare it so that it becomes a very agreeable and wholesome aliment, such as the bread we now generally eat. Nothing appears so easy at first sight as to grind corn, to make a paste with the flour and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and to bake this paste in an oven. They who are accustomed to enjoy the advantages of the finest <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> inventions, without reflecting on the labour it has cost to complete them, think all these operations <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> and trivial. However, it appears very certain, that for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time men no otherwise prepared their corn than by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> and forming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> viscous cakes, not very agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and of difficult digestion, before they were able to make bread of good taste and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, as we have now. It was necessary to invent and complete ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> corn, and separating the pure flour with little trouble and labour; and that inquiries <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather some happy chance, which some observing person availed himself of, should discover, that flour, mixed with a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water, is susceptible of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a> which almost entirely destroys its acidity, heightens its taste, and renders it proper to make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> bread, very agreeable to the taste, and of easy digestion. This essential operation, on which the good quality of bread depends, is entirely of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>. It would add to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> cultivators of chemistry, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> to them so useful and important a discovery; but, unhappily, it is too probable that they had no share in it. The ancient chemists were engaged in other pursuits than that of bread and other common objects. They hoped to make <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; and what is bread in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with gold? However that be, to the fortunate <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of raising the paste before baking we owe the perfection of the art of making bread. This operation consists in keeping some paste or dough, till by a peculiar spirituous fermentation it swells, rarefies, and acquires a smell and taste quick, pungent, spirituous, somewhat sour, and rather disagreeable. This fermented dough is well worked with some fresh dough, which is by that mixture and moderate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> disposed to a similar but less advanced fermentation than that above mentioned. By this fermentation the dough is attenuated, and divided; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is introduced into it, which being incapable of disengaging itself from the tenacious and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> paste, forms in it small cavities, raises and swells it: hence the small quantity of fermented paste which disposes the rent to ferment, is called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAVEN">leaven</a>, from the French word <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVER">lever</a>, signifying to raise. When the dough is thus raised, it is in a proper state to be put into the oven; where, while it is baked, it dilates Bread dilates itself still more by the rarefaction of the air, and of the spirituous substance it contains, and it forms a bread full of eyes or cavities; consequently light, and entirely different from the heavy, compact, viscous, and indigested masses, made by baking unfermented dough. The invention of beer, or wine of grains, furnishes a new matter useful in the making of bread. This matter is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROTH">froth</a> which forms upon the surface of these liquors during fermentation. When it is mixed with dough, it raises it better and more quickly than ordinary leaven. It is called yeast or barm. By means of this, the finest lightest bread is made. It often happens, that bread made with leavened dough has a fourth and not agreeable taste; which may proceed from too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a quantity of leaven, or from leaven in which the fermentation has advanced too far. This inconvenience does not happen to bread made with yeast; because the fermentation of this substance is not too far advanced, or because more <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is given to that finer bread. It may be asked, Why, since dough is capable of fermenting spontaneously and singly, as we see from the leaven, a substance is added to dispose it to ferment? The true reason is, That all the parts of a fermenting substance do not ferment at the same time, nor to the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; so that some parts of this substance have finished their fermentation, while others have not yet begun. The fermentable liquors which contain much <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYDROMEL">hydromel</a>, and must of wines, give proofs of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>; for, after these liquors have become very vinous, they have still very distinctly a saccharine taste; but all saccharine matter is still susceptible of fermentation; and, in fact, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> vinous hydromel, or must, or even new beer, be distilled, so that all their ardent spirit shall be separated, and the residues diluted with water, we shall see a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> fermentation take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and a new quantity of ardent spirit formed. The same thing precisely happens to dough, and still more sensibly, from its viscosity and want of fluidity; so that if it be left to ferment alone, and without the help of leaven, as the fermentation proceeds very slowly and insensibly, the parts which ferment first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have become four and vapour before all the rest be sufficiently attenuated and changed, by which the bread will acquire a disagreeable taste. A mixture of a small quantity of leaven with dough effectually prevents this inconvenience; because the effect of this leaven, and of all fermenting substances, is to dispose to a similar fermentation all matters capable of it, with which it is mixed; or rather, by means of leaven, the fermentation of all the parts of such substances is effected more nearly at the same time. Bread well raised and baked differs from unfermented bread, not only in being less compact, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a>, and of a more agreeable taste, but also in being more easily masticable with water, with which it does not form a viscous mass, which circumstance is of great importance in digestion. It is observable, that without bread, or somewhat of this form, no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> seems to live. Thus the Lapps, having no corn of their own, make a sort of bread of their dried fishes, and of the inner rind of the pine, which seems to be used, not so much for their nourishment as for supplying a dry food. For this mankind seem to have an universal appetite, rejecting bland, slippery, and mucilaginous foods. This is not <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> accounted for, but seems to depend on very simple principles. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of our food depends on the mixture of the animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> in every stage. Among others the saliva is necessary, which requires dry food as a necessary stimulus to draw it forth, as bland, slippery, fluid aliments are too inert, and make too short flay in the mouth, to produce this effect, or to cause a sufficient degree of manducation to emulsify that liquor. For this reason we commonly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> dry bread along with animal food, which otherwise would be too quickly swallowed. For blending the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and water of our food nothing is so fit as bread, assisted by a previous manducation. For which purpose, bread is of like <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> in the stomach, as it is proper that a substance of solid consistence should be long retained there. Now the animal fluids must be mixed with our aliments, in order to change the acetylicity it undergoes. But liquid foods would not attain this end, whereas the solid stimulates and emulsifies the glands of the stomach. The bread then appears to be exceedingly proper, being bulky without too much solidity, and firm without difficulty of foliation. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> we meet with various denominations of bread; as, 1. Panis filigenesus, called allo Chamber's mundus, athleticus, ifungia, colophius, and robys, answering to our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> bread; being made of the purest flour of the best wheat, and only used by the richer sort. 2. Panis secundus or secundarius, called allo similacrus or similagineus, the next in purity; being made of fine flour, only all the bran not sifted out. 3. Autopyrus, called allo syncomitus and confusaneus, made of the whole substance of the wheat, without either retrenching the finer flour or coarser bran; answering to our <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> bread. 4. Cacabaceus, apparently the same with what was otherwise denominated fordides, as being given to dogs; furfuraceus, furfureus, or furfuratius, because made in great part of bran; and, in the middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, bilis, on account of its brownness; sometimes allo leibo. There were other sorts of bread, denominated from the manner in which they were made, or the uses they were applied to; as, 1. The militaris, which was prepared by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> and officers in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> with their own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; for which purpose some had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, others pounded the corn in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, and baked it on the coals. 2. Clibanites, that baked in an oven, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> from that baked on the hearth or under the embers. 3. That called subcinereus, or sub cinere coctus; sometimes allo reveratus, because it was to be turned in the baking. 4. Nauticus, answering to our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-biscuit, and denominated accordingly bis coctus, because baked several times over to make it keep the longer. Other kinds of bread were denominated from their qualities and accidents; as, 1. The panis ficetus, that which had been long baked; such as were the bis coctus, naval and buccellated bread. 2. Madidus, a sort made of rye or bear, sometimes also made of fine flour, wherewith they smeared their faces, by way of a cosmetic, to render them smooth. 3. Acidus, or sour bread, which was acidulated with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>. 4. Azymus, that unleavened or unfermented. The French have also a great variety of breads; as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s queen's bread, alamode bread, bread de Segovie, de Gentilly, quality-bread, &c. all prepared in peculiar manners by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAKERS">bakers</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. The bread de Gonelle excels all others, on account of the waters at Gonelle, a town three leagues from Paris. It is light, and full of eyes, which are the marks of its goodness. Pain de menage, is that which each family bakes for itself. Spice-bread, pain d'epice, denotes bread baked and iced over with the foam taken off sugar in refining houses; it is sometimes also made with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> and other sorts of leavening, and answers to what the ancients call panis mellitus. Among us, bread is chiefly divided into white, wheaten, and household; differing only in degrees of purity. In the first, all the bran is separated; in the second, only the coarser; in the third, none at all: so that fine bread is made only of flour; wheaten bread of flour and a mixture of the finer bran; and household, of the whole substance of the grain, without taking out either the coarse bran or fine flour. We also meet with ymnel bread, manchet or roll bread, and French bread: which are only so many denominations of the finest and whitest bread, made of the purest flour; except that in ill-roll bread there is an addition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>; and in French bread, of eggs and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> also. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>, and several of the northern counties of England, they have several sorts of oaten bread; as, 1. The bannock, which is an oat-cake, kneaded only with water, and baked on the embers. 2. Clap-bread, which is made into thin hard cakes. 3. Bitchinets bread, which is made of thin batter, and made into thin soft oat-cakes. 4. Riddle-cakes, which are thick and four, have but little leaven, and are kneaded stiff. And, 5. Jannock, which is oaten bread made up into loaves. Add to these, peafe-bread, much used in many parts of Scotland; being bread consisting either wholly of the flour of pease, or of this and oat-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> mixed: the dough, sometimes leavened, sometimes made only with water, is formed either into bannocks or cakes, and baked over the embers; or into what they call baps, i.e. a kind of flatfish rolls, and baked in the oven. In the statute of affize of bread and ale, 51 Hen. III. mention is made of wafel-bread, cocket bread, and bread of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREET">treet</a>; which answer to the three kinds of bread now in use, called white, wheaten, and household bread. In <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, they heretofore distinguished bread by the names esquires bread, panis armigerorum; monks bread, panis conventualis; boys bread, panis puerorum; and servants bread, panis famulorum, called also panis servientalis. A like distribution obtained in the households of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> and princes; where, however, we find some other denominations; as messengers bread, panis nuncius, that given to messengers as a reward of their labour; <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>-bread, panis curialis, that allowed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> for the maintenance of his household; eleemosynary bread, that distributed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> by way of alms. It is for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> that the food of the poor should be as various as possible, that, in time of dearth and scarcity of the ordinary kinds, they may not be without ready and cheap resources. To the discovery of such resources several benevolent philosophers having successfully turned their inquiries, we shall lay before the reader the result of their experiments. 1. Bread of Potatoes. Potatoes, previously deprived of their skin, cut into thin slices, and put between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, will dry in a heat somewhat less than 300° Centigrade. By this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> they lose about two-thirds of their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, and they may then be reduced to a fine powder. A little of this powder thrown upon the fire sends out a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, accompanied with a smell resembling burnt bread. As this smell is perceived from all farinaceous vegetables, when treated in the same manner, M. Parmentier thinks it may be considered as the characteristic of the presence of an amylaceous matter. This smell does not, however, he observes, arise from the amylaceous or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> part separately, but from both taken together. The powder of potatoes, obtained in the manner described above, has the smell and taste of wheat; and, like it, is devoured by rats and mice; but, even when most finely powdered, it has not the feel or brightness of the flour of wheat; although, on a chemical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a>, it yields the same products. It is also nutritious, and keeps well for a long time. Finding so great a similarity between the meal of wheat and what may be called the meal of potatoes, M. Parmentier next endeavoured to make bread of them when mixed in different proportions. His trials were made with one-fourth, one-third, one-half, and two-thirds, of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-POTATO">potato</a>-meal, the remainder being flour from wheat. These proportions, with the addition of a little <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and yeast, yielded bread which was well tasted, but which had fermented little, was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, and covered with hard brown crusts. Bread made from the meal of potatoes alone, with the addition of salt and yeast, was eatable, but very heavy, unfermented, and exceedingly brown. This bread, from the meal of potatoes alone, was apt to crumble into powder. To give it more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADHESION">adhesion</a>, he mixed with the meal a decoction of bran, or a mixture of honey and water; either of which made it lighter and more fermented: it obtained also a crust of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, became well tasted, and sufficiently adhesive. M. Parmentier obtained bread also, well fermented, and of a good colour and taste, from a mixture of raw potato-pulp with meal of wheat, or potato-meal, with the addition of yeast and salt. Potatoes, when used for making bread, are not readily disposed to ferment; without which, bread is very insipid, and not easily digested. But M. Parmentier found, from a variety of experiments, that good bread might be made from equal quantities of flour and potato-meal. He concludes, therefore, with recommending the mixture of potatoes, in times of scarcity, with the flour of wheat, instead of employing rye, barley, or oats, as has frequently been done. When grain is altogether wanting, he recommends the use of bread made from a mixture of the amylaceous powder of potatoes and of their pulp, this mixture being fermented with leaven or with honey. The meal of this root, when diluted with hot water, acquires a tenacious and gluey consistence. However fair the meal of potatoes may be, it always gives a gray colour to the bread made by mixing it with the flour of wheat. Bread: but a mixture of the pulp of potatoes with the flour of wheat does not produce brown-coloured bread. M. Parmentier made bread, very much like that of wheat, by a mixture of the following four substances, viz., four ounces of amylaceous powder of potatoes, one dram of mucilage extracted from barley, one dram of the bran of rye, and a dram and a half of glutinous matter dried and powdered. 2. Bread from different Vegetables not commonly in Use. Although <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-chestnut has not hitherto been employed, yet it is certain that wholesome bread, without any bitterness, may be obtained from it. M. Parmentier advises, that the fruit, after the skin is taken off, and the juice pressed from it, be made into a paste. This paste must be diluted in water, and then strained through a sieve. A milky-coloured liquor is thus separated, which, on standing, deposits a fine powder. This, being dried, is without either smell or taste, and very fit for aliment; the mass from which it is procured retaining the bitterness of the fruit. The roots of the bryonia, when treated in the same manner, yielded a similar white powder. By the same treatment also, fine, white, infusible, inodorous powders may be procured from the roots of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRIS">iris</a>, gladiolus, ranunculus, lomatia, arum, dracunculus, mandragora, colchicum, filipendula, and helioborus; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which grow spontaneously, and in great abundance. Of acorns bread has frequently been made; and to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, in some countries, they are in common use. The method of preparation which M. Parmentier recommends is, that they be deprived of their cover by boiling, then dried and powdered, and afterwards baked in the same manner as the flour of wheat. When fully ripe, and made into a paste, they were deprived of their astringency by merely pressing their juice from them. The mass remaining after the pressing, when dried, was easily reduced to a fine powder by no means disagreeable. The graminum caninum arvensis, in its appearance, approaches to corn; and some naturalists have considered it as the original <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> from which all our grain is produced. Its roots are sweet-tasting, and have long been employed in making pitans. In the preparation of them for bread, it is only necessary that the roots should be cleaned, cut small, dried, and pounded. This powder, M. Parmentier observes, does not dissolve in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water or spirits; but it does in boiling water, which it renders thick and cloudy, and, upon cooling, the whole mass obtains a gelatinous consistence. Upon a chemical analysis, it yields an acid empyreumatic oil, which possesses a singular odour, resembling that which is perceived on <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> the plant. The fleshy residuum, calcined in the air, gives a fixed alkali. These properties incontestably prove, that it contains an amylaceous (A) matter similar to that of grain, which appears to be the nutritive part of vegetables. This amylaceous matter, formed into a jelly, and diffused in water, keeps for a long time without suffering any change; it then turns acid, and at length putrefies. The amylaceous matter of acrid and poisonous plants, although innocent and nutritive, cannot be converted into bread without the addition of some mucilaginous substance. In times of great scarcity, common bran will answer the purpose; but when potatoes are to be had, the addition of a proper proportion of these is to be preferred. M. Parmentier gives an account of the bread which he obtained from the amylaceous powders of the different vegetables mentioned above, with the addition of potatoes and a small quantity of common leaven of grain. This bread appeared in general to be well fermented; it was of a good white colour, and free from any disagreeable odour; but to the taste, it was somewhat insipid; which, however, he imagines, might have been corrected by the addition of a proper quantity of salt. As the resources against scarcity here pointed out can be procured only at particular seasons, the author proposes a method for preserving the matter thus obtained. For this purpose, he advises, that bread prepared in the manner mentioned above should be carefully (a) M. Beccari of the Bolognian academy has discovered in the flour of wheat two distinct substances. The one he terms an animal or glutinous matter; the other, an amylaceous matter or vegetable paste. The gluten has been supposed to be the nutritive part of corn, from its not dissolving unless in vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>; from its assuming a fleshy form in boiling water; from its supposed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> to the animal lymph; and, lastly, from the similitude which the products it affords, on a chemical analysis, bear to those obtained from animal substances. M.
