Parmentier, however, from various experiments, was led to conclude, with the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">Model</a> of Petersburg, that the gluten or animal matter of Beccari exists in the bran, and is not the nutritive part of the wheat. Having made experiments with four different kinds of flour, it appeared that the quantity of animal matter was always proportioned to the coarseness of the flour. Hence, were this gluten the nutritive part, the coarsest bread, or that which contained most bran, would afford the greatest quantity of nourishment. The contrary of this, however, is now known to be fact. The amylaceous part, or, as some have termed it, the fecula, of wheat and other vegetables, is a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a>, not soluble in spirit of wine, vinegar, or cold water. It contains more acid, and less water, than the ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>. It is found in many of these plants that make the nourishment of men and other animals. Hence M. Parmentier concludes it to be the nutritive matter. Though we are not to consider the glutinous matter as the nutritious part of vegetables, yet it is a very necessary ingredient. It is that which preserves the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a> of the paste in fermenting bread; it is that which forms the viscid pellicle, and stops the air in fermentation; gives the favourite taste to bread; occasions it to be light, to ferment, and which forms the small cells seen in it. It is found especially near the cortical part of grain; and this accounts for its being found in the greatest quantity in coarse brown meal. It is this gluten which renders wheat a superior aliment to the other grains and roots. Bread, fully dried, reduced to powder, and then kept in a clofe cask. By this means, he is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that it may be preserved for a very long time, and will always be ready to make an agreeable and wholesome panada by the addition of a little butter and salt. M. Parmentier, in order to discover the degree of power wherewith this alimentary powder nourished, made himself the subject of experiment; and found, that three ounces of it for dinner, and as much for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, made into panada with water, was a sufficient quantity of aliment for a day. From his discharge by stool while he used it, he had reason to believe that it is almost totally alimentary. He concludes with recommending it not only as useful in times of scarcity, but as a proper substitute for farina-biscuit, and as a species of food well adapted for armies and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>. 3. Cheap method of making wholesome Bread, when wheat-flour is dear, by mixing turnip with it*. At the time I tried this method, bread was very dear, inasmuch that the poor people, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> where I live, can hardly afford themselves half a meal a-day. This put me upon considering whether some cheaper method might not be found than making it of wheat-meal. Turnips were at that time very plentiful. I had a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of them pulled, washed clean, pared, and boiled; when they were become soft enough to mash, I had the greatest part of the water pressed out of them, and afterwards had them mixed with an equal quantity in weight of coarse wheat-meal; the dough was then made in the usual manner, with yeast or barm, salt, water, &c. It rose very well in the trough; and after being well kneaded, was formed into loaves, and put into the oven to be baked. I had at the same time some other bread made with common meal in the ordinary way. I baked my turnip bread rather longer than the other. When they were drawn from the oven, I caused a loaf of each sort to be cut; and found, on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, the turnip-bread was sweeter than the other, to the full as light and as white, but had a little taste (though nowise disagreeable) of the turnip. Twelve hours afterwards I tasted my turnip-bread again, when I found the taste of the turnip in it scarce perceptible, and the smell quite gone off. On examining it when it had been baked 24 hours, had I not known that there were turnips in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, I should not have imagined it; it had, it is true, a peculiar sweetness, but by no means disagreeable; on the contrary, I rather preferred it to the bread made of wheat-meal alone. After it had been baked 48 hours, it underwent another examination, when it appeared to me to be rather superior to the other; it ate freer and moister, and had not at all abated in its good qualities: to be short, it was still very good after a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>; and, as far as I could see, kept as well as the bread made of common wheat meal. "In my trials of this bread by the taste, I was not satisfied with eating it by itself; I had some of it spread with butter; I tasted it with cheese; I ate of it toasted and buttered, and finally in boiled milk and in soup; in all these forms it was very palatable and good. Bread, in Medicine. Besides the alimentary, bread has also medical qualities.—Decoctions, creams, and jellies of bread, are directed in some dispensaries. Bread carefully toasted, and infused or lightly boiled in water, imparts a deep colour, and a sufficiently agreeable refringent taste. This liquor, taken as common drink, has done good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in a weak lax state of the stomach and intestines; and in bilious vomiting and purging, or the cholera morbus; examples are related in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> essays of several <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of this kind cured by it, without the use of any other medicine.—In Westphalia there is a very coarse bread eaten, which still retains the opprobrious name given it by a French traveller of Bonjournickel, "good for his horse <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NICKEL">Nickel</a>." It is the same with what the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> called panis furfuraceus, or panis impurus, from its not being cleansed from the husks; and panis aer, from the blackness of its colour: though we learn from Pliny, that the Romans for 300 years knew no other bread. The Germans* make Hoffman, two sorts of waters by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> from this bread; the one with, the other without, the addition of a spirituous liquor: to both which great virtues are ascribed. That without anything spirituous, is made out of the juice of craw-fish, may-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a>, rose-water, nutmegs, and saffron, distilled from a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantity of this bread. This is esteemed a great restorative, and given in hectic habits. The other is distilled from this bread and Rhein wine, with nutmegs and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>. This is given in all the disorders of the stomach, vomiting, loss of appetite, and other complaints of the same kind: and besides these, there is a spirit distilled from it by the retort in the dry way, which, when separated from its fetid oil, is esteemed a powerful sudorific, and very valuable medicine in removing impurities of the blood. Bread is also medicinal, applied externally, as is vulgarly known*. Mr Boyle assures us he drew a menstruum from bread stronger than aquafortis, and which Phil. Works alridged, vol iii. p. 572. Bread Tree. See Artocarpus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Bees-Bread. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEE">Bee</a>. Cassia Bread. See Jatropha, Botany Index. Earth Bread†. In the lordship of Mofcau in the Upper Lufatia, a sort of white earth is found, of German E-which the poor, urged by the calamities of the wars phemonides, which raged in those parts, make bread. It is taken out of a hill where they formerly worked at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> has somewhat warmed this earth, it cracks, and small white globules proceed from it as meal; it does not ferment alone, but only when mixed with meal. Mr Sarlitz, a Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, was pleased to inform us, that he has seen persons who in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> lived upon it for some time. He assures us that he procured bread to be made of this earth alone, and of different mixtures of earth and meal; and that he even kept some of this bread by him upwards of six years: he further says, a Spaniard told him, that this earth is also found near Geronne in Catalonia." Eucharist or Sacramental Bread, in the Protestant churches, is common leavened bread, in conformity to the ancient practice. In the Roman mass, azymous or unleavened bread is used, particularly in the Gallican <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, where a sort is provided for this purpose called pain e chanter, made of the purest wheaten flour pressed between two <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> plates graven like wafer-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a>, being first rubbed with white wax to prevent the patte from sticking. The Greeks observe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> ceremonies in their making the eucharist bread. It is necessary the person who bakes it have not lain with his wife the day before; or, if it be a woman, that she have not conversed with her husband. The Abyssinians have an apartment in their churches for this service, being a kind of facility. F. Sirmond, in his disquisition on azymous bread, shows from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>, that anciently there were as many ceremonies used in the Latin church in the preparation of their unleavened bread as are still retained in the eastern churches. He cites the example of Queen Radegonda, who distributed with her own hands in the church, the bread which she herself had made. It appears also from the dispute of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Humbert against the Greeks, that in the Latin church no bread was used for the eucharist, but what was taken out of the facility, and had been made by the deacons, subdeacons, and even priests, who rehearsed several psalms during the process. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> writers enumerate other species of bread allotted for purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; as, 1. Calendariae, that anciently offered to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KALENDS">kalends</a>. 2. Prebendariae, the same with capitulariae, that distributed daily to each prebendary or canon. 3. Benedictus, that usually given to catechumens before <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, in lieu of the eucharistic bread, which they were incapable of partaking of. The panis benedictus, was called also panagium and culogium, being a sort of bread blessed and consecrated by the priest, whereby to prepare the catechumens for the reception of the body of Christ. The same was used afterwards, not only by catechumens, but by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a> themselves, as a token of their mutual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> and friendship. Its origin is dated from the 7th century, at the council of Nantz. In the Gallican church we still find panis benedictus, pain benit, used for that offered for benediction, and afterwards distributed to pious persons who attend divine service in chapels. 4. Consecrated bread is a piece of wax, paste, or even earth, over which several ceremonies have been performed with benedictions, &c. to be sent in an Agnus Dei, or relic-box, and presented for veneration. 5. Unleavened bread, panis azymus. The Jews eat no other bread during their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSOVER">passover</a>; and exact search was made in every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, to see that no leavened bread was left. The usage was introduced in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of their hasty departure from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, when they had not leisure to bake leavened. 6. Shew-bread was that offered to God every Sabbath-day, being placed on the golden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> in the holy of holies. Horse-Bread is made of wheat, oats, and beans; to which sometimes are added aniseed, gentian, liquorice, fennel, eggs, and ale; and sometimes rye and white wine are used. For <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>-horses three sorts of bread are usually given with success, for the second, third, and fourth nights feeding: they are all made of beans and wheat worked with barm; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> consisting chiefly in the proportion of the two former. In the first kind, three times the quantity of beans is used to one of wheat; in the second, equal quantities of both; in the third, three times the quantity of wheat to one of beans. Sago-Bread. See Sago. * See Affix * of Bread. The price and weight of bread is regulated by the magistrates according to the price of wheat. We have divers tables of the weights of the loaves both of wheat, wheaten, and household bread, at every price of wheat. If bread want one ounce in 36, the baker formerly was to suffer the pillory: now, to forfeit 5s. for every ounce wanting; and for every defect less than an ounce, 2s. 6d.; such bread being complained of and weighed before a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> within 24 hours after it is baked or exposed to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> within the bills of mortality, or within three days in any other place. It is to be observed, bread loses weight by keeping: in some experiments recited by Bartholomew, the diminution was near one-fourth in six months. The same author affirms us, that in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a> they make bread which keeps 30 or 40 years; and that they are there fonder of their old hard bread, than elsewhere of new or soft; since the older it is, the more agreeable it grows. For their great feasts, particular care is taken to have the oldest bread; so that, at the christening of a child, they have usually bread which had been baked perhaps at the christening of his grandfather. It is made of barley and oat-meal baked between two hollow <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Bread-Room, in a ship, that destined to hold the bread or biscuit. The boards of the bread-room should be jointed and caulked, and even lined with tin-plates or mats. It is also proper to warm it well with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> for several days before the biscuit is put into it; since nothing is more injurious to the bread than moisture. Breadth, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, one of the three dimensions of bodies, which multiplied into their length constitutes a surface. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">Break</a>, in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, signifies to divide a thing into several parts with violence. In the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, to break ground, is to open the trenches before a place. Among sportsmen, to break a horse in trotting, is to make him light upon the hand in trotting, in order to make him fit for a gallop. To break a horse for hunting, is to supple him, to make him take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of running. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAKERS">Breakers</a>, a name given by sailors to those billows that break violently over rocks lying under the surface of the sea. They are distinguished both by their appearance and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, as they cover that part of the sea with a perpetual foam, and produce a horrible and terrible roaring, very different from what the waves usually have in a deeper bottom. When a ship is unhappily driven among breakers, it is hardly possible to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> her, as every billow that heaves her upwards serves to dash her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with additional force when it breaks over the rocks or sands beneath it. Breaking, in a mercantile style, denotes the becoming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKRUPT">bankrupt</a>. See Bankrupt. Breaking-Bulk, in the sea-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is the same with unloading part of the cargo. Breakspear, Nicholas. See Adrian IV. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BREAM">Bream</a>. See Cyprinus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> Index. To Bream, to burn off the filth, such as grats, ooze, shells, or sea-weed, from a ship's bottom, that has gathered to it in a voyage, or by lying long in a harbour. This operation is performed by holding kindled furze, faggots, or such materials, to the bottom, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> incorporating with the pitch, sulphur, &c., that had formerly covered it, immediately loosens and throws off whatever filth may have adhered to the planks. After this, the bottom is covered anew with a composition of sulphur, tallow, &c., which not only makes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">Breast</a> makes it smooth and slippery, so as to divide the fluid more readily, but also poisons and destroys those <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> which eat through the planks in the course of a voyage. Breathing may be performed either when the ship lies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGROUND">aground</a> after the tide has ebbed from her, or by docking, or by careening. Breast, in Anatomy, denotes the fore-parts of the thorax. See Anatomy Index. Smiting the breast is one of the expressions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENITENCE">penitence</a>. In the Romish church, the priest beats his breast in rehearsing the general confession at the beginning of the mass. Breasts, or Mamme, in Anatomy. See Anatomy Index. The breasts are usually two; though we also meet with instances of trimamie or women with three breasts*, and even some with four, all yielding milk alike†. Breast-Hooks, in Ship-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">Building</a>, are thick pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> incurvated into the form of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, and used to strengthen the fore-part of the ship, where they are placed at different heights directly across the stem, so as to unite it with the bows on each side. The breast-hooks are strongly connected to the stem and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAWSE">hawse</a>-pieces by tree-nails, and by bolts driven from without through the planks and hawse-pieces, and the whole thickness of the breast-hooks, upon whose inside these bolts are forelocked or clinched upon rings. They are usually about one-third thicker, and twice as long, as the knees of the decks they support. Breast-Plate, in antiquity, a piece of armour worn to defend the breast, originally believed to be made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, twisted into small cords, but afterwards made of brafs, iron, or other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, which were sometimes so exquisitely hardened, as to be <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> against the greatest force. Breast-Plate, in Jewish antiquity, one part of the priestly vestments anciently worn by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-priests. It was a folded piece of the same rich embroidered stuff of which the ephod was made; and it was set with twelve precious stones, on each of which was engraven the name of one of the tribes. They were set in four rows, three in each row; and were divided from each other by little golden squares or partitions in which they were set. The names of these stones, and that of the tribes engraven on them, as also their disposition on the breast-plate, are as follows: | Sardine | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMERALD">Emerald</a> | Ligare | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERYL">Beryl</a> | |---------|---------|--------|-------| | Reuben | Judah | Gad | Zebulun | | Topaz | Sapphire | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGATE">Agate</a> | Onyx | |---------|----------|-------|------| | Simeon | Dan | Asher | <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> | | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARBUNCLE">Carbuncle</a> | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAMOND">Diamond</a> | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMETHYST">Amethyst</a> | Jasper | |-----------|---------|-----------|--------| | Levi | Naphtali| Issachar | Benjamin | This breast-plate was fastened at the four corners; those on the top to each shoulder by a golden hook or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> at the end of a wreathed chain; and those below, to the girdle of the ephod, by two strings or ribbons, which had likewise two rings and hooks. This ornament was never to be severed from the priestly garment! and it was called the memorial, to put the high-priest in mind how dear those tribes ought to be to him, whose names he wore on his breast. It is also called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREASTPLATE">breastplate</a> of judgment, because it had the divine oracle of Uriim and Thummim annexed to it. See Uriim and Thummim. Breast-Plate, in the manege, the strap of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> that runs from one side of the saddle to the other, over the horse's breast, in order to keep the saddle tight, and hinder it from sliding backwards. Breast-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">Work</a>, in fortification, the same with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">Parapet</a>. Breath, the air inspired and expelled again in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of respiration. The ancients were very watchful over the last breath of dying persons, which the nearest relations, as the mother, father, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, or the like, received in their mouths. Breathing, the same with Respiration. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRECHIN">Brechin</a>, a town of Scotland, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGUS">Angus</a>, situated in W. Long. 2. 18. N. Lat. 56. 40. It consists of one large handsome street, and two smaller; and is on the side of a small hill, and washed by the river Southelk, over which there is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of two large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>. At the foot of the town is a long row of houses independent of it, built on ground held in feu from the family of Northesk. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough, and, with four others, sends a member to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. In respect to trade, it has only a small share of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> manufacture. It lies at no great distance from the harbour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTROSE">Montrose</a>; and the tide flows within two miles of the town; to which a canal might be made, which perhaps might create a trade, but would be of certain service in conveying down the corn of the country for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>. Brechin was a rich and ancient bishopric founded by Pemant's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> I. about the year 1150. At the Reformation, Tur in its revenues, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> and in kind, amounted to 700l. Scotland a-year; but, after that event, were reduced to 150l. chiefly by the alienation of lands and tythes by Alexander Campbell, the first Protestant bishop, to his chieftain the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Argyll.—The Culdees had a convent here. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> Leod was witness to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> made by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> David to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_ABBEY">new <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of Dunfermline. In after times, they gave way to the Mathurines or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> Friars. The ruins of their house, according to Maitland, are still to be seen in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> Wynd.—Here was likewise an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> called Maison de Dieu, founded in 1266, by William de Brechin, for the repose of the souls of the kings William and Alexander; of John earl of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, and of Huntingdon his brother; of Henry his father, and Juliana his mother. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBINUS">Albinus</a> bishop of Brechin, in the reign of Alexander II. was witness to the grant. By the walls which are yet standing, behind the west end of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> street, it appears to have been an elegant little building. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is a Gothic pile, supported by 12 pillars; is in length 166 feet, in breadth 61: part is ruinous, and part serves as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-church. The west end of one of the aisles is entire: its door is Gothic, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> consists of many <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDINGS">mouldings</a>; the window of it neat tracery. The fleche is a handsome tower, 120 feet high; the four lower windows in form of long narrow openings; the belfry windows adorned with that species of opening called the quatrefoil: the top battlemented, out of which rises a handsome spire.—At a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> small distance from the aisle stands one of those singular round towers whose use has so long baffled the conjectures of antiquaries. These towers appear to have been peculiar to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; in the last they are frequent; in the former, only two at this time exist. That at Brechin stood originally detached from other buildings. It is at present joined near the bottom by a low additional aisle to the church, which takes in about a fifth of its circumference. From this aisle there is an entrance into it of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a>, approachable by a few steps, for the use of the ringers; two handsome bells are placed in it, which are got at by means of six ladders placed on wooden semicircular floors, each resting on the circular abutments within side of the tower. The height from the ground to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is 80 feet; the inner diameter, within a few feet of the bottom, is 8 feet; the thickness of the wall at that part, 7 feet 2 inches; so that the whole diameter is 15 feet 2 inches; the circumference very near 48 feet; the inner diameter at top is 8 feet 7 inches; the thickness of the walls 4 feet 6 inches; the circumference, 38 feet 8 inches; which proportion gives the building an inexplicable elegance: the top is roofed with an octagonal spire 23 feet high, which makes the whole 103. In this spire are four windows placed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> on the sides, resting on the top of the tower; near the top of the tower are four others facing the four cardinal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>: near the bottom are two arches, one within another, in relief; on the top of the outmost is a crucifixion: between the mouldings of the outmost and inner are two figures; one of the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>; the other of St John, the cup, and lamb. On each corner of the bottom of this arch is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of certain beasts; one possibly the Caledonian bear; and the other, with a long snout, the boar. The stone-work within the inner arch has a small slit or peep-hole, but without the appearance of there having been a door within any modern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>: yet there might have been one originally; for the filling up confills of larger stones than the rest of this curious rotund. The whole is built with most elegant masonry, which Mr Gough observed to be composed of 60 courses.—This tower hath often been observed to vibrate with a high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. The castle of Brechin was built on an eminence, a little south of the town; it underwent a long siege in the year 1393; was gallantly defended against the English under Edward III.; and, notwithstanding all the efforts of that potent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, the brave governor Sir Thomas Maule, ancestor of the family of Panmure, held out this small fortress for 20 days, till he was slain by a stone <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> from an engine on the 20th of August, when the place was instantly surrendered. The family of Panmure have now a noble house on the site of the old castle.—Brechin is also remarkable for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought near it, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the rebellion raised in 1452, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of the earl of Douglas in Stirling castle. The victory fell to the royalists under the earl of Huntly. The malecontents were headed by the earl of Crawford, who, retiring to his castle of Finhaven, in the frenzy of disgrace declared, that he would willingly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, to obtain the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> that fell to the share of his antagonist.

BRECKNOCK

Pages 466-466
or Brecon, a town of Brecknockshire in Wales, and capital of the county. It is called by the Welch Aber Hondey, and is seated at the confluence of the rivers Hondey and Usk, over which there is a handsome stone bridge. It is an ancient place, containing three churches, one of which is collegiate, and is seated at the west end of the town. The houses are well built. Here was formerly a stately castle, and a strong wall, through which there were three gates, that are all demolished. It sends one member to parliament. It is well inhabited, which is in some measure owing to its being the town where the affizes are kept; and there is here a considerable woollen-manufactory. The markets are well supplied with cattle, corn, and provisions. W. Long, 3. N. Lat. 52. O.

BRECKNOCKSHIRE

Pages 466-466

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, bounded by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RADNORSHIRE">Radnorshire</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; Cardiganshire and Caernarmonshire, on the west; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORDSHIRE">Herefordshire</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONMOUTHSHIRE">Monmouthshire</a>, on the east; and by Glamorganshire and Monmouthshire, on the south. It is 35 miles in length, 30 in breadth, and about 100 in circumference. It is surrounded with hills, which renders the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> in the valleys pretty temperate. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> on the hills is very stony, but the streams descending from thence into the valleys render them fruitful both in corn and grass. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> commodities here are corn, cattle, fish, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OTTER">otter</a>'s fur, besides <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of cloth and stockings. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USK">Usk</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WYE">Wye</a>, and the Yrvon. The chief <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Brecknock, Bealt, and Hay. Two miles to the east of Brecknock is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> lake, called Brecknock Meer, and by the Welch Llyn Sowddan; it is two miles in length, and nearly the same in breadth. It contains plenty of otters, tench, perch, and eels. The county sends one member to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It is in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Landaff, and contains 61 parishes, and is divided into five <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>.

BREDA

Pages 466-468

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Dutch Brabant. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, populous, well built <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, regularly fortified after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> way, and is one of the strongest places on the Dutch frontiers. It is seated on the river Meck, in a marshy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, which may be overflowed and rendered inaccessible to an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. It is 4000 paces in circumference, and contains upwards of 2000 houses. The town is of a triangular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and the ramparts are all planted round with elms. At every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> there is a gate built with brick. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is a noble structure, remarkable for its fine spire, which is 362 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a> of Angelbert II., <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a>, is a curious piece, adorned with several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> suitable to the occasion. In 1577 the garrison delivered this city to the States-general; but it was retaken in 1681 by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CLAUDE">Claude</a> de Barlaimount, assisted by the baron de Fresin, who was prisoner therein. In 1590, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Maurice took it again from the Spaniards. In 1625 it was invested by Spinola; when it endured a siege too remarkable not to deserve a particular detail. The citadel, which formed the residence of the princes of that family, was surrounded by a ditch of prodigious depth filled with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and a strong wall defended by three great bastions; and the arsenal was celebrated for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and the vast quantities of arms and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> stores it contained. Spinola, perfectly acquainted with the strength of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, thought he should expose his whole army to imminent destruction, should he attempt an assault before he had regularly carried carried on his approaches. He even resolved upon reducing the city by famine, as the method attended with least danger to his army; and accordingly began with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> trenches round, for the space of four miles, erecting forts and redoubts at certain distances. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the garrison, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> thousand infantry, and several troops of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, composed of English, French, and Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, took the most vigorous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> for their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. The English were under the command of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Morgan, who had frequently distinguished his valour in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the States; the French were directed by Colonel de Haueterive; and the Dutch troops were subject to the immediate orders of Colonel Lohre, though the whole received their instructions from Justin de Nassau, the governor. The first advantage was gained by Baglioni, who seized a large convoy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> and stores coming up the river, converting the boats into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. This loss dispirited the besieged, and reduced them to a stated allowance of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>; and what added to their misfortunes, though they were ignorant of it, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Prince Maurice, from whom they were in hopes of receiving relief. Meanwhile Spinola prosecuted the siege with the utmost diligence and vigour. On his pushing his trenches near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a>, the besieged began a terrible fire to retard his approaches, and kept it up with such vehemence and obstinacy, that Spinola was in hopes they must soon surrender for want of ammunition. But here he formed a false judgment of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> of Justin de Nassau, who finding he could not accomplish his purpose by his firing, resolved to try the effect of water. With this view, he stopped up the course of the river Marck; and having formed a large basin of water, opened the sluices, swept away men, horses, and houles, in an inundation, and overflowed the whole country. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> force of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a> fell upon Spinola's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, and he exerted his utmost ability to remove the consequences. He dug large pits, and cut out ditches and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> to receive the water; but these being filled, and the whole ground covered over, so as to appear one uniform <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of water, served only to entrap his cavalry. The inundation was augmented by the rains which happened to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>; a mortality among the soldiers and horses ensued; and of his whole army, Spinola had scarce twelve thousand men fit for service by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>. With these inconsiderable remains, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of vast extent were to be defended, the works were to be advanced, the fallies from the garrison repulsed, and provisions to be conveyed into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, while Spinola, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, was confined to a sick-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>. In the garrison, an epidemical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> and scarcity likewise prevailed; but the excellent regulations made, and strictly observed, enabled the town to hold out three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four months beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> expected. The magistrates bought the corn for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAKERS">bakers</a>; obliging them to sell the bread to the inhabitants and garrison at a price affixed, and returning the overplus of their pay to the soldiers. A variety of other prudent regulations were established by the magistrates and governor, such as we do not find equalled by any instances recorded in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> upon a similar occasion, and all evincing the steadiness, sagacity, courage, and ability, of Justin de Nassau. A kind of rivalship appeared between him and Spinola, which should best fulfil their several duties. The Spanish general caused himself to be carried about the works in a litter; he inspected and directed every thing; and displayed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> of full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> at the time his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was in imminent danger from an acute malady. He ordered several breaches in the lines to be repaired. These the Hollanders had made by sap, with a view of introducing succours to the besieged. He drove piles into all the ditches and canals through which their boats could <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>. He made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a>, to clear off the waters of the river Marck; and succeeded in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> by dint of perseverance, vigilance, and conduct. He was now reinforced with a body of eight thousand foot, and one thousand five hundred horse; many of the sick were perfectly recovered by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> care; and his army was again become formidable, amounting to twenty-five thousand infantry, and eight thousand cavalry. Nor was Prince Henry idle, who now succeeded to the titles and dominions of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Maurice, and was elected governor of Holland, Zeeland, Guelderland, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, and Overijssel. He prefled France for assistance, and was joined by a body of cavalry under the conduct of the count de Rouff and the marquis de Rambures. With this reinforcement; and a body of German infantry, he attacked the enemy's lines, and after an obstinate conflict was repulsed. He advanced a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time; but Spinola, who entertained a high <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of his valour and conduct, did not choose to wait for him in his lines; he marched out with the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his army, seized upon a convenient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, and obliged the prince a second time to retire towards Boileduc. Henry, finding no prospect of being able to relieve the garrison, sent a permission to the governor to surrender on the best conditions he could obtain. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, which was figured with no name, fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the besiegers, and Spinola sent it open, by a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>, to Justin de Nassau, offering him an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>; but that intrepid governor, suspecting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> was forged, because it was anonymous, replied civilly, that a permission was not an order to surrender; and that he should better follow the prince of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>'s intention, and show his respect for Spinola, by continuing to defend the city to the last extremity. By this time the garrison was diminished by disease, fatigue, want, and hardship, to half the original <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>; but Justin put on such a countenance, as concealed his situation from Spinola. He frequently fell out upon Baglioni's quarters, where the Italians were perishing with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, the whole subsistence of the besiegers depending on the contributions raised in the neighbouring territories. This inconvenience produced a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUTINY">mutiny</a> in the camp, that could not be appeased without applying violent remedies, and executing within sight of the whole army the chief <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>-leaders. One of the mutineers blew up Spinola's chief <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a>, valued at two hundred thousand livres. Urged more by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> than compassion for the besieged, Spinola sent a message to the governor, exhorting him not to force him to extremities, which might be attended with fatal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to a brave garrison; but Justin, with equal art and dissimulation, answered, that Spinola was certainly ill served by his spies, as he appeared wholly unacquainted with the state of affairs in Breda, which was fully provided for a siege of several months, and defended by soldiers who preferred death to the necessity of surrendering. At that time the besieged were not informed of the death of the prince of Orange. They flattered themselves with the hopes of speedy succour, and were entirely ignorant of Prince Henry's late disappointment. When they wrote to the army an account of their miserable condition, Henry returned an answer, written with his own hand, and signed with his name, apprising them of the death of Maurice, the unsuccessful attempts made to raise the siege and throw in succours, the great inferiority of his troops in point of numbers, and the death of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James, whereby he was disappointed of a strong reinforcement; concluding, that he left the city entirely to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of the governor and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officers. Jutfin was thunderstruck with the contents of this letter. He had hitherto concealed the total want of provision and ammunition from the enemy, and his own garrison, except a few officers and other persons in whom he repose confidence. The colonels Hauterive and Morgan would listen to no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>, saying, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of their several countries was concerned, and that they were responsible for the conduct of the English and French forces. They therefore required an express order from the prince of Orange to surrender, notwithstanding they pined under the united pressure of fatigue, scarcity, and disease. Jutfin acquainted the prince with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, and he sent back an order to surrender, threatening with capital <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> whoever should disobey; but he requested that the garrison would first acquaint him by a certain number of fires, lighted up in different parts of the city, how many days they should be able to hold out. Upon receipt of this order, eleven fires were kindled; but as the prince had sent a duplicate of the order by another messenger, and this fell into the hands of the enemy, Spinola was now acquainted with the desperate circumstances of the besieged. By this acquisition he likewise discovered the mystery of the eleven fires: a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> was assembled to deliberate whether they should lay the eleven days, and then oblige the garrison to surrender at discretion, or immediately offer conditions worthy of so brave a garrison. The Spanish officers were of the former opinion; the count de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERG">Berg</a> and Spinola supported the latter. At last the marquis, determined to pursue the dictates of his noble generosity, sent such terms as could not be refused. The count de Berg conducted the negociation. Two separate capitulations were drawn up, one for the garrison and the other for the city, and both the most honourable and advantageous that could be devised. They were accepted, and the garrison marched out on the 6th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, after having sustained a siege for ten months, whereby they were diminished two thirds; nor was the loss inferior on the part of the inhabitants. Spinola drew up his army to salute them, and, surrounded by his field officers, paid particular compliments to the governor, the colonels Morgan, Hauterive, and Lohre. He distributed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> among the soldiers, ordered the sick and wounded to be treated with the utmost tenderness, conveyed the rest in the manner most commodious for them to Gertruydenburgh, and displayed all the fenti- ments of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> in the regard paid to the valour and merits of his enemies. Breda was retaken by the prince of Orange, for the United Provinces, in 1637. There was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGRESS">congress</a> held there, and peace concluded, in 1667, between the Dutch and the English. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 4. 45. N. Lat. 51° 35'. Breda, John Van, painter of history, landscape, and conversations, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> in 1683, the son of Alexander Van Breda, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> who was much esteemed for landscapes, views of particular scenes in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, with a variety of animals and figures. He was instructed by his father: and having the advantage of a good example and a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>, added to his own great application, he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his studies with his father till he was 18 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Among the variety of capital paintings which were at that time in the possession of John de <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">Wit</a> at Antwerp, Breda fixed upon those of Velvet Breughel, which he copied with extraordinary success; and he was also employed for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years in copying the pictures of several other great masters; which he performed with such incredible exactness as scarcely to leave it in the power of any judicious person to distinguish the originals from the copies. Having at length established his reputation in Holland, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> with Ryfbrack the sculptor, and there gradually rose into such esteem, that he was visited by persons of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, and particularly patronized by the unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Derwentwater, who was beheaded for rebellion in 1715. He found so much encouragement in London, that he was employed by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, and could scarce execute the large demands for his performances. After a residence of some years in England, he returned to Antwerp loaded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, the honourable testimonies of English liberality, as well as of his own merit; and in the year 1740, when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XV. arrived in that city, he so far honoured this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> as to purchase four of his pictures: One represented Christ at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of Tiberias; another, Christ performing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>; and the other two were landscapes, with a number of figures, so exquisitely drawn and finished that it would be difficult to distinguish them from those of Velvet Breughel. He certainly approached nearer to those great masters whose manner he imitated, namely, Breughel and Wouvermans, than any other artist of his time. His landscapes are in the style and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the former; and his conversations, historical figures, fairs, skirmishes, or battles, are in the manner of the latter. His colouring is good; his touch neat; his skies and distances <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and beautiful; and his taste of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> agreeable. He had as much fire in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, and perhaps more genius, than Breughel, in those subjects which he painted in the style of that master; his figures are generally well placed, his grounds skilfully broken; every small figure hath its particular character, and occupies its proper place; and, in short, he is a painter of such a rank, that the value and estimation of his works must always increase. He died in 1750. BREECH of a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a>, or cannon, the end next the touch-hole.

BREECHES

Pages 468-469

a garment worn by males, reaching from the girdle to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, and serving to cover the hips, thighs, &c. Breechings. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> had nothing in their dress answering to our breeches and stockings; instead of which, under their lower tunics and waistcoats they sometimes bound their thighs and legs round with silken scarves <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fasciae, called tibialis and femorata. Breeches appear to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> peculiar to the barbarous nations, especially those inhabiting the colder countries of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; whence Tacitus calls them barbarum tegmen. We find mention made of them among the ancient Getæ, Sarmatæ, Gauls, Germans, and Britons; they also obtained among the Medes and Persians, as being a people of Scythian origin; they also afterwards got footing in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, some pretend, as early as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Augustus; but without much foundation, that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s breeches, mentioned by Suetonius, being apparently only swaths tied over his thighs. However this be, breeches were at last received into Italy, and grew so highly in fashion, that it was thought necessary, under Honorius and Arcadius, to restrain them by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and expel the bracarii or breeches-makers out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>; it being thought unworthy of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> that commanded the world, to wear the apparel of barbarians.

BREECHINGS

Pages 469-469

in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> with which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> guns are lashed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fastened to the ship's side. They are thus called, because made to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> round the breech of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a>.

BREEDING

Pages 469-469

in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MORAL_SENSE">moral <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes a person's deportment <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> behaviour in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> offices and decors of social <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In this sense we say well-bred, ill-bred, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of breeding, &c. Good-breeding is hard to define; none can understand the speculation but those who have the practice. Good-breeding amounts to much the same with what is otherwise called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> urbanity. Good-breeding is near to virtue, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of itself <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a man a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the way towards the same. It teaches him to rejoice in acts of civility, to seek out objects of compassion, and to be pleased with every occasion of doing them good offices. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHAFTESBURY">Shaftesbury</a> compares the well-bred man with the real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>: both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> aim at what is excellent, aspire to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and carry in view the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of what is beautiful and becoming. The conduct and manners of the one are formed according to the most perfect ease, and good entertainment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; of the other, according to the strictest <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of mankind: the one according to his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> in his private station; the other according to his rank and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Horace seems to have united both characters, Quid verum atque decens curo et rogo, et omnis in hoc sum. See the article Good Manners. BREEDING of Horses. See Equus. BREEDING of Fish. The necessary qualities of a pond, to make it serve well for breeding fish, are very different from those which are to make it serve for the feeding of them, insomuch that some particular ponds serve only for one of these purposes, and others for the other; and scarce ever the same pond is found to answer for them both. In general, it is much more rare to find a good breeding pond than a good feeding one. The best indications for a good breeding pond are these; Breeding that there be a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of rushes and grass about its sides, with gravelly shoals, such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-ponds usually have: when a pond has this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, and takes to the breeding of fish, it is amazing what a progress will be made in a little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The spawn of fish is prodigious in quantity; and where it succeeds, one is able to produce many millions: thus, in one of these breeding ponds, two or three melters, and as many fishawners, will, in a very little time, flock the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. When these ponds are not meant entirely for breeding, but the owner would have the fish to grow to some size in them, the method is to thin the numbers, because they would otherwise starve one another, and to put in other fish that will prey upon the young, and thin them in the quickest manner. Eels and perch are the most useful on this account; because they prey not only upon the spawn itself, but upon the young fry from the first hatching to the time they are of considerable size. Some fish are observed to breed indifferently in all kinds of waters, and that in considerable plenty; of this nature are the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ROACH">roach</a>, pike, and perch.

BREENBERG

Pages 469-469

Bartholomew, an excellent painter, was born in 1620. He is best known by the name of Bartolomeo, an appellation bestowed upon him, for distinction sake, by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of Flemish painters at Rome called Bentvueghels. He was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>; but in the early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> went to Rome. His studies in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> were attended with such success, that his pictures were held in the highest estimation. He greatly excelled in landscapes, and these he enriched with historical subjects. The figures and animals which he introduced were very spirited, and drawn in a masterly manner; especially when they were not larger than the size in which he usually painted them. He died in 1660, aged 40 years. He also etched from his own designs a set of 24 Views and Landscapes, ornamented with Ruins.

BREEZE

Pages 469-469

a shifting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> that blows from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> for some certain hours in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> or night; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> and some parts of the East and West Indies. Breezes differ from easterly or trade-winds, as the former are diurnal, or have their periods each day; and the latter are anniverary, and blow at a distance from land. The sea-breezes rule by day, and the land-breezes by night; so that, dividing their empire, they remain constant as the seasons of the year, or course of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, on which they seem to depend: not but that they appear sooner or later, stronger or weaker, in some places than in others; and vary the alternative according to the several latitudes, situations, and soils, &c. of the countries where they are found. See the article Wind. BREEZE-Fly. See Tabanus, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BREGENTZ

Pages 469-469
or Bergentz, a town of Tyrol in Germany, situated at the east end of the lake of Constance, in E. Long. 9° 40' N. Lat. 47° 36'.

BREHAR

Pages 469-470

one of the Scilly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, lying almost directly west of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>'s end in Cornwall, about the distance of 30 miles. It lies between the isles of Mi-carol, Guel, Trefcau, and Samson. It is the roughest and most mountainous of them all, and not many years since, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREHONS">Brehons</a> since, there were only two families in it, but now there are 13. There are a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> houles called the town of Brebar; and there are several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARROWS">barrows</a> edged with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, in which they buried considerable persons in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times; besides many monuments of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRUIDS">Druids</a>. Some are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that this with the rest made but one <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, which is the reason why so many antiquities are now found in most of them.

BREHONS

Pages 470-470

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> judges among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Irish, by whom <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> was administered, and controversies decided. These faxes were a distinct tribe <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> family, to whom competent lands were allowed in inheritance. In criminal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the brehon had the eleventh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of all the fines; which could not but be considerable at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when murders, rapes, robberies, and the like offences, were only subject to pecuniary commutations. Brehon-Laws, or Leges Brebonices, denote the general maxims or rules of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> observed by the brehons, and having the force of laws throughout all the provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. Several fragments of the leges brebonice are still extant in public and private <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>. The most complete collection is that belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Chandos; containing 224 sheets <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> written, full of abbreviated words, and not very legible. By the statute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KILKENNY">Kilkenny</a>, made under Edward III., it is enacted that no English subject shall submit to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> by the brebon law, on the penalty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>. Notwithstanding which, many were still under a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of being concluded by the Irish laws and customs, till the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> was settled on an English bottom by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James I.

BREMEN

Pages 470-470

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, populous, and very strong town of Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same name, with an archbishop's see, secularized in favour of the Swedes, but now belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>. The river Weser runs through the middle, and divides it into the old and new town. In September 1739, while the inhabitants were asleep, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> of powder was set on fire by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, and all the houses were shaken, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there had been a violent earthquake, which threw them into a terrible consternation. The town is divided into four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, each of which has a burgomaster; and in the middle there is a large market-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, with the statue of Rolando. Bremen drives a very large trade for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, with France, England, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, and in return takes back other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, with which it supplies Westphalia and the countries about Hanover. It also gets a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> by its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>; the trade for blubber with the south of Germany is very considerable. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 45. N. Lat. 53. 40. Bremen, a duchy of Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, lying between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Weser and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>; of which the former separates it from the duchy of Oldenburgh, and the other from that of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is fertile, and well peopled. It formerly belonged to the Swedes, but was afterwards sold to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, as elector of Hanover, in 1716. In the winter it is subject to inundations. In 1617, on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTMAS_DAY">Christmas-<a </a>class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, several thousand cattle were drowned, besides several hundred of men; and the country was so covered with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, that it has cost immense sums to repair the dykes. Bremen is the capital town. Bremen-Veerd, a town of Germany, in the circle of Lower Saxony, and duchy of Bremen. It is an open town, seated on the river Oost, and was formerly the place of residence of the archbishop. E. Long. 8. 35. N. Lat. 53. 58.

BRENNAGE

Pages 470-470

Brennagium, in middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers, a kind of tribute paid in lieu of bran, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bran itself, which the tenants were obliged to furnish for the support of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>'s hounds. The word is also written brennage, brenagium, and brenaige, bernagium, bernaticum, and brennaticum.

BRENNUS

Pages 470-470

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> among the Gauls, who, about 388 years before the Christian era, entered <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> with a powerful <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> conquests there; defeated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and sacked Rome. The capitol alone was defended; and Camillus coming to its relief, drove the Gauls not only out of Rome, but out of all Italy. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Rome.

BRENT

Pages 470-470

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, with a market on Saturdays, and two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, on May 13th and October 10th, for horned cattle. It is but a small <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and lies on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>, being 26 miles south-west from the former, and 198 west by south of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 7. N. Lat. 50. 30. Brent-Goose, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of goose with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> neck, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> collar round; usually confounded with the barnacle, though in reality a distinct species. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANAS">Anas</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BRENTFORD

Pages 470-470

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to the west. It is divided into old and new Brentford, in which last are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and market-houfe, and where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> elections are held. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, well stocked with public houles, and is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, in W. Long. 0. 10. N. Lat. 51. 26. BRENTWOOD <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Burnwood, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> in England; it stands on a rising ground in the road from London to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLCHESTER">Colchester</a>, and has several good inns. E. Long. 0. 25. N. Lat. 51. 38.

BREREWOOD

Pages 470-470

Edward, a very learned English mathematician and antiquary, was the son of Robert Brerewood a tradesman, who was thrice mayor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>; and born in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the year 1565. He was educated in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> learning at the free school in Chester; and afterwards admitted, in 1581, of Brazen nofe-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. In the year 1596, he became the first professor of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> in Gresham-college in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; where he led the same private and retired course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> that he had before done in Oxford. He died there of a fever, upon the 4th of November 1613, much lamented. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learner into antiquity and curious knowledge; but is remarkable for having never published any thing during his lifetime. After his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> came out the following works. 1. De ponderibus et pretiis veterum nummorum. 2. Inquiries touching the diversities of languages and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> parts of the world. 3. Elementa logica in gra-

BRESCIA

Pages 470-471

a strong and handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, with a bishop's see and a good citadel. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Bresciano in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, and is seated in an agreeable plain on the river Garza, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10° 5'. N. Lat. 43° 31'.

BRESCIANO

Pages 471-471

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by the Grifons and the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>; on the east, by the lake <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GARDA">Garda</a>, the Veronese, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>; on the south, by the duchy of Mantua and the Cremonese; and on the west, by the Cremafo, the Bergamofo, and the Valletina.
